en: Preface to the Commentary on the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*:
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* is, in essence, a wondrous scripture of universal application within the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
How can this be known? It is precisely because the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma across the five periods each has its own specialized focus:
the *Avataṃsaka* specializes in the Sudden; the *Āgama* specializes in the Small Vehicle; the *Prajñāpāramitā* specializes in Emptiness; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* specializes in the Perfect;
and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa* specializes in the Permanent. As for the Vaipulya period, however, there is nothing to which it is exclusively devoted, yet there is nothing to which it is not devoted.

This has already become a time for universal application; this scripture’s teaching is adapted to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra) style so that it is not restricted to any single point, yet there is nothing it does not correctly and universally encompass.
Therefore, it is called the wondrous scripture of the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden Teaching that penetrates all directions.
As the verse of praise by the Elder Ratnakūṭa to the Buddha says: "The Dharma is taught as neither existent nor non-existent; all phenomena arise through causes and conditions."
"There is no self, no agent, and no recipient; yet the karma of good and evil does not perish.

This refers exclusively to the Perfect [Teaching], while simultaneously encompassing the doctrines of the *Avataṃsaka*, *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Prajñāpāramitā*, and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras. Furthermore, it says: "When he first sat beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power;
attaining the extinction of ambrosia, he perfected the Way of Enlightenment. Without mind, intention, or volitional activity, he completely crushed and subjugated [all adversaries]."

"O you heterodox practitioners! The Wheel of Dharma has been turned thrice throughout the great universe; that wheel is originally and eternally pure. That devas and humans have attained the Way serves as its testimony;
thus the Three Jewels have appeared in the world. This refers specifically to the Lesser Vehicle, capturing the minor teachings of the Āgamas.
Furthermore, it says: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings understand according to their respective types."
Each attains understanding, and all believe that the World-Honored One has spoken in their own language; this is the extraordinary power of the Buddha’s unique dharma. As it says:
"When the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, some feel fear, some rejoice, some develop weary detachment, and some sever their doubts."
This is the supernatural power of the unshared dharma. This is precisely what is dedicated to the Vaipulya (fangděng), thereby universally encompassing all the Mahayana teachings:
the Perfect-Sudden, the Esoteric, and the Indeterminate. Therefore it is said: "There is nothing to which one is exclusively devoted, yet there is nothing to which one is not devoted."

Someone may raise an objection, saying: "Since this sutra is not specialized in any one thing, yet there is nothing it does not specialize in, does it also fully encompass all the various partial and gradual teachings of the Lesser Vehicle?
I respond: "It is not so. Since it is said to be 'not specialized in any one thing,' how could it be specialized in the Lesser Vehicle or in the partial and gradual?
Nevertheless, since it is also said to be 'there is nothing it does not specialize in,' this means that it destroys the Lesser to establish the Great, and harmonizes the partial with the Perfect."

Returning to the Perfect, one realizes the gradual as the sudden; it is like Mount Sumeru encompassing all colors, which all become the color of sapphire, or like the wish-fulfilling jewel raining down treasures, all of which become a treasury of jewels.
There is nothing specialized, yet there is nothing that is not specialized—is this not found therein? These are no idle words.

One may see this for oneself by entering the sutras. Should those who read this scripture happen to encounter it even once, if they can integrate and harmonize [the teachings] through it, then whether great or small, complete or partial, all will return to the correct track of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of this sutra.

Although the works of the master and disciple from Guanzhong survive as established interpretations, and the commentaries of the Zhiyi of the Chen and Sui dynasties have already been lost, nevertheless, [the lineage of] Jing...
It is titled *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning). Since it is brilliantly clear and worthy of contemplation, the Dharma-gate of the inherent nature (*xingju*) is likewise vividly manifest before one's eyes.
Therefore, without neglecting what was previously perceived, the full meaning of the text is preserved. Whenever a critical juncture remained unopened, I have briefly applied the steel hammer;
whenever a knotty point was not yet resolved, I have slightly employed the ox-knife. Thus, I shall strive to outshine the five hundred elders and further...
I request that the Sugata Śākyamuni open his lips to explain this. It is titled the *Wúwǒ Shū* (Commentary on Non-Self) to the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*.
My intention is to employ the "not-I" (*búwǒ*) of Māṇavaka to govern the two "non-selves" (*èrwú*) of Kūrma.
May those who read it alone consider whether this commentary by an old monk is indeed as it should be.
On the fifth day before the full moon of the late spring in the year of Yi Chou (1625), the fifth year of the Huangming Tianqi era,
the *Śramaṇa* Chuandeng of Youxi on Mount Tiantai set his brush to paper at the Eastern Hall of the Unblinking Eye within the *Śūraṅgama* altar.
(The *Fozu Tongji*, in the original biography of Master Luoxi, states that the traces of the Tiantai teachings extend far back to Huisi...)
History has long been in turmoil; since the destruction by fire during the Huichang era, fragmented steles and broken scrolls have left those who transmit them without reliable evidence.
The Master constantly lamented this and strove to collect these materials. Previously, he obtained only a single commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* from an ancient repository in Jinhua.
Later, because the King of Wuyue dispatched ten envoys to the country of Japan to seek out Buddhist scriptures, [he was able to acquire more].
After he returned, the King built a temple for him and inscribed the name "Dinghui" (Jeweled Creek) upon it; he was granted the title Jingguang (Pure Light).
Jingguang transmitted this commentary to Baoyun, who in turn transmitted it to Siming. Siming once composed a brief commentary on it to circulate it.
From this we know that although other doctrinal texts were scattered to the lands beyond the sea, the old commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* [remained].
All is well in China).

In explaining this sutra, we shall first determine whether the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) exists, and only thereafter enter the text for detailed commentary.

Now, when a sutra possesses chapters, its thematic significance remains unconfused; when chapters possess an introductory sequence, their logical threads can be drawn out. Moreover, the two types of introduction—the general and the specific—are common to all scriptural collections.
For instance, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* first displays the six auspicious omens, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* prefaces the discourse with a dream.

Because of this golden drum, it has been possible to proclaim and expound [the teaching] for one period. If the great outline can be raised, then the establishment of the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) is something esteemed in common by all sūtras.
Yet, at the very beginning of this specific sūtra, it is preceded by the "Chapter on the Buddha-land.
Following the entry into the sūtra and the exposition of the five matters, the elder presents a parasol, and the divine application is unfathomable; thus, there is the gāthā.
As for the eulogies, they are interspersed and flow gracefully; is it not the case that the two sequences—the general and the specific—are clearly distinguishable?

That they are not currently placed [at the beginning] is certainly not due to the failure of the compilers to establish them; rather, it is likely a corruption or omission from the translation process.

Regarding the titles and order of the chapters: some were proclaimed by the Buddha himself, as in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*; some were established by the compilers, as in the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā*; and some were added by the translators.
Just as with Kumārajīva, I now wish to augment the meaning, yet I also fear incurring offense and thus intend to desist.

It appears that in my commentary (*shu*), there may be points that deviate from the essential gates of the meaning; therefore, regarding the scriptural text (*jingwen*), I shall maintain its traditional value, while for the commentary, I shall establish the meaning anew.
As the Great Master of Siming once said: "The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* takes the causes and conditions of the Buddha-land as..."
As the *Zhengzong* (Orthodox Tradition) lacks a "Preface Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), various masters have taken the half-chapter on the Buddha-land as the introductory section.
Thus, the ancients also divided it according to its meaning into three parts, following the standard classification: first, the Introductory Section; second, the Orthodox Section;
and third, the Propagation Section. The Introductory Section is further divided into two: beginning with the five matters such as "Thus have I heard," it extends throughout [the text].
This is the introduction. Next follows: "At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was the son of an elder named Ratnākara," ending with the verse of praise:

"I prostrate to the One who is like space, having no dependence. This is the separate introduction (*prastāvanā*). Here it ends; next follows the main body (*mūla*), the "Chapter on the Buddha-land" (*Buddhakṣetraparivarta*).
Thus, Ratnākara addressed the Buddha, saying, "I wish to hear about attaining the purity of a buddha-field. In this way, it proceeds.

Not only will the two meanings of the introduction (*nidāna*) and the main body (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) become clear through this, but it is as plain as pointing at one's own palm that the title of the "Buddhakṣetra" chapter should serve as the heading for this text.

Next, entering the commentary on the sutra, we shall follow the usual practice of dividing it into two parts: first, the explanation of the sutra’s title; second, the explanation of the sutra’s text. Regarding the explanation:

The title is divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the translator; second, an explanation of the scriptural title. According to conventional practice, one first explains the scriptural title and subsequently explains the translator.
The present work differs from this because the old commentary first indicates the translator and only later explains the scriptural title.
Since the original commentary has been preserved until now, it is for this reason that [the following] is stated. First, regarding the translator:
Kumārajīva, the Tripiṭaka Master of the Yao Qin dynasty, was translated as "Dongshou" (Child-Life) by Master Sengzhao. He was a native of Kucha. During the Eastern Jin period, later...
The Yao clan of the Qin dynasty held Chang’an and honored [Kumārajīva] as their National Teacher.
During the Hongshi era, the Qin ruler issued an edict for eight hundred śramaṇas, including Sengqie, to receive Kumārajīva’s instructions and translate sūtras and śāstras at Caotang Monastery.
In total, ninety-eight works comprising four hundred and twenty-one fascicles were produced, with Sengrui, Sengzhao, Daochang, and others serving as scribes to record the translations.
This constitutes the first [point].

○ Second, the explanation of the title of the sutra is divided into two parts. First, listing the ancient commentaries. Second, the initial explanation of the first title, which is divided into two parts. First, the heading:
*The Sutra Spoken by Vimalakīrti*.
Second, the explanation.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Vimalakīrti—whose name means 'Pure Fame' in the language of Qin—is one of the five hundred youths.

Having come from the Land of Wondrous Joy to travel within this realm, and having fulfilled all that was required, he is about to return to his native land. He desires to manifest his profound purity."
Virtue nourishes all living beings, and manifesting one's traces awakens those of the age; these matters must necessarily have their causes.

Therefore, while he commanded his companions to go to the Buddha, he alone did not go. From his not going, one knows that he was ill. How do we know this? Five hundred companions followed the Great Way together;
in advancing toward virtue and cultivating goodness, they were invariably united in both movement and stillness. Now, [he remains behind] in the Pure Land.

Among these assemblies, it is one of the greatest undertakings that they are not held together. This clarifies that there is illness; because there is illness, there is an assembly for inquiring after the sick.
The assembly for inquiring after the sick arises from the gathering at the Pure Land; the gathering at the Pure Land arises from the skillful means of Vimalakīrti.
Thus, the origin of this sutra from beginning to end truly has its basis here. If we observe it from the perspective of his own discourse:
Thus, the various sages are equal in their merit. Tracing back from the root, this merit originates with Vimalakīrti;

by investigating its source, it is therefore called "The Teaching of Vimalakīrti. Master Zhao said: "Sūtra" means "constant. Although antiquity and the present differ, the path of awakening does not change.
The multitudes of evil cannot obstruct it, and the various sages cannot alter it; hence it is called "constant."
II. Explanation of the subsequent title, in two parts. First, the heading:
One name is "Inconceivable Liberation.
Second, the explanation.
Master Zhao said: "Subtle, remote, profound, and deep—it cannot be fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles; this is the inconceivable.
Exercising mastery without obstruction, such that worldly entanglements cannot bind it—this is liberation. This sutra begins with the Pure Land and concludes with the Dharma-offering;
although what is elucidated therein varies, its inconceivable liberation is one and the same. Therefore..."
In general, these are used as titles. The former names the sutra after a person; this names the sutra after the Dharma.
Naming the sutra after the Dharma serves to indicate its ultimate purpose; naming the sutra after a person serves to show that the Way was propagated through that individual.
II. Expanding upon the present commentary has two parts. First, a general presentation of the fivefold profundity.
Formerly, when the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai explained the title of this sutra, he employed the fivefold profound meaning (*pañca-gambhīrārtha*):

namely, "person and dharma" as the name (*nāman*); "true nature liberation" as the essence (*śarīra*); "the causes and effects of the Buddha-land" as the thesis (*abhiprāya*); and "expedient and real, subduing and gathering" as the function (*kriyā*).
As for their application: fresh butter serves as the pedagogical characteristic. II.
The individual explanations of the five layers, part five. First, the explanation of the titles, in two sections. First, the explanation of the primary title.
Now, I shall clarify this by means of the meaning of the teaching. Regarding the first [type of] title, which is based on person and dharma: Vimalakīrti is the person.
The sūtra that is spoken is the Dharma. If one follows the sequential titles, it would be named simply after the Dharma.
However, since the initial title includes both person and Dharma, there is a distinction between the person who speaks and the person about whom it is spoken.

According to the scriptural text, the Buddha is the person who speaks, while Vimalakīrti is the person about whom it is spoken. Now, since the title is given as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, [it indicates the latter].
Thus, "person" does not refer exclusively to the Buddha. Although ultimately one returns to the Buddha as the source, for now we shall follow the title and take Vimalakīrti as the speaker.

As for the "Dharma" that is spoken, it consists of true nature and liberation, the causes and effects of the Buddha-land, and the provisional and ultimate, as well as the methods of subduing and gathering—all of which are the teachings expounded.
Indeed, everything taught in this single sutra is none other than its essence, its school, and its power.
This is because of the three dharmas. Now, dharmas are taught through persons; since the realization of the dharma is what constitutes a person, the person is designated according to the dharma.
As there are already three dharmas, how could a person lack them? Thus, the person is named in accordance with the dharmas:
"True Nature Liberation" (bhūtatathatā-vimukti) is the essence of the *dharmakāya* realized by Vimalakīrti, while "Buddha-land Cause and Effect" is the *prajñā* realized by Vimalakīrti.

This is the essence [of the teaching]. The provisional and the real, as well as the methods of subduing and gathering, are the functions of liberation arising from the fundamental substance (*tattva*) of Vimalakīrti.
Since the Dharma is neither vertical nor horizontal, and persons are likewise beyond thought and discourse, there is no Dharma apart from persons, and no persons apart from the Dharma.
Because person and Dharma are designated in union, it is called the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*. Regarding the word *sūtra*, there are two interpretations: it means "constant" (*nitya*).
It is said: "Dharma. The old commentary preserves only one meaning, thus explaining the sūtra as "constant" (*nitya*).

If it were to be supplemented, it should state: "Furthermore, 'sūtra' means Dharma. Although the Buddhas of the three periods differ, there is no discrepancy in the path they follow to achieve enlightenment.
Since they have practiced it themselves and further awakened others to it, it is called a 'sūtra. 2. Explanation of the subsequent title.
The former [title] combines the person with the Dharma for its name; this [title] receives its designation based on the Dharma alone.

"Inconceivable" is spoken in contrast to the conceivable states of the partial teachings (*pradeśa-śāsana*), the perfect teachings (*paripūrṇa-śāsana*), the stages of cause (*hetu-bhūmi*), and the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Now, those who are bound within the cage of the three realms (*tridhātu*) and immersed in the delusions of the five destinies (*pañcagati*) are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). And the two...
Having mounted [this vehicle], one is able to understand and liberate oneself, remaining serene beyond the myriad burdens of existence.

Yet, the minor practices of the Śrāvakas are like those of a gazelle leaping alone, never looking back at its herd; the faction of the Pratyekabuddhas is like deer longing for their group—what is the use of such mere dwelling in a settlement?
These can liberate one from *bhava* (existence), but they have not yet liberated one from *śūnyatā* (emptiness).
To be liberated for oneself while not liberating others is something that can be conceptualized.

Therefore, those of the Two Vehicles exhaustively destroy the existence of the triple world to return to emptiness, and exhaustively cling to the non-existence of nirvana to establish it as a reality.
Because they only destroy the triple world to return to emptiness, [they fail to extend this] toward all sentient beings, even down to sovereigns and ministers.
To treat father and son, husband and wife, brothers and friends with a mere long bow, regarding them as if they were strangers on the road—this is what constitutes the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Only in *nirvāṇa* do they cling to it as something existent;

thus, they remain stubbornly attached to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, as well as to vision, wisdom, clarity, and awakening, regarding them as sweet as clarified butter (*sarpis*). This is why it is called... [the Lesser Vehicle].

This is the school of Emptiness (*śūnyatā*). As for the playful exercise of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), the purification of Buddha-fields, entering fire and water, and the transformation and salvation of sentient beings—these are utterly useless to one whose mind is withered, just as lotuses do not grow on high plateaus or dry land.
Like scorched sprouts or rotten seeds, they cannot become vessels of the Dharma. The Tathāgata’s rebuke of them was precisely to this effect:
how could such persons possibly tread the path of Great Beings or perform the deeds of Great Beings? Thus it is said: "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not what a donkey can endure;
one does not pour the great ocean into a cow's footprint. All such reproaches and censures are directed at those of this sort.
This is hypothetical. It is not so for those of the Bodhisattva vehicle; for they are able both to benefit themselves and to benefit others.
Thus, while realizing emptiness, they do not abide in emptiness. Turning this empty mind toward existence, they destroy inherent nature and destroy marks.
They practice and study universally, knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, providing the medicine according to the illness so that it may be ingested and applied. First, by means of...

His supernormal powers were awe-inspiring, and later he proclaimed the teachings through his wisdom and eloquence. Yet, while he was able to attain liberation within emptiness (*śūnyatā*), he had not yet attained liberation within the Middle Way (*madhyama*).
Or, while he was able to penetrate deeply into the "mere middle" (*kevala-madhyama*), he had not yet penetrated deeply into the perfect middle (*pariniṣpanna-madhyama*).
Although he drove the ox-cart and was thus called a follower of the Mahāyāna, it was not the Great White Ox-Cart of the Supreme One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). As for the Tripiṭaka...

The Bodhisattva subdues and observes the afflictions of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, yet does not sever them; they traverse the conditions of the provisional to deliver sentient beings.
This is precisely what the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* means when it says that one uses a vessel of poison to store ambrosia.

Since such a state has not yet reached liberation, how can one speak of the conceivable or the inconceivable? Generally, there are three kinds of liberation: true nature, perfect purity, and purity through skillful means. Vertically...
To clarify this: traversing the three stages of cultivation, the "purification through skillful means" allows the two vehicles to attain realization;
the "perfect purification" allows Bodhisattvas to enter [the path]; and "true nature" is realized and known only by Buddhas.
Having thus proceeded through these distinct stages to achieve completion, all are accessible through the expression of the mind; this is the inconceivable liberation. When fully possessed—

To speak of this: it is that which is elucidated in the Perfect and Sudden Supreme Vehicle. It is fully present within the single mind of the beginner; it is cultivated within a single thought-moment of the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*);

and it is realized within the single mind of the stage of fruition. That which is the originally existing ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) wherein all phenomena are subsumed is the "perfectly pure liberation" (*pariśuddha-vimukti*).
That which is the originally existing conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) wherein all phenomena are fully contained is the "skillful means pure liberation" (*upāya-śuddha-vimukti*).
That which, within the Middle Truth of the Original Existence, governs all phenomena is true nature and liberation. This is nature; it is not cultivation.
It is the Three Truths; it is not the Three Contemplations. Therefore, what is called "cultivation" is that which illuminates and realizes in accordance with this nature.

Illuminating and realizing the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-satya) results in perfect, pure liberation, wherein all phenomena are obliterated; this is termed "Emptiness. Illuminating and realizing the Conventional Truth (Saṃvṛti-satya)...
The liberation through the purity of skillful means establishes all phenomena; this is termed the "provisional.
The illumination of the Middle Truth is the liberation through the purity of nature; it encompasses all phenomena and is termed the "Middle.

Since the three truths are already complete within a single mind, the three contemplations are likewise cultivated within a single mind, and the three types of liberation are realized within a single mind. Therefore, directly...
Perfect purity is not [identical to] non-perfect purity; perfect purity must necessarily possess the true nature of skillful means. Direct skillful means is not [identical to] skillful means;

skillful means must necessarily possess the true nature of perfect purity. Direct true nature is not [identical to] true nature; true nature must necessarily possess skillful means and perfect purity.
Nevertheless, although there is a single thought-moment of simultaneous cultivation, because of the varying depths of the destruction of delusions, that which is realized is not [identical].

There is no sequential order. Thus, through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), views and afflictions (*kleśa*) are shattered and perfect purity is realized; through the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*), the dust-like delusions are shattered and skillful means are realized;
through the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), ignorance (*avidyā*) is shattered and true nature is realized.

Although the stages of realization are sequential, the principle is not sequential; therefore, the contemplations themselves also possess no sequence. While the cause is indeed sudden and perfect, one must defer to the fruit before it is fully realized.
Because these are integrated, even when discussed in terms of causes, they remain conceivable— such as the room in the "Inconceivable" chapter containing a vast seat,
a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru, the ocean entering a pore without disturbing the fish and turtles, or taking up a world and casting it elsewhere.

He causes people to be neither aware nor cognizant of it; he expands a day into an eon (*kalpa*) and shortens an eon into a day, yet there is no distinction whatsoever between extension and contraction.
These are all matters pertaining to the sages of the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*), and thus seem beyond the realm of those at the initial stage of resolve (*ādikarmika*).

This is especially so in the case of Vimalakīrti, who was a Tathāgata of Golden Grain (*Suvarṇa-kaṇa*); having already come together with five hundred elders from the Land of Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*), he sought its...
The fundamental and the manifested (honji-suijaku) are indeed equal in rank. Is it not in this that the title "Inconceivable Liberation" resides?

Nevertheless, while the fruit is presented, its primary purpose is to reveal the cause; and while the cause is revealed, its primary purpose is to lead toward the fruit. There are depths and shallows within the cause, yet the intent lies in the initial mind. As it is said:
"The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings," and "practicing on what is not the Path."
To penetrate the Buddha-way, the guidance provided here relies on diligent verbal instruction. How could those who have perfected their names not admire this?
Yet, one must know the fundamental tenets within it. Why is this so? It is because the title "Liberation" (vimukti) refers to but one aspect of the Three Virtues;
when spoken of in terms of the Three Truths, its meaning resides in the Provisional (saṃvṛti). As the ancients said: "Unthinkable..."

This provisional [reality] is not a partial provisional reality. This provisional reality, which fundamentally possesses all dharmas, refers to the nature-endowment of the three thousand [realms], the ten realms and their thousand suchnesses;
it is precisely emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. That is to say, true emptiness is not merely empty, and perfect middle is not merely middle.
Therefore, the first of the four gates is precisely this inconceivable provisional reality.
As for these three thousand worlds: one thousand belong to the provisional names of sentient beings and Buddhas; one thousand belong to the primary retributions of sentient beings and Buddhas;

and one thousand belong to the secondary retributions of sentient beings and Buddhas. Because they abide within a single nature, the more they are integrated, the more they are differentiated; the more they are dispersed, the more they are unified.
Interfusing and unimpeded, each possesses universality and inclusiveness; this is the essence of the unchanging *tathatā* (suchness), yet each also possesses the function of responding to conditions.
Since it is unchanging while responding to conditions, it responds to conditions while remaining unchanging.

Therefore, within the fruit, the primary manifests within the dependent, and the dependent manifests within the primary; the small manifests within the large, and the large manifests within the small. One.
The infinite becomes one, and the one appears within the tip of a single hair, manifesting a jewel-king land;
sitting within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel—it is all rooted in this. Thus, the title "Inconceivable Liberation" is likewise rooted in this.
II. Distinguishing the Essence.
Regarding the second point—that the essence consists of true nature and liberation: the meaning of the three liberations has already been explained as above.

However, the previous explanation of the names was general, because it encompassed the three dharmas collectively. Now, the explanation of the essence is specific, because it distinguishes the three dharmas individually. This is the Chapter on the Essence.

Since it is distinct from the *dharmakāya*, it alone is designated as having true nature (*tathatā*) as its essence. Within the contemplation and realization of the truths, it is further distinguished within the three truths;
and within the three truths, it is further distinguished as the Middle Way. Although it resides in a single nature, that one necessarily possesses the three.
That is to say, the direct *dharmakāya* is not merely the *dharmakāya*; the *dharmakāya* must necessarily possess *prajñā* and liberation (*vimukti*). This is...
It is like the case of one sovereign and two ministers: although they can govern and direct, the sovereign is noble in essence and, being autonomous, is called the King.
Furthermore, it refers solely to the true nature, the *dharmakāya*.
○ Third, the Thesis of the Three Clarities:
Regarding the thesis that the cause and effect of the Buddha-land constitute the core principle, the aforementioned true nature resides only in its ontological essence.

Although there is no duality between the living being and the Buddha, that which sentient beings possess has not yet at all entered the realm of cultivation. Therefore, in order to realize this essence, one must—
The arising of boundless great function lies in the essential doctrine of the causes and effects for purifying Buddha-lands. The purity of the Buddha-land is the fruit;
the practice for purifying the land is the cause. Therefore, the Elder Ratnakūṭa made a request on behalf of the assembly, wishing to hear how one attains the purity of a Buddha-land, saying:
"I pray that the World-Honored One will explain the practices for purifying the lands of all Bodhisattvas. This is because... [the text is incomplete].
This cause and effect cannot realize this true nature of liberation. Thus, the aforementioned true nature belongs to the *dharmakāya*, while the present cause and effect belong to *prajñā*.
There are three types of *prajñā*: the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*), which corresponds in meaning to the Middle Way;

the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), which corresponds in meaning to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); and the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*), which corresponds in meaning to... [text ends].
It is as if it were said: "For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to construct a palace upon an empty plot of land;
they may do so at will without hindrance. But if they attempt to do so in empty space, it can never be accomplished.

Is this not because while emptiness exists, it equally illuminates both the ultimate and the conventional, such that through their mutual fusion, it constitutes the essential core of this single scripture?
Section Four: The Function of the Teachings.
Regarding the fourth point, that provisional and ultimate [truths] and subduing and gathering constitute the function:

Now, when the Perfected One benefits sentient beings, he takes the provisional and ultimate as his essence and subduing and gathering as his function. However, gathering is the fundamental mind, whereas subduing is not the fundamental mind; therefore, it is said: "The four..."

The gathering of dharmas (*dharmasaṃgraha*) is the pure land of a bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who have been gathered through liberation come to be born in that land.
However, if one merely gathers them without first practicing subduing, it will not succeed; one must first employ subduing.
This is like Śākyamuni’s manifestation in the Sahā world, where he first employed subduing; whereas Amitābha’s vow to attain purity and tranquility was followed by gathering. Such is the Dharma.
He preached on suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; he began with "refutation" (zhé). He spoke of the Dharma as a jade grove and a crystal pond;
he showed it through "gathering" (shè). By showing the gates of the Hīnayāna, he demonstrated that by practicing them one attains the Way; this was preceded by "gathering.
Those who were like scorched sprouts or rotten seeds, unfit to be vessels for the Dharma, were subsequently subjected to "refutation. Such Dharma-gates are too numerous to be enumerated individually.
All these are based on the ultimate person’s reliance upon the foundation of provisional and ultimate truth to apply the functions of *śāntika* (appeasement) and *dāruṇa* (subjugation).

Thus, there are those whom the gift of material wealth cannot subdue; instead, the practitioner turns to them and begs from them. This is because giving is used to arouse their joy, while begging is used to break their stinginess.
Or there are those whom kind speech cannot subdue; instead, the practitioner turns to them and rebukes them with harsh words.

Kind speech is used to encourage their progress; reprimand is used to effect their retreat. Sometimes that which is beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) cannot encompass them, and one instead proceeds to oppose and take it away from them.
Beneficial conduct is used to accord with their dispositions; opposition and taking it away serves to conflict with their will.
Sometimes that which is shared purpose (*samānārthatā*) cannot encompass them, and one instead proceeds to act differently from them.

That which is identical is used to lead them forward; that which is different is used to cause them to retreat. Yet, some are gathered through the Real (shí), while others are refuted through the Expedient (quán);
some are refuted through the Real, while others are gathered through the Expedient. It is like performing a play on the spot or joining in song according to the melody:
it may be done in a barbarian tongue with coarse forms, or it may be done in the Han language with elegant substance. This is like the "Spring Wind" [melody].
The "White Snow" may be so; the "Ba Songs of the Low Villages" may also be so. That Bodhisattvas are called "those who sport with supernatural powers" truly seems to be like this.
V. Judging the Teachings.
Regarding the fifth, *navanīta* (fresh butter), as the characteristic of the teaching: the mutual generation of the five flavors is recorded in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The Great Master employed this to judge the Tathāgata’s dispensation of the Dharma across five periods. First, "milk produced from the cow" is a metaphor for the Buddha’s initial preaching of the *Avataṃsaka*.

Second, "curd produced from milk" is a metaphor for the gradual teaching bestowed after the sudden [teaching], specifically the preaching of the four *Āgama* sūtras during the twelve years following [the *Avataṃsaka*].
Third, the production of cream from curd represents the period within eight years after the Buddha preached the Āgamas, during which the four teachings were expounded together.
Fourth, the production of clarified butter from cream represents the twenty-two years following the Buddha’s teaching of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras).
It is said that after the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* was preached, the *Ghṛta* (clarified butter) emerged from the *Manda* (fresh butter).

This serves as a metaphor for the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* within the eight years following the Buddha’s *Prajñā*, and the preaching of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* on a single day at midnight.
This sūtra is categorized among the *Vaipulya* (Extensive) teachings; for instance, when the great disciples were rebuked by Vimalakīrti, they all recounted past events. Thus, one should know [this].
Regarding the Vaipulya (fangděng), the Great Master [Zhiyi] judged this period to be the time for preaching the "Full" (mǎn) in contrast to the "Half" (bàn).
Nevertheless, within that interval, there are some sutras that preach the purely perfect (chúnyuán), and others that preach the perfect by contrasting the specific (bié) with the general (tōng).
This sutra precisely corresponds to the teaching of the "Full" through the contrast of the general and the specific; although it also contains elements contrasted with the general...
Regarding the meaning of "distinct," it is precisely while addressing the partial that one speaks of the perfect.
Nevertheless, within this, the meaning of the perfect is most consummately complete, such as the identity of birth-and-death with nirvāṇa, and afflictions with bodhi;
for instance, the liberation of the Tathāgata is to be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings, and the practice of non-paths leads to the penetration of the Buddha-way, and so forth.

How could there be a Perfect and Sudden teaching superior to this? Therefore, although it is generally categorized as belonging to the "Fresh Butter" (Sarpis) stage of the doctrinal classification, poison has been placed within that fresh butter;
for this "butter" is a teaching that kills people. The initial explanation of the title of the sutra is hereby concluded.

II. Explanation of the Scriptural Text. Following the standard practice, this is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the introductory section (nidāna); second, the explanation of the main body (śarīra);
and third, the explanation of the dissemination section (pariṇāmanā). Regarding the title of the first part, the introductory section:

according to the usual convention, as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, where the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta) is first indicated and followed by the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta), by analogy with that, how could this [text] lack such? Thus, we know it is not a [mere] non-scripture.

The absence of this [title] in the text is due to the abridgment of the translator. Therefore, although the present commentary designates it as "Buddha-land" (Foguo) based on the scripture, the exegesis must first set forth its general and specific meanings;
it is only upon reaching the subsequent chapter that the meaning of "Buddha-land" is formally explained.
The text is divided into three parts: first, the title of the chapter according to the translation.
Preface to the First Chapter, "The Buddha-land," of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, according to the primary meaning.
This follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in designating the first chapter as the "Introduction" (*Nidāna*). As the *Wenju* states:
"Preface" (*nidāna*) means sequence, cause, and narration. This sutra is likewise so; these five matters are placed at the beginning of the sutra to establish the sequence.
The verses of offering and praise constitute the opening of the inspiration. As for the questions and answers that resolve doubts, these belong to the "Correct Teaching" (*samyak-artha*);
this differs from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Nevertheless, they are not anything other than the introductory lead-in to the correct exposition. This is the narration.

This is an exposition. Because it possesses these three meanings, it is called the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta). As for "chapter" (parivarta), the Sanskrit term is *varga*, which here is translated as "chapter.
A "chapter" carries the sense of a category; herein, the phrases and sentences are grouped according to their thematic categories and demarcated as *vargas*.
Therefore, it is titled "The First Introductory Chapter."
III. The Correct Explanation of the Sutra Text has two parts: first, the general introduction; second, the specific introduction. The general introduction consists of six items:

first, the essence of the Dharma heard; second, the person who upholds it; third, the harmony between hearing and upholding; fourth, the teacher who expounds it; fifth, the place upon which it relies;
sixth, the companions who hear and uphold it. Master Tiantai said: "These six matters are also called the 'Seal of Certainty' (Yinding Xu) introduction."
Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time place these words at the beginning of their sutras, it is called the "General Preface" (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*), as it is common to all sutras.
It is also called the "Postscript," as it was established by those who compiled the teachings. It is also called the "Preface," as it was placed there by the Buddha's own behest.
It is also called the "Preface for Refuting Error," as it counters and refutes the *āgama* of the non-Buddhists. It is also called the "Preface for Establishing Faith."
Introduction: This is so that those who hear it may have no doubts. These six explanations collectively constitute the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*.
First, the essence of the Dharma as it was heard is thus.
The Great Master of Tiantai said: "Regarding the 'old interpretation' of *ru-guang-ming* (suchness-light), it is identical to the name itself; thus it is called 'non-erroneous.

The words and phrases transmitted by Ānanda are like pouring water from one vessel into another—they are of the same kind as the Buddha’s own words, and therefore they are termed 'such' (*ru*) because they are not different.

The principle underlying the text is accurate and without error; thus, what was previously called 'non-erroneous' is now affirmed as 'is' (*shi*). To speak briefly: the text is suchness, and the principle is suchness."
This is so. When Master Sengzhao annotated the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa*, he used the phrase "Thus" (*evam*) as a term denoting faith and compliance.

Through faith, the principles of what is spoken are realized; through compliance, the way between teacher and disciple is perfected. Whether a scripture is extensive or concise, it cannot be transmitted without faith;
therefore, he stated at the outset, "Thus. The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha said: "Thus" signifies determination. It is the determination of number and the determination of principle.

Certainty. When the Buddha preached this sutra, there were a certain number of phrases and sentences; if there were more, it would result in the slander of exaggeration, and if there were fewer, it would result in the slander of diminution.
Ānanda transmitted it like pouring water from one vessel to another—neither more nor less—and thus the count is fixed.

The principle of signlessness taught by the Buddha is neither existent nor non-existent; if "existent," one falls into exaggeration, and if "non-existent," one falls into diminution. Ānanda transmitted it accordingly.
There is neither increase nor decrease; therefore, the principle is definitive. Nāgārjuna explains that "thus" (*evam*) is a term of faith and compliance.
One who has faith says, "This matter is thus"; one who lacks faith says, "This matter is not thus. These four interpretations each rely upon a specific *siddhānta*.
The old commentaries are general in their language and do not clarify what kind of principle is expressed by the text as being "thus."
As for the principle by which the text is interpreted, what is presented here is not yet fully explicit; it is merely according to the *loka-siddhānta* (worldly standpoint).

Master Zhaol relied on faith as the *pudgala-viniścaya* (intent regarding persons). The principles and texts of the Tripiṭaka are definitive as the *pratipakṣa-viniścaya* (intent of counteractive treatment).
Nāgārjuna’s faithful adherence is thus the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth). The Great Master said: "One should provide both a general and a specific interpretation. Generally...
Regarding the term "shì" (釋): the Buddha taught according to the characteristics of the dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and Ānanda transmitted them according to the characteristics as he heard them;

therefore, it is called "ru" (如). The Buddha explained according to the characteristics of the dharmas, and Ānanda received them according to the characteristic of the ocean (*sāgaralakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called "shì" (是). Regarding the separate explanation:
outsiders say that "Ān" (阿) signifies "auspicious" (*kalyāṇa*). Since the words deviate from the principle, they are not "ru" (如); since the principle differs from the words, they are not "shì" (是).
This is not so. It cannot be that the *āyu* (the syllable "A") exists at the beginning while the middle and end are all auspicious.

Because the text accords with the principle, it is called "thus" (*yathā*); because the principle accords with the text, it is called "is" (*iti*). This refutes the heterodoxy of the non-Buddhists and establishes the orthodoxy of the Tripiṭaka;
therefore, it is termed "Thus" (*evam*). Furthermore, the opening of the Tripiṭaka sūtras states: "Thus, the two truths are each distinct."

Therefore, it is not "as" (yathā) because its principle is shallow; it is not "is" (tathā) because [in the Tripiṭaka] the two truths are not mutually identical. In the Mahāyāna, because the two truths are identical in nature, it is called "as"; because its principle is profound, it is called "is.
This refutes the differences of the Tripiṭaka teachings and establishes the commonality of the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) Teaching; thus it is termed "Thus" (evam).

Furthermore, although the three types of people hear it together, they each understand it differently, and thus it is not "as. Because their realization and entry [into the truth] vary in degree of excellence, it is not "is."
That which is heard by Bodhisattvas alone is the "Thus" (tathā); that which is realized by Bodhisattvas alone is the "Is" (evam).

This refutes the shallowness of the Shared Teaching and establishes the profundity of the Distinct Teaching; therefore, it is called "Thus" (tathatā). Furthermore, this is the passage clarifying the "Middle" by departing from the extremes.
If one holds that there is a Middle Way existing outside of the two truths, that is not so. The very nature of words is detached;
this is precisely Suchness (tathatā). All dharmas are the Buddha-dharma; this is designated as "is. This refutes the separation characteristic of the Separate Teaching (biejiao).

It establishes the "immediacy" (*jika*) of the Perfect Teaching (*enkyō*); therefore, it is called "Thus" (*nyoze*). Since this sutra belongs to the Vaipulya class, it universally addresses various capacities and natures;

thus, there is no fault in its manifold explanations. For one who understands through the contemplation of the mind (*kanjin*), "Thus" (*nyo*) refers to the contemplation being in profound accord with the object, while "Is" (*ze*) refers to the object being identical to correct contemplation.
As the sutra says: "One who performs this contemplation is said to possess correct contemplation. If...

"To contemplate otherwise is called 'erroneous contemplation'—this is precisely the meaning. Someone asked: "The interpretation of the meanings of the Buddhist scriptures has been a universal standard since ancient times;
however, regarding the contemplative interpretations of the Dharma-gates, there is much empty and redundant proliferation. It would be better to simply abandon them. He replied:
"In Zhiyi’s *Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, this very question was originally raised. I shall now cite the dialogue preserved in the *Zongjing Lu* to elucidate it for you."
Know that what I take as my primary authority is not erroneous. His commentary asks:

"Why do you suddenly, in various places, explain the Dharma-gates in relation to the contemplation of the mind by making such statements? It is not necessarily the Buddha’s intention that it should be so. He answers:

"If one were to say that there is no explanation of the meaning through the Dharma-gates within the sutras, [one must consider] this 'Universal Manifestation of Form' chapter of the *Buddhamārga* (Buddha-way) section of this sutra..."
The Bodhisattva Śariputra asked Vimalakīrti, "Householder, who are your father, mother, wife, children, relatives, and kinsmen?
The Great Being replied in verse: "The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas...
Since Vimalakīrti was a lay bodhisattva, how could he be without parents, a wife, children, or a home? Yet, why did he not answer according to these worldly facts?

To answer by summarizing all according to the dharma-gate of internal practice, one should know that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not give rise to the dharmas of the Path, yet they manifest the affairs of ordinary beings.
Although they manifest these worldly affairs, they all outwardly represent the dharmas of the Path.

For example, when the Buddha entered parinirvāṇa between the twin trees, with four branches withered and four flourishing—how could one simply interpret this as being about the trees? Furthermore, such is the reality of the Tathāgata.
These all symbolize the partial and the complete, the withered and the flourishing. Now, being at the Āmra Grove in Vaiśālī, he wishes to preach the Dharma-gate of the inconceivable liberation.
Without abandoning the Way, he manifests traces identical to those of ordinary beings;
by dwelling in Vaiśālī, does this not symbolize the Dharma-gate of the ultimate stage? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies ten cities and ten groves—how could it be merely this?
The world is like a city and its gardens. As stated in the "Bodhisattva Conduct" chapter of this sutra:
"In all the majestic deportment of the Buddhas, whether advancing or halting, there is nothing that is not a Buddha-activity. How can one interpret these as merely mundane affairs?

One fails to contemplate the inconceivable teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, nor the matters expressed through their skillful means and secret manifestations. Furthermore, the Lotus Sutra says:
If one wishes to preach this sutra, one should enter the Tathāgata’s chamber, don the Tathāgata’s robe, and sit upon the Tathāgata’s seat.
The Tathāgata’s chamber is the mind of great compassion; the Tathāgata’s robe is gentleness and patience;
the Tathāgata’s seat is the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Question: Is it possible to [attain] the Mahayana of the sudden teaching of the *Avataṃsaka*?

While various Dharma gates are generally elucidated by way of practice (*caryā*), how can this Vaipulya sutra and the teachings of the Hīnayāna also elucidate their meaning by way of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*)?

The answer is: since this sutra states that "the liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings," if one does not rely on contemplative practice, how could it be consistent with this text?
If [one does not rely on it], then [it would be like] not using the Āmra grove of Vaiśālī...
Regarding the various Dharma-gates in the Grove of Trees, one cannot explain them by means of contemplating the mind alone.

How could one seek the liberation of all Buddhas within the mental activities of sentient beings? If one does not seek liberation within mental activity, how can one abide in inconceivable liberation?
If one does not abide in inconceivable liberation, how can one, in a single...
Within the pores of his skin, he beholds all Buddha-lands and manifests transformations with sovereign mastery, as clarified in the "Inconceivable" chapter (*Acintya-parivarta*).

Furthermore, how can one attain the purification of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, whereby all lands of the ten directions appear within one's own body?
Moreover, how can one attain that which is spoken in the verses of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*: "All immeasurable worlds..."?
Infinite Buddha-lands arising from the mind all manifest within a single pore. As was previously asked:

if it is not permissible to explain the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) by means of contemplating the mind, why is it that in the Śrāvaka sūtras, when the Buddha taught the eleven dharmas to a cowherd, each one was internally correlated with a bhikṣu’s contemplation of the mind? Such are the examples.
Is it not the case that the Vaipulya and Tripiṭaka sūtras clarify the meaning of contemplating the mind in relation to all dharma-gates?
Thus we know that both definitive teachings and non-definitive teachings are all definitive, because they are but the One Mind. Furthermore, the Commentary asks:

"The Profound Meaning (Xuanyi) frequently clarifies contemplating the mind in various places; this was already feared to be excessive. Now, as the text is being entered, it is done so again. Will it not..."
Does this not disrupt and confuse the scriptural teachings? Answer: The purpose of expounding the scriptures is fundamentally for entering the Path.

If a worthy person who cherishes the Path practices contemplation wherever they go, how could there be one who seeks the sacred texts of Nirvana yet fails to practice contemplation? It is simply that skillful exposition is appropriate;
it does not merely avoid damaging the literal meaning of the text, but also ensures that contemplative wisdom becomes clear and distinct, thereby discerning the various Dharma-gates. It is not...
What has been attained through contemplation? Could there be any fault of disruption or confusion?
○ Second, those capable of upholding [the teaching].
Thus have I heard.

Master Shi said: "If one does not say that [the Dharma] was heard, then it would mean that I myself possess the Dharma. If I myself possessed the Dharma, then my mind would have something to which it clings.
If the mind has something to which it clings, then strife and confusion will inevitably arise. If one says that it was heard, then I have no Dharma."
Since I have no self, there is nothing to which I cling. Whether gain or loss, right or wrong, these all return to what has been heard.
Since I have no clinging, others likewise have no contention. Without clinging and without contention, from what cause could dispute arise? This sutra refers to this as "Thus have I heard."
Paramārtha said: "I" has the meaning of a vessel. First, a distracted mind is called a covered vessel because it lacks the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

Second, a forgetful mind is called a leaking vessel because, though it may acquire [knowledge], it loses it; it lacks the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Third, an inverted mind is called a defiled vessel because it takes what is not as what is;
it lacks the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Ānanda is free from these three faults and is solely a vessel for that which is good.
Because there was a direct transmission, he said, "I have heard.
The *Śāstra* explains: when the faculty of hearing is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, and one applies the mind to listen attentively, these conditions harmonize;
thus, it is called "hearing. Ānanda recounted the Buddha’s final instructions to the assembly; because he received them directly and without error, he said:
I have heard that the Great Master of Tiantai explained that "self" (*ātman*) has four meanings: namely, self-self; self-no-self; no-self-self; and self-no-self non-duality.

These are correlated with persons of the four faculties. "Hearing" (*śruta*) likewise has four meanings: namely, hearing-hearing; [hearing-no-hearing; no-hearing-hearing; and hearing-no-hearing non-duality].

"Hearing what has not been heard," "hearing what was not heard," and "neither hearing what has not been heard nor hearing what was not heard" correspond to the four types of individuals according to their spiritual faculties (*indriya*).
There are four kinds of Ānanda, namely: Ānanda of Joy (*Nandika*), Noble Ānanda (*Bhadrika*), Ānanda the Keeper of the Treasury (*Koṣṭhila*), and Ocean Ānanda (*Sāgara*).
These four names were established based on four types of conditions (the *Koṣṭhila* appears in the *Āgama-sūtra*; the other three appear in the *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna-sūtra*).

The Joyful Ānanda is "I am I," for he hears by means of hearing; having personally attended the Buddha of the sixteen-foot body and upheld the Dharma of the Tripitaka, he says, "I am I, I hear, I hear.
The Worthy Ānanda is "I am not-I," for he hears by means of not-hearing;

having personally attended the Buddha who is the unified body of the sixteen-foot and the *vairocana* (excellent) forms and upheld the teachings of the *abhiṣeka* (empowerment), he says, "I am not-I, I hear, I do not hear."

I have heard that the Elder Ānanda is "no-self and yet self. Because he hears what is unheard by using the hearing of non-hearing, and because he personally received the Buddha’s special physical body and upheld the distinct teachings of the Dharma, it is said:
"No-self and yet self; I do not hear, yet I hear. O Sea-like Ānanda, "self" and "no-self" are non-dual.
Because he does not hear by means of non-hearing, and because he personally received the Buddha of the Dharma-body and upheld the perfect teachings of the Dharma, it is said: "Self."

There is no self and thus no duality. In its function, it is neither heard nor not heard. Although this sutra belongs to the Perfect and Sudden teaching, it also extends to the teachings and listening of the Three Vehicles;
since each understands according to their own voice, it is necessary to distinguish them.
Regarding the contemplative understanding: if one practices the contemplation of loathing the lower while grasping for the higher, this is "I" and "my hearing-hearing.
If one practices the two types of analytical contemplations—breaking down the substance to enter emptiness from the conventional—this is "I" and "non-I," and "hearing-not-hearing.

If one practices the contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional, this is "non-I" and "I," and "not-hearing-hearing. If one practices the Middle Way contemplation, this is the "True I."
"Having heard it or not having heard it. This sutra takes the causes and conditions of the Buddha-land as its primary theme; it pertains solely to the latter type.
III. Hearing, Retaining, and Harmonious Union.
At one time.
Master Zhao said: "The Dharma King has initiated his auspicious reign; this is a time of sublime assembly. Paramārtha said: "In times of prosperity, arrogance prevails;
in times of decline, one indulges in the five desires. Both of these—excess and deficiency—are states in which one is unfit to hear the Dharma."
Only when one is at ease—neither indulgent nor arrogant—is that itself the "one time. The Great Master said:

"When sentient beings elicit the Buddha and the Buddha’s compassion accords with their capacity, at the moment when capacity and response merge as one, it is also the moment of awakening to the true realization of the Truth (satyadarśana)."
When the Dharma-eye is clear and bright, illuminating the world, and when the Buddha-eye shines upon it, they are said to be "one.

If one were to think first and then perceive later, they would not be one; rather, it is called "at one time" because at the moment of sudden awakening when discursive thought and perception are falsely severed.

Regarding "contemplative understanding": entering emptiness from the conventional is simultaneous with the Truth; entering the conventional from emptiness is simultaneous with the capacities of sentient beings;
and the correct contemplation of the Middle Way is simultaneous with the *dharmatā*. Therefore, it is called "simultaneous."
○ Fourth, the explanation of the Teacher:
the Buddha.

Regarding "Buddha," Paramārtha states that there are three meanings: omniscience (which distinguishes him from non-Buddhists), and compassion (which distinguishes him from the two [types of practitioners]).
Vehicle. This is distinct from the small *bodhisattvas*; other people do not possess it. The *Śāstra* clarifies that "Buddha" is the ninth title. "Buddha" means awakening (*buddha*).
One awakens to the mundane and supramundane, the permanent and impermanent, the conditioned and unconditioned, and so forth;
because of this clear and great enlightenment, one is called a Buddha. The Great Master said: "As for 'Buddha,' based on omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), there is the six-foot Buddha."

Based on the knowledge of the aspects of the path (mārgajñatā), there is the Honored One of Extraordinary Appearance (vairocana-vigraha) measuring sixteen feet; based on the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā), there is the Dharma-body Buddha (dharmakāya-buddha).
These three Buddhas cannot be said to be either identical or different; they are neither identical nor different, yet they are so.

Regarding contemplative understanding: through the contemplation of emptiness, one realizes that all phenomena have a single characteristic; through the contemplation of the provisional, one realizes that all phenomena have manifold characteristics;
and through the contemplation of the middle way, one realizes that all phenomena possess neither the characteristic of identity nor difference, yet do possess both identity and difference.
V. The Place of Reliance.
It is located in the Āmra Grove at Vaiśālī.
This is explained in two parts. First, "located" (*zài*) is explained by means of "dwelling" (*zhù*). Master Tiantai said: "'Located' refers to a temporary state."
To "be" (vartate) means to remain for a long duration; this is merely a way of speaking. Therefore, "being" is here explained by "abiding" (sthiti). As for "abiding":
the Buddha is the one who abides, and the Vairaṇyāmravana grove is the place where he abides. According to the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, there are eight modes of abiding.
1. Abiding within the great trichiliocosm; 2. Abiding in the place of reliance, namely the Āmra Grove of Vairaṇyā; 3.
Abiding in the manifestation of the lifespan of the fivefold Dharma-body; 4. Abiding in majestic deportment that benefits sentient beings; 5.

Celestial abiding, which is abiding in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); 6. Brahma-abiding, which is abiding in the four immeasurables of loving-kindness and compassion; 7. Noble abiding, which is abiding in the three [knowledges] (*trividyā*).
Obscure. Abiding in the eight great stations (*mahāsthāna*). This refers to abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The *Śāstra* explains that the four abidings encompass eight dharmas:

the celestial abiding (*devasthāna*) and the Brahma abiding (*brahmasthāna*) encompass the celestial abiding; the meditative abiding (*samādhisthāna*) and the noble abiding (*āryasthāna*) encompass the fivefold life-sustaining abiding;

and the Buddha-abiding (*buddhasthāna*) encompasses the abiding in the great stations. Furthermore, there is the abiding in traces (*vyañjanasthāna*), such as the city of Vaiśālī, which encompasses the reliance on the majestic power within those boundaries.
Regarding the three abodes of the ritual forms, the Great Master said: "The Buddha of the six-foot body abides in the True Truth (*satyadharma*).

The Buddha of the combined body of the six-foot and the *viśeṣa* (extraordinary) form abides in both the True and the Middle. The Buddha of the *viśeṣa* body abides in both the Conventional and the Middle. As for the Dharma-body Buddha..."

This refers to abiding in the Middle Way. In my humble opinion, this sutra explains that when the Buddha first abides, he clarifies the various stages of abiding; he abides in the Land of Common Residence for Ordinary Beings and Sages.
Next, he abides in the Truth of Reality (*satyadharma*); he abides in the Land of Expedient Means with Remainder.

Next, he abides simultaneously in both Reality and the Middle; he abides in the Land of True Reward. Finally, the Dharma-body abides in the Middle Way; he abides in the Land of Eternal Quiescent Light. As stated in the following passage of the sutra:

[The Buddha] said, "Clear! Śāriputra replied, "I see this land as full of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines; thorns, gravel, and sand; mountains of earth and stone; and it is filled with filth and impurity.
It is a place where ordinary beings and sages dwell together. This was exactly what the Brahma King Śikhin saw:
like the palace of the Lord of Freedom (Īśvara), it was likewise a land where ordinary beings and sages dwelt together. Then the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately the world—
The realm is adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels. By citing this single section, the two aforementioned lands can both be discussed.

For those who practice through contemplation and understanding: when conventional wisdom abides in the mundane, one abides in the Land of Common Residence; when the contemplation of emptiness abides in the ultimate, one abides in the Land of Adornment.
Conveniently, the provisional contemplation (*parikalpita*) abiding in the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) is precisely abiding in the *sahā-pratibhāsa* (Real Reward) land;

the middle contemplation (*paratantra*) abiding in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely abiding in the *śānta-prabhāsa* (Tranquil Light) land. Next, to correctly explain the dwelling places: Vaiśālī is also called Vyeśālī, Viśālī, or Vaiśālī.
This is called Vaiśālī. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) calls it the Kingdom of Vaiśālī; the old transliteration was *Piśālī*. Master Kumārajīva said:
"Vai" refers to what is suitable for rice fields, and "śālī" means "broad and magnificent. Its terrain is level and its appearance is grandly adorned.
The *Jingming lüeshu* (Brief Commentary on the Vimalakīrti) states: "In this [language], it is called 'Vipula-vyūha-śuddha' (Broad, Majestic, and Pure).

That land is vast and level, hence it is named 'Broad'; its cities and towns are magnificent, hence it is named 'Pure. Some masters translate it as 'Excellent Rice,' because it produces fine non-glutinous grain that surpasses that of other lands.
Others say it means 'Excellent Path,' because the country has a path that is polished and straight; others say it means 'Excellent Way.'"
The people of the kingdom delighted in the Right Path and naturally cultivated benevolence and righteousness; they required no sovereign ruler.
Five hundred elders together practiced the Dharma, and among the people throughout the land, there were none who did not turn toward it with joy.
As for the Āmrapālī Grove, it was named after the tree; that is to say, this famous grove existed in the city of Vaiśālī, which these five hundred elders established.
In the vihāra, he invited the Buddha to enter the rains retreat, where the Wheel of Dharma was constantly turned; this was because there were many such trees in the garden.
The *Fanyi mingyi ji* states: "The correct term is āmra, or āmrāvati; Zhaò translates it as 'pear' (*nài*)."
Its fruit resembles a peach but is not a peach; it is also translated as "difficult to distinguish. In the past, Jīvaka’s mother was named Āmrapālī;
she was born from within this tree, and thus she was a human being of moist-birth origin.

Regarding "interpretation through contemplation": contemplating this mind as the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), wherein it is fully endowed with all phenomena and capable of producing the noble sprouts of the Dharma-body, is the meaning of *vi* [vastu].
Contemplating this mind as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), wherein its essential nature and magnitude pervade the entire Dharma-realm, is the meaning of *pra*.

Contemplate this true reality of the mind: its essential nature is pure and unstained; this is the meaning of "purity. Contemplating this, one sees that it is simultaneously the ultimate, the conventional, and the middle.
To mention one is to include all three; to speak of the three is to express the one. They are difficult to differentiate; this is the meaning of *amala*.

Sixth, the four types of companions who hear and uphold [the Dharma]: first, the assembly of Śrāvakas who have attained the fruit; second, the assembly of Bodhisattvas; third, the miscellaneous assembly;
and fourth, the assembly of Śrāvakas practicing the cause. If these were to be arranged in sequence according to the Great and Small Vehicles, the Bodhisattvas should come first.

That this is not the case today is as the ancient masters have said: they categorized them according to the proximity of their physical forms and conduct. Śrāvakas have forms that emerge from the mundane net;
their conduct is close to that of the Tathāgata, and they realize the sūtras, thus they are listed first. Deva-mānuṣas have forms that differ and attire that is distinct;

their conduct does not consist of serving [the Buddha], and they realize the sūtras with a degree of remoteness, thus they are listed later. Bodhisattvas do not regulate their physical forms, and their conduct has no fixed station.
As for their dwelling, they differ from the laity and yet are distinct from the monastic community; situated between the "eldest" and the "youngest," they occupy the position of the "middle brother.
This is explained in terms of factual circumstance. If explained in terms of principle, the śrāvakas rejoice in nirvāṇa, while devas and humans are attached to saṃsāra.
Each has its own partiality; the Bodhisattva neither delights in nor clings to them, but dwells in the center to seek the ultimate essence, and thus remains between the two.
The intent of the *Śāstra* is likewise. Now, first, the assembly of Śrāvakas who have attained the fruit is enumerated.
He was together with a great assembly of eight thousand bhikṣus.

The *Śāstra* clarifies that "together" (*saha*) signifies the sense of being in common. Taking up the seven points, one interpretation of "common" refers to: being at one time, in one place, and observing one precept.
It is one mind, one vision, one path, and one liberation. It is called "Great" (*mahā*) because it signifies "much" and "superior.
Its capacity and measure are so venerable that it is revered by great beings such as celestial kings; thus it is called "Great. It transcends the ninety-five types of heterodox paths;
thus it is called "Superior. It possesses comprehensive knowledge of both internal and external scriptures; thus it is called "Much. The Great Master said: Now...
It is called "Great" because it possesses the Great Way, the Great Function, and the Great Knowledge.

It is called "Victorious" because its Way is victorious, its Function is victorious, and its Knowledge is victorious. It is called "Abundant" because its Way is abundant, its Function is abundant, and its Knowledge is abundant.

The "Path" (mārga) is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*); it surpasses the non-Buddhist practitioners of all-knowledge (*sarvajña*). The "Activity" (*prayoga*) is the shared foundation of mindfulness (*sādhāraṇasmṛtyupasthāna*);

it excels the non-Buddhist practitioners of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). The "Knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the foundation of mindfulness of objects (*ālambanasmṛtyupasthāna*); it far exceeds the non-Buddhist practitioners of the four Vedas.
If explained according to the teachings (*śāsana*), "venerated by great beings" refers to the interpretation within the Tripitaka. Here, "great" means venerated by Arhats of great power.

Furthermore, "many" refers to the universal knowledge that arising and ceasing are themselves the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing; "superior" refers to surpassing the three baskets and four gates.
This is the explanation according to the Shared Teaching (*p'ung-chiao*). Moreover, "great" refers to being revered by Arhats of great power who have realized the nature of dharmas;

"many" refers to knowing all the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; "superior" refers to surpassing those of the Two Vehicles. This is the explanation according to the Distinct Teaching (*pieh-chiao*).
Furthermore, "great" means that which is revered by all the great bodhisattvas. "Many" means that which knows the immeasurable dharma-realm in its entirety.

"Victorious" means surpassing all other bodhisattvas. This is the interpretation according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). It is precisely because, although his manifest traces are those of a śrāvaka, [he is in truth a bodhisattva].

The mind is identical to that of a bodhisattva. Upon hearing the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, one practices according to the depth of one's capacity; from the outset, there is no fixed position.

For those who practice through contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*), the contemplation of emptiness (*kong-guan*) is considered "great," the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*) is considered "many," and the contemplation of the middle way (*zhong-guan*) is considered "supreme.

Furthermore, proceeding directly from the contemplation of the middle way, the nature of the mind is vast and expansive like empty space; therefore, it is called "great. By simultaneously negating the two extremes, one enters into quiescent extinction.
"Ocean": thus it is called "Victorious. It simultaneously illuminates the two truths and possesses great capacity for inclusion. Because one mind contains all minds, it is called "many.
Regarding "bhikṣu," Master Zào says: in the Qin language, it means "pure livelihood through begging. One who destroys afflictions and is able to maintain the precepts is [a bhikṣu]. Fearful...
"Māra" and so forth is a single term in India that encompasses these four meanings. Since there was no corresponding term in the Qin language to translate it, the original name was retained.
Master Kumārajīva said: "At the beginning, one leaves the home of wife and children; one should support oneself by begging for alms to maintain a pure livelihood.
At the end, one leaves the home of the triple world; one must destroy afflictions and maintain the precepts to guard oneself. Possessing these two meanings, the celestial Māras are terrified."
Regarding his departure from the household life, the *Śāstra* states: "Frightening Māra," "Destroying Evil," and "Beggars. Māra delights in birth and death;

once [the practitioner] has left the household life and further converted others so that they all transcend the three realms, they act contrary to Māra’s intent. Māra attempts to restrain them by force, yet he instead becomes bound by the five fetters, remaining nothing but sorrowful and terrified.
For this reason, he is called "Frightening Māra. Those who have left the household life must necessarily destroy [the impurities of] body and speech.

There are seven evils; therefore, it is called "destroying evil. Now, for those living at home, there are three lawful means of livelihood: first, agriculture; second, commerce; and third, service. These are used to sustain one's body and life.
For those who have left the household life, the Buddha did not permit these; rather, they must sustain themselves solely by begging for alms.

When the body is at peace, the Way endures; thus they bring benefit and merit to their donors. These three principles support one another, which is precisely the meaning of a *bhikṣu*. As the Great Master said above:
What has been explained above is entirely the purport of the Tripitaka Teaching. If one seeks the Truth by traversing through conditions, this is called "the mendicant" (bhikṣu);

if one destroys the delusions regarding the principle that obstructs [realization], this is called "destroying evil. Practicing in this manner and fearing the four māras constitutes the meaning of the Shared (Sādhāraṇa) Teaching. If one seeks the Principle by traversing through the three truths, this is called "the mendicant";
if one eliminates the pervasive and specific delusions, this is called "destroying evil. Fearing the eight māras and ten māras constitutes the meaning of the Distinct (Pratyekabuddha) Teaching.

If one seeks the flavor of the true mark within birth and death itself, one is called a "beggar for the Dharma" (bhikṣu). To realize that afflictions are identical to bodhi is called "destroying evil.
That the realm of Māra is identical to the realm of the Buddha is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

As for "explanatory contemplation" (*guan-jie*): to contemplate that the single thought-moment of the mind is as pure as empty space, unbroken by the shackles of the two extremes, with equal and great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) that is non-abiding and non-attached—this is called "leaving home.
To sustain the life-force of the Dharma-body through the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) is called being a "beggar" (*bhikṣu*).
To contemplate that the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vāsabhūmi*) are themselves bodhi—this is called "breaking [through]."
Evil. All extremes and inversions are none other than the Middle Way; this is precisely what terrifies Māra. As for the term "assembly" (*saṃgha*):
in India it is called *saṃgha*, which here is translated as "harmonious assembly. A single person is not called an assembly; from four people upwards, one is called an assembly.
There is harmony in affairs, meaning there is no separate group; there is harmony in the Dharma, meaning there is no separate principle. The Buddha always...

He was accompanied by a certain number of people. In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, he is accompanied by eighteen thousand people; in other sūtras, it is frequently stated that he is accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty people;
whereas this present sūtra states that he is accompanied by eight thousand people. The *Śāstra* (Treatise) elucidates four types of saṃgha.
Those who do not rely on pure precepts are called monks who break the precepts; those who do not understand the laws and regulations are called foolish monks;
