He skillfully knows the destinations to which sentient beings go and come, as well as the movements of their minds.
Master Zhao said: "He thoroughly knows the coming and going within the six realms of existence, as well as the beauty and evil of the mental activities."

Deng said: "The coming and going through the six realms of existence is the fruit; the beauty or evil of one's mental conduct is the cause. To observe the cause and know the fruit, or to see the fruit and know the cause—just as it is said:
'If you wish to know the causes of your past lives, look at what you are experiencing in this life; if you wish to know the fruits of your future lives, look at what you are creating in this life.
These are words intended to encourage faith, much like the divinations of the milfoil stalks and the tortoise shell."
This is not true skillful knowledge. A bodhisattva thoroughly understands that the provisional and the real aspects of all phenomena are mutually identical, and that good and evil intersect.
Although Aṅgulimāla was an evil person, because his Buddha-nature was fully matured, he immediately attained liberation.
Although the bhikṣu Sunakṣatra was a good person, because his evil nature was fully matured, he was prophesied for hell. Only through such thorough comprehension can one be called truly skilled.

"Knowing" refers to the practitioner of contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*). They contemplate that the nature of the single thought-moment (*ekacitta*) encompasses the ten realms (*daśadhātu*), which intersect and mutually integrate.

Although an evil thought may arise, if one contemplates it with the wondrous observation (*miao-guan*), it immediately becomes the realm of Buddhahood. Although a wholesome thought may arise, if one [contemplates] it as the discrimination of sense-objects (*viṣaya-vikalpa*)...
Following this is the nature of sentient beings.
(17) The seventeen qualities adjacent to the Buddha’s merit:
proximity to the peerless, equal-free wisdom of the Buddha; the ten powers; the fearlessnesses; and the eighteen unique qualities.

Master Kumārajīva said: "The wisdom of all Buddhas has no equal; yet this [wisdom] is equal to that of the Buddha. Furthermore, regarding the dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), there is nothing to compare it with;
only the Buddha is its equal. Bodhisattvas are adjacent to it but have not yet attained it; therefore, it is called 'near'."

Deng said: The *Fahua shiqian* states that the bodhisattvas praised by Vimalakīrti are all at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), whose rank is adjacent to Sublime Enlightenment (*tathāgata-jñāna*).
Therefore, it says they are "near to the Unequaled. For the Buddha is called "the Unequaled," and because they are the most excellent among the unequaled, they are called "equal to the equal.
Equal Enlightenment is close to this; thus, by citing what it is near, it refers to the "Buddha’s Sovereign Wisdom. By means of this...

Contemplation: What has been praised above consists entirely of the virtues of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambuddha). How could one possibly compare these to the merits of the seventh stage and above, whether in their general or specific aspects?

As for contemplative understanding: one contemplates that the originally inherent Dharma-realm of the Bodhisattva and the originally inherent Dharma-realm of the Buddha are adjacent to one another. Therefore—

It is said that one approaches the peerless, unequaled sovereign wisdom of the Buddha. Furthermore, by contemplating that one's own dharma-realm is identical to the Buddha's dharma-realm, it is therefore said that one approaches the peerless, unequaled sovereign wisdom of the Buddha.
Eighteenth: Manifesting evil while remaining free from it.
He closes the gates to all evil realms (*apāya*), yet manifests his body within the five destinies (*gati*).
Master Zao said: "The Dharma-body is without birth, yet there is nothing it does not manifest. Because it is without birth, the gates to the evil realms are closed. [Because it is without birth...]
Because they are unborn, they manifest their bodies within the five realms of existence.
The Lamp says: "The gates of the evil destinies are open and unbarred for the five realms; they are barred and not opened for those of the Two Vehicles;

for Bodhisattvas, because they lack the causes for evil paths, the gates are barred, yet because they possess a heart of compassion, the gates are also opened. To 'bar' them means to sever [the causes] forever."
Regarding the opening of evil: the opening arises from the profusion of inherent evil. This inherent evil is fundamentally undefiled;
therefore, although it manifests as evil, it is not truly evil. Thus, the various Bodhisattvas constantly open and constantly close the gates of the evil realms;
they constantly close while constantly opening.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that cultivated evil is itself innate evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*); no cultivated evil can be found apart from it. This is called "closing the gates to all evil destinies.
By means of the three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, one treats cultivated evil as being of the nature of innate evil. It gives rise to the five realms of existence to manifest its body;
it is precisely because of this that it is able to manifest its body at the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).
19. Capable of curing all ailments, he acts as a Great King of Physicians.
Skilled in treating all maladies, he dispenses medicine according to the specific ailment, enabling it to be taken and practiced.
Master Zhao said: "The Dharma-medicine skillfully heals; this illustrates the Great King of Physicians."
Deng said: "Previously, skillfully understanding the characteristics of phenomena is called 'identifying the medicine'; knowing the faculties of sentient beings is called 'knowing the illness.
Once one can both identify the medicine and know the illness, one may then administer the Dharma-medicine according to the illness, causing them to take it and practice it.
As the *Miaozong* says: 'The causes and conditions of all phenomena must be investigated from beginning to end; [one must address] the heavy layers of views and afflictions.'"
In number, they are like dust motes or grains of sand. With a heart of great compassion, one observes them all and studies them all; this is called "knowing the illness.

Regarding all dharmas and all gateways, one breaks through their intrinsic nature and their marks, applying each specific remedy with complete mastery; this is called "recognizing the medicine. According to the depth or shallowness of the afflictions, one knows whether the faculties are raw or mature.
Through supernormal powers one causes wonder and awe, and through wisdom and eloquence one proclaims the teaching, ensuring that the four *siddhāntas* are appropriate to the occasion.
"Each is made to obtain benefit. Thus one administers the medicine, only then being willing to take it and practice it.

Regarding "contemplative understanding," the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) states: "When practicing the entry from the conventional into emptiness, one first contemplates the dharma of the true cause and conditions.
This dharma—whether internal or external, intimate or distant—is distinct; one must diligently and joyfully cultivate it without weariness. This is..."

The *loka-siddhānta* (worldly consensus) initiates the initial contemplation. If one wishes to contemplate the conventional (*prajñapti*) in order to enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one must recognize what is appropriate for the individual (*pudgala*).
If it is suitable to cultivate insight (*vipaśyanā*), one should initiate it with the three factors of enlightenment: investigation (*dharmapravicaya*), vigor (*vīrya*), and joy (*prīti*).

If it is suitable to cultivate tranquility (*śamatha*), one should initiate it with the three factors of enlightenment: equanimity (*upekṣā*), relinquishment (*tyāga*), and concentration (*samādhi*). Mindfulness accompanies both; this is what is meant by "according to suitability."
The wholesome mind then arises. If there is the affliction of mental sinking or floating, one must employ the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial method).
When the mind sinks, it is treated by mindfulness, discernment, exertion, and joy. When the mind floats, it is treated by equanimity, relinquishment, and concentration.

If one skillfully employs these for others, their roots of goodness will become thick; if one skillfully employs them as a remedy, their afflictions will become thin. Regarding the seven factors of enlightenment...

Within this, by relying on any one awakening, one suddenly feels as if [the world] has vanished. By cultivating and training according to these factors of awakening, one can give rise to true illumination and perceive the primary truth (*paramārtha*).
This constitutes employing the four *siddhāntas* to initiate the contemplation that proceeds from the conventional to the empty, thereby accomplishing all-knowledge and giving rise to the wisdom-eye.
If, however, one proceeds from the empty to the conventional contemplation, one skillfully employs the four *siddhāntas* to attain the Way.

The Dharma-eye of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) is also like this. If one cultivates the contemplation of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way and skillfully employs the four *siddhāntas*, the attainment of the Buddha-eye of all-encompassing wisdom is likewise so.
If one contemplates with the threefold contemplation in a single mind, skillful application is also like this.
This is called contemplating the mind as the Great King of Physicians, who skillfully cures all ailments, providing medicine according to the disease, and causing [the patient to be healed].
One attains the practice of wearing [the robes].
○ Third, the general conclusion on the two virtues, in three parts. First, praising the virtue of self-benefit, in two parts. First, the adornment of the primary retribution:
"All immeasurable merits are fully accomplished."
Master Zhao said: "There is no virtue that is not complete.
Daoping said: "The thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth—these are the adornments of this body.
Although he is a bodhisattva, he also possesses the three bodies; these present adornments [belong to the nirmāṇakāya]."
This praises the *saṃbhogakāya*. It is the ultimate state of all Buddhas, which Bodhisattvas attain in part. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"Profoundly penetrating the nature of both sin and merit, he shines universally throughout the ten directions. His subtle and wondrous *dharmakāya* is endowed with the thirty-two marks and adorned with the eighty secondary characteristics.
He is venerated by devas and humans, and revered by dragons and spirits. He is able to...
Adornment is the *saṃbhogakāya*. That which adorns the body is the *dharmakāya*; that which is venerated and looked up to by devas and humans is the *nirmāṇakāya*.

Regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guanjie*): by means of the wondrous contemplation of the one mind, one illuminates the three truths within the single realm. That which is capable of illuminating is the *saṃbhogakāya*; that which is illuminated is the *dharmakāya*.
When the realm and contemplation are in perfect accord, that which can give rise to adaptive application is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
II. Adornment of the Secondary Environment (Upādāya-saṃbhoga).
All immeasurable Buddha-lands are adorned and purified.
Master Zao said: "Sentient beings are immeasurable, and their preferences differ; therefore, immeasurable pure lands are cultivated to respond to them."
This is what he delights in.
The Lamp said: "In all Buddha-lands, there are two meanings: horizontal and vertical.

Speaking horizontally, there are various distinctions among the co-residence of ordinary beings and sages, as is briefly the case with the Land of Ultimate Bliss in the West and the Land of Medicine Master in the East."
As for the land: there are ordinary beings and sages dwelling together within it; this refers to a pure land adorned with various kinds of splendors.
Described vertically, there are four distinct types: first, the Pure Land of Common Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages, which is the abode of those who suppress or sever delusions;
second, the Pure Land of Residual Existence through Skillful Means, which is for those who have already severed the two views of the Two Teachings (the Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha vehicles).

Regarding the abodes of those who have attained the fruit: first, the lands where those on the causal stages of the two vehicles reside; second, the Pure Lands adorned by retribution for the three truths, which are the abodes of Bodhisattvas of the Separate and Perfect Teachings who have destroyed the delusions of ignorance;
third, the Land of Constant Quiescent Light, which is the abode of those who have attained the ultimate fruit of the Perfect Teaching.
Now, since the immeasurable Buddha-lands are adorned and pure, and these are already assigned to the ultimate fruit, the aforementioned three kinds of Pure Lands— [are assigned accordingly].
For this reason, the Bodhisattva completely adorns and purifies them all.

As for the contemplative interpretation: one contemplates that within a single thought-moment of oneself, the three thousandfold world-realm is fully present; of these, one thousand lands pertain to the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution).

By subduing the three delusions through the three contemplations, one adorns and purifies the Land of Common Residence (*sahā-loka-dhātu*). By perfectly destroying view-delusions and thought-delusions through the three contemplations, one adorns and purifies the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*).
By perfectly destroying the delusions of dust-like ignorance (*rajas-avidyā*) and fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), one adorns and purifies the Land of Reward (*vipāka-bhūmi*).
When the three delusions are ultimately exhausted, one adorns and purifies the Land of Tranquil Light (*śānta-prabhāsa*).
II. Praising the Virtue of Benefiting Others, in two parts: First, the benefits obtained through seeing and hearing;
there is no one who sees or hears who does not receive benefit.
Second, that the merit is never spent in vain.
"Whatever one does is not in vain. Dīpaṃkara said:
"The mind of an ordinary person employs various delusive thoughts; thus, although there may be virtuous deeds, all that is done is empty, and therefore its merit is wasted.
The mind of a Bodhisattva dwells in the Way at every thought-moment; whatever virtuous deeds they perform, none are not [efficacious]."
Because it is real, its merit is never wasted. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* says: "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling on anything.
Because the Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind without dwelling, their merit is not in vain.

Regarding "contemplative understanding": one is able to use perfect contemplation to observe the mind. Whatever actions are undertaken, among all various affairs, there is nothing that is not the locus of the mind arising in non-abiding;
therefore, one's efforts are never in vain.
○ Third, a general conclusion praising [the merits].
Thus, all such meritorious qualities are fully perfected.
(End of Volume One) Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Volume Two.
Written by the Tiantai Mountain monk Youxi Chuan Deng. Part Four:
Listing the Names of the Assembly, Thirty-Four. First: Listing the Three Bodhisattvas who derive their names from contemplation.
Their names were Bodhisattva Equal Contemplation, Bodhisattva Unequal Contemplation, and Bodhisattva Equal-and-Unequal Contemplation.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Equal Contemplation" refers to the four immeasurables toward sentient beings; "Unequal" refers to the wisdom that discriminates among all phenomena.
"Equal and unequal" refers to these two aspects combined.

The *Deng* says: "Equal contemplation" means that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. "Unequal contemplation" means that although they possess Buddha-nature, it does not preclude the distinctions among the ten realms.
"Equal-and-unequal contemplation" means to simultaneously embrace both and simultaneously relinquish both.
Furthermore, "equality" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "inequality" refers to the provisional (*prajñapti*); and "both equality and inequality" refers to the middle (*madhyama*).
Moreover, as for emptiness: when one is empty, all are empty; there is nothing—neither provisional nor middle—that is not empty.
Thus, although the three Bodhisattvas are distinguished as three persons, they share a single essence, each possessing three functions.
The explanation through contemplation can be understood.
Next, two bodhisattvas who derive their names from mastery are listed:
Samādhi-viśeṣa-vaśavartin Bodhisattva and Dharma-viśeṣa-vaśavartin Bodhisattva.

If one explains them in their sequential order: by means of the first [of the three] meditations, one enters the unequal; by means of the subsequent equal and unequal, one enters the universally equal.
Through these three meditations, one attains the Samādhi of the Sovereign King. Furthermore, through this samādhi, one attains mastery over all phenomena.
Indeed, the Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated here as "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*). As for the "Samādhi of the Sovereign King," it refers to the second...
Fifteenth is the Samādhi of the King of the Twenty-five Existences (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava-rāja*). The Bodhisattva contemplates the twenty-five existences:

contemplating each one as equal, contemplating each one as unequal, and contemplating each one as both equal and unequal. By attaining samādhi regarding all phenomena, he is called "King" because of his sovereignty.
Thus, by contemplating the hells, he attains the Samādhi of Freedom from Defilement (*vimala-samādhi*); by contemplating animals, he attains the Samādhi of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-samādhi*).
[This is] obscure; it is fully contained within the *Dharmasaṃkhyā*. For this reason, the Bodhisattva’s name is derived from actual attainment; he is titled the Sovereign King of Samādhi.
When one contemplates these dharmas and personally attains samādhi, then within each and every dharma, there is nothing in which one does not attain sovereignty and act as king.
Therefore, he is called the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of Dharmas. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Dharma-King who destroys existence. This is indeed [the case].
The Tathāgata first destroyed their existence and subsequently attained mastery over existence; now the Bodhisattva also partially attains this.

Regarding the practitioner of contemplative understanding: they contemplate that a single moment of mind is fully endowed with the ten realms, thereby accomplishing two kinds of duality—those within the realm and those outside the realm.
The fifteen modes of existence are observed through the three types of contemplation: equal contemplation, unequal contemplation, and both equal and unequal contemplation.
Thus, that which is cultivated as evil is itself inherently evil; one attains sovereign mastery over the ten dharma realms like a king, and achieves meditative concentration and the Dharma.
These are the two great Bodhisattvas.
Third, listing the two bodhisattvas who derive their names from their characteristics:
Bodhisattva Dharmalakṣaṇa and Bodhisattva Prabhālakṣaṇa.

Regarding "Dharmalakṣaṇa," all phenomena (*dharmas*) constitute their characteristic. These phenomena possess the characteristic of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of conventionality (*saṃvṛti-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of the middle (*madhyama-lakṣaṇa*). This...

These three marks take the markless as their mark; this is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). By awakening to this true mark, one enters the stage of perfection (*pariniṣpanna*) and draws near to the Tathāgata.
Because they have reached the ultimate true mark, they are named Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-mark (*dharmalakṣaṇa-bodhisattva*). Regarding this true mark:
He gives rise to the light of wisdom regarding the provisional and the real; for this reason, he is further named Bodhisattva Guangxiang (Light-Aspect).

As for the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that a single thought-moment is fully replete with all phenomena, and that these phenomena are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.
In terms of the object of contemplation, it is the aspect of dharmas; in terms of the subject of contemplation, it is the aspect of light.
○ Fourth, listing the two bodhisattvas who receive their names from their adornments:
Bodhisattva Light-Adornment and Bodhisattva Great Adornment.
"Radiant Adornment" (Guāngyán) refers to adorning the dharma-nature of the three virtues with the radiance of the three wisdoms.
"Great Adornment" (Dàyán) refers to adorning the essential substance of the principle of the three truths with the vast, great, and supreme three wisdoms.
The explanation through contemplation can be understood.
Fifth, two bodhisattvas are listed according to their names derived from their accumulations:
Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa and Bodhisattva Prakṛtikuśala (Discriminating Accumulation).
As for "Accumulating Jewels" (Ratnakūṭa): it means to accumulate the Three Jewels within oneself to await the needs of all sentient beings.
As for "Discerning Accumulation": it means that while the Three Jewels exist within, one bestows them externally to benefit all sentient beings.

Indeed, a Bodhisattva’s own practice must necessarily include the transformation of others, and the transformation of others must necessarily include self-benefit; these are simply manifested separately.
First, regarding the virtue: they merely receive each other’s names reciprocally.

As for the interpretation through contemplation (*guanjie*): one contemplates that the three *tathāgatagarbhas* are fully endowed with all dharmas; this is called "Treasury Accumulation" (*Ratnakūṭa*).

By means of the three types of cessation-and-contemplation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*), one destroys the delusions that can obscure them, and through great eloquence (*pratibhāna*), one opens the various treasuries to bestow [their contents].
People.
○ Sixth, listing four bodhisattvas named after their hands:
Bodhisattva Jewel-Hand (Ratnapāṇi), Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal-Hand (Ratnamudrāpāṇi), Bodhisattva Constantly Raised Hand (Nityotkṣiptahasta), and Bodhisattva Constantly Lowered Hand (Nityādhaḥkṛtahasta).
Now, the hand possesses the function of lifting and pulling; thus it lifts and pulls people out of fiery pits, out of the mud, and out of traps.
Furthermore, it possesses the function of giving and receiving; thus it gives and receives clothing and food, gives and receives precious treasures, and gives and receives scriptures.
It is one and the same hand that has these two functions. So it is with the Bodhisattva.
Whether it be the Treasure Hand, the Seal Hand, the Raised Hand, or the Lowered Hand, there is nothing that does not pertain to this matter.
Therefore, sometimes he preaches the Dharma of Emptiness, in order to pull sentient beings out of the fiery pit of views and craving.

Sometimes he preaches the Dharma of Provisionality, in order to pull sentient beings out of the mire of attachment to emptiness. Sometimes he preaches the Dharma of the Perfectly Interfused Middle Way.

This is to rescue sentient beings from the pitfall of ignorance. Having already extracted them from their suffering through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one further bestows happiness upon them through great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
Thus, having extracted them from their views and attachments, one must necessarily grant them the bliss of *nirvāṇa*;
having extracted them from their clinging to emptiness, one must necessarily grant them the bliss of wondrous, unimpeded function.
Having already uprooted their ignorance, one must necessarily bestow the bliss of the secret treasury.
For those who practice through contemplative understanding: the perfect contemplation of true emptiness is the uprooting of the suffering of the three delusions;

the perfect contemplation of wondrous provisionality is the bestowing of the bliss of the three virtues; and the perfect contemplation of the Middle Way is that which uproots and bestows simultaneously, bestowing as it uproots.
This means "immediate extraction.
○ Seventh, listing three bodhisattvas who receive their names from the mind:
Bodhisattva Constant Sorrow (Sadāprarudita), Bodhisattva Joyful Faculty (Nandiyashas), and Bodhisattva King of Joy (Nandirāja).
Regarding "constant sorrow": it arises from the Bodhisattva’s mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).

Out of pity for sentient beings who endure the sufferings of the nine realms of affliction and birth-and-death, [the Bodhisattva] desires to uplift them; there is no moment when this is not present, nor has there ever been a single thought of abandoning them.
Therefore, they are called "Constant Sorrow" (*nitya-paritāpana*). As for the "Root of Joy" (*muditendriya*) or "King of Joy":

from the Bodhisattva’s great heart of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*), he loves sentient beings and, possessing the bliss of the Buddha-fruit’s wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), desires to bestow it upon them. He rejoices in their attainment of that bliss;

having long since become a root, it is deep, firm, and difficult to uproot—hence it is called the "Root of Joy. If one is constantly sorrowful or constantly joyful without attaining the Middle Way, then [it becomes]...
Regarding this view of attachment: although it involves both sorrow and joy, one maintains it with meditative concentration and rules with sovereign mastery;
therefore, it is called the "King of Joy. Now, although the names of these three individuals differ in their designations, the essence of the Bodhisattva remains the same.

The meanings must necessarily complement one another. That is to say, through the mind of compassion (*karuṇā*), one uses constant sorrow to extract [beings] from suffering and must bestow joy upon them;

through the faculty of joy (*muditā*) and the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one bestows joy and must extract their suffering. All are Perfectly Awakened beings who bestow innate bliss and extract innate suffering.
As the *Vajracchedikā* says: "I have brought all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa, yet in reality, no sentient being has attained parinirvāṇa."
One who has attained deliverance is such that, though there may be suffering, they do not suffer; though there may be joy, they do not rejoice.
Therefore, regarding this compassion, there is none that does not acknowledge them as king, and they attain mastery.

Regarding "interpretation through contemplation": one contemplates that the nature of the single thought-moment possesses the ten realms. The nine realms are suffering; with constant compassion, one desires to extract them from it.

The Buddha-realm is bliss; with constant joy, one desires to bestow it upon them. Yet, since this bliss and suffering are inherent to the nature itself, what need is there for bestowing or extracting?

Thus, in extracting there is no extraction, and in bestowing there is no bestowing. Therefore, one constantly bestows while constantly extracting, and constantly extracts while constantly bestowing—this is the threefold [contemplation] within a single mind.
Contemplation. He is called the Sovereign King.
○ Eighth, one Bodhisattva is named after his eloquence:
the Bodhisattva Melodious Voice (Ghoṣadatta).
This Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings by constantly employing the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

In accordance with the capacities of sentient beings for the four types of teaching, he preaches the teachings of sudden, gradual, partial, and perfect enlightenment. His various merits are all fully perfected;
however, because this Bodhisattva’s resolve is focused specifically on using eloquence and vocal resonance to perform the Buddha-work, he alone receives this particular name.
○ Ninth: One bodhisattva is named after a treasury (garbha).
This is the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha.
Since this name for the bodhisattva is identical to that in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, it should be explained according to that sūtra’s account of the bodhisattva’s own declaration.

This explains the origin of the name "Universal Pervasion" (Yuantong). The Sūtra says: The Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha addressed the Buddha, saying, "Under the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I attained the body of boundless extent.

At that time, I held four great precious jewels in my hands, which illuminated the Buddha-lands as numerous as motes of dust throughout the ten directions, transforming them into empty space. Furthermore, within my own mind, I manifested a great..."

The perfect mirror emits ten kinds of subtle and wondrous jewel-lights from within, flowing and permeating the ten directions to the very limits of empty space, reaching all the realms of the Sovereign Banners.
These enter into the mirror and penetrate my body; my body becomes identical to empty space, without mutual obstruction.

My body is able to skillfully enter lands as small as motes of dust, extensively performing the Buddha-work and attaining great accordance. This great supernormal power arises because I have contemplated that the four elements have no basis, that false thoughts arise and perish, and that space is non-dual and the Buddha-lands are fundamentally the same.

By illuminating this sameness, I attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). When the Buddha asked about perfect penetration, I replied that through my observation of space— *Note: The provided text ends mid-sentence; the full passage from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* continues with:* "...I entered the Samādhi of the Wondrous King of Liberation and perceived the nature of all phenomena. I then entered the Samādhi of the Universal Radiance of the Tathāgata’s Wisdom and saw that the bodies of all Buddhas are equal to empty space. I then entered the Samādhi of the Non-duality of All Dharmas and saw that the lands of all Buddhas are equal to empty space. I then entered the Samādhi of the Non-differentiation of All Dharmas and saw that the minds of all sentient beings are equal to empty space.

I then entered the Samādhi of the Non-obstruction of All Dharmas and saw that the wisdom of all Buddhas is equal to empty space. I then entered the Samādhi of the Non-difference of All Dharmas and saw that the liberation of all Buddhas is equal to empty space. Having attained these ten kinds of Samādhis, I then entered the Samādhi of the Non-arising of All Dharmas and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas."*
"Entering the samādhi of the Infinite Space, its wondrous power is perfectly luminous; this is the foremost. The preceding passage describes the essence of what has been realized.
"The body is able to skillfully enter... and the following four phrases describe the function that arises therefrom.
Such is its great essence and great function; it is not something that even those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment can approach or equal.
How could one possibly reach the sovereign wisdom of the Buddhas?

As for "contemplative understanding," it means contemplating that within the ten realms of the mind, the threefold world, the five aggregates, and the lands—including all four great elements—are fully present.
The entire body is illumination; that is, the four great precious jewels and so forth.

The ten realms within a single mind interpenetrate one another, and furthermore, within the manifestation of the Great Perfect Mirror and other such images in one's own mind, the two types of retribution—the environment and its inhabitants—are infinitely layered and inexhaustible.
This refers to the various *dhvajarāja* lands entering into the mirror and so forth; each assembly may be understood by observing them accordingly.
Ten: listing the three bodhisattvas named after jewels.
Bodhisattva Holding the Precious Torch, Bodhisattva Jewel Valor, and Bodhisattva Jewel Vision.
"Torch" refers to the ability to illuminate, thereby destroying the profound darkness of ignorance within oneself and others.

"Valor" refers to benefiting others while simultaneously benefiting oneself, possessing such diligent and courageous effort that there is no indolence. "Vision" refers to perceiving one's own Buddha-nature, and likewise...
In perceiving the nature of persons, he causes both self and others to leave suffering and attain happiness.
All are named "Treasures" because they have wondrously realized the single essence of the Triple Gem; in both the mundane and supramundane realms, there is nothing superior to this.

Regarding contemplative understanding (*guanjie*): the threefold cessation-and-contemplation within a single mind is as bright as a precious torch, capable of destroying the darkness of ignorance in both oneself and others.
It illuminates that the three delusions are themselves the three Buddha-natures, proceeding directly forward without slackening.
Through these three types of cessation-and-contemplation, one perceives that the nature of one's own mind is itself the Buddha-nature.
Eleventh, two bodhisattvas are listed who derive their names from nets:
Bodhisattva Imperial Net (Indrajāla) and Bodhisattva Luminous Net.
"Imperial Net" refers to the Indrajāla of Śakra, the Lord of Devas; this net is composed of wish-fulfilling maṇi jewels.
It is for this purpose that [this work] was composed. It manifests light shining universally, layer upon layer, infinitely. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:
"The gateway of the Buddha's teaching is also like this. Here, we clarify the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground realized and realized-by the Bodhisattvas;
the three thousand phenomena inherently possessed by their nature are each and every one illuminated, like Indra’s net, where each and every part pervades all others, layer upon layer, without end.
It is so. The Bodhisattva Mingwang (Net of Light) is likewise.
The interpretation and understanding may be known by analogy with this principle.
○ Twelfth: One Bodhisattva is listed, named after that which has no conditions (*anālambana*).
The Bodhisattva of Objectless Contemplation (*anālambana-vipaśyanā*).

Regarding objectless contemplation: it is the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), wherein one contemplates that both one’s own realm and the Buddha-realm are fully endowed with the true Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

It is free from all relative oppositions; it is neither existent nor non-existent. One thereby gives rise to the four great vows (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) of objectless compassion, and by means of this very [contemplation], one...
One cultivates the three contemplations of non-conditionality (*anālambana*) and uses them to transform and deliver sentient beings, all of whom ultimately return to non-conditionality alone.
The principles for the contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*) may be known by analogy with this meaning.
○ Thirteen: One Bodhisattva is named after wisdom. [He is] Bodhisattva Huìjī (Accumulation of Wisdom).

"Huìjī" is like Zhìjī (Accumulation of Wisdom) from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. "Jī" means accumulation. The three types of knowledge (*trividya*) and the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) are constantly accumulated and constantly...
It is an accumulation that is able to illuminate the three virtues, shatter the three delusions, and manifest the three bodies;
this is precisely because the three bodies all possess the meaning of being an accumulation.
Regarding "contemplative understanding" (guanjie): one contemplates the three truths by means of the three contemplations, thereby illuminating the three kinds of delusive fetters;
thus it is called the "Accumulation of Wisdom" (huiji). ○ Fourteenth, one bodhisattva is named according to his preeminence.

The Bodhisattva Jewel-Victorious (Ratnavijaya) surpasses all the world with the jewel of the supramundane Dharma, causing them first to obtain worldly jewels and subsequently to obtain the great jewels of the supramundane;
he is thus the Great Jewel Dharma-King.

Regarding the practitioner of contemplative understanding: the principle-realm that is contemplated is like a wish-fulfilling jewel; it is unsurpassed by anything else, yet it can surpass all that is mundane and supramundane.
To be able to contemplate in this way is to attain the Buddha-way.
Fifteenth: One Bodhisattva is named after the devas.
He is the Deva-rāja Bodhisattva.
Since the devas are already honored, he is the king among the devas; more honored than the honored. Since the devas are already sovereign, he is the sovereign among the devas.
O King, he is further sovereign. Having awakened to the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha*), the Bodhisattva has already become the Honored One among all phenomena;
now, as a son of the Dharma-King, he may be called the Honored One of the world, having attained great mastery over all phenomena.

As for the practitioner of contemplative understanding: they contemplate that the three truths are fully present within the single mind, and have already awakened to the Middle Way within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Furthermore, they are able to contemplate the sentient beings of the twenty-five realms of existence as being inherently endowed with nature, each and every one subtle and wondrous, conforming to the true nature, and realizing that there is no phenomenon of birth-and-death characterized by delusion or defilement. This may be called attaining mastery over all phenomena.
Sixteenth, one bodhisattva is named after that which is destroyed.

This is the Bodhisattva Destroyer of Māras (*Mārabhañjaka*). There are four meanings to a bodhisattva destroying Māra: there is destroying while not yet having destroyed; there is not yet having destroyed while having already destroyed; and there is destroying.

Yet it is not destroyed. Its destruction is like that of Śākyamuni’s attainment of enlightenment and his subduing of the demonic enemies; its non-destruction is as described in the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra*.

One knows that the suchness of the realm of Māra is the suchness of the realm of the Buddha. If the suchness of the realm of Māra is the suchness of the realm of the Buddha, then there is one suchness and no dual suchness.
Thus, in the realm of the Buddha there is nothing to be grasped, and in the realm of Māra there is nothing to be abandoned. This contemplation realizes that Māra is none other than the Buddha.
It is not necessarily by destroying Māra. That which is "not destroyed yet destroyed" is like the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
it is as when the Tathāgata preached this Dharma, and all the celestial Māras were bound by the five fetters. That which is "destroyed yet not destroyed" is as described in this sutra:
the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīśvara was deluded by a celestial Māra, and Vimalakīrti subdued him to beg for a heavenly maiden. For...
His teaching was to delight himself in the joy of the Dharma and to transform others through the lamp of inexhaustibility. Eventually, all were transformed;
he finally returned his daughter, allowing her to live as she pleased. This is what is meant by "destroyed yet not destroyed. He is now called the Destroyer of Māra.
This is both destroyed and not destroyed.

Regarding the "explanation through contemplation": when one contemplates that the nine dharma-realms within a single thought-moment are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, then they are destroyed.

That cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil means they are not destroyed. Since there is no cultivated evil to be discussed, it is "not destroyed yet destroyed," and "destroyed yet not destroyed."
Destruction is also included therein.
○ Seventeenth: One bodhisattva is named after lightning—namely, the Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta (Lightning-Attained).
Vajra said: "All conditioned phenomena are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows; they are like dew and like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way.
The metaphor of lightning clearly illustrates that all phenomena are unobtainable. Furthermore, he said:
"'To obtain'—this refers to a bodhisattva who has already entered into the dharma of non-attainment. Within that which cannot be obtained, I therefore 'obtain' it."
Therefore, he is named the Bodhisattva Vidyutprāpta. Vajra said: "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere.

This is it. As for the contemplative explanation (*guan-jie*): one contemplates all phenomena within a single thought-moment and investigates them through the four modes of being (*catur-bhava*). One realizes that nothing can be apprehended; although there is nothing [to be found],...
It is attained. There is the bliss of the Buddha-realm inherently present; I desire to obtain it. There is the suffering of the nine realms inherently present;
I desire to uproot it. This is what is meant by "attaining through the lightning-like observation of the mind."
○ In the eighteenth section, one bodhisattva is named after the king:
Bodhisattva Sovereign King (Vaśavartin-rāja).
The meaning and the contemplation are both explained according to the exposition of Bodhisattva Dharma-Sovereign King (Dharmavaśavartin-rāja).
19. One Bodhisattva is named according to their functional application:
the Bodhisattva Adorned with Virtuous Marks (*Guṇalakṣaṇavyūha*).

This is a Bodhisattva of the first *vihāra* (abiding) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), who has already partially realized the pure *dharmakāya*. However, this is merely the "unadorned" (*su*) *dharmakāya*; it is not yet [the fully perfected one].
Because there is adornment, one must cultivate various practices to adorn the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa* and *anuvyañjana*) so as to accomplish the reward-body (*vipākakāya*).

Once the wisdom of the reward-body accords with the Dharma, one can subsequently manifest responsive transformations. Because this bodhisattva is diligent in adorning his body through meritorious qualities, he is specifically designated by that title.
According to the adornments of the Buddha-fruit, all possess their respective causes and karmic actions. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Just as..."
The dharmas thus attained are adorned by the powers of meditative concentration and wisdom. "Power" refers to their efficacy, while "virtue" refers to their function;
this is because the merits of a bodhisattva all possess the power and function to destroy evil and give rise to goodness.
Regarding contemplative understanding: the object of contemplation is the virtue of the Dharma-body; the contemplating wisdom is the virtue of Prajñā;
the breaking of delusions through the perfection of contemplation is the virtue of Liberation; and the diligent cultivation of contemplative wisdom is the adornment of the marks of merit.
○ Twenty: One bodhisattva is named after his fearlessness in preaching the Dharma;
this refers to the Bodhisattva Siṃhanāda (Lion’s Roar).
Regarding the meaning and contemplation, both follow the description of his virtues and his fearlessness in expounding the Dharma, which is explained within the *Siṃhanāda-sūtra*.
Twenty-one: Two bodhisattvas are named after their voices.
They are Ghoṣadeva Bodhisattva and Parvata-saṃghaṭṭita-ghoṣa Bodhisattva. Regarding "Ghoṣadeva":
the sound of this bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma is like that of the Dragon King Sāgara when he is about to send down a great rain.
One must first cause the sound of thunder to vibrate throughout the great trichiliocosm, so that all sentient beings may be made aware in advance and observe strict vigilance;
only then shall the great rain descend, enabling the three types of grasses, the two types of trees, and the hundred grains and sprouts to grow and flourish.

It is the same for the Bodhisattva. When he is about to let fall the great rain of the Dharma, he must first thunder forth the sound of the Dharma, so that the capacities of the three types of grass and two types of trees, and the multitude of the hundred grains and sprouts, may each achieve their growth.

Regarding the phrase "the sound of mountains clashing": the nature of a mountain is eternally still; being still, it does not clash; not clashing, there is no sound. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Destruction..."
One’s reputation is as immovable as Mount Sumeru. The *Analects* says, "The benevolent person delights in mountains," and further states, "The benevolent person is tranquil.
It is clear that the mountain is immovable and cannot be struck. Nevertheless, there are three causes and conditions by which a mountain can be moved.
What are these three? First, at the time of the destruction of a kalpa, there is the Vairambha wind, which can strike Mount Sumeru and reduce it to something like a speck of dust.
First, when the dust settles. Second, when the Great Tree Kinnara King performs music, the waves of the great ocean surge, and the seven golden mountains of Mount Sumeru are shaken;
as they move, they inevitably strike one another, and as they strike, they produce sound.
Third, through the power of those who have attained the Way and the spiritual power of the Buddha, the earth of the trichiliocosm can be made to tremble in six ways.
Thus, Mount Sumeru also surges and submerges. It is the same with the Bodhisattva’s destruction of delusions and preaching of the Dharma:

the first metaphor illustrates the destruction of the delusions of views and thought by preaching the Dharma of the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*); the second metaphor illustrates the destruction of the delusions of "dust and sand" by preaching the Dharma of the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*);
and the third metaphor illustrates the destruction of the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*) by preaching the Dharma of the Middle Way.

Regarding the contemplative interpretation (*guanjie*): one cultivates three kinds of contemplation within a single mind to shatter the three kinds of delusion and reveal the principle of the Three Truths;

this is the "Sound of Mountains Striking One Another. Furthermore, regarding the previous "Sound of Thunder" contemplative interpretation: one contemplates that a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*) contains the ten dharma-realms (*daśadhātus*).

When delusion is shattered, the realms are revealed—this is like the sound of thunder followed by a downpour of rain, whereby the three types of grasses and two types of trees each receive their nourishment and grow.
[This is] the long version.
○ Twenty-second: two bodhisattvas are named after elephants.
They are Gandhahastin Bodhisattva and Śvetagandhahastin Bodhisattva.

The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* clarifies the metaphor of three animals crossing a river—namely, the elephant, the horse, and the hare. The hare floats upon the surface; the horse reaches the middle; and the elephant goes straight to the bottom.
This illustrates that those of the three vehicles who realize the Dharma possess varying degrees of depth. Only the Bodhisattva realizes it to its ultimate source and bottom.
Among elephants, the fragrant elephant (*gandhahastin*) is superior; if it is a white fragrant elephant, it is even more excellent.
Furthermore, this is the greatest among the bodhisattvas; thus, the white fragrant elephant is the *mahāsattva* among bodhisattvas.

As for the "contemplative understanding," the person of the Perfect Teaching contemplates the principle of the three truths, just as the fragrant elephant exhausts the source and reaches the bottom. Moreover—
To contemplate that one is all, and all is one, is to contemplate the greatest among the great. (O) Twenty-three:
Two Bodhisattvas are listed; they are named according to their courageous engagement in the two benefits [of self and others].

The Bodhisattva Constantly Diligent and the Bodhisattva Unceasing are courageous in their upward quest for the Buddha-way and their downward transformation of sentient beings; they are always diligent and tireless.
Even when they have attained the Buddha-way, they continue to practice the cause while bearing its fruit, vowing that as long as sentient beings have not attained Buddhahood, [they will not rest].
One does not grasp at *nirvāṇa*. These two great Bodhisattvas fill the inexhaustible ocean of the four great vows of non-action.

As for contemplative understanding: it is the perfect contemplation of the inherent nature; one contemplates that the Buddha-realm inherently possesses bliss that can be shared, and thus seeks the supreme [enlightenment].
This is the Buddha-way. Fundamentally, there are the sufferings of the nine realms that may be uprooted; this is the downward transformation of sentient beings.
To advance toward this goal in every thought-moment, without distraction or regression, and without end, is precisely what is meant by constant diligence without rest.
○ Twenty-fourth: One Bodhisattva is named after his birth.
The Bodhisattva Wondrous Birth (Miaosheng).
Within the six realms of existence, there is birth within birth; thus, one does not attain that which is wondrous. The followers of the Two Vehicles [do not attain it] within birth...
Even those who are born do not attain its subtlety. Only the Bodhisattva, while taking birth within the six realms of existence, is without birth;
while remaining non-arising in the Two Vehicles, they manifest arising. Thus, arising is non-arising, and non-arising is arising; birth and non-birth are both merged in obscurity.
Therefore, it is called "wondrous birth" (*miao-sheng*). Regarding the contemplative understanding:

through the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one subdues and destroys the afflictions of views and thoughts; thus, within birth there is no birth. Through the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*), one subdues and destroys the afflictions as numerous as motes of dust;

thus, within non-birth there is a blazing birth. Through the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), one subdues and destroys ignorance (*avidyā*); thus, within birth there is no [birth].
Birth. Birth without birth; birth and non-birth are both darkened in mystery.
○ Twenty-fifth: A Bodhisattva is named according to his adornment:
the Huayan (Avataṃsaka) Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva uses the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices to adorn the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya), thereby harmonizing it with the Dharma Body (dharmakāya).

Subsequently, from the root of the Dharma and Reward Bodies, they manifest responsive traces. Thus, the Avataṃsaka is the essential matter for all Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samayaksaṃbodhi).
That this Bodhisattva alone receives this title may be said to mean that he has grasped its fundamental principles.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: "The flowers of the causes of the myriad practices" refers to the contemplation of entering the conventional (prajñapti-praveśa-vipaśyanā). "Recompense wisdom" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā).
When these two contemplations are combined, they adorn the contemplation of the Middle Way; this is precisely the Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
○ Twenty-sixth: One Bodhisattva is named after Avalokiteśvara.

Regarding the name "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva," Master Tiantai’s *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Guan Shi Yin Pusa Xuanyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Chapter of the Lotus Sutra) explains the name as follows: "Avalokita" means that which is able to...

It is called "contemplation" (*guan*) because it is the act of observing. Subject and object are perfectly interfused; existence and non-existence are both fully realized. It illuminates the ultimate nature and examines both the root and its branches;

therefore, it is termed "contemplation. "World-Sound" (*Shi-yin*) refers to the objects of contemplation. These objects consist of the myriad phenomena in constant flux, separated and distinct from one another, with various beings uttering diverse cries.
Yet all alike receive liberation from suffering. Through the Bodhisattva’s vast compassion, they are universally saved at once. All...

Because they are able to bring about liberation, they are called Avalokiteśvara. This is an instance where both the object and the wisdom are raised together, and the subject and the object are designated in unison.

Regarding the interpretation of "contemplation" (*guan*), one should cite the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* in which the Bodhisattvas themselves describe their realization of perfect penetration: "First, within the faculty of hearing, I entered the stream and forgot the object.
Once that which was entered had become still, the two characteristics of movement and stillness were clearly seen not to arise. Thus, gradually increasing, my hearing..."
When what is heard is exhausted, and one does not dwell even in that exhaustion of hearing; when the perceived object is realized as empty, and emptiness-awareness reaches ultimate perfection;
when both emptiness and the object of emptification are extinguished—once birth and death have ceased, quiescent extinction manifests before one. This is Avalokiteśvara.
27. One Bodhisattva is listed by name derived from his attainment of great power:
the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-saṃcodana-sūtra*: "Wherever I set my foot, it causes the three-thousandfold world system and the palaces of Māra to tremble."
Therefore, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Regarding the interpretation of "contemplation" (guan): the three kinds of cessation (samatha) serve as his feet; planting them upon the ground of the Truths, they cause the ten dharma-realms to tremble.
All places where views and craving abide are entirely shaken and moved (from the *Wenju*).
○ Twenty-eighth: One bodhisattva is named after the Brahma-net (Brahmajāla).
The Bodhisattva Brahmajāla—“Brahma-net” being like Indra’s net (Indrājāla) in the palace of Śakra—is used as a metaphor for the dharma-gate of the intrinsically inherent nature that he has realized.
It is like the pearls in Brahma’s net: their substance is perfectly round, translucent, and mutually inclusive, unfolding in infinite layers without end.

Regarding the contemplative interpretation: one contemplates that within a single thought-moment, the nature is replete with the three thousand [dharmas]. This substance, magnitude, and virtue are inconceivable.
29. One bodhisattva is named after his precious staff: the Bodhisattva Ratnadaṇḍa.
Regarding the three uses of a staff in the world: it can support the elderly. According to ancient rites, when one grows old, the court bestows a staff upon them. (6)

"To carry a staff in one's village at age ten, and to carry a staff in the state at age seventy," is precisely this principle. It is that which allows one to bear burdens and that which enables one to exert effort.
The *Analects* states, "To grow old and not die is to be a thief"; using a staff to strike one’s own shin is an illustration of this. The same applies to the *khakkhara* (monastic staff):

it is for the sake of old age and illness, for the sake of the robes and bowl one carries, and as a symbol of shame like the "willow whip" used to discipline; thus, it may be used to support the elderly.
In the analogy of cultivation, bearing a burden may be likened to emerging into the conventional (出假), and exerting oneself may be likened to entering emptiness (入空).
The staff is called a "treasure" precisely because it refers to the supramundane Triple Gem, which is worthy of honor and preciousness.

Regarding "contemplative understanding": one takes the cultivation of the three contemplations within a single mind as a staff; by means of it, one emerges from suffering; by means of it, one assists others;
and by means of it, one brings the perfection of awakening and practice to completion—this is precisely what is meant.
○ Thirty ranks: one Bodhisattva is named from "Invincible" (Anabhibhūta).
An Invincible Bodhisattva is one whom others cannot surpass, yet who can be surpassed by others; this is the lower rank. One who can surpass those below, yet...
To be unable to be surpassed by those above is the middle rank. To be able to surpass those below while no one above can surpass oneself is the upper rank.

Now, although this Bodhisattva manifests as dwelling in the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and is thus called an "upper person" (upari-puruṣa), he has in fact realized Wondrous Enlightenment (pratyakṣa-bodhi) and is thus called an "unsurpassed person" (anuttara-puruṣa); therefore, he is named "Unsurpassable" (Anabhibhū).

Regarding the perspective of contemplative understanding: although the cultivation of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) surpasses that of ordinary beings, it cannot surpass the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).
Although the contemplation of the provisional surpasses that of the śrāvakas, it cannot surpass that of the Buddhas.

Since the Middle Way Contemplation (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*) can surpass those below while having nothing superior above it, and because "one emptiness is all emptiness" and so forth, all three contemplations may be described as having no superior.
31. One bodhisattva is named after his adornment of the land:
Adorned-Land Bodhisattva (*Bhūmyalaṃkāra*).
Regarding "adornment of the land," it is as requested below by Ratnakūṭa: "I wish to hear how one attains a pure buddha-field. Thus said the Tathāgata.
That which is revealed therein is none other than the principle of adorning the land; this can be understood from the preceding explanation. Regarding the contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*):

within the three thousand realms inherently possessed by nature (*xingju sanqian*), there are one thousand realms of land. The lands of the six classes of ordinary beings are the Land of Common Dwelling (*tongju-tu*).
The lands of the two vehicles are the Land of Expedient Means (*fangbian-tu*). The lands of the bodhisattvas are the Land of Real Reward (*shibao-tu*). The Buddha...
The land is the Land of Tranquil Light. When deluded, one is deluded along with others; covered by the three delusions, all four lands are defiled.
When awakened, one is awakened along with others; revealed by the three contemplations, all four lands are pure.
○ Among the thirty-two rows of bodhisattvas, two are named after their topknots (*uṣṇīṣa*):
the Bodhisattva Golden Topknot and the Bodhisattva Pearl Topknot.
According to the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Yingluo jing*), there are six kinds of necklaces used as adornments for bodhisattvas, namely: iron, jewels... [and so forth].
The jewel necklace adorns the Bodhisattvas of the stage of the ten faiths. The copper-jewel necklace adorns the Bodhisattvas of the stage of the ten abidings;

these belong to the nature of cultivated seeds (*śikṣā-bīja-gotra*). The silver-jewel necklace adorns the Bodhisattvas of the stage of the ten practices; these belong to the nature of innate seeds (*prakṛti-bīja-gotra*).
The gold-jewel necklace adorns the Bodhisattvas of the stage of the ten transferences; these belong to the nature of the path-seeds (*mārga-bīja-gotra*).
Lapis lazuli jewel necklaces adorn Bodhisattvas of the ten stages; this is the nature of the noble lineage (*āryagotra*).
Maṇi jewel necklaces adorn Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); this is the nature of Equal Enlightenment.

Crystal jewel necklaces adorn Buddhas at the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*prajñābuddhi*); this is the nature of Wondrous Enlightenment. Since the necklaces upon their bodies are already sixfold...
The same applies to their head ornaments. Thus, when the sutra speaks of a "golden topknot," it refers to those whose stage is the tenth stage of Dedication (*daśamī-pratipatti*).

A "jeweled topknot" refers to those whose stage is Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Although these adornments are distinct in their provisional manifestations, they are mutually embellished in reality, for all Bodhisattvas draw near to the sovereign wisdom of the Buddha, who is equal to the unequaled.
Section 33: One Bodhisattva is named after his compassion—Maitreya Bodhisattva.
"Maitreya" translates as "The Compassionate One" (Cishi). This is because this Bodhisattva constantly covers all sentient beings with the three types of compassion.
The meaning of "compassion" (*maitrī*) will be explained in detail below. Regarding the contemplative understanding:

compassion directed toward phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*) corresponds to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); compassion directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*) corresponds to the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*); and unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) corresponds to the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*).

By means of these three contemplations, one equally contemplates the inherent presence of the ten realms within the nature; this is how the three forms of compassion universally encompass all sentient beings.
34. One Bodhisattva is named after his virtue:
the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī Dharma-Prince.
"Mañjuśrī" signifies "Wondrous Virtue," because he has long realized the subtle and wondrous three virtues (*triguṇa*). He is also called "Great Wisdom."
Because they possess great wisdom.

Regarding "contemplative understanding," this refers to contemplating the three truths within one mind, which are the subtle and wondrous three virtues (*triguṇa*). The capacity for such contemplation is precisely the three great types of wisdom.
According to the list provided in the sutra, there are forty-nine individuals in total; of these, the first forty-eight each rely upon one [truth].
Regarding the reception of titles based on virtue, one such as Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva could rival them all with a single person;
yet, if one were to summarize them by means of a single virtue, among all virtues, only three virtues would be supreme, encompassing all other qualities.
This is because all of them are collectively presided over by the Three Virtues.
Furthermore, among these forty-eight individuals, each one can individually match the multitude, and each possesses a single virtue that encompasses all virtues.
Now, the reason why Mañjuśrī alone is placed at the end yet stands as the foremost above the entire assembly, being titled "Dharma Prince," is indeed...
Apart from the Tathāgata himself, those whom he honors reside in the chamber of Vimalakīrti within the Dharma-realm of Quiescent Light (*jigguang*).
Without the three virtues (*triguṇa*), there would be no dwelling; without great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), there would be no opening.
Furthermore, during the period when guest and host engage in their discourse, only Mañjuśrī is capable of responding. Therefore, those who read this sutra should reflect upon its name.
They contemplated the meaning, and thereafter attained realization.
(5) Summary of the Total Number:
Such as these were thirty-two thousand people.

III. The Section on the Enumeration of the Miscellaneous Assembly is divided into nine parts. The *Fahua wenju* states: "What was formerly called the 'assembly of ordinary beings' includes sages herein;
what was formerly called the 'assembly of laypeople' includes those on the Path herein; and what was formerly called the 'assembly of devas' includes nāgas and ghosts herein."
All [of these] were unsuitable. Now, by summoning the diverse assembly, the intention is comprehensive. First, regarding the celestial hosts, there are three groups. First, the Brahmā kings;
furthermore, there are ten thousand Brahmā kings such as Śikhin and others, who have come from the other four continents to the place where the Buddha is to listen to the Dharma.
Master Zhao said: "Śikhin is the name of a Brahmā King; in the Qin language, it means 'topknot.
Next was Śakra, followed by twelve thousand other Śakras who also came from other four-continent worlds and sat in the assembly."
Master Kumārajīva said: "To mention those who come from the four continents is to rely upon these four continents to clarify the Brahmā heaven.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of heavens: first, the terrestrial heavens; second, the celestial heavens.
Śakra resides at the summit of Mount Sumeru, which is a terrestrial heaven. Moreover, he is the lord of the earth. To mention Śakra is to include all terrestrial heavens."
The Brahmā King encompasses all the deities of the Ākāśānantyāyatana heaven.

Furthermore, it is commonly known that Śakra attained the stage of the Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) and the Brahmā King attained the fruit of the Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), and they frequently come to listen to the Dharma; therefore, the assembly of the sūtra is described as those "known by all" (*vijñātaka*), serving as witnesses for the gathering.
Moreover, all sentient beings honor and serve the Brahmā Heaven; since those whom they revere and esteem have come, it is thereby known.
"Other people will surely arrive. Zhaor said, "In a single Buddha-field there are ten billion sets of four continents (cāturdvīpaka).
Each set of four continents has its own Śakra and Brahmā; therefore it is said that 'others' [will come]. Alternatively, they may have come from other Buddha-fields."
"Third, the remaining devas, as well as other devas of great majesty and power.
Zao says: "This refers to the devas other than those mentioned above—the Brahmā and Śakra devas."
Deng said: The *Fahua wenju* states that the Śakra mentioned in the *Āgamas* is an Anāgāmin.

The *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies that those who pose difficult questions regarding Prajñā are all named Śakradevendra. In the Separate and Complete Teachings, it is explained that Śakradevendra has attained the Śūraṅgama Samādhi;
their internal realizations differ, surpassing [the former] by two thousand twenty-four kalpas of the Bhadrakalpa.
He will become a Buddha in a future kalpa, named the World-Honored One Without Attachment (Aśoka). Furthermore, in the passage below, the Brahma King Śikhin says to Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, you have had this thought, saying that this buddha-field is impure. Why is this?
As for me, I see this land as pure, like the palace of the Lord of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven. By observing it in this way, he not only realized the initial stage of the Hīnayāna..."
The second and third fruits.

Regarding the liberation through contemplation: one contemplates that the nature of the mind in a single thought-moment possesses the celestial realms. Being "empty," it is the Śakra-devānām-indra heaven;
being "provisional," it is the other heavens; being "middle," it is the Brahmā heaven.
Next, regarding the assembly of nāgas:
Master Kumārajīva said, "There are two kinds of nāgas: first, snake-nāgas; second, space-nāgas."
Deng said: "In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is listed that there are eight dragon kings. All dragons have three afflictions:
first, hot winds and hot sands strike their bodies, burning their skin, flesh, and marrow, causing them great suffering;

second, fierce winds suddenly arise and blow away their palaces, causing them to lose their precious ornaments, garments, and the like, and their dragon bodies manifest themselves, causing them great suffering."
Third, when the nāgas are enjoying themselves, the garuḍas enter their palaces to seize and devour the newly born nāga infants, or they may eat all the nāgas.
Thus, the nāgas are filled with fear and tormented by distress.

However, only the nāgas of Lake Anavatapta at the summit of the Snowy Mountains in the West are free from these three afflictions; apart from those who dwell in Anavatapta, all other nāgas possess them.
It is difficult [to understand]. People of the world know only the dragon’s majestic power, its enjoyments, and its long life, and thus they envy it;
they do not realize that the suffering resulting from the dragon’s karmic retribution exceeds that of humans.
Furthermore, there are dragons among the heavens, dragons in the seas, and dragons in the mountains—all of whom are the dragons among dragons. Moreover, there are those who...
The "Dragon among Men. For instance, Zhao Taizu Kuangyin was born at Jiamaying Camp and was raised by a holy nun.
One day, while the child was still swaddled in his cradle, he suddenly transformed into a dragon. The maidservant, startled, let go of him in her panic, causing him to fall to the ground.
The holy nun sighed and said, "My startling my child will cause him to attain the empire late; the proof that he is a 'dragon among men' is manifest. Yet, in the interval between these events...

There are those who possess the true recompense of fruition, and there are those who manifest through expedient means; these are variously different. Furthermore, there are those who hear the Dharma while in their dragon bodies and thereby attain the Way.
As stated in the *Fahua Wenzhu*: "There are those whose original abode is the eternal, blissful, self, and pure, yet whose traces reside in the Anavatapta Lake;
there are those whose original abode is the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting Physical Bodies, yet whose traces appear with many heads."
These examples are not exhaustive. When the Buddha is called a "great dragon among men," it is because he is likened to one whose spiritual transformations are unfathomable.
When a Bodhisattva is called a "dragon-elephant" that tramples [all things], it is because he is likened to one capable of undertaking great tasks.

Regarding the perspective of contemplative understanding: one contemplates that True Suchness (tathatā) is unchanging yet capable of responding to conditions. Whether manifesting as a Buddha or as the nine grades of beings, it is the unchanging nature responding to conditions;
there is no difference from True Suchness itself. This is the great dragon of my own mind.
III. The Assembly of Spirits.
Regarding "spirits," Master Kumārajīva said: "Spirits receive a mixed retribution of both good and evil; they resemble humans and devas, yet they are not humans or devas."
Deng said: "The spirits are gathered by the six realms of existence and subsumed within the realm of ghosts. For spirits are the elders of ghosts;
since they can lead other ghosts, how could they not be subsumed within the realm of ghosts? It is only that in discussions of spirits and heavens throughout antiquity and today,"

The principles are often confused; I shall now distinguish them by means of yin and yang, as well as food and drink. Those who hide by day and manifest by night, fearing yang and delighting in yin, are ghosts.
Those who emerge at sunrise and cease at night, fearing yin and delighting in yang, are humans.

Those for whom there is no interval between yin and yang, and whose hiding and manifesting are not constant, are heavenly beings. As for those who consume solid, portioned food and habitually employ both the savory and the raw, they are [humans].

Humans are such beings. Those who inhale its vital energy and receive a mixture of raw flesh and blood are ghosts. Those who naturally enjoy food and drink yet loathe pungent odors and raw blood are heavenly beings (*tian*).
From this we know that when those in the world perform sacrifices to Heaven (*jiaotian*), they invariably use sacrificial animals.

If Heaven does not respond (*ge*), what is the purpose of using them? If Heaven does respond, one must realize it is not [the Great] Heaven that responds; it is merely the mountains, rivers, peaks, and marshes.
They are all ghosts and spirits. Thus we know that the ancient practice of using sacrificial animals to offer sacrifices to Heaven was an extreme form of profanation.
To use the three sacrificial victims to worship one’s ancestors is, in truth, to treat them as ghosts and thus profane them.
Now, these various deities who have come to this Dharma assembly have all increased their majestic spiritual power by relying on the Buddha’s might; they have grown by virtue of the Dharma causes.
All such merits are already inconceivable; how much more so for one who manifests divine traces and abides in the rank of a Bodhisattva—this is truly beyond the reach of thought.

As for the contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*): one contemplates that the single thought-moment is simultaneously birth and Buddhahood, simultaneously Buddha and birth, and simultaneously empty and provisional.
This is precisely the center. Its divine subtlety is immeasurable; the subtlety of the mind and spirit is thereby attained.
○ Fourth, the host of yakṣas. Yakṣa.
Master Shi said: "In the language of Qin, this means 'noble person,' but it also means 'light and agile. There are three kinds: first, those on the earth;
second, those in empty space; and third, the celestial yakṣas. The terrestrial yakṣas can only bestow material wealth; therefore, they cannot ascend into the air."
Because the celestial yakṣas gave him chariots and horses as offerings, he was able to fly. When the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma, the terrestrial yakṣas proclaimed it;
the celestial yakṣas heard it. The celestial yakṣas proclaimed it; the Four Heavenly Kings heard it. In this manner, it continued up to the Brahma Heaven.
Deng said: "These three yakṣas do not merely proclaim their announcements when the Buddha turns the wheel of Dharma;
they must also chant them when a person of the world first leaves the household life. There are two reasons for this:

first, as an auspicious report, because the devas of great majesty and virtue give rise to joy; second, as a portent of misfortune, because the māras of the desire realm give rise to terror. However—"
"Rather, good fortune and misfortune reside elsewhere; it is not the yakṣa itself. Thus, within this there are likewise two paths: the provisional and the real.
What is now called 'proclaiming the report' is entirely the manifestation of bodhisattvas."

Regarding the practitioner who contemplates through understanding: practicing the contemplation of the provisional corresponds to the earth yakṣas; the contemplation of emptiness corresponds to the space yakṣas; and the contemplation of the Middle Way corresponds to the celestial yakṣas.
When one contemplates by means of these three contemplations, it is equivalent in meaning to raising the cry of proclamation; the Pāpīyas of the three delusions all give rise to terror.
The gods of the Three Virtues all dwell in joy.
Fifth, the host of gandharvas. Gandharva.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The Celestial Music Deity dwells upon a mountain of jewels on the earth.
When the heavens wish to produce music, signs emerge from the body of this deity, and only then does he ascend to heaven."
Deng said: "Gandharva" is translated here as "Fragrance-Olfactory. They take fragrance as their food and are also called "Fragrance-Skandhas," for fragrance issues from their bodies.
These are the deities of worldly music belonging to the Heavenly Emperor. The *Lotus Sūtra* fully enumerates four types. Jingxi said:
Regarding worldly music: it uses the mundane to manifest the ultimate truth. The four *gandharvas* may be correlated with the four teachings as explained in the commentary.
Regarding contemplative understanding: contemplating that a single thought-moment is endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity is precisely the four *gandharva* kings.
6. The Assembly of Asuras. Regarding "Asura," Master Shi [Kumārajīva] said:

"In the Qin language, it means 'one who does not drink wine. Its origins are found in the *Zàbǎozàng jīng* (Sutra of the Miscellaneous Jewel Treasury). This constitutes one of the six realms of existence (*ṣaḍgati*). They are male."
The Ugly Woman became upright and possessed great power; she constantly fought with the devas. Dīpaṃkara said:
The *Fahua wenju* states that this [name] means "Wineless. She gathered flowers from the four continents and fermented them in the great ocean;
despite the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the flavor did not change. Because she vowed to sever anger and jealousy, she is called the Wineless Deity (*Asurā*). It is also...
Yunbuenduan (Yun: "not upright") says that Master Tianmi (Tianmi An) calls it *zhìliàng* (質諒). *Zhìliàng* means straightforward faith. This spirit is sycophantic and crooked;
its name does not correspond to its characteristics. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that there are four types of asuras: first, those born from eggs.

The first belongs to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*); the second is birth from a womb; the third belongs to the realm of humans; the fourth is birth from transformation; and the fifth belongs to the realm of animals.
Among these, the asuras also differ in terms of provisional and ultimate [reality]: provisionally, they manifest in order to transform their own kind;
ultimately, they are produced by a mixture of good and evil, and by the influence of flattery and jealousy.

Regarding contemplative understanding: one contemplates that the cultivated evil (xiū-è) is precisely the inherent evil (xìng-è). When the inherent evil is interfused, there is no longer any cultivated evil to be discussed; this is "no wine.
Furthermore, one contemplates that the cultivated evil of the heavenly realms is precisely the inherent evil; thus, one does not perceive a heavenly realm as attainable—this is "no heaven.
The entirety of the Buddha constitutes the nine [realms], which is provisional transformation; the entirety of the nine constitutes the Buddha, which is the true path.
○ Seventh, the assembly of garuḍas.
Regarding "garuḍa," Master Shi [Xuanzang] said: "The divine golden-winged bird."
Deng said: The *Fahua wenju* states that *garuḍa* means "golden-winged" (*jīnshì*) in this language; its wing-feathers are golden, and it dwells atop a great tree spanning the four continents.
The distance between its two wings is three million six hundred thousand *li*. Some say that Zhuangzi calls it the *péng*;
when the *péng* flies, all other birds follow as its wings. It is also called the phoenix (*fènghuáng*), though it is said that the current [bird] is not the true phoenix.
They tread upon living grass and eat the kernels of bamboo; they nest and suckle among paulownia trees. The golden-winged bird eats dragons—how can such a creature be of this same class?
The garuḍa possesses divine power: the male transforms into a celestial son, and the female changes into a celestial maiden.

Their transformed dwelling contains a jeweled palace, and there is food and drink of a hundred flavors; yet, as retribution for their habit of eating dragons, they are unable to consume the embryos within a womb.
The egg-born can consume two; the moisture-born can consume three; and the transformation-born can consume four. The *Sūtra on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* states:

"In one day, he consumes one dragon king and five hundred small dragons in the eastern mountain range; it is the same in the other three directions. This cycle repeats itself. His lifespan is eight thousand years.
As his life draws to a close, he loses his power and wishes to consume the dragon’s offspring; the mother dragon then devours him with a roar."
