He was not permitted to eat and immediately became enraged. He passed through Mount Vajra, across the ocean, and through the earth-wheel, but he could not pass through the wind-wheel.
The wind repelled him, and he surged back through the original opening to Mount Vajra. This occurred seven times, after which he died upon the mountain peak.
His flesh split open and fire erupted, threatening to burn the Jewel Mountain. Nanda rained down rain to extinguish it; his flesh rotted away, leaving only his heart.
It is buffeted by the wind-wheel seven times and falls upon a mountain, where it becomes a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). When a dragon obtains it, he immediately becomes a king.
As for the contemplative interpretation: one contemplates that while True Suchness (*tathatā*) is unchanging, it gives rise to the nine realms of conditioned evil through defiled conditions;

this is like the *garuḍa* (golden-winged bird) who creates karma to devour dragons. One contemplates that while True Suchness is unchanging, through pure conditions it transforms conditioned evil into its original nature.

Evil, in its essence, is interfused with the nature of the Buddha-realm’s goodness; this is like a bird dying and obtaining a wish-fulfilling jewel, thereby attaining great wealth and abundance, and ascending to the precious throne of the Dharma King.
8. The Assembly of Kiṃnaras.

Regarding the *kiṃnara*, Master Kumārajīva said: "In the language of Qin, it means 'neither human nor non-human. They have horns upon their heads; when humans see them, they wonder whether they are humans."
Is he not a non-human (amanuṣya)? For this reason, he was named accordingly; he is also a celestial musician deity (*devakinnara*). He is slightly inferior to the gandharva. The Lamp says:
The *Fahua wenju* states that he is a deity of the Dharma-pleasures of the Heavenly Lord. He dwells on the Ten Treasure Mountains and possesses extraordinary physical marks;
whenever the Buddha preaches the Dharma, he goes there to perform music, while the various devas play stringed instruments and sing, and the pañcaśikha [deities] likewise [perform].

Regarding the verses on the Dharma-gates: formerly it was said that *Dharmatāṃjani* recites the Four Noble Truths, *Pratītyasamutpādāṃjani* recites the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, *Mahāṃjani* recites the Six Perfections, and *Dhāraṇyāṃjani* recites the former three.
Now it is said that they recite the four Dharma-teachings.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": to contemplate that sounds and voices are phenomena produced through causes and conditions is to present the Dharma-gate of the Tripitaka.
To say, "I declare them to be empty," is to present the Dharma-gate of the Shared Teaching. To say, "They are also called provisional names," is to present the Dharma-gate of the Distinct Teaching.
To say, "They are also called the meaning of the Middle Way," is to present the Dharma-gate of the Perfect Teaching.
○ Ninth, the assembly of mahoragas.
All the mahoragas and their like came to the assembly.
Master Zao said: "Mahoraga means a great python. These eight classes above all possess great divine powers."
[The Buddha] has the power to transform his own body and sit to listen to the Dharma.
Deng asked: "If one asks why the eight classes of beings can transform their own bodies, what form do they take? [The Buddha] replied: "The human form.
This is because all ten realms take the human form as their basis; it is only the adornments that differ in terms of superiority or inferiority."
It is precisely because the mind is taken as the vessel for receiving the Way, while the physical form is the bowl that contains the mind.

Furthermore, the human path dwells exactly at the juncture between clarity and turbidity, and between ascent and descent; thus, those who receive the Way find it easy, and those who attain the Way are many.

Therefore, the Buddha manifests his traces within the mundane world solely within the realm of humans, and even when the eight classes of beings participate, they all manifest in human forms. This is true even for the superior devas.
Even their own bodies become hidden and do not appear; how much more so for other things! As for devas and humans, they proceed from the superior to the inferior;

those of other realms look up to the excellence [of the human realm] while concealing their own inferiority. That a person can receive the Way and its excellence is such as this—that one may participate in their kind—is something for which one ought to rejoice;
it is something for which one ought to cultivate oneself.

Regarding "interpretation through contemplation": one contemplates that the cultivated evil of the animal realm is identical to the cultivated evil of the human realm; that this cultivated evil is, in its essence, identical to the Buddha-realm.
To contemplate how what is not the Way penetrates through to the Buddha-way—this is what is meant.
IV. The Assembly of Śrāvakas Cultivating the Causes, Part Two:
The Two Groups of the Homeless—The Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs.
Master Zao said: "Ni" (尼) is a name for women. The aforementioned eight thousand bhikṣus are specifically designated as those who have attained the Way.
Deng said:

"These two groups of renunciants are not entirely without attainment of the Way; they are either those who have attained the first three fruits of the path, or those at the stages of the outer or inner ordinary beings (pṛthagjana).
Therefore, they are listed separately as a distinct category at the end."

Regarding those who practice through contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*): when they cultivate the three types of *śamatha*, their delusions are merely suppressed but not severed, as if they have not yet attained the Way.
If they cultivate the three types of *vipaśyanā*, the delusions are immediately shattered and severed, just as the previous eight thousand [beings] all attained the Way.
Second, the two assemblies of householders:
both *upāsakas* and *upāsikās* came together to the assembly hall.
Master Zhaò said: "The meaning [of these terms] is 'faithful man' (*xìnshì nán*) and 'faithful woman' (*xìnshì nǚ*)."
Deng said: "Furthermore, it is translated as *upāsaka* (lay male devotee) and *upāsikā* (lay female devotee).
This refers to laymen who, having received and maintained the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, are fit to serve as attendants (*upāsaka*) to the ordained bhikṣus;

and laywomen who, having received and maintained the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts, are fit to serve as attendants (*upāsikā*) to the ordained bhikṣuṇīs. However, there are also those who manifest through provisional means while practicing the ultimate reality."
There are two kinds of differences. First, as for the great Bodhisattvas, they transform those of their own kind through "sameness of purpose" (sābhoga); what indeed could they not accomplish?
Second, as for those who practice through contemplative understanding, they contemplate the oneness of the Two Jewels; they prevent all that is improper and cease all evil—this is the virtuous mind.
Sincerity is the man; compassion is the woman.
This concludes the initial general introduction.

Next is the specific introduction, also known as the introductory section on the occasion of the teaching. It has two parts: first, the manifestation of the occasion; second, the praise. The first part [the manifestation of the occasion] has six sections.
First, the great assembly surrounds [the Buddha]. Second, he preaches the Dharma for the assembly. Third, the Buddha manifests his supreme body. Fourth, the elder offers a parasol.
Fifth, the Buddha displays supernatural transformations. Sixth, the assembly marvels at the rarity of this event. First, the great assembly surrounds [the Buddha].
At that time, the Buddha was respectfully surrounded by an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands.
Among those gathered at the Āmra Grove were those who were constant companions and co-residents, namely the eight thousand bhikṣus;

there were also those who had assembled for the occasion, such as the members of the eight classes of beings and the sons of householders; and there were those who dwelt in between, staying there only occasionally.
Those who have newly arrived are the assembly of bodhisattvas. This great multitude makes no distinction between the holy and the ordinary, nor does it differentiate between the black and the white.
They all dwell together in this single land of manifested transformation; they all possess the same capacity for the Perfect and Sudden teaching;

they all respond to the same Sole and Extraordinary Buddha; they all hear the same Perfect and Sudden Dharma; and they all obtain the same Perfect and Sudden benefit. This is the great purport of this sutra.

Furthermore, regarding the practitioner who resolves through contemplation (*guan-jie*): they contemplate that the Buddha-realm is inherent within the single mind, residing amidst the nine realms that are also inherently present.

Each realm is mutually inclusive, forming a重重 (repeatedly layered) and inexhaustible totality; this is precisely what is meant by the Buddha being reverently surrounded by hundreds of thousands of followers.
Second, he preaches the Dharma for the assembly.
Regarding this preaching of the Dharma:
it is like when, on Vulture Peak, he was about to preach the Lotus Sutra, he first preached the *Anantārtha-sūtra*.
This serves as the introductory exhortation. For in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the infinite is clarified as being one;

thus, the infinite is clarified as opening up the one to become the infinite. Master Tiantai said: "Opening is the sequence for merging," just as in worldly arithmetic, one first multiplies and subsequently divides.
This sutra is likewise: because it is about to expound the principles of the Perfect and Sudden teaching, it first explains the Dharma.
This must have been intended as an introductory exhortation; it certainly existed in the original scripture, though the translator merely omitted it.
That such a sudden-and-perfect teaching was used to introduce a sudden-and-perfect teaching can be known without further divination.
Regarding contemplative understanding: with the threefold contemplation within a single mind, one contemplates the dharma-gate of the inherent nature.
This is precisely the Buddha preaching the wondrous Dharma for the great assembly. Third, the Buddha manifests his supreme body.

It is like Sumeru, the king of mountains, manifesting upon the great ocean; seated securely upon a lion throne adorned with various jewels, it eclipses all the assembled multitudes who have come together.
Master Zhao said: "Sumeru is the Vajra Mountain where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resides. In the language of Qin, it is called 'Wondrously High' (Miaogao)."
Situated in the midst of the great ocean, its peak rises three million three hundred and sixty thousand li above the water;
so too does the Tathāgata stand amidst the fourfold assembly, his majestic appearance transcendent and his radiance eclipsing the multitude, like a mountain of gold manifesting upon the vast ocean.

Deng said: "The Buddha has three bodies, namely the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body. As for the two bodies of Dharma and Reward, which the Buddha enjoys for his own use, they are set aside and not discussed here;
we shall discuss only the Response-body. This Response-body varies in its degree of excellence, such as the ten-thousand-foot [thousand-zhang] body in the Avatamsaka Sūtra."

The inferior response body is like that described in the Āgamas as being one *zhang* and six *chi* in height. These two types of response bodies both arise from the entirety of the Dharma-body and the Reward-body;

thus, they are the entirety of the response body functioning as the Dharma-body and Reward-body. It is like the entirety of water manifesting as waves, such that the entirety of the waves is immediately the water.

This is the state where non-duality appears as duality, and duality is non-dual. Furthermore, within these two types of response bodies, one distinguishes between the permanent and the impermanent; the inferior response body is...

The permanent [manifestation] is not manifest through the supreme response; as in the case of the *Avataṃsaka* over twenty-one days, the response is not permanent. At the Deer Park for eighty years, its response was permanent.
Therefore, that which is permanent does not appear, while that which is not permanent does appear; this is the inevitable principle of the natural order.
There is no need for verbal dispute. Furthermore, within the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*), one may behold a superior body.
There are instances where manifestation is required and instances where it is not; those such as the *Avataṃsaka* and this present sutra are cases where manifestation is required.

However, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, as seen by the Dragon Girl and the Dragon King, because their spiritual capacities (*indriya*) were perfected, even the inferior [manifestation] was sufficient.
Because he beholds the supreme, he reveals the wondrous within his speech, declaring it the "subtle and wondrous Dharmakāya.

While the Buddhas possess the forty-eight marks of purity, subtle wonder, and tranquil extinction, the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) in this present sutra belong to what must be manifested. Therefore, it says:
"It is like the King of Mountains, Sumeru, appearing upon the great ocean, seated securely upon a lion throne of various jewels, eclipsing all [other mountains]."
[The Buddha said to] the assembly: "How does this differ from the body of the King of Mount Sumeru in the *Avataṃsaka*?
It is because his body ought to be manifested; therefore, his environment (*upabhoga*) also ought to be manifested. As the subsequent text says:
'Thereupon, the Buddha pressed the earth with his toe, and immediately the trichiliocosm was adorned with hundreds of thousands of various precious jewels.'"
Just as the Buddha Ratnavyuha’s immeasurable land of jewel adornments was such that the entire great assembly marveled at its unprecedented nature,
and each saw themselves sitting upon a precious lotus flower— yet because Śāriputra possessed the faculties of a follower of the Lesser Vehicle,
he could not immediately perceive the sublime within the inferior, and thus doubted this land, taking it to be impure— so too was it with the Brahmā Śikhin, who said:
I see that the land of Śākyamuni Buddha is pure, like the palace of the sovereign deva (Īśvara). This is because their spiritual capacities are perfected;
they need not wait for a manifestation, as they are able to perceive the sublime within the inferior.

Regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guanjie*): contemplating that the mind is itself the Middle is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Contemplating that the mind is itself emptiness is the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Contemplating that the mind is itself the Provisional is the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Contemplating the Provisional as identical to the Middle manifests the Supreme Response-body. Contemplating the Provisional as identical to emptiness manifests the Inferior Response-body.
Contemplating the Provisional as simultaneously identical to both emptiness and the Middle manifests the Body of Ten Cubits and Six Feet.
4. The Four Elders Offer Canopies.
At that time, in the city of Vaiśālī, there was the son of an elder named Ratnākara, who was accompanied by five hundred sons of elders.
Carrying seven-jeweled parasols together, they came to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves at his feet, and each offered their own parasol to the Buddha in common worship.
Master Zao said: "Ratnakūṭa is also a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body; he constantly comes to the Tathāgata together with Vimalakīrti."

To propagate the Way of the Buddha, he now alone, accompanied by five hundred people, went to visit the Buddha; this was intended to provide the occasion for inquiring after his illness and to open the gateway to this scripture.
According to the practice of the noble and eminent of India, each held a parasol made of the seven precious gems as an offering to the Buddha.
V. The Five Buddhas Display Supernatural Transformations (2). First, regarding the substance of the transformed canopy:
through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, all the precious canopies were merged into a single canopy, which completely covered the trichiliocosm.

Master Kumārajīva said: "There are two purposes for manifesting such supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*). First, by manifesting immeasurable supernatural transformations, it is revealed that his wisdom must be profoundly deep.
Second, because Ratnākara offered what was most precious to him, he will surely obtain a fruit as precious as his offering;
what is accomplished in future lives will certainly be as wondrous as this. This clarifies how a small cause can produce a great result."
Regarding the four things manifested within the two canopies: first, the world is manifested.
The vast and extensive characteristics of this world are all manifested therein.
Master Zhao said: "Because it is not broad, it pervades the eight extremities; yet the land is not narrow, for it is manifested within the canopy."
Next, he manifested all the mountains:
furthermore, within this trichiliocosm, there were Mount Sumerus, Cloud Mountains, Mount Mucilinda,
Mount Mahāmucilinda, Fragrant Mountains, Jewel Mountains, Gold Mountains, Black Mountains, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains.
Regarding "mountains, the great ocean, rivers, streams, and springs," Master Kumārajīva said:
"Sumeru Mountain; in the language of Qin, it means 'Wondrous High Mountain. There are ten mountains made of precious jewels, with Sumeru situated in their midst and the other nine surrounding it.
An alternative version states: "Manifesting within the great ocean, the mountain is golden in color, as is the sea."
Just as clear water reflects and enhances one another, so too does the manifestation of the causal marks cause the golden light to appear.
Thus far, this Buddha-world has been manifested.
III. Manifesting the various palaces.
Furthermore, the sun, moon, and stars, as well as the celestial palaces, the dragon palaces, and the palaces of all the honored deities, all appeared within the precious canopy.
Fourth, the manifestation of Buddhas and their preaching of the Dharma:
moreover, the Buddhas of the ten directions and their preaching of the Dharma also appeared within the precious canopy.
Master Zhaolun said: "In order to manifest that the excellence of the Buddha-lands varies and is not uniform, he appears throughout the ten directions.
These sons of noble families have all long since resolved their minds on the Way, yet they have not yet cultivated the Pure Land.
Desiring to inspire their aspiration for the Pure Land through the sentiment of their current offerings, he manifested it within their parasols."
The group of six monks marveled at its rarity.

At that time, the entire great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural power, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. With palms joined, they paid homage to the Buddha, gazing up at his venerable countenance without averting their eyes for even a moment.
Master Shi said, "Faith and joy arise from within, and their signs manifest externally.
Daoping said, "The six preceding sections are called the 'Separate Introduction' (bie xu), also known as the 'Introductory Section on Origination' (faqi xu).
They describe the causes and conditions that give rise to this sutra. For example, prior to the main body of the Lotus Sutra, five matters serve as the origination: first,"
1. The assembly gathers; 2. Manifestation of auspicious omens; 3. Arising of doubt and reflection; 4. The posing of questions; 5. The answering of questions.
These sections cite specific instances as seals of verification; they need not be identical in every detail. Their immediate cause for arising is one in meaning.

First, the great assembly surrounds [the Buddha], signifying that the capacities of those present in this assembly who can strike the resonance are perfect. Next, he preaches the Dharma for the assembly, signifying that this assembly responds to the capacity.
The benefit derived from the preaching of the Dharma is great. First, the Three Buddhas manifest their sublime bodies;

this signifies that the response of the assembly gathering according to conditions is extraordinary. Second, the Elder presents the parasol; this signifies that the cause for generating the aspiration for enlightenment within this assembly is vast.
Third, the Buddha displays supernatural transformations; this signifies that the fruition achieved by this assembly is ultimate.
The Six Groups of Monks marveled at its rarity. This indicates that the benefit obtained by the assembly hearing the Dharma in this gathering was profound;

there is no time to discuss other matters. Only the Elder’s offering of the parasol and the Tathāgata’s supernatural transformations—these two causes and conditions—carry a far-reaching symbolic significance.
Were these not expressed in accordance with the ultimate truth of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun), they would cause...
For those who attempt to construct [a fixed interpretation], there is no path. Was it not the Elder who offered the parasol? Was his sentiment of reverent aspiration not in vain?
When the Sugata manifested supernormal powers, was it not merely an empty display to examine the capacities of sentient beings? The essential purport of this single sūtra is nearly obscured.
Is it the Tathāgata who proclaims it? Is it Ānanda who compiles it? Is it those who transmit it to this land? Regarding these matters—
It is clear that explaining the meaning of the sutras cannot be dispensed with. Now, I shall clarify this by means of two points:

first, regarding the defiled function of the jeweled canopy, it symbolizes one’s own practice (*sva-caryā*); second, regarding the pure function of the jeweled canopy, it symbolizes transforming others (*parārtha*).

Within the two points concerning one’s own practice: first, discarding the canopy to offer it to the Buddha; second, taking afflictions themselves to constitute wisdom. Regarding transforming others, there are likewise two points.
First, proceeding from cause toward fruit; second, arising from essence to function. Regarding the first, the defiled functions symbolize one’s own practice:

the five hundred elders represent sentient beings of the five destinies; the five hundred jeweled canopies represent that sentient beings of the five destinies possess the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).
As for the five hindrances: first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill-will; third, the hindrance of ignorance... [and so forth].

Namely: first, the hindrance of sensual desire; second, the hindrance of ill will; third, the hindrance of sloth and torpor; fourth, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse; and fifth, the hindrance of doubt.

Since these five hindrances are the cause of the five destinies, and the five destinies are the fruit of the five hindrances, and since these five factors are prized and esteemed by the world, they are therefore called "jewels."

Regarding the statement that there are five hundred [beings] within the five paths (*pañca-gati*): each path possesses five [qualities], resulting in twenty-five. When these are combined by way of cause and effect, they become fifty.

Furthermore, since the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of this cause and effect is interfused, and each one further possesses ten [aspects], they constitute five hundred. As for those who first abandoned the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) to make offerings to the Buddha—the five hundred elders discussed—these were all bodhisattvas by nature. Original Text: 五道而言五百者。道道具五。成二十五。約因果合論。成五十。而此因果。其體性融。一復具十。成五百葢。初棄五葢以供佛者。論五百長者。皆菩薩人。本 Translation: Regarding the statement that there are five hundred [beings] within the five paths: each path possesses five [qualities], resulting in twenty-five. When these are combined by way of cause and effect, they become fifty. Furthermore, since the essential nature of this cause and effect is interfused, and each one further possesses ten [aspects], they constitute five hundred.
As for those who first abandoned the five hindrances to make offerings to the Buddha—the five hundred elders discussed—these were all bodhisattvas by nature.
There are no five hindrances; even if they were present, why would one necessarily abandon them? It is simply that, manifesting the path of transformation, one gathers those of a similar kind.
If one did not demonstrate their abandonment and removal, by what means could the cycle of rebirth in the five realms for all sentient beings ever cease?
Therefore, he renounced his cherished pleasures to make offerings to the Buddha. He redirected what was precious to Youyou toward that which is considered light by the field of merit (puṇyakṣetra).

Hoping that the Buddha would bestow upon him the power of great wisdom and supernormal faculties (abhijñā) to transform and convert him, so that through these very acts he might realize the ultimate principle—transforming the light into the heavy and accomplishing unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).
Therefore, the following verse says: "Now I offer this humble canopy to the World-Honored One;
within it appear my trichiliocosm, the palaces where devas, nāgas, and spirits dwell, as well as those of gandharvas and yakṣas—all that exists in the world is fully seen.
Out of compassion, the One of Ten Powers has manifested these miraculous transformations; seeing this rarity, the assembly all praises the Buddha. Now I prostrate."
The Honored One of the Three Realms. Second, as for "transforming delusions into wisdom": the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are subsumed under the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).
For five hundred elders who had long since realized the path wherein afflictions are identical to bodhi, in order to deliver sentient beings, they manifested as the sons of elders in Vaiśālī.
Possessing these five hindrances, they first awakened to the realization that afflictions are identical to bodhi.
By this, he accomplishes the Bodhisattva path. Now, from within that Bodhisattva path, he manifests the appearance of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
Only people know that the Bodhisattva has become a hindrance; they do not know that the Elder’s hindrance is in fact no hindrance, and that the hindrance is itself Bodhi.
For this reason, he uses this precious canopy to make an offering to the Buddha, hoping that the Buddha, by means of his great wisdom and supernatural powers, will—
By means of transformation and conversion, one hopes to realize supreme bodhi through these very afflictions;
thus, the following verse states [etc.]. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "All sentient beings possess the mark of bodhi;
all sentient beings are ultimately quiescent, which is the mark of nirvāṇa, and they do not undergo further extinction. It also says: "Without severing the afflictions, one enters nirvāṇa."

This is what constitutes sitting in meditative repose (*pratisaṃlayana*). Furthermore, it is said that greed, anger, delusion, the four inversions, and the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) constitute the seeds of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the two intentions for transforming others: first, as for "turning from causes toward the fruit," this refers to the Bodhisattva’s transformation of others through the cultivation of the causes of the three types of compassion.
Here, the hindrances function as a covering; thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* describes the spreading of canopies and covers. The Great Master... [text ends]
This serves to manifest compassion. Now, the Elder’s offering of the parasol is likewise; it is intended to symbolize the thirty kinds of compassion found in this sutra.
As the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" states: At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: [text continues]
"How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings? Vimalakīrti replied, "It is, for example, like a master of illusions... (and so forth).
Mañjuśrī said, "If a bodhisattva contemplates in this way, how should they practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*)?
Vimalakīrti replied, "Once a bodhisattva has made such an observation, they think to themselves: 'I shall preach such a Dharma to sentient beings.'"

This is precisely true compassion (*maitrī*). It is also said that one practices the compassion of quiescence (*śānti*) because there is nothing that arises. Generally, thirty kinds of compassion are enumerated;
though there are thirty types of compassion, they may be condensed into three. Of these, the compassion of the Middle Way without conditions (*anālambana*) consists of fourteen.

1. True Compassion (*bhūta-maitrī*) (etc.); this is compassion taking the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as its object—this is the seventh. 1. Non-feverish Compassion (*anupatāpa-maitrī*) (etc.);
this is compassion taking conventional birth (*saṃvṛti-satya-utpatti*) as its object—this is the ninth. 1. Bodhisattva Compassion (*bodhisattva-maitrī*) (etc.).

Although these are expanded into thirty when classified, they comprise only three types of compassion when condensed. Therefore, the Elder’s offering of the parasol is unified with the Buddha’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*).
To speak of its meaning, there are only three types. First, five hundred elders each offered one parasol, totaling five hundred.
This symbolizes that the object of compassion based on conditions for birth resides within the five realms of existence. Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "There are three kinds of loving-kindness (*maitrī*):
loving-kindness directed toward sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*), which does not involve the mind actively grasping at sentient beings, yet [compassion] arises naturally toward them."

Regarding the present benefit, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "I do not actually go; rather, it is through the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness that I am able to cause sentient beings to see such things.
Next, when offering a parasol to the Buddha, since the Buddha’s seat is so high, the parasol must necessarily be held aloft in the air.

It was like scattering flowers as an offering to the Buddha; however, the canopies remained suspended in the air. Since space has no basis, this symbolizes the *maitrī* (loving-kindness) that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).

Thus, the *Śāstra* says: "Regarding *dharmālambana-maitrī*, one contemplates phenomena without a [discursive] mind, yet all phenomena are naturally and universally illumined, just as the sun shines upon things without making any distinctions.
Next, through the majestic spiritual power (*anubhāva*) of the Buddha, he caused all the precious canopies to merge together.
It forms a single canopy that universally covers the trichiliocosm. Having first offered the canopy, it next rested upon the void;
now, the canopy and the void have merged into one, universally covering the world.

This precisely symbolizes the Middle Way of unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*), which both illuminates and negates simultaneously, and again both negates and illuminates simultaneously. This essence of compassion is all-pervasive, universally encompassing all.

Because it universally covers all, it is unified as one, illuminating the three thousandfold world-systems. The *Śāstra* states: "Unconditioned compassion (*apratyaya-maitrī*) does not involve the mind contemplating principles;
rather, it naturally abides within the equality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). This very state serves as the cause for turning toward the fruit;
this very state serves as the arising of function from the essence. Why is this? It is because [the practice of] the five hundred elders..."

This is its canopy, yet its position lies within the conditions for birth. That which is called "being without a mind that clings to objects" means that one spontaneously manifests benefit for all sentient beings.

If one does not turn this back toward the objectless condition of the Dharma, those who do not understand it will mostly fall into the rank of the *piṭaka* bodhisattvas, performing the six perfections while remaining entangled in attachment and false views. Now, I offer this [to you].
The Buddha scattered them into the air; thus, these conditions of birth immediately became conditions for the Dharma.
This is what is called "contemplating the Dharma without a mind," whereby all phenomena are naturally and universally illumined, like the sun shining upon objects without making any distinctions.
The Tathāgata further manifested his majestic power, causing all the precious canopies to merge into a single canopy that completely covered the trichiliocosm.
The realm (*dhātu*). That is to say, taking the two conditions of arising and phenomena as objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī-karuṇā*).

This refers to contemplating principle without a [discursive] mind, naturally abiding within the equality of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); this is the meaning of turning the cause toward the fruit.
As for "arising function from the essence," it is this jeweled canopy that unifies the three into one, serving as the [shelter] for all Buddhas.
The general essence of the fruit of realization is the essence of objectless compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*), which is the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The essence of compassion for phenomena (*dharmanimitta-maitrī*) is the virtue of wisdom (*prajñā*). The essence of compassion for sentient beings (*sattvanimitta-maitrī*) is the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*). Together they form a single canopy.

To speak precisely of its essence, it universally covers the three thousand worlds; to speak precisely of its function, it is said that the vast and long characteristics of this world are all [contained therein].
The center appears; even the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions appear within the precious canopy.
Is this not the mutual manifestation of the profound interpenetration between the environment and its inhabitants, and the reciprocal interfusion of sentient beings and Buddhas?

This very state constitutes the Great Body; this very state constitutes the Great Function. To wondrously realize the inherent nature of all things—can this not be believed without words? Why [doubt it]?
This very [compassion] constitutes its great function. Now, "canopy" (vai) takes the sense of covering;
yet the multitudes of beings within the ten realms dwell intermingled amidst the three realms, suffering from the affliction of feverish distress and longing for coolness.

They stand in eager anticipation within the blazing house on fire, no less than the three types of grass, two types of wood, and the sprouts of the hundred grains, which look toward the compassionate clouds to provide universal coverage.

The rain of Dharma falls equally upon all. If one were to divide that which is indivisible, the canopy of compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*) covers those within the five destinies (though there are six destinies within the realms;

here "five destinies" is used because asuras are subsumed within the four modes of birth). The canopy of compassion based on phenomena (*dharmālambana-karuṇā*) covers those within the two realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
The canopy of unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-karuṇā*) covers those...

These exist within the two realms of the Bodhisattva and the Buddha. Furthermore, although the sentient beings reached by these ten realms all reside within the five destinies (*pañcagati*), they actually reside mostly within the human realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, when the Buddha manifests birth, he does so constantly within the human path.
However, these three types of compassion are fundamentally one essence; though there are specialized applications for each, in reality, they are raised [as a whole].
One is precisely three; speaking of three is precisely one. To speak thus, the "Preface to the Offering" is of no small significance.
Its underlying meaning truly constitutes the warp and woof of the entire chapter.
One who explains it should grasp its main framework and extract its essential points, gathering them together here, so that those who hear this scripture may reflect upon it.

Regarding its meaning: for those who have not yet cultivated compassion, there is a path from which they may follow. Now, based on this, the chapter is divided into eight sections: first, clarifying the five hindrances regarding the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*);
second, clarifying the three bodies of the field of respect (*gaurava-kṣetra*); third, clarifying the identity of the nature and characteristics of delusion;

fourth, clarifying the mutual interpenetration of the rational essence; fifth, clarifying the three types of wisdom as the cause of compassion; sixth, clarifying the three types of compassion as the fruit of virtue; seventh, clarifying... [text ends].
The essence of compassion consists of three virtues, and its function is clarified through eight aspects of the three liberations. These eight meanings accord with the essence of the Four Great Vows.
Indeed, the Bodhisattva’s four great vows are established based on the objects of the Four Noble Truths: first, based on the object of the Truth of Suffering, one vow is established:
"I vow to deliver boundless sentient beings. Here, the five hundred sons of elders represent the sentient beings of the five realms of existence.

This refers to the realm of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*). To eliminate the fruit of suffering, there is nothing more fundamental than severing its cause. The five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are precisely the causes of suffering.

Because they function as obscurations, they also accord with the meaning of "compassion" (*maitrī*); therefore, this constitutes the first vow. Second, based on the realm of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), one makes a single vow:
"I vow to sever the countless afflictions. Now, these five hundred sons of elders understand the five hindrances and other such afflictions...
The fact that the nature of vexation is fundamentally empty is itself bodhi. Therefore, he used the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*) to scatter them into emptiness as an offering to the Buddha.

The Buddha, knowing his intention, employed his majestic spiritual power (*ṛddhibala*) to cause all those precious canopies to merge into a single canopy that universally covered the great trichiliocosm.
This was able to manifest the function of the canopy; furthermore, it accorded with the meaning of compassion (*maitrī*), and thus it was the next vow. Third, relying on the Path.

Regarding the object of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), one establishes a vow: "I vow to learn the immeasurable Dharma-gates. Regarding the object of the Truth of Cessation, one establishes a fourth vow:

"I vow to accomplish the unsurpassed Buddha-way. Herein, the compassion directed toward the conditions of rebirth and the conditions of phenomena is turned toward unconditioned (*anālambana*) compassion.
The three types of compassion at the stage of the cause are the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*); the three types of compassion as the fruition of virtue are the Truth of Cessation.

This is the truth. Furthermore, its capacity to manifest [the goal] accords with the meaning of compassion (*maitrī*). Thus, these four great vows (the *caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) constitute the initial arousal of the armor of resolve (*saṃnāha*) at the very start of the mind;
they represent the arising of function from essence. This is precisely the culmination of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) in responding to the perils of the world.
Following this principle, I shall explain them as eight [sections]. First, I clarify the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*) that are the objects of compassion (as detailed in the *Mahā-...*).

Within the twenty-five expedient means of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there is the discernment of the characteristics of the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and the methods for abandoning them. A practitioner who cultivates the Perfect Teaching must consult these when necessary.

Now, sentient beings within the five realms of existence are a class of people who lack understanding; they are immersed in the pleasures of the five hindrances. Because of them, they create karma, and because of them, they transmigrate in saṃsāra.
Unaware and unknowing, they take suffering to be pleasure. Thus, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas vow to extract them from this state. This is the correct [teaching].
This constitutes the object of compassion. Within this state, those who awaken to and weary of suffering feel sorrow for that very suffering and look upward toward bliss.
Now, there is nothing greater than the Buddha as the ultimate source of bliss; yet, to look upward and seek it, one cannot do so unless moved by sincere resonance.
This is a sign of sincere resonance; it cannot be communicated except through the giving of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).
Now, these five hundred elders, on behalf of suffering sentient beings, have offered five hundred jeweled canopies to the Buddha.

Thus, although the material wealth they have sacrificed is finite, because this material gift can communicate the Dharma, the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*) is inexhaustible. As the Sūtra says: "If one can be equal toward food... and so forth.
All dharmas are also equal. Since all dharmas are equal, they are likewise equal in regard to food. It was solely because of this wondrous response that he looked upward to reach the Buddha;
thus, by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, all the jeweled canopies were merged into a single canopy, universally covering the trichiliocosm.
Indeed, while material giving is inherently limited, the gift of Dharma is limitless.

Furthermore, their nature is fundamentally harmonious and pervasive, reaching everywhere without exception. The Tathāgata, by virtue of this nature, harmonizes, penetrates, encompasses, and pervades them;
thus, he causes all the jeweled canopies to merge into a single canopy that covers the entire great trichiliocosm.
Were it not for the fact that the essence of this nature is fundamentally wondrous, how could the Tathāgata intentionally effect such a transformation?
Indeed, the five hundred jeweled canopies are the *traces* (迹), while their nature of interpenetration is the *essence* (本). Those who are deluded forget the essence and cling to the traces;
those who have awakened take the traces as the means to reach the essence. Although essence and trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability (*acintya*).

Furthermore, the five hundred jeweled canopies are the traces, while their synthesis into a single canopy that universally covers the great trichiliocosm is the essence. Thus, it begins from the essence...
These are considered the "traces" (*ji*), and thus there are five hundred. Now, by following these traces to return to the source, they are unified into a single canopy.
Thus, although the source and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability (*acintya*). Next, to clarify the three bodies (*trikāya*) as the field of respect (*gurutīrtha*):

while the essence of the field of respect is universal, we now take the Buddha as the field of respect; this is the most supreme of all fields. For the Buddha manifests responsive transformations (*nirmāṇakāya*).
As for his traces: his physical body is identical to that of ordinary beings; though he surpasses a Wheel-Turning King, it is merely by a factor of two.
If one were to use a single canopy from a householder to cover a single body of the Tathāgata, it would already suffice. Now, we offer five hundred precious canopies.
Each then manifested a single body, which served as a single canopy. Who would say this were impossible?
The Tathāgata then caused all those precious canopies to merge into one, using this single canopy to cover his single body.

Is this not following the traces to return to the source—uniting the five hundred responsive bodies that correspond to the five realms of existence into one retributive body (*vipākakāya*)? Indeed, it is the retributive body.

Wisdom is *prajñā*. Responsive traces are liberation (*vimukti*). Now that these two practices have been unified into a single essence, it is appropriate to call this very unity the "one nature of the Dharma-body" (*dharmakāya-ekasvabhāva*).
In the past, one descended from the fundamental source to manifest traces;
now, one follows those traces to return to the source. Those who are deluded forget the source and cling to the traces; those who are awakened realize the source through the traces.
The fundamental and the manifested, though distinct, are inconceivably one. Yet, were it not for this field of compassion, one could not move the Buddha;

were it not for this field of reverence, the Buddha could not respond by appearing. When the fields of compassion and reverence are mysteriously united, the Way of resonance and response is fully revealed.
This is the reason why the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* on the Inconceivable Liberation was preached.
Regarding the identity of the nature and characteristics of the three delusions: the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) constitute the general substance of the three delusions.

When categorized vertically, these five hindrances comprise the two types of view-delusion and thought-delusion belonging to both the internal and external realms (*dhātu*). While the dull afflictions (*dauṣthulya-kleśa*) correspond to the back of the blade, the dull must necessarily coexist with the sharp;

furthermore, the single hindrance of restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) is sufficient to encompass both types of view-delusion and thought-delusion, which correspond to the sharp edge of the blade. Therefore...

These five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are alternative names for the three delusions: the delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi*), the delusion of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the delusion of the dust-sands of ignorance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
To speak of them categorically, these five hindrances constitute the great calamities of the turbidity and agitation of birth and death, both within and beyond the triple world (*traidhātuka*).

Specifically, the three hindrances of greed (*lobha*), anger (*vyāpāda*), and restlessness-with-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*) have movement as their essential nature; the two hindrances of delusion (*moha*) and sleep (*middha*) have stillness as their essential nature.
Obscurity. That which obstructs emptiness and stillness is *dṛṣṭi* (views) and *saṃjñā* (perceptions). That which hinders transformation and guidance is the dust-like afflictions (*kleśa*).
That which clouds the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is ignorance (*avidyā*). To agitate these three factors is the calamity of movement;
to obscure these three factors is the malady of obscurity. Sentient beings in the five realms are deluded by them, and thus they become their emotional attachments. Five...
The elder Śata understood this; therefore, he attained wisdom. Thus, Vimalakīrti said: "To practice what is not the Path is to penetrate the Buddha-Path.
Mañjuśrī said: "The sixty-two views constitute the seed of the Tathāgata.

This is because those who perceive the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) cannot give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is like a high plateau or dry land..."
Lotus flowers do not grow from dry land; they arise only from low-lying, damp mud. (And so forth.

It is precisely because the Elder understood these five hindrances—that delusion is transformed into wisdom—that he offered five hundred precious canopies to the Buddha, hoping that the Tathāgata would illuminate and discern them for him.
Thus, the clarity of the Three Truths is the fundamental source; as for the three delusions—
This is a trace of the dark [ignorance]. Those who are deluded cling to the trace and forget the source; those who have awakened take the trace as the very means to reach the source.
Although the source and the trace differ, they are one and the same in their inconceivability.

As for the "interfusion of the principle and the phenomena" (li-xing rong-tong) in the Four Ming [Commentaries], the Tathāgata clearly perceived this meaning and demonstrated that principle and phenomena are interfused; therefore, he caused all the precious canopies to merge into a single canopy, covering everything.
The five hundred precious canopies throughout the trichiliocosm represent that the dust motes are themselves transformational guidance;

their synthesis into a single canopy represents that view-delusion and affliction-delusion are themselves emptiness and quiescence. Their universal covering of the trichiliocosm represents that ignorance is itself the dharma-nature.
Furthermore, their pervading the entire trichiliocosm represents the essence of movement being stillness, manifesting as one.

All things are thus. The "manifestation" (biao) is the function of luminosity within obscurity. Now, the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) and the three delusions (*trividha-moha*) are the essence of the unchanging *tathatā*.
Their ability to follow along with the five destinies is the function of defiled conditions. Since the beginning, the essence does not change as it follows conditions;

at the end, it follows conditions without changing. The unchanging essence is the fundamental source (*mūla*); the five hindrances that follow conditions are the traces (*li*). For those who are deluded...
Those who forget the source cling to the traces; those who awaken realize the source through the traces. Although source and trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Furthermore, the five hundred jeweled canopies follow the traces of pure conditions; their unification into a single canopy that universally covers the great trichiliocosm is the unchanging source.
Without the source, there would be no way to manifest the traces; without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the source.

Although the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are one in their inconceivability. Yet, were it not for the five hundred elders, there would have been no means to awaken to the delusion regarding the five traces—that nature and characteristics are identical;
and were it not for the Tathāgata, there would have been no means to manifest the harmonious integration of the principle-body.
The way of mutual resonance is interwoven, and the principle of the deluded nature is one; this is the reason for the teaching of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* on the inconceivable liberation.
Regarding the statement that "the five vidyās have compassion as their cause and the three knowledges as their essence," the three types of compassion belong to the category of the fruit.

The fruit is achieved through causes, and these causes consist of the three types of wisdom. Compassion based on sentient beings takes birth as its condition; its essence belongs to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Since the obstacles as numerous as motes of dust hinder transformation and guidance, they cannot be cleared away without relying on conventional wisdom (*jñāna*). Compassion based on phenomena (*dharma*) takes the ultimate reality as its condition; its essence belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The views and afflictions obstruct emptiness and stillness; were it not for the wisdom of emptiness, they would not be revealed. Unconditioned compassion has its essence in the Middle Truth;
ignorance clouds the Dharma-nature, and were it not for the wisdom of the Middle, it would not be made manifest. Therefore, the Bodhisattva desires to reveal the three types of compassion.

One must cultivate the three types of wisdom. Therefore, one first cultivates the wisdom that enters emptiness from the conventional, thereby destroying and eliminating views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and accomplishing compassion based on phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).

Next, one cultivates the wisdom that enters the conventional from emptiness, thereby destroying and eliminating the "dust-sand" [afflictions] and accomplishing compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).

Finally, one cultivates the wisdom that enters the Middle Way from both emptiness and the conventional, thereby destroying and eliminating ignorance (*avidyā*) and accomplishing [compassion based on the non-arising of phenomena].

"Compassion without conditions. This is still explained according to the sequential and distinct [aspects]. If, however, one speaks of the three wisdoms in their perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), then "one is empty, and all are empty":
there is neither the provisional nor the middle that is not empty.

Thus, the wisdom of emptiness not only destroys the views and afflictions (*jiansi*) to manifest the compassion for dharmas and conditions, but also destroys the dust-like afflictions and ignorance (*chensha wuming*) to manifest both the compassion for sentient beings and the compassion without conditions.
Cultivate compassion. (And so forth. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said: "Just as this illness of mine is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of sentient beings are neither real nor existent.
When one contemplates in this way, if thoughts of attachment or false views arise toward sentient beings, they should be abandoned immediately.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions and yet gives rise to [compassion].

Regarding great compassion: those whose compassion is based on attachment and views will experience weariness and aversion toward birth and death. If one can be free from these, there will be no weariness;
wherever one is born, one will not be obscured by attachment and views, and one’s births will be without bondage.
One is able to preach the Dharma to untie the bonds of others. As the Buddha has said: "It is impossible for one who is themselves bound to untie the bonds of another;
it is possible for one who is themselves unbound to untie the bonds of another. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bondage.
Speaking from this perspective, if a bodhisattva wishes to accomplish the three types of compassion, they must necessarily cultivate contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).

This clearly demonstrates the destruction of fetters and attachments. It is further said: "Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to fetters. What is meant by fetters? What is meant by liberation?
To be greedily attached to the flavor of dhyāna is the fetter of a bodhisattva; to be born through skillful means is the liberation of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, there is bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means, and liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means; there is bondage through skillful means lacking wisdom, and liberation through skillful means accompanied by wisdom.
He explains this himself: "What is meant by 'bondage through wisdom lacking skillful means'?

It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity, yet fails to discipline himself within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness."
I prostrate. This is called "bondage by wisdom lacking skillful means. Now, to further explain what has been explained:
although this text is divided into four phrases, when combined they constitute only two meanings, namely, skillful means and wisdom.

It is merely because of the separation of [the acts of] adorning Buddha-lands and maturing sentient beings from the planting of the roots of all virtues that there are four; this is the first meaning.
To be bound is to be bound in both ways. For if one adorns Buddha-lands and brings sentient beings to maturity through craving and views, one is bound to existence (*bhava*).
If one seeks self-discipline within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one is bound to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Next, regarding the meaning of "understanding," it means understanding both together: namely, not adorning the Buddha-lands with craving or views is to understand existence (*bhava*).
To discipline oneself through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness without weariness is to understand emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The same applies to the subsequent meanings. Thus, wisdom is the knowledge of emptiness that takes phenomena as its object through compassion; skillful means is...
The arising of wisdom based on the conventional is the compassion with conditions (*sopāya-karuṇā*).

To be without attachment to both the empty and the conventional, such that the two wheels proceed together, is the middle-way wisdom, which is the compassion without conditions (*anupāya-karuṇā*). It continues: "If one dwells in an unconquered mind, this is the way of fools;
if one dwells in a conquered mind, this is the way of the śrāvakas. Therefore, a bodhisattva should not dwell in either."
To subdue the unsubdued mind—being free from these two extremes is the practice of a bodhisattva.

All twenty-eight kinds of bodhisattva practices clarify the dharma of departing from the two extremes in order to manifest the Middle Way; none of them are other than the contemplative wisdom of the three types of compassion.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice," the Buddha told the bodhisattvas: "There is that which is exhausted and that which is inexhaustible."
This is the Dharma-gate of liberation; you should study it. What is meant by "exhaustion"? It refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). What is meant by "non-exhaustion"?

It refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). As for a bodhisattva, they do not exhaust the conditioned, nor do they dwell in the unconditioned. What is meant by "not exhausting the conditioned"?
It means not being separated from great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), not abandoning great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and deeply generating the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).

Without neglecting or forgetting [these teachings], they teach and transform sentient beings without ever becoming weary. Regarding the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they constantly mindfully practice them in accordance with the Dharma.
They protect and uphold the True Dharma, not sparing even their own bodies or lives. (And so forth. Why is it that they do not dwell in the unconditioned?

It means that while they cultivate and study emptiness, they do not take emptiness as a realization; while they cultivate and study signlessness and wishlessness, they do not take signlessness or wishlessness as a realization.
As proof... (and so forth). Now, "not exhausting conditioned phenomena" means not departing from great kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) and not abandoning great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
To deeply resolve upon the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*) and never forget it—this is precisely to exhaust conditioned phenomena while never exhausting them;
it is to emerge into the provisional while constantly entering into emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "Not abiding in the unconditioned" means practicing and studying emptiness and signlessness (*animitta*).

It is non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). One does not take emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and non-action as a means of realization; rather, one enters into emptiness while constantly emerging into the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

Thus, there is both simultaneous negation and constant illumination, and simultaneous illumination and constant negation. This is none other than the cultivation of the contemplative wisdom of the three types of compassion.
This is precisely what the thirty-two bodhisattvas each taught as entering the gate of non-dual dharma (*advayadharmamukha*).
Non-duality (*advaya*) is the principle of the fruit realized by all Buddhas. The "gate" (*mukha*) is the objective realm of the three truths (*triratna*) as they are contemplated.
"Entry" (*praveśa*) is the contemplative wisdom of the three types of compassion.
Some enter through emptiness (*śūnyatā*), some enter through the provisional (*upāya*), some enter through the middle (*madhyama*), and some enter by using words to dispel words.
There are those who enter by means of "wordlessness" to dispel words; this is the pedagogical gate (*upāya-mukha*). It clarifies the four gates for entering the Way.
Beyond the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), each possesses a corresponding proposition of wordlessness. This is briefly as the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara said: "Arising and ceasing constitute duality.
The Dharma is fundamentally unarisen; now it is unceasing. To attain this Dharma of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is to enter.
The Dharma-gate of Non-duality takes the Middle Way as the entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality; this is precisely Middle Wisdom. The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said:
"To accept and not to accept constitute duality. If one does not accept any phenomenon, then it cannot be apprehended.
Because it cannot be apprehended, there is neither grasping nor abandoning, neither action nor practice. This is the entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality."
To enter by means of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is to enter the gate of non-duality; this is the wisdom of emptiness. The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said:
"To delight in nirvāṇa and not to delight in the world constitutes duality. If one does not delight in nirvāṇa and does not feel aversion toward the world, then there is no duality.
This is entry into the gate of non-duality. Thus, by means of the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—...

This constitutes the Dharma-gate of Non-duality; it is the wisdom in which emptiness and the provisional proceed together. Therefore, when these are gathered and returned to their source, they are nothing other than contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*);
when one turns back and directs oneself toward them, they are without exception compassionate causes. Now, these five hundred sons of elders manifest their traces within the five destinies;

as compassion belongs to the conditions of birth, and since this is a complete cultivation in which the provisional is identical with the empty and the middle, for this reason, by means of the five...

A canopy of a hundred jewels is scattered into the void as an offering to the Buddha. To scatter it into the void is to realize that the provisional nature of the conditions of birth is itself the emptiness of the conditions of phenomena.
To offer it to the Buddha is to realize the simultaneous provisional-emptiness of both the conditions of birth and the conditions of phenomena.
Thus, within the state of objectlessness (*anālambana*), one takes phenomena as they are to be the principle (*li*), turning the cause toward the fruit.

Now, the two types of compassion—emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the void (*ākāśa*)—are the fundamental basis; the five hundred instances of compassion based on sentient beings (*sattvālambana*) are the provisional manifestations.

Without the foundation of the two compassions of emptiness and the void, there would be no way to extend the provisional manifestations of the five hundred instances of compassion based on sentient beings; nor, without those provisional manifestations of compassion based on sentient beings, [could the fundamental basis be realized].
The traces of the five hundred [bodhisattvas] cannot manifest the foundation of the three types of compassion within emptiness. Those who are deluded cling to the traces and forget the foundation;
those who have attained awakening penetrate the foundation and realize it within the traces. Although the foundation and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

Sixth, regarding the three types of compassion as the merit of the fruition: the former explained the three wisdoms as the causes of compassion; here, the three types of compassion are explained as the fruition of that merit.
Indeed, the three types of compassion inherent in the fruit of enlightenment are fundamentally complete as the cause; however, they remain unmanifest because they are shrouded by the three delusions.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva first cultivates provisional compassion (*jia-ci*), which destroys the "dust-like sands" [of ignorance] so that the compassion directed toward sentient beings (*yuan-ci*) becomes manifest.

Next, he cultivates the compassion of emptiness (*kong-ci*), which destroys the afflictions of views and thought (*jian-si*) so that the compassion directed toward phenomena (*fa-yuan-ci*) becomes manifest. Next, he cultivates the compassion of the Middle Way (*zhong-ci*), which destroys... [the delusion of ignorance].

When clarity arises, the compassion that is without objective conditions (*anālambana-maitrī*) becomes manifest. These three types of compassion are named after the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Great Wisdom), yet their meanings are fully contained within the present sutra;

they differ only in how they are categorized—either combined or expanded. In the *Śāstra*, thirty types of compassion are condensed into these three; in this sutra, these three types of compassion are expanded into thirty.
Specifically, the single category of "compassion without objective conditions" is expanded into fourteen: first, the compassion of ultimate reality (*bhūta-tattva-maitrī*).

1. Compassion that observes sentient beings as they truly are. 2. Compassion of quiescence, because there is nothing produced. 3. Equal compassion, because it is equal throughout the three periods of time. 4.

Non-dual compassion, because there is no conjunction between the internal and external. 5. Indestructible compassion, because it is ultimately exhaustive. 6. Firm compassion, because the mind is indestructible. 7.
Pure compassion, because the nature of all phenomena is pure. 8. Boundless compassion.

1. The compassion like space, because it is like empty space; 2. The compassion of the Tathāgatas, because they have attained the mark of suchness; 3. The compassion of the Buddhas, because they awaken sentient beings;
4. Spontaneous compassion, because it is obtained without cause; 5. Bodhi-compassion, because it is of one equal flavor; 6.
Great compassionate love, because it guides by means of the Mahāyāna; 7. Compassion of peace and happiness, because it causes them to attain the bliss of the Buddha. [Opening]

Loving-kindness with dharmas as its object constitutes seven types: first, unfeverish loving-kindness, because it is free from afflictions; second, non-contentious loving-kindness, because nothing arises [from it];
third, arhat-like loving-kindness, because it has destroyed the thieves of the fetters; fourth, incomparable loving-kindness, because all cravings have been severed.
Fifth is the compassion that is never weary, because it is empty and selfless. Sixth is the compassion of the profound mind, because its practice is unmixed.

Seventh is the compassion that is non-deceptive, because it is not false or artificial. By expanding upon the compassion based on sentient beings, there are nine types: first is the compassion of a bodhisattva, because it brings peace to sentient beings.
1. The compassion of the gift of Dharma, because there is no withholding or regret. 2. The compassion of ethical discipline, because it transforms those who violate the precepts.

3. The compassion of patience, because it protects both self and others. 4. The compassion of diligence, because it bears the burden of sentient beings. 5. The compassion of meditative concentration, because it does not relish its flavor. 6.
The compassion of wisdom, because there is nothing for which the proper time is unknown. 7. The compassion of skillful means, because it manifests everything.
Because it is manifest, there is the ninth, the unhidden compassion (*anigūḍha-maitrī*), for the direct mind (*ṛju-citta*) is pure.
Now, by the power of his supernormal transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), the Tathāgata causes all these precious canopies to merge into a single canopy that completely covers the trichiliocosm.

The five hundred precious canopies represent the compassion based on living beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*); their merging into a single canopy represents the compassion based on phenomena (*dharmālambana-maitrī*). It completely covers the trichiliocosm.
The "Great Trichiliocosm" represents the compassion of non-conditionality (*apratihata-maitrī*).

Without the foundation of the two types of compassion—non-conditionality and conditioned by phenomena (*dharmālambana*)—it would be impossible to manifest the traces of five hundred births conditioned by sentient beings. Without the traces of those five hundred births conditioned by sentient beings, it would be impossible to reveal the foundation of non-conditional and phenomenon-conditioned compassion.
Those who are deluded forget the foundation to cling to the traces; those who are awakened reach the foundation through the traces.
Although the fundamental and the manifested differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
When merged and unified, it is not through the cause of the three wisdoms of the five hundred elders that the fruit of the threefold compassion of Śākyamuni Tathāgata can be turned toward them;
nor is it without the fruit of the threefold compassion of Śākyamuni Tathāgata that the cause of the three wisdoms of the five hundred elders can be gathered. Thus, cause and fruit intersect.
When the stimulus and the response meet, the Way is communicated; this is the reason for the teaching of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* on the inconceivable liberation.
Seventh, regarding the three virtues of the essence of compassion: the essence of unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*) is precisely the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*).

This is also symbolized by a canopy that completely covers the trichiliocosm. The essence of the *dharmālambana-maitrī* (compassion directed toward phenomena) is the virtue of *prajñā*; this is symbolized by a single unified canopy.
The essence of the *sattvālambana-maitrī* (compassion directed toward sentient beings) is the virtue of *vimukti* (liberation); this is symbolized by five hundred precious canopies.
Regarding these three virtues, there are both primary retributions (*pratyaya-vipāka*) and secondary environments (*niśraya*). With respect to the primary retribution, [it refers to] the Buddha’s...

Regarding the three bodies (*trikāya*): in terms of the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment as retribution), the Buddha’s *sukhāvati-prabhāsvara-kṣetra* (the Land of Peaceful Light and Wondrous Radiance) also encompasses both the *vipākakāya* (retribution body) and the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body).
As for the Tathāgata’s primary retribution—the three bodies—the *Commentary on the Sūtra of Contemplation of Amitāyus* states: "The Dharma-body... (and so forth); "The Reward-body... (and so forth);
"The Response-body... (and so forth). This is as seen in the "Chapter on the Vision of Akṣobhya Buddha," where at that time the World-Honored One questioned Vimalakīrti...
“Māṭhara, you wish to see the Tathāgata; by what means do you contemplate the Tathāgata? Now, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya is the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body).
Yet Vimalakīrti thoroughly understands that this emanation is itself the *dharmakāya* and the *saṃbhogakāya*. Therefore, he replied to him as follows.”
Just as one contemplates the true mark of one’s own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha. To contemplate the body is to contemplate one’s own physical body as the true-mark Dharma-body;
how could it be otherwise for the Tathāgata? Therefore it is said: "To contemplate the Buddha is likewise.
Extending this principle further, it says: "I contemplate the Tathāgata: he does not come from the past, he does not go to the future, and he does not abide in the present."

One does not contemplate form (*rūpa*), nor the suchness (*tathatā*) of form, nor the nature (*dharmatā*) of form; one does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the suchness of consciousness, nor the nature of consciousness.
Now, form is the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body); the suchness of form is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body); and the nature of form is the nature of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
Thus, this is not only a contemplation of the three bodies as equal, but also a contemplation in which the three bodies are simultaneous.

It is sent forth. Furthermore, it says that it does not arise from the four great elements and is identical to empty space; it continues until it says that it cannot be displayed through any verbal expression or conceptual discrimination.

That there is nothing which is not the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) used to clarify the dharma-body (dharmakāya) and reward-body (sambhogakāya)—and as for what is said in the middle, that it is "not on this shore, not on the other shore, and not in the middle stream" while transforming sentient beings—this is stated explicitly.
The Dharma-body and Reward-body manifest as the Response-body. Just as it is with the Buddha Akṣobhya, so it is with Śākyamuni Tathāgata and all Buddhas of the ten directions.
Yet, were it not for the essence of the Dharma-body and Reward-body, there would be no trace of the manifestation of the Response-body;
and were it not for the trace of the Response-body, there would be no way to reveal the essence of the Dharma-body and Reward-body. Those who are deluded forget this fundamental source.
By adhering to the traces, the awakened one realizes the fundamental through the traces. Although the fundamental and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Regarding the three virtues of the dependent retribution, these are the eternally quiescent and luminous Pure Land (*nitya-prabhāsvara-śuddha-kṣetra*) where all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwell.

"Eternal" (*nitya*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "luminous" (*prabhāsvara*) is Prajñā; and "quiescent" (*śānta*) is Liberation (*vimukti*). These are the three dots of the syllable *ī*, neither vertical nor horizontal. If...
To treat these as separate or to extend them horizontally and vertically would deviate from the essence of the Dharma. For example, regarding the ten-foot square room where Vimalakīrti dwelt:
explained according to its underlying meaning, it is replete with the three virtues. Thus, a single ten-foot square room symbolizes the Dharma-body and the virtue of permanence.
Thinking that Mañjuśrī and his great assembly were about to arrive, he immediately employed his supernatural powers to empty the room and remove all its contents,
thereby manifesting the virtue of the light of Prajñā, which can accommodate thirty-two thousand people as well as thirty-two thousand lion thrones,
manifesting the virtue of the tranquility of liberation. Thus, this chamber of tranquil light is like a person entering a grove of campaka trees.
One hears only the fragrance of the *campaka* flower and does not smell any other scent;
likewise, upon entering this room, one smells only the fragrance of the merits of all Buddhas and takes no pleasure in the fragrance of the *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*.

Furthermore, eight unprecedented phenomena are constantly manifested in this room, precisely because this room of ten feet square is itself the land of eternal quiescent light (*nityapraśāntaprakāśa*). Moreover, this is in accordance with what Śākyamuni manifests.
The dwelling land is clarified by this: that which was seen by Śāriputra and the great assembly as a defiled realm is the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment) land.
That which was seen by the Brahma King Śikhin, as well as that manifested when the Tathāgata pressed down his toe, is the *nirmāṇakāya* (manifestation/retribution) land.

The essential substance upon which these two lands depend, as well as the principle by which they are manifested, is the *dharmatā-niṣyanda* (constant quiescent light) land. Therefore, [it is] the Jewel...
Within the canopy, the three-thousandfold world-system and the teachings of the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear therein.
This is precisely because the environment and its inhabitants, the sentient beings and the Buddha, are non-dual, perfectly interfused, unimpeded, and inconceivable.
However, were it not for the fundamental nature of the Dharmakāya Prajñā, there would be no way to manifest the liberation of the Nirmāṇakāya.
The trace is not the trace of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of liberation; without it, there would be no way to manifest the foundation of the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā*.

Those who are deluded forget the foundation to cling to the trace; those who awaken penetrate the trace to attain the foundation. Although the foundation and the trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Eighth, regarding the three liberations as the function of compassion: the essence of the fruit of compassion resides in the three virtues (*triguṇa*). And...
The function of the essence of compassion resides in the three liberations (*vimokṣa*).

As the sutras clarify regarding inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), a single hair can contain the great ocean and a mustard seed can encompass Mount Sumeru. Such a great function is titled "inconceivable liberation";

thus, it is clear that the function of the essence of the fruit resides in liberation. However, there are three types of liberation: namely, liberation through intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-vimokṣa*). For...
The function of the Dharma-body is called "perfectly pure liberation" (*pariśuddha-vimukti*). The function of Prajñā is called "skillful means-pure liberation.
The function of Liberation is as follows: if one clarifies essence and function from the standpoint of their respective natures, then "nature-purity" (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) constitutes the essence.

The remaining two serve as its functions. Thus, the title is explained through five aspects. Taking true nature (*dharmatā*) as the essence (*svabhāva*), we now consider it in terms of the three virtues (*triguṇa*).
Since the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is the essence, both Prajñā and Vimukti are its functions. If these are symbolized by a jeweled canopy (*ratnacchatra*):

the canopy has the meaning of "sheltering," which symbolizes the liberation of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha-vimukti*); the canopy has the meaning of "removing feverish heat," which symbolizes [the liberation of] purification...

The "pure canopy" (*śuci-vitāna*) signifies the meaning of attaining cool serenity (*śītala*), representing perfect and pure liberation (*pariśuddha-vimukti*). This is its primary symbolic meaning. As for other interpretations:
the five hundred elders each offered a precious canopy; this represents the way of their spiritual resonance (*pratyaya*).

The World-Honored One accepted them and merged them into a single canopy that universally covered the great trichiliocosm; this represents the way of his responsive manifestation (*anupratyaya*). This may thus symbolize resonance.
