This should be considered inconceivable. May all these jeweled canopies merge into a single canopy that universally covers the great trichiliocosm, suspended in mid-air, neither rising nor descending;
this may symbolize the inconceivability of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). Bells are suspended on all four sides, emitting harmonious and elegant sounds;
this may symbolize the inconceivability of preaching the Dharma. They merge into a single canopy and form its sovereign; this is the original [intention].
These five hundred [disciples] serve as his retinue; this can represent the inconceivability of the *parivāra* (retinue).

That the sentient beings of the trichiliocosm receive his protection, have their feverish afflictions removed, and obtain the benefit of coolness—this can represent the inconceivability of the *anugraha* (benefit).

With these two aspects fully manifested, the Buddha’s transformation of beings is complete. Question: How does this compare to the ten kinds of "wondrousness" (*daśa-prakāra-miṭhya*) in the "trace gate" (*jia-men*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*?
"What is the same and what is different? He replied: "They are different yet the same; they are the same yet different.

They are different because that [text] elucidates the ten wonders (*daśa-prakāra-vaipulya*), whereas this elucidates the eight inconceivables (*aṣṭāv-acintyāni*); thus they are different. They are the same because, although there is a difference in the names established,"

In terms of their summarized meaning, these two sections are roughly equivalent. Herein, the third section clarifies that the nature and characteristics of delusion are identical; the fourth clarifies the interpenetration of the true nature.
These may correspond to the first "Excellence of the Object" (*viṣaya-prakarṣa*) in the *Xuánwén*. Herein, the fifth section clarifies that the cause of compassion consists of the three wisdoms;
this may correspond to the second "Excellence of Wisdom" (*jñāna-prakarṣa*) in the *Xuánwén*. Herein, the first section clarifies the five hindrances as the objects of compassion.
The second clarifies the three bodies of the field of respect (*gurutu-kṣetra*), which corresponds to the third "Excellence" (*miaoxing*) in the *Xuanyiwen*.

Herein, the fifth clarifies the three wisdoms as the cause of compassion, and the sixth clarifies the three types of compassion as the essence of the fruit; these correspond to the fourth "Excellence of the Stages" (*weimiao*).
Herein, the seventh clarifies the three virtues as the essence of compassion, which corresponds to the fifth "Excellence of the Three Dharmas" (*sanfa miaoxing*).
Within this, the eighth [section] clarifies the three functions of the essence of loving-kindness (*maitrī*).

It corresponds to the sixth, the "Excellence of Response," the seventh, the "Excellence of Supernatural Powers," the eighth, the "Excellence of Preaching the Dharma," the ninth, the "Excellence of the Retinue," and the tenth, the "Excellence of Benefiting Others" in the *Xuánwén* (Profound Text).
Regarding "the same yet not the same": that [text] clarifies the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s opening of the provisional and revealing the real;

thus it establishes ten gates to encompass the non-differentiation of the three—sentient beings, Buddhas, and the mind—and each of these fully possesses both the two subtleties of the relative and the absolute.

This present sutra, however, is a Vaipulya (Extensive) teaching that establishes the provisional for the sake of the real, rebukes the partial and disparages the small, extols the Great, and praises the Perfect. For the sake of the Dharma...
When Hua [Zhi] composed the *Nǎoyǐn* (Introduction to the Essentials), he did not merely distinguish between the formal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Exoteric and Esoteric;

he also differentiated subtly between their underlying principles. Yet, the marvelous is precisely the inconceivable, and the inconceivable is precisely the marvelous; thus, they are both different and the same.
Now, I shall first clarify that the response of resonance is inconceivable. Generally speaking, "function" is "response. Response is not...

The stimulus does not reach the response. "Stimulus" refers to the opportune moment (*nimita*). The opportune moment is not connected unless there is a response. For example, when five hundred elders each offered a precious parasol, this was the stimulus.
The Buddha, by means of his supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), caused all those precious parasols to merge into a single parasol that universally covered the great trichiliocosm;

this was the response. It was not the case that the stimulus of the five hundred precious parasols did not connect [with the response], nor was it the case that the Tathāgata’s supernormal power did not [act].

It would be inappropriate for all the jeweled canopies to merge into a single canopy; rather, it is through the mutual resonance of cause and response that the transformative Dharma of this single period is fully manifested.
If one follows the specific wording of the text, the five hundred sons of elders serve as the stimulus;
yet these five hundred elders merely act as the catalyst. Generally speaking, however, it refers to the entire assembly in the Āmra Garden.
There were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas and eight thousand bhikṣus present together with them;

these, along with the bodhisattvas from other directions who had come to receive benefit and depart, as well as the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings manifested within the precious canopy throughout the trichiliocosm, all served as responsive capacities capable of being moved.
Although there were no lack of distinctions among the ten realms therein, when one observes...
Whether sown, ripened, or shed, all are without exception taken as the dependent origination of the Buddha-realm.
If one discusses their manifestations, there are two: first, Śākyamuni; second, Vimalakīrti. For while Śākyamuni manifested supernatural powers, Vimalakīrti likewise manifested supernatural powers.
Śākyamuni preached the Dharma, and Vimalakīrti likewise preached the Dharma. Yet, at the beginning, Āmrapālī sent someone to inquire after his illness;

at the end, Vimalakīrti led the assembly back to the garden. Although during this interval the two struck one another like the rhythmic tapping of a mallet on a sounding block, and guest and host engaged in a protracted exchange, once the ultimate source was reached, it was Śākyamuni alone who served as the master and presided over the assembly.

This is indeed so. As the Profound Text (*Xuánwén*) states: "It is like a single moon that neither descends nor ascends, yet according to the length or shortness of the rivers and the dimensions of the vessels, it appears everywhere at once, without before or after.
This is the inconceivable, wondrous response to wondrous conditions. If explained in terms of differentiation, then the bodies of the ten realms respond universally, and the Dharma...
The "Universal Gate" chapter of the Lotus Sūtra opens into thirty-two kinds of response bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*).
If one should appear in the form of a Buddha, it is the present Śākyamuni Buddha; if one should appear in the form of a Bodhisattva, it is the present Mañjuśrī and other great Bodhisattvas;
if one should appear in the form of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, it is the present Vimalakīrti and other venerable ones.
This is it. Those who should appear in the forms of the eight classes of beings, such as devas and nāgas, are the Brahmā king Śikhin with his topknot and the celestial maidens in this hall.
Those who should appear in the form of a celestial Māra are, as the sutra describes, those who act as Māra kings throughout the immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions;
most of these are bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation.
This is [the case of] the Bodhisattva who, through the power of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), teaches and transforms sentient beings by manifesting as the King of Māras.
When it is appropriate to appear in the form of a Brahmin or others, it is as described in the sutra: there may be someone who begs for hands, feet, ears, or nose.
Such beggars are, for the most part, Bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*) who, through the power of skillful means, go forth [in such forms].
Test this: it is that which causes one to be firm and steadfast. One should manifest in the bodies of elders, householders, and the like;
thus, the present Vimalakīrti and his five hundred elder sons are such manifestations. Such appearances are not limited to these alone.

However, without the fundamental basis of the Dharma-body and Reward-body of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there would be no way to manifest the traces of the various capacities of beings across the five paths of rebirth;

and without the traces of the various capacities of beings across the five paths of rebirth, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental basis of the Dharma-body and Reward-body of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The deluded forget their origin and cling to the traces; the awakened take the traces as the means to reach the origin. Although the origin and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability.

Furthermore, were it not for the fundamental dharmakāya and saṃbhogakāya of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, there would be no way to manifest the traces of the response-bodies (nirmāṇakāya) throughout the ten realms.
And were it not for the traces of the response-bodies throughout the ten realms, there would be no way to reveal the dharmakāya and saṃbhogakāya of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
This is the foundation. Those who are deluded forget the foundation to cling to the traces; those who awaken reach the foundation through the traces.

Although the foundation and the traces differ, they are one in their inconceivability. Second, regarding the clarification of the inconceivability of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), the *Xuánwén* states:

The preceding section has distinguished between mechanical responses and spiritual resonance; yet, as the subtle principle is difficult to manifest, it must rely on supernatural powers to startle and move the senses, appearing as auspicious signs that secretly represent the underlying truth.
The world observes that when a spider hangs from a ceiling, joyful events are about to occur, and when a magpie calls, a traveler is arriving.

If even these minor occurrences carry omens, how could great matters lack auspicious signs? Using the near to represent the distant should likewise be understood in this way. [The text continues with] the *sīng* (necklace/ornament).
The *Lüeyun* states: "The name 'spirit' (*shen*) refers to the nature of the celestial mind (*tianxin*); 'penetration' (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom (*huixing*).

'Celestial mind' means the innate, natural nature; 'nature of wisdom' means unimpeded penetration. The *Dichijing* states: "'Spirit' means difficult to fathom or know; 'penetration' means being without obstruction.

Though the words differ, their meaning is the same. Furthermore, there are six kinds: namely, the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*), knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), and [knowledge of] past lives...
Life, body, and as one wishes; untainted—these six kinds are still merely general summaries.
If we speak in terms of the distinctions between the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), then there is again the case of one being immeasurable and the immeasurable being one;

the large appearing within the small, the small appearing within the large, the primary appearing within the dependent, and the dependent appearing within the primary, and so forth. This is like the five hundred sons of elders who made their offering.
Five hundred precious canopies are immeasurable; they combine to form a single canopy. This is the first [point]:
causing all the precious canopies to merge into one canopy, taking the immeasurable as one. Although they merge into a single canopy, the number five hundred is not destroyed;
thus, one becomes the immeasurable. Each of the five hundred precious canopies possesses its own manifest measure (pratyakṣa); though small, they universally cover the great.

A thousand [parasols] are vast; they combine to form a single canopy, which is the manifestation of the great within the small. Although it is a single canopy, it does not obstruct the five hundred distinctions;
this is the manifestation of the small within the great. The jeweled canopy is the *parinirmita* (dependent retribution);

the manifestation of the various Tathāgatas preaching the Dharma is the *sambhoga* (primary retribution). The Buddhas preaching the Dharma appear within the canopy; this is the manifestation of the primary within the dependent.
The Buddha’s body is pure; it is that which manifests as the support within the manifested body. This constitutes the fundamental basis for the supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) throughout this sutra.
The various inconceivable liberations and supernatural powers described in the subsequent text all flow forth from this.
Now, to specifically set forth their characteristics, there are many kinds. For example, a single room of ten feet square can contain three [people].
There were twelve thousand lion thrones, each eight thousand four hundred *yojanas* in height.
Upon them sat thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, each having transformed their own bodies to be forty-two thousand *yojanas* tall.
Śāriputra said, "Householder, this is unprecedented! Such as this..."
The room was then able to accommodate this high and vast seat without obstructing anything within the city of Vaiśālī.
Furthermore, it did not crowd the villages, towns, cities, or the palaces of the devas, nāgas, rājas, ghosts, and spirits throughout Jambudvīpa and the four continents.
Vimalakīrti said, "Śāriputra, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas possess..."

Liberation is called the inconceivable. If a bodhisattva dwells in this liberation, he can place Mount Sumeru, with all its height and breadth, inside a mustard seed without it increasing or decreasing; the original appearance of the king of mountains, Sumeru, remains as it was.
Yet the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings and the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven do not perceive or know where they have entered; only those who are ready for deliverance [perceive it].
To see Mount Sumeru enter into a mustard seed— this is called the inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation—
and for a space of ten feet to accommodate a seat, both of which represent the manifestation of the great within the small; furthermore,

to cause the waters of the four great oceans to enter a single pore without disturbing the fish, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, or any other aquatic creatures, while that great ocean remains as it was in its original state.
This is the manifestation of the support within the reality; it is also the manifestation of the reality within the support.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation may seize the trichiliocosm as if it were a potter’s wheel, place it upon his right palm, and hurl it beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, yet the sentient beings therein would neither perceive nor know it.
Having gone there, he returns them once more to their original places, such that no one at all has the perception of coming or going;
yet this world remains as it was in its original state. This is mastery over going and taking.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there are sentient beings who delight in dwelling long in the world and can be liberated thereby, the Bodhisattva immediately manifests seven days as a single day.

He causes those sentient beings to perceive it as one *kalpa*. Alternatively, for those who do not wish to remain long and are ready to be liberated, the Bodhisattva shortens one *kalpa* into seven days, causing those sentient beings to perceive it as seven days.
This is what is meant by being able to extend and able to shorten time. Furthermore, Śāriputra, a Bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation can, with a single...
The magnificent adornments of all Buddha-lands are gathered into a single land and shown to sentient beings; this is what is meant by "able to gather" and "able to collect.
Furthermore, a Bodhisattva places the sentient beings of a single Buddha-land upon his right palm and flies to the ten directions.
He manifests everything everywhere, yet does not move from his original place; this is movement without moving, and non-movement while moving.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, as for the offerings made to all Buddhas by sentient beings throughout the ten directions, a bodhisattva causes them all to be seen within a single pore;
this is being fully endowed with and being able to manifest. Furthermore, Śāriputra, regarding the worlds of the ten directions...
All winds, the Bodhisattva is able to inhale into his mouth without them causing any harm; nor does he cause the trees to be pushed or broken.
This is "moving while remaining at peace. Furthermore, when the worlds of the ten directions are consumed by fire at the end of an eon, he takes all that fire into his own belly;
the fires continue their work as before, yet they do no harm. This is...

That which was perilous was immediately made secure. Furthermore, from below, passing through Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he took a single buddha-land and placed it above, passing through countless worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, as if holding a date leaf on the point of a needle without causing any disturbance.
This is because his taking and placing accord with the nature of reality (dharmatā), yet he establishes them without leaving a trace. Moreover,
Śāriputra, a bodhisattva dwelling in the inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernormal powers, manifest the body of a Buddha, and even the body of a wheel-turning king—
this refers precisely to bodies corresponding to the ten realms and so forth. They can transform all the sounds of sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
including their superior, middling, and inferior voices, causing them to become the voice of a Buddha and produce [the Dharma].
The sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the various teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions—all these are universally made audible within it.
The various [manifestations] mentioned previously were all the supernatural power of form;
this is the supernatural power of sound. Such diverse transformations are inconceivable. Furthermore, it is like wishing to bring forth fragrant food.

He served the great assembly with food. Thereupon, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested before the gathering a transformed bodhisattva whose physical marks and signs were radiant and whose majestic virtue was so preeminent that it eclipsed the entire assembly. He addressed them, saying:
"Go to the region above, across as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges Rivers. There is a land named *Saṃbhava*."
"O Fragrance! The Buddha there is named Sugandhakūṭa. He is currently seated together with various bodhisattvas for a meal. Go to him and speak these words on my behalf:
'Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One. He pays you boundless respect and inquires after your well-being.'"
"I hope you have little illness and little affliction, and that your physical strength remains at ease. I pray for the remnants of the World-Honored One’s meal;
I shall perform the work of a Buddha within this Sahā world, so that those who delight in inferior teachings may attain the Great Way, and also cause the fame of the Tathāgata to be heard everywhere.
At that time, the transformed bodhisattva immediately rose above the assembly toward the zenith and paid homage.
He fully recounted his respectful greetings and his request for alms-food.
Once that manifested bodhisattva had accepted the bowl of food, he went with those nine million bodhisattvas to the house of Vimalakīrti.
Vimalakīrti immediately manifested nine million lion-thrones, and all the bodhisattvas sat upon them; together with the great assembly, they partook of the fragrant food.
[He offered] rice. (And so forth. This was a divine transformation that takes the distant as near, the small as great, the few as many, and the coarse as sublime.

Furthermore, wishing to go to the Buddha’s presence together with Mañjuśrī, he immediately used his supernatural power to take all the great assembly, along with the lion throne, and placed them upon his right palm; he then proceeded to the Buddha’s presence. Moreover, with his right [hand...]
"Taking the world of Wondrous Joy with his hand and placing it here in this land," and so forth—these are all inconceivable divine transformations.
Someone may ask: "Why are the divine transformations described in this sutra so numerous? The answer is: "This sutra is taught within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class;
it is precisely at the time when the partial is criticized, the small is rejected, the great is praised, and the perfect is extolled. Yet, regarding the Śrāvakas of the past Āgama..."
Having already attained the fruits of the Path, they contemplate only emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Consequently, they do not give rise to even a single thought of delight regarding the bodhisattvas’ playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*) or the purification of buddha-fields (*buddhakṣetra-pariśodhana*).

For this reason, the introduction to this sutra takes the manifestation of supernatural power through the jeweled canopy as its theme, and the opening chapter takes the purification of the buddha-field as the request. This is precisely because [the author] intends to...

To contravene their long-held inclinations and set aside their minor practices, he causes them to feel shame for the small and aspire toward the great, thereby allowing them to obtain the nourishment of "fresh butter" (sarpis).
Thus, as a prologue for the Lotus Sūtra’s method of opening up provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality, his supernatural powers and pure lands are particularly abundant therein.
Therefore, at that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard this Dharma-gate of the Bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and said to Śāriputra:
"It is as if someone were to manifest various forms and images before a person who is blind."

It is not that they do not see it. Among all the śrāvakas who hear this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, who would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? Why then have we eternally severed our roots?

Regarding this Mahāyāna, those who have already become like withered seeds [of potential] should all weep aloud upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation, their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.

This very section of the Vaipulya sūtra disparages the partial and rejects the small, while extolling the Great and praising the Perfect; it serves to cause the śrāvakas to feel shame for the small and to aspire to the Great.
However, it is not that the basis of inconceivable liberation cannot produce the traces of various inconceivable supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*).
Without the traces of inconceivable supernatural powers, there would be no means to manifest the basis of inconceivable liberation.
Those who are deluded forget the basis to cling to the traces; those who have awakened reach the basis through the traces. This is the basis.
Although their manifestations differ, they are one in their inconceivability. Regarding the third point, the inconceivability of the teaching of the Dharma:

this section shares with the preceding [section on] supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) two perspectives—separation and integration. To speak of them separately, there are sentient beings who attain liberation through the benefit of the forms manifested by supernatural powers;
as the sutra clarifies regarding Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed, it says that only those who are capable [of such perception] may perceive it.
"Those who are delivered are able to see it"—this is precisely its meaning. Furthermore, it is also like the case of the Pratyekabuddha who manifests signs;
he cannot preach the Dharma, but by manifesting supernatural powers alone, he causes people to obtain benefit. This is of the same category.

While there are naturally those among sentient beings who must obtain deliverance through hearing the Dharma and gaining the benefit of a Śrāvaka—this being the common course—now we shall clarify this by combining these points.

Having first startled and moved them with supernatural powers to inspire joy and delight, he now proceeds to proclaim the teachings through wisdom and eloquence, adapting them to what is appropriate for each.

It is like the Dragon King sending down rain: he must first gather the clouds of compassion and thunder the lightning of the precepts, so that the three types of grasses and two types of trees may first find relief and stand up tall and expectant, only then does the rain fall.
With the rain of the Dharma, the entire land is thoroughly saturated; those of superior, middling, and inferior faculties each attain growth. The Buddha-dharma is likewise;

therefore, following the supernormal powers, the exposition of the Dharma is clarified. While there is certainly no occasion to discuss it at other times, this sutra is preached within the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) period, wherein the "Full" (Pūrṇa) teaching is presented in contrast to the "Half" (Ardha).
Although it is called the "Full" teaching, it possesses the correctness of both censure and praise.

Yet, the majority belong to the Sudden and Perfect (yuantun) teaching. Although they are dedicated exclusively to the Sudden and Perfect, this does not preclude their being compatible with the Shared and Distinct teachings.
For example, the thirty-two bodhisattvas each spoke on entering the gate of non-duality; while Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti certainly represent the Sudden and Perfect, [the others do not].
Do not other bodhisattvas also simultaneously master both the general and the specific? Furthermore, as the verse from the *Ratnakūṭa* says:

"The teaching of the Dharma is neither existent nor non-existent; all phenomena arise through causes and conditions. There is no self, no agent, and no recipient; yet the karma of good and evil is never lost.
This is a eulogy of the Perfect and Sudden Dharma. At the very beginning, under the Bodhi tree, by his power...
"Subduing Māra," and so forth—this is a retrospective praise of the Hīnayāna teachings expounded during the Āgama period.
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their own kind," and so forth—this is a direct praise of the Vaipulya period.
The four teachings are discussed together; the sudden, gradual, secret, and indeterminate are raised as a unity. When the Great Master expounded the *Avataṃsaka*, he used this analogy:
"Next, it illuminates the level ground, and its reflection appears in ten thousand waters;

according to the square or round shape of each vessel, and following the movement or stillness of the waves, one Buddha-land is shown such that purity and impurity differ, and a single body is manifested such that the large and small vary, while a single voice speaks."
The Dharma is understood differently by each according to their kind. Some feel fear, others joy; some feel weary and detached, while others sever their doubts.

Through his inconceivable and unique spiritual powers, they perceive purity and impurity, hear praise and censure, smell the scent of *campaka* flowers or not, see flowers clinging to the body or not, and experience wisdom as manifold or not manifold.
This serves as a true analogy for how the Vaipulya teachings manifest lands and bodies.
The various ways of teaching the Dharma through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) differ in many respects.

For example, when the Buddha taught the practice for purifying the Buddha-land to Ratnakūṭa, he stated in general terms that the categories of sentient beings constitute the bodhisattva’s buddha-field.
When analyzed in detail, this consists of three minds and twenty practices. As for the three minds: first, the straightforward mind; second, the profound mind; and third, the great [mind].

The "Mind-vehicle" consists of twenty practices: namely, the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), the four methods of attraction (*catuḥ-saṃgrahavastu*), skillful means (*upāya*), the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), the teaching on the removal of the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), self-guarding of precepts and conduct, and the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*). It further states:

"If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, they should purify their own mind. To the extent that the mind is purified, the Buddha-field is purified. (From the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra-nirdeśa*)
The practice of purifying Buddha-lands can be cultivated by Bodhisattvas of all four teachings. The Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka-piṭaka) perform the six perfections as concrete practices;
their cultivation is based on the Āgamas. Since they have not yet destroyed delusions, they still fall within the realm of craving and views.

Now, in the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtras), which directly confronts the "half" teaching to expound the "full," there are the three minds and twenty practices that encompass the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect teachings for Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles.
One can practice them all. If one understands that these mental activities are immediately empty (*śūnyatā*), they are classified as entering the Shared Teaching (*pṛthagjana-śāsana*).

If one understands the "limited middle" (*prādeśika-madhyama*), they are classified as entering the Distinct Teaching (*bhedaka-śāsana*). If one understands the "perfect middle" (*pariniṣpanna-madhyama*), they are classified as entering the Perfect Teaching (*paripūrṇa-śāsana*).
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Expedient Means," Vimalakīrti, on account of his physical illness, extensively expounded the Dharma; he first spoke of the faults and afflictions of the body.
This is also the common object of contemplation for the four teachings. It proceeds to say: "O virtuous ones, this [body] is to be loathed;
you should instead delight in the Buddha-body. Why is this? The Buddha-body is the Dharma-body, born from immeasurable merits," and so forth.
The various merits thus enumerated, when brought together and traced back to their source, likewise apply to all four teachings. At present, however, we are in the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra) period.
Since the practice of the *pāramitās* has already been refuted, it can likewise be understood that the subsequent three [pāramitās] are also being cultivated.
Furthermore, in the "Chapter on the Disciples," the Buddha rebukes Śāriputra, saying: "As for true *pratisaṃlayana*, it is not manifesting body or mind within the triple world;

this is *pratisaṃlayana*. It is the non-abiding of the true mind within or without; this is *pratisaṃlayana*. Although this uses the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) to rebuke the Lesser Vehicle (*xiao*), it serves as a critique.

The meaning also applies both generally and specifically. If one says that while remaining unmoved by various views, one cultivates the factors of enlightenment and enters nirvana without severing the afflictions—this precisely uses the Perfect and Sudden teaching to critique the Hinayana.
Such various instances are too numerous to enumerate. As for his rebuke of Maitreya, he taught the twenty-five dharmas as bodhi;

for the youth Prabhāvyūha, he expounded the thirty-two practices of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Although these are perfect and sudden (*yuantun*), their meaning also encompasses the common and distinct (*tongbie*) teachings.
Furthermore, as for his rebuke of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, he subdued the celestial māras and preached to the various demonesses.
The Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Lamp: this employs the perfect to critique the partial, thereby establishing the perfect and sudden.

It transforms demons into Buddhas; this is cited as an illustration, so other instances need not be listed exhaustively. Now, the Perfect Teaching is the root, while the other teachings are its traces.
At the beginning, the real is employed to bestow the provisional; at the end, the provisional is integrated to return to the real. Those who are deluded forget the root and cling [to the branches].
Regarding the "trace" (*ji*): the awakened one reaches the fundamental through the trace. Although the fundamental and the trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
As for the "inconceivable retinue" according to Siming, the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) clarifies six kinds of retinues, all of which are present in this sūtra as well.
I shall now set forth their characteristics. First is the retinue of the rational nature (*lixing*). The sūtra says: "All sentient beings..."
It is thus; even Maitreya is likewise so. Second, regarding the birth of a retinue through karma:
the Tathāgata, in previous lives, once established the seeds for the conditions of Buddha-nature. Life after life, he brought them to completion, ripened them, delivered them, and liberated them.
Even in this very life, some may hear the teaching and attain the Way, becoming a constant following of the assembly, serving as close spiritual kin or inner retinue; or else—
They attain the Way and join the assembly of the laity as external kinsmen. Regarding those who wish to be born among kinsmen:

although they have not yet severed suffering due to karmic ties from previous lives, they vow to be born among internal kinsmen, so that even enemies and others may, by means of this, receive the Way.
If one attains the Way, they become an internal retinue; if not, they become an external retinue, as described in other sutras regarding those such as Devadatta.
As for the retinue of the four supernormal powers, it refers to those who encountered a Buddha in a previous life.
Having given rise to true insight into the Truths (*satyadarśana*), their births were not yet exhausted; they may have been in the higher realms or in other directions.
Now, these Buddhas manifest as *paricchinna-buddhas* (segmented Buddhas), and whether by the power of vows or through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), they descend to this lower realm.
Just like those who come from the land of the Buddha Gandhottamakūṭa, they come here to Vaiśālī with bodhisattvas from other directions, hear the Dharma, obtain benefit, and depart.
The Bodhisattvas and others are such examples. Regarding the fifth, the retinue of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body):

there are those who, being identical to the Buddha’s ultimate *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, manifest as a *nirmāṇakāya*, such as Mañjuśrī, who was King Nāgeśvara Buddha, and Vimalakīrti, who was the Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa.
There are also those such as Bodhisattvas at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), who arise from the partially realized *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* as *nirmāṇakāyas*.

The body [of the emanation] is exemplified by Maitreya and others. Whether for the sake of maturing others, for the sake of maturing oneself, or for the sake of original conditions, all such instances are termed the retinue of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Sixth, regarding the retinue of the Dharma-gates: this is exemplified by the Bodhisattva Samantadarśin.
He asked the layman Vimalakīrti, "Who are your father, mother, wife, children, relatives, and kinsmen? Who are your officials, subjects, and acquaintances?
Where are your slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages? Vimalakīrti replied, "The Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas;
Expedient Means is their father. All teachers of the multitudes are born from these two."
The joy of the Dharma serves as his wife; the mind of compassion is his daughter; the virtuous and sincere mind is his son; ultimate emptiness is his house.
His disciples are the various afflictions, which he turns according to his will. The factors of enlightenment are his spiritual friends;

through these, he achieves perfect awakening. This is the retinue of this Dharma-gate. The various categories of sutras are exceedingly numerous; the student may approach them according to their own inclination.

It is so. If one discusses the fundamental and the manifested within this context, the retinue of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) takes the dharma-body and reward-body as its basis, while the response-body itself is the manifestation.
Yet, without the basis, there would be no way to manifest; without the manifestation, there would be no way to reveal the basis.

Those who are deluded forget the basis to cling to the manifestation, whereas those who have awakened use the manifestation to reach the basis. Although the basis and the manifestation differ, they are inconceivable.

First. As for the remaining three, they take past seeds as the fundamental and present activity as the trace; thus, although the fundamental and the trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Fifth, regarding the clarification of the inconceivability of benefit: whatever the Buddhas do is never in vain. The *Śāstra* says:
"When the Buddha enters the King-Samādhi, he first emits light to illuminate those who have come before, and subsequently emits [light]..."
Regarding the latter, "the radiance of light": it is like catching fish with a net, where both those caught first and those caught later are not in vain;

likewise, seeing the light and hearing the Dharma are never fruitless. The present sutra says: "The Jewel of the Dharma shines universally and rains down the rain of Dharma," which refers to the dual benefit of body and speech.
The Elder Ratnakūṭa said: "The Great Sage, the Dharma King, to whom all turn; those who observe the Buddha with a pure mind are without exception filled with joy. Each...
To see the World-Honored One before oneself is the unique power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi-viśeṣa-dharma*).

This means that according to their respective past roots of capacity (*indriya-mūla*), sentient beings perceive the Buddha’s body differently. Furthermore, it is said: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each understand it according to their kind;
all say that the World-Honored One speaks in their own language. This is the unique power of spiritual transformation.
This statement means that sentient beings each hear the Dharma differently according to their respective innate capacities (*gotra*). It further says:
"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind; they all receive and practice it, thereby obtaining its benefit.

This is the inconceivable power of the Buddha’s unique qualities. This means that upon seeing his body and hearing the Dharma, each obtains benefit according to their own faculties and vessels (*indriya-bhājana*).
They are different. Furthermore, it is said: "The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet some feel fear, some feel joy, some develop weary detachment, and some sever their doubts;
this is the inconceivable power of his unique qualities. This refers to the various differences in the benefits obtained.
That some experience joy is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint), wherein they obtain the benefit of joy.

If there is fear, this is the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (human-centric standpoint): being earnestly reverent and fearful, one practices goodness with diligence and thereby attains the benefit of wholesome rebirths.
If one gives rise to weary detachment (*nirveda*), this is the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial standpoint): attaining remedial dharmas and becoming weary of and detached from afflictions (*kleśa*).

One obtains the benefit of destroying evil; or, for those who sever doubt, one severs delusive uncertainty and attains the benefit of entering the principle of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

These four *siddhāntas* relate in meaning to the four teachings. This sutra speaks of the "complete" (*pūrṇa*) in contrast to the "half" (*ardha*), and speaks of the three teachings—Shared (*sādhāraṇa*), Distinct (*vaiśeṣika*), and Perfect (*paripūrṇa*)—in contrast to the *piṭaka*.
Furthermore, for those who have newly entered the *piṭaka* during the period of the Vaipulya [sutras], they should obtain the minor benefit; it is necessary...

Regarding the benefit of this sutra and its treatise, there are two aspects: the exoteric and the esoteric. As for the exoteric aspect, it is as stated at the conclusion of the "Buddha-kṣetra" chapter:
thirty-two thousand devas and humans seeking the vehicle of the śrāvaka realized that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent.

They distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye. Eight thousand bhikṣus, no longer grasping at any phenomena, attained the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of outflows.

This illustrates how hearing [the Mahāyāna] leads to great awakening while [hearing the Hīnayāna] leads to small [awakening], thereby obtaining the benefit of both the *Āgama* (Zàng) and *Vaipulya* (Tōng) teachings—as seen in the "Expedient Means" chapter and the way Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma according to the needs of those who came to inquire after his illness, causing countless people to all resolve upon the unsurpassed path.
I believe that this obtains the benefit of generating the mind of enlightenment according to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, while also encompassing the benefits of the two preceding teachings.
Furthermore, it is like when Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for Maudgalyāyana; at that time, eight hundred lay devotees all generated the aspiration for the unsurpassed Way.
Furthermore, when Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for Subhūti, two hundred devaputras attained the pure Dharma-eye.
Again, when Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for Rāhula, thirty-two sons of elders all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
Again, when he preached the Dharma for Maitreya Bodhisattva, two hundred devaputras attained [the stage of] non-arising.
He attained patience regarding beings. Furthermore, while preaching the Dharma for the youth Prabhāvyūha, five hundred devas and humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
While preaching the Dharma for the demonesses, he caused twelve thousand celestial maidens to resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed path.
And while preaching the Dharma for the elder Sudatta, he caused the lowliest beggar in the city to resolve his mind [upon the unsurpassed path].

They resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path. Furthermore, when Mañjuśrī led the assembly into Vimalakīrti’s room to hear the Dharma and witness the miraculous transformations, eight thousand devaputras among them all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path.

Moreover, when this "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" was being preached, five thousand bodhisattvas all entered the dharma-gate of non-duality and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Furthermore, at the Gandhavyūha...

In this chapter, when the ten matters of the good Dharma and so forth of the Sahā world were expounded, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed path, and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the entire great assembly was filled with great joy; thus they collectively obtained the benefit of joy. As for the hidden intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), it serves incidentally to censure the partial [teachings].

To disparage the Lesser Vehicle so that those of the Śrāvaka vehicle, upon hearing the Great Vehicle, do not slander it; and upon hearing this disparagement, do not become angry; but rather gain the benefit of feeling shame for the Lesser and aspiring to the Great.
Thus, for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, it serves as the skillful means (*upāya*) for "opening the provisional and revealing the real," gaining the benefit of transforming curd into fresh butter.
If one unifies these three benefits through the three applications of the precious canopy: [the first is] generating the mind for the Unsurpassed Way, entering into the...
The patience toward living beings (*sattvakṣānti*). This is the benefit of obtaining protection. The Bodhisattva attains a pure Buddha-field and sports with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).

This is the benefit of being able to reach the state of coolness (*śītala*). Attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye, not grasping at any phenomena, and the liberation of the mind through the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
This is the benefit of removing feverish affliction. Nevertheless, it is because he wishes to cause sentient beings to attain the opening of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
It is the root of great benefit. Therefore, as a provisional means, it allows beings to attain the traces of the benefits of the three vehicles and the seven stages of expedient means.
Those who are deluded forget the root and cling to the traces; those who awaken reach the root through the traces. Although the root and the trace differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Thus, were it not for the inconceivable great substance of the three virtues, one could not attain the three liberations.
This is the inconceivable great function; it is not that the three liberations cannot manifest this inconceivable great function.
There is nothing that can fail to reveal the inconceivable great essence of the three virtues. Both essence and function are vast; both principle and phenomena are perfect.
This is the reason for the teaching of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the Sūtra on the Inconceivable Liberation of Vimalakīrti.

Regarding contemplative understanding (*kuan-jie*): one contemplates that the single-mind nature inherently possesses the five destinies, taking these as the objects of compassion for the five destinies and vowing to deliver them;
this is the arising of *pratyaya-compassion* (compassion based on conditions), such as when the five hundred sons of the elders offered the jeweled canopies.

Next, one contemplates them so that they become empty, which accords with the two vehicles inherent in the nature; this is *dharma-compassion* (compassion based on dharmas), such as the five hundred jeweled canopies.
It is cast into the void. Contemplate these five paths as no different from Buddha-nature. The suchness of sentient beings is identical to the suchness of Maitreya;
this is non-conditioned great compassion. It is like causing all precious canopies to merge into a single canopy.

This is the general contemplation. As for the specific contemplation: contemplate that the causes and effects of the five paths are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature, which is itself Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, the cause and effect of the Buddha-realm have never been different from the nature of the five destinies;

yet, while the nature of the five destinies is devoid of suffering and yet possesses suffering—this suffering being pitiable—the nature of the Buddha-realm is devoid of pleasure and yet possesses pleasure—this pleasure being venerable.
This is precisely the pair of compassion and reverence. Contemplating the five destinies and the five hindrances, afflictions and birth-and-death are...
This Bodhi and Nirvana are the pair of the nature of delusion and the nature of reality.

Contemplating the ten realms within the one mind as empty, provisional, and middle is called the "three causes" in practice and the "three compassions" in fruition; this is the pair of cause and effect.
Contemplating the one mind as empty, provisional, and middle is itself the three virtues, and these three virtues are fully present.

The feet possess the great function of no fixed direction; this is the unity of essence and function. Within this, the miraculous responses, supernatural powers, the preaching of the Dharma, the retinue, and the benefits can be understood through observation.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of understanding: one contemplates that within a single thought-moment, the nature is fully endowed with the five destinies.
These five realms of existence constitute the object of the *maitrī* (compassion) based on sentient beings; they are the five hundred precious canopies.
To contemplate them as empty is the object of the *maitrī* based on phenomena; this is symbolized by scattering the precious canopies into space.

To realize that these nine realms are themselves the Buddha-realm is to perceive the inherent presence of the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, universally traversing provisional names, substantial dharmas, and the various lands.
He then caused these precious canopies to merge into a single canopy that completely covered the trichiliocosm.
*The Commentary on the Non-Self of the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Fascicle Two.
*The Commentary on the Non-Self of the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Fascicle Three.
Written by the Tiantai Mountain monk Youxi Chuandeng.
Part Two: Eulogies (2). First, the introduction provided by the narrator:
The son of a householder, Ratnakūṭa, immediately before the Buddha spoke in verse as a eulogy, saying:
Master Kumārajīva said: "Previously, he made offerings with his body; now he makes offerings with mind and speech. Previously, he sustained [the Sangha] with material wealth;
now he sustains it with the Dharma. Furthermore, although the assembly has witnessed these transformations, they do not yet know the source from which these transformations arise.
Desiring to lead them to investigate the ultimate basis of these events so that their faith and joy may deepen further, he praises him with verses."
II. The Two Elders Speak in Verse. Part One: General Praise. Section One: Praising the Preeminence of Both Form and Mind. Subsection One:
Praising the Preeminence of Form.
His eyes are pure, long, and wide, like blue lotuses.

Master Sengzhao said: "Among the five sensory faculties and the hundred skeletal members, the eyes are the most prominent. Since one acts upon beholding a person's countenance, the eyes are praised first.
In India there is the blue lotus flower; its petals are long and broad, with the blue and white clearly distinguished.
Because they possess the marks of a Great Man’s eyes, it is used as a metaphor."
Deng said: "Of the ten parts of the human face, seven are occupied by the features; of the ten parts of the facial features, seven are occupied by the eyes.
Thus, although the Buddha possesses the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics, these marks and characteristics are most abundant in the blue-lotus eyes.
Therefore, in the *Ratnakūṭa*, its excellence is singled out for praise; by this, the inclusion of the remaining features can be understood. If...
To speak exhaustively, it should be understood according to verses such as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*’s praise: "The Buddha’s face is like the pure, full moon," and so forth;

this is the intended meaning within these words. As for the external meaning, it is precisely because the elder offered the parasol that his intention was expressed through compassion, and the Buddha’s compassion is primarily embodied in the eyes. As it is said: "If the mind is upright, then..."
The pupils are clear and bright. Thus, the praise of the eyes is essentially a praise of compassion. As the *Samantabhadra-dvāra* states: "Beholding sentient beings with compassionate eyes;
the accumulation of merit is as vast as an ocean. Yet, there are the blue-lotus eyes of the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇakāya*), up to the blue-lotus eyes of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Although only one eye is praised here, the four eyes and five eyes are all fully intended.

Regarding the practitioner who resolves through contemplation: they contemplate the ten realms within one mind and perceive that there is the bliss of the three truths to be bestowed; they constantly desire to bestow this upon them.
This is what is meant by the purity and vast cultivation of the contemplative mind, which is like a blue lotus.
II. Praising the Supremacy of the Mind.
Once the mind is purified, one has already transcended all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
Master Zào said: "The body is the gate for the form; the mind is the master of virtue. Therefore, the author designates these two as the opening verse of the hymn.
Furthermore, the ocean of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is profound and vast, without limit. Were it not for the Tathāgata’s pure true mind, none could cross it.
Dēng said: "The defiled mind is this shore; only meditation can ferry one across. If one becomes attached to the flavor of meditation, that meditation will in turn become a defilement."
Therefore, one must further cross over this shore of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). This encompasses mundane *dhyāna*, supramundane *dhyāna*, and even the supreme-supramundane *dhyāna*.
Through these successive stages, one may discuss both distraction (*vikṣepa*) and concentration (*samādhi*).

Thus, while the fundamental mundane *dhyāna* is termed "concentration" when compared to the distracted ground of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is already considered distracted from the perspective of the four supramundane noble ones (*ārya*).
How much more so, then, regarding the Tathāgata’s supreme dhyāna? Therefore, the subsequent passage says: "What is called bondage? Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is the bondage of a bodhisattva.
The *Vajracchedikā* states: "Those who understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like a raft should abandon even the Dharma itself."
How much more so for that which is contrary to the Dharma! This is the ocean of the flavor of meditative concentration; only the Buddha, the Sage, is able to cross it.
Third, praising the excellence of his karma:
"Having long accumulated pure karma, it is called immeasurable."
Master Zhao said: "Because one has accumulated the three pure karmas over incalculable eons, one's reputation is immeasurable.
Master Deng said: "There are three impure karmas: greed, anger, and delusion; these are the impurities of mental karma."
It is said: killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct—these are the impurities of bodily action (*kāyakarman*). It is said:

false speech, frivolous speech, harsh speech, and divisive speech—these are the impurities of verbal action (*vākkarman*). As for pure action, there are two types of goodness: cessation (*saṃvara*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Regarding the three aforementioned impure actions, one abandons them entirely. This refers to non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, and so forth.
It is so. This refers to purifying one's karma; it is not merely the purification of karma itself. Now, as for the purification of karma:

it is not only the absence of greed, anger, and delusion, but also the capacity for integrity, moderation, benevolence, compassion, and wisdom. It is not only the abstention from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, but also the ability to release living beings, practice charity, and bestow pure Dharma upon others.
It is not only the avoidance of false speech, frivolous talk, divisive speech, and harsh words, but also...
One who is able to speak with sincerity, truthfulness, and honesty; who skillfully reconciles disputes and litigation; and who causes others to possess beautiful virtue—this constitutes pure karma.
Now, in praising the Tathāgata’s purity of mental karma, it is shown that the three delusions are thoroughly purified and the three wisdoms are perfectly realized.
When the karma of the body is pure, the two types of death are forever extinguished and the three virtues are perfected.
When the karma of speech is pure, the five modes of speech are like lute strings and the eight qualities of voice resound far and wide.
Only after one possesses the virtue of a renowned name does that name subsequently become universally heard throughout immeasurable realms; this is indeed true.
Regarding contemplative understanding: to contemplate that the single thought-moment is originally empty and quiescent is the purity of mental action (*manas-karman*).

Since even the mind cannot be apprehended, how could the ten realms exist? This is the purity of physical action (*kāya-karman*). To proclaim and extol this in accordance with reality is the purity of verbal action (*vāk-karman*).
4. Praising the Supremacy of Compassion:
He bows his head because he leads the multitudes to tranquility.

The verse says: "His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses"—this refers to the tranquility of his physical form. "His mind is pure, having already transcended all meditative absorptions"—this refers to the purity of his heart.

The mind is quiescent; having long accumulated pure karma, it is called "immeasurable. This is the quiescence of karma. Those who possess these three yet are not quiescent are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Those who are quiescent in themselves but not quiescent for others are those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Those who are quiescent both for themselves and others, yet still abide in the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*), are [Bodhisattvas].
The Bodhisattva, who brings both self and others to tranquility and reaches the further shore, is the Tathāgata.
When the Elder Ratnākara addressed those who do not readily humble themselves before others, he said: "To bow with reverence and respect when one cannot immediately do so is difficult.
Indeed, those who surpass others by means of wealth are merely wealthy; those who surpass others by means of rank are merely noble. He did not [speak thus] because of...

That one does not surpass others on account of wealth or nobility is due solely to the Way (*dào*). To surpass others by means of the Way, and furthermore to cause them to surpass [others], is simply to lead people by means of the Way.
Therefore, for one who lowers themselves before others despite possessing wealth and honor, it is merely a matter of outward appearance and dress.
One who humbles others through the Way wins their hearts' submission. One who guides others through the Way wins their submission yet again.
Now, you say that you lead the multitude to tranquility; therefore, we bow our heads.
Since the Tathāgata has already triumphed by means of the Way and is further able to guide others through the Way, we thus bow our heads and prostrate ourselves at his feet.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": to contemplate that the afflictions of a single moment of mind are themselves bodhi, and that birth-and-death are themselves nirvana, is quiescence (*śānti*).
Furthermore, to use this dharma to teach others in turn is to lead the multitude toward quiescence.
2. Praising the inconceivable miraculous transformations:

Having seen the Great Sage manifest throughout the infinite lands of the ten directions by means of his miraculous powers, and having heard all the Buddhas therein preaching the Dharma, everything was thus seen and heard.
Master Zhaolun said: "Since the divine transformations of the merging canopy have already been seen and are unfathomable,

it is even more rare that within it the lands of the ten directions and the various Buddhas preaching the Dharma appear, so that the entire assembly in this Sahā world can all see and hear them from afar."
Deng said: "The Master has already provided a comprehensive account with this verse praising the Buddha’s merits.

As for that which cannot be fully exhausted by praise, it lies solely in the single circumstance of offering the canopy. My own intention was profound, yet the Buddha’s response to me was far-reaching.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he caused all the precious canopies to merge into one."
It forms a single canopy that universally covers the great trichiliocosm, manifesting everywhere throughout the lands of the ten directions along with the Buddhas preaching the Dharma;

thus, the entire assembly is able to see and hear it. Within this, the entirety of the transformative path of a single career and the merit of the four pairs and eight ranks of noble ones are fully contained.
For this reason, the Elder first praised it in general with this verse. What follows below consists of various [details].

Regarding the verses of praise: if one were not to expound upon their meaning, yet the observer could grasp what lies beyond the words, then more than half of the intent of this entire scripture would already have been contemplated.
The method for observing and interpreting them is the same as explained above.
III. Praising the Universal Bestowal of the Wealth of Dharma:
The Dharma-king’s power of Dharma transcends all living beings; he constantly bestows the wealth of Dharma upon all.
Master Zao said: "A secular king uses worldly power to overcome the people, and thus his grace can extend throughout a nation. A Dharma-king, however, uses..."
The power of his Dharma surpasses all others; thus, he is able to provide spiritual succor to boundless realms. He is able to skillfully discern the distinct characteristics of all phenomena.
From this point down to the phrase "karma does not perish," the entire passage extols the gift of Dharma.
II. Specific Praise in Three Parts. First, praise for the merit of the initial teaching of the sudden [vehicle] in two parts. First, praise for the excellence of internal realization:
"He is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena, yet he does not waver from the ultimate truth (paramārtha). Having already attained self-mastery over all phenomena..."
Therefore, I prostrate before this Dharma King.
Master Zao said: "The primary truth (paramārtha) refers to the meaning of the single characteristic (ekalakṣaṇa) of all dharmas.

Although one may differentiate the various distinct characteristics of dharmas, they do not deviate from that single characteristic. This is the unsurpassed path of the Dharma King. Now, as for worldly kings... [text ends]
This resides within the people. The Dharma King exercises sovereign mastery over the Dharma. The Dharma has no fixed characteristics; it is distinguished according to what is appropriate.
For those who favor difference, he distinguishes differences without contradicting unity. For those who favor unity, he distinguishes unity without contradicting difference.
Although unity and difference are distinguished as distinct, both accord with the characteristics of the Dharma; thus, he attains sovereignty.
Deng said: "The meaning of Ratnakūṭa’s words is this: sentient beings take wealth as their power, and thus they possess mastery over wealth;
they are able to bestow wealth as a gift upon all. The Dharma King takes the Dharma as his power, and thus he possesses mastery over the Dharma;
he is able to universally bestow the wealth of the Dharma upon all. What constitutes 'wealth' here? It is precisely each of them offering a jeweled canopy to the Tathāgata."

What constitutes this Dharma? It is the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha that causes all the precious canopies to merge into a single canopy, universally covering the trichiliocosm and the entire assembly.
Within this canopy, everyone perceives everywhere the various signs of the Buddha’s birth, as well as the primary and secondary dharmas (the person and his environment).
Furthermore, this is not a method of giving distinct from material offerings; it is simply a matter of understanding—
The gift of material wealth leads to mastery of the gift of Dharma; as material things are equal, so too are all phenomena.
Therefore, the power of the Dharma King surpasses that of all living beings, for he constantly bestows the wealth of Dharma universally upon all. Yet even this is merely a conventional appearance.

As for using these characteristics to manifest the Dharma, it is as previously explained: the manifestation of compassion and reverence, delusion and principle, cause and effect, essence and function, are all inconceivable.
These pertain to the great purport of this sutra and the fundamental intention behind its teaching of the Dharma.
Truly, it is said that one who possesses mastery over the Dharma transcends all sentient beings, constantly bestowing the wealth of the Dharma universally upon all. Well done!
To be able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena is to engage with existence (*saṃsāra*). To remain unmoved within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is to abide in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
It is precisely through discernment that one remains unmoved; it is precisely through remaining unmoved that one discerns.

Thus, one constantly engages with existence while always abiding in emptiness, and always abides in emptiness while engaging with existence. It is like a precious canopy manifesting to all—how could it ever [be otherwise]?
Are existence and non-existence not of divergent natures? To summarize them and bring them back to their source, they can be exhausted in two words:
it is said that he has attained mastery over all dharmas; therefore, we prostrate before this Dharma King. This is why the Tathāgata is called the Dharma King.
This is precisely because one has attained mastery over all phenomena. This praises the excellence of internal realization.

As for contemplative understanding: to contemplate that the single thought-moment inherently possesses the ten realms as being identical to emptiness is to be a Dharma King whose Dharma power surpasses all sentient beings.

To contemplate it as identical to the provisional (provisional existence) is to bestow the wealth of the Dharma upon all through its eternal nature. To contemplate it as identical to the Middle Way is [to realize the ultimate].
Simultaneously negating both extremes is the immovability of discrimination; simultaneously illuminating both extremes is having attained mastery over all phenomena.
○ Second, praising the subtlety of the teaching of the Dharma.
The teaching of the Dharma is that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent; they arise through causes and conditions.
There is no self, no creator, and no experiencer; yet the karma of good and evil never perishes.
Master Zhao said: "If one wishes to say it exists, existence does not arise of itself; if one wishes to say it is non-existent, when conditions assemble, form appears.

That the assembly of forms is not called 'non-existence,' yet that which is not non-existent is not called 'existence. Furthermore, because there is existence, there is non-existence; if there were no existence, what would there be to be non-existent?
Because there is non-existence, there is existence; if there were no non-existence, what would there be to exist? Thus, that which exists of itself does not truly exist."
"That which is non-existent by itself is not non-existent. This is the correct teaching of the Dharma King. Regarding the statement that "all phenomena arise due to causes and conditions":
existence does not arise from conditions, nor does non-existence arise from conditions; it is because phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent that they arise from causes and conditions.
The treatise says: Because phenomena follow conditions, they do not exist; because they arise through dependent origination, they are not non-existent. They are without self and without an agent.
There is no experiencer. All phenomena arise from conditions; there is no separate, true sovereign. Therefore, there is no self.
Since it is because of a self that one can perform good or evil and receive calamity or fortune, and since phenomena are devoid of self, there is neither one who acts nor one who receives.
Furthermore, it is said that "the karma of good and evil does not perish" means that if there were no agent...
If there were no recipient [of karma], then one should not experience blessings for doing good or calamities for committing evil.

Yet, the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings are transmitted from one to another; beauty and ugliness arise therefrom. The way of retribution follows in a continuous succession, just as sound harmonizes with its echo and a straight form produces a straight shadow.
This is the natural principle, without deviation even by a hair’s breadth. Why, then, should it depend on anything else?
"Is it always born from a self? The Lamp said:
"This is a retrospective praise of the essential Dharma taught at the very beginning of the *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra].
This verse is identical to the four lines of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*. The Treatise says: 'Of those phenomena produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty; they are also called'"
It is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*). It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). The first [verse] corresponds to the fourth;
the second corresponds to the first; the third corresponds to the second; and the fourth corresponds to the third. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* proceeds from the derivative toward the fundamental;

therefore, it first explains dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and subsequently explains the Middle Way. This verse proceeds from the fundamental toward the derivative; therefore, it first explains the Middle Way and subsequently explains dependent origination.

They arise, meet, and return to one another; they are different yet identical. Now, this verse will be explained through four interpretations: first, an interpretation based on the unchanging nature following conditions;
second, an interpretation based on the principle-body of the three truths; third, an interpretation based on the three contemplations of the gate of cultivation;

and fourth, an interpretation based on the four teachings according to the capacities of beings. Regarding the first, the interpretation based on the unchanging nature following conditions: "The preaching of the Dharma... [is not...]
It is neither existent nor non-existent; it is the unchanging essence of *tathatā*. The essence of *tathatā* is by nature the Middle Way.
If one speaks of its existence, the four modes of being (*catuskoṭi*) are profoundly absent; if one speaks of its non-existence, it is fully endowed with all phenomena.
This principle extends throughout the ten directions without limit and remains eternally as it is through ten thousand ages. Like the Vajra King, it is permanently abiding and indestructible.
Therefore, the Tathāgata has constantly proclaimed this in various sūtras, such as the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
That phenomena arise by means of causes and conditions is the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā) in accordance with conditions.

This is truly because the unchanging essence of True Suchness—like a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel and is thus capable of both good and evil—is able to follow along with defiled or pure conditions. As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "It is able to follow along with defiled and pure conditions."
It fully constructs the ten dharma-realms. This is because the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), while remaining immutable, is able to follow conditions (pratyaya).

That is to say, it can follow the pure conditions of the three contemplations to fully construct the Buddha-dharma realm; it can follow the defiled conditions of the three delusions to fully construct the nine dharma realms.
Therefore it is said: "All phenomena arise due to causes and conditions; there is no self, no creator, and no experiencer. This is precisely [the meaning].
Because the substance of True Suchness (tathatā) is unchanging, although it is said to manifest all phenomena by following conditions, it does so precisely while its substance remains unchanging.
Precisely because it is unchanging, it is the function of following conditions; its substance is fundamentally empty.
There is absolutely no creator or sovereign, nor is there any karma created, nor any recipient of retribution.
Therefore, it is said: "No self, no creator, no recipient. Yet, the retribution for good and evil does not perish; this is the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Although it remains unchanging while following conditions, its fundamental nature is empty; thus, there is no self, no creator, and no recipient.
Nevertheless, this does not obstruct the functional utility of differentiation according to conditions.

Thus, following pure conditions, one does not lose the retribution of wholesome karma and thereby accomplishes the Buddha-way; following defiled conditions, one does not lose the retribution of unwholesome karma and thereby accomplishes the nine realms.
Second, regarding the explanation of the three truths as the principle-substance: in both this section and the subsequent passages, it is necessary...

Returning to the *Avataṃsaka*, it explains the sequence in the same manner as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions" refers to the objective realm of the dependent origination of the ten realms.
"I say they are empty" means that the very substance of the dependent origination of the ten realms is emptiness.

"Without self, without creator, and without experiencer" refers to the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It is also called "provisional designation," which refers to the entirety of the dependent origination of the ten realms.

The substance is itself provisional; yet the retribution for good and evil does not perish. This is the realm of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). It is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

The dependent origination of the ten realms is, in its very place, entirely the Middle. To teach that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent is the realm of the middle truth (*madhyama-satya*).
It is precisely because phenomena arise through conditions that they are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way. To mention one is to include all three;
to speak of the three is to include the one. Regarding the three as explained in terms of the three contemplations within the gate of cultivation:

"Phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent" refers to the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way. "Because of causes and conditions, all phenomena arise" refers to the objective realm contemplated by the three contemplations.

"Without self, without agent, and without recipient" refers to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is also termed "provisional name," referring to the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*).

This is the dharma produced through causes and conditions, which is simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle. Thus, by mentioning one, all three are implied; by speaking of the three, they are simultaneously one.
These three dharmas, when spoken of in terms of the object of contemplation, are called the Three Truths (*trīṇi satyāni*); when spoken of in terms of the subject...

Contemplating these [truths] is called the "Three Contemplations" (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). They are in fact a single dharma; it is only by distinguishing them according to their cultivated nature (*xiùxìng*) that they are designated as "truths" (*satya*) or "contemplations.
Therefore, Master Jingxi said: "The three truths and three contemplations are not three; three, one, and one are nowhere to be found.
Though the names 'truth' and 'contemplation' differ, their essence is identical. Thus, the two—subject and object—are not two. This is the fourth point.
Regarding the explanation according to the four teachings as assigned by chance: "Phenomena produced from causes and conditions" refers to the Tripitaka Teaching of the Lesser Vehicle.

The Buddha’s exposition of the Tripitaka belongs to the initial stage of the Lesser Vehicle. Because non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to the view that all phenomena arise spontaneously (*svabhāva*), he taught the doctrine of phenomena produced from causes and conditions to refute this;
that is, he taught that all phenomena arise precisely because of causes and conditions. Now, regarding production from causes and conditions...
The Dharma was originally taught to refute heterodoxy. If its causes and conditions were not refuted, one would still remain bound by birth and death;
therefore, he established the teaching that "my teaching is itself emptiness" in order to refute those causes and conditions, whereby the Teaching of Commonality (Tongjiao) can arise.

This is precisely the state of being without self, without an agent, and without one who receives [karmic results]. Now, the fundamental purpose of the Emptiness School (Śūnyatāvāda) is to transcend birth and death.
If one clings to this emptiness as the ultimate goal, then one becomes like a withered sprout or a rotten seed; such a person does not become a vessel for the Dharma.
Therefore, the Tathāgata used a wedge to extract a wedge, teaching the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness, so that one may cultivate the pure Buddha-lands and roam therein.

The practice of the Bodhisattva’s play of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) constitutes the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*). Therefore, it is said that these are also called "provisional names" (*jiaming*);

thus, the retribution one receives does not perish. Now, the Initial Teaching is for the purpose of destroying existence (*yu*) to enter emptiness (*kong*), while the Subsequent Teaching is for the purpose of destroying emptiness to emerge into the provisional.
These merely practice the two extremes and have not yet realized the Middle Way (*zhongdao*). Therefore, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is taught to reveal the Middle Way.
To melt it away and penetrate it so that it is neither biased nor leaning; therefore, it is also called the meaning of the Middle Way.

This is precisely the teaching that phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent. Regarding the contemplative interpretation, it may be understood by following the explanation according to the three contemplations.
II. Praising the Merit of the Initial Teaching of the Gradual [Path], Part Three. A. Praising the Three Jewels, Part One: Praising the Buddha Jewel.

At the beginning, beneath the Bodhi tree, he subdued Māra by his power; having attained the realization of the path to the extinction of ambrosia (*amṛta*), he was without mind or will and without perception or activity, yet he utterly defeated all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Master Zhaoluo said: "That which is governed by the power of the Way—how could it be opposed by the armies of Māra?

From this point down to the passage on the Sea of Ritual and Law, he praises the original accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s merit. Master Kumārajīva said: "The Sanskrit text says 'Nirvāṇa-Amita' (Silent Extinction and Ambrosia);
