This body is impermanent, not abiding for even a single moment, like a flash of lightning, a torrential waterfall, a magical illusion, or a mirage. It is also like drawing on water, where as soon as one draws, it flows away and merges back together.
This body is easily destroyed, like a great tree standing on the edge of a steep riverbank. This body will not last long, like a tiger or a wolf...
It is devoured by owls, crows, eagles, vultures, and starving dogs. What person of wisdom would take pleasure in this body?
It would be easier to contain the waters of the great ocean within the hoofprint of an ox than to fully describe the impermanence, impurity, and foul stench of this body.
One might as well roll the great earth into balls the size of jujube fruits, gradually reducing them until they are like *ting-li* seeds or even down to atoms;
yet one could never fully describe the faults and afflictions of this body. Therefore, it should be abandoned like spittle or snot.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": to be able to contemplate the body in this manner is itself the cultivation of contemplation.
II. Second, the teaching that one should take pleasure in the Buddha-body. This has two parts. First, the heading:
"O virtuous ones, this [body] is something to be weary of; you should take pleasure in the Buddha-body."
Now, when the foundation of the Dharma-realm is first established, the processes of rejection and acceptance take precedence.

Within these two gates of rejection and acceptance, the essentials lie in the cultivation of delight and aversion. If one fails to understand this, will they not end up accepting that which should be rejected and rejecting that which should be accepted?
Furthermore, regarding those things to be rejected and accepted, there are both fundamental and derivative aspects; therefore, its...

Regarding that which is to be delighted in and loathed: there is both mind and body. Previously, I demonstrated the various faults and afflictions of the advancing body, speaking only of its derivative aspects.
For although the derivative depends upon the fundamental for its arising, the fundamental in turn relies upon the derivative for its sustenance.

Therefore, a practitioner of the path of contemplation who first succeeds in loathing the derivative—the physical body of birth and death—is able to resolve the derivative in order to sever the fundamental.
As for this text, in demonstrating that which one ought to rejoice in, it addresses both the fundamental and the derivative, and presents both body and mind together.
Thus, the statement "one should rejoice in the Buddha-body" is it not intended to speak of the derivative?
Furthermore, the statement "arising from immeasurable merit" is it not intended to speak of the fundamental? Being thus, these two should be combined.
Seek it thus: by using that which is the root of what one delights in to govern that which is the root of what one loathes and suffers from,

then the branches of what one loathes and suffers will depart of their own accord without needing to be removed, and the branches of what one delights in will be attained of their own accord without needing to be sought.
II. Explanation of the Two [Aspects]. First, showing the fruit that is produced. Why is this so?
The Buddha-body is precisely the Dharma-body. Master Zhaolun said:
"The Sūtra states that the Dharma-body is the body of empty space. It is without arising, yet there is nothing that does not arise. No...
It possesses form yet is not limited by form. It transcends the realm beyond the three worlds and cuts off the sphere of the conscious mind.
It cannot be subsumed by the aggregates or sense bases, nor can it be reached by words of praise. Cold and heat cannot cause it affliction; birth and death cannot transform its essence.
Thus, as a thing, it is subtle and wondrous, without sign, and cannot be said to exist, yet it fully responds to the myriad phenomena.
Its form cannot be said to be non-existent, for it encompasses the eight extremities of the universe. It cannot be said to be small, for its subtlety enters the infinitesimal gaps between atoms.

It cannot be said to be large, for it can enter [the subtlest realms]. Thus, it is able to enter life and emerge from death, penetrating and permeating the transformations of the infinite, manifesting in diverse ways across different regions.
This should not be sought through baseless inquiry. This is something that those of the Two Vehicles do not recognize, and even those in their final birth before Buddhahood do not behold;
how much less could ordinary people, who lack the eye of wisdom, dare to apply their thoughts to it? I have merely relied on the sincere words of the sutras to roughly indicate its profound ultimate.
Thus, when the Dharma-body is in heaven, it is heavenly; when it is among humans, it is human. How could one possibly abandon it in favor of what is near?
"Does one seek the Dharma-body far away from the sixteen-foot [form]?
Deng said: "The Buddha has three bodies: the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Response-body. The Dharma-body is inherently possessed;
this is that which is common to all Buddhas and sentient beings. The Reward-body is accomplished through cultivation; it is what arises now from immeasurable merit."
This is so. It manifests as the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is what is meant by mercury mixed with pure gold being able to coat various forms and images;
likewise, the merit combined with the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) appears and proceeds everywhere in response.

However, although the Dharma-body is said to be universal, within it one must distinguish between concealment and manifestation. Because sentient beings are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), it is therefore concealed.
Yet it is not manifest; it is produced only by the Buddhas through the cultivation of immeasurable merit. Therefore, it is manifest and not concealed.
Is it not the case that retributive wisdom (*vipākajñāna*) is that which manifests, and the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is that which is manifested?
Thus, the present passage demonstrates the Dharma-body by referring to that which is manifested. The subsequent passage demonstrates the immeasurable merit by referring to that which manifests.
As for this, Master Zhaogong’s commentary identifies the *dharmakāya* as the "body of empty space.
While this may be acceptable when speaking in terms of what is manifested, it ultimately fails to harmonize with the subsequent chapter, leaving practitioners without a clear direction.
Furthermore, if one speaks in terms of the *nirmāṇakāya*, its responding to the myriad things cannot be considered non-existent; yet [the commentary] also says, "it is heaven while being in heaven."

"To be human and yet human" is a principle of total fusion; it is not intended to establish the relationship between the fundamental and the derivative, nor to encourage cultivation through such designations.

Regarding "contemplative understanding": the single object of contemplation, which is the threefold truth, is called the Dharma-body; the contemplating subject consists of the three contemplations within a single mind.
This is called the *saṃbhogakāya*. Because the object and the contemplation are in perfect accord, enabling the arousal of great function, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya*.
[Section] Two: Showing the causes that give rise [to these bodies], in three parts. First, a general explanation.
It is born from immeasurable merit and wisdom.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The Dharma as it has been attained is adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom.

Here, "immeasurable merit" indicates his concentration (*samādhi*) and blessings (*puṇya*), while "immeasurable wisdom" indicates his insight (*prajñā*). Although that which is able to adorn [is] indeed...
Immeasurable. In a single word, concentration, wisdom, and merit are all fully present; there is nothing that is not complete therein.
○ Second, the specific explanation of the twelve [aspects]. First, they arise from the fivefold merits.
It arises from precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation.
The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) states: "The Buddha is endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body: first, unconditioned precept as the body of precept;
second, untainted pure dhyāna as the body of concentration; third, untainted wisdom as the body of wisdom; fourth, the three kinds of liberation as..."
The body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*). The five [factors] consisting of non-arising constitute the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*).

Regarding the practitioner of contemplation: at the time of contemplating the mind, when no perversions or errors enter, this is the body of precepts (*śīla-kāya*). When deluded thoughts subside and cease, this is the body of concentration (*samādhi-kāya*).
When things are perceived with perfect clarity, this is the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*). When the three delusions are thoroughly suppressed, this is the body of liberation. Originally...
It is neither born nor does it perish; it is the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation.
Second, it arises from the four immeasurables;
it arises from loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.

The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are fully explained as in the first section. First is the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). The mental state that is able to bestow happiness upon others is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).

When a practitioner, while in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), brings to mind sentient beings and wishes for them to obtain happiness, a state of concentration arises among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*);
this is called the "concentration of loving-kindness" (*maitrī-samādhi*). This is associated with loving-kindness; the mind is free from malice and free from resentment.
Free from resentment and affliction, it is well-cultivated and attained as liberation; vast and immeasurable, it pervades the ten directions.

This is called the immeasurable mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*). Second is the immeasurable mind of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*): the mind capable of uprooting the suffering of others is termed "compassion.

When a practitioner, within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), contemplates sentient beings undergoing suffering and brings them to liberation, [this arises] among the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).
This concentration is called the concentration of compassion (*karuṇā-samādhi*). It is associated with compassion; the mind is free from anger, resentment, malice, and vexation.

Through skillful cultivation, it is attained as liberation—vast, immeasurable, and pervading the ten directions. This is the immeasurable mind of compassion. Third is the immeasurable mind of joy (*muditā*).
To rejoice in others' attainment of happiness and to give rise to a heart of gladness is called joy. If the practitioner...

While in meditative concentration, when one contemplates sentient beings so that they may be free from suffering and attain happiness and joy, a state of concentration arises among the mental factors;
this is called the concentration of joy (*muditā-samādhi*). This is associated with joy, and the mind is without ill will, resentment, enmity, or affliction.
When one has skillfully cultivated and attained liberation that is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions, this is called the immeasurable mind of joy (*muditā*).
Fourth is the immeasurable mind of equanimity (*upekṣā*): when one possesses a mind free from both hatred and attachment toward others, it is termed equanimity.

When the practitioner, within meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), brings to mind sentient beings who are objects of hatred or love and causes them to attain equanimity, [this arises] among the mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).

This concentration is called the concentration of equanimity (*upekṣā-samādhi*). It is associated with equanimity; the mind is without anger, without resentment, without enmity, and without affliction.
Having skillfully cultivated it, one attains liberation; it is vast, immeasurable, and pervades the ten directions. This is the immeasurable mind of equanimity.
Third, it arises from the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*):
it arises from the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience and gentleness, diligent application of energy, meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi,
extensive learning, and wisdom.

Master Zhao said: "Dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas; samādhi refers to the four formless concentrations (ārūpya-samāpatti); liberation refers to the eight liberations (vimokṣa); and samāpatti refers to the three samāpattis.
These are all specific practices of the perfection of meditation (dhyāna-pāramitā). 'All' refers to the aforementioned six perfections. Pāramitā is the Qin term for 'reaching the other shore.
The 'other shore' is the shore of true reality (bhūta-lakṣaṇa). It refers to the various practices cultivated after attaining non-arising (anutpāda)."
All things are in accord with the true mark (dharmatā); there is no further discrimination.
○ Fourth, arising from skillful means.
Arising from skillful means.
As explained above.
○ Five: Arising from the Six Supernormal Powers.
It arises from the six supernormal powers.
Master Zhao said: "From the seventh stage upward, one possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Unless these six supernormal powers are employed to manifest unconditioned transformations, it is impossible to perfect the ultimate body."
6. Arising from the Threefold Knowledge (*traividyā*).
It arises from the Threefold Knowledge.

Master Zao said: "The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*) constitute the Threefold Knowledge."
7. It arises from the factors of enlightenment;
it arises from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
8. It arises from tranquility and insight.
It arises from *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

*Śamatha* is concentration (*samādhi*), and *vipaśyanā* is wisdom (*prajñā*). This interpretation has been established since ancient times. Yet, it was not known that there are three types of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*:
gradual, non-sequential, and sudden-perfect (*candian*). These encompass a vast scope and extend far and wide; were it not for those who are mature and experienced...
One studies, yet none are able to penetrate it; students ought to devote their whole hearts to this.
○ Ninth: It arises from the Ten Powers and so forth;
it arises from the Ten Powers, the Four Fearlessnesses, and the Eighteen Unshared Dharmas.
10. It arises from abandoning evil and giving rise to good;
it arises from abandoning all unwholesome dharmas and gathering all wholesome dharmas.
11. It arises from reality.
Arising from reality.
Twelve: arising from non-negligence;
arising from non-negligence.
III. Third, the general conclusion:
From such immeasurable pure dharmas, the body of the Tathāgata is born. III.
Third, the general conclusion returning to the source: the root of illness.
"O virtuous ones! Those who wish to attain the Buddha-body and sever all the illnesses of sentient beings should resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.
(4) Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Benefit."
In this manner, the elder Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma to those who had come to inquire after his illness as was appropriate for each,
causing countless thousands of people to all resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Now, although the myriad dharmas are numerous, they consist of nothing more than their nature (xing) and characteristics (xiang). The divergence of these natures and characteristics arises from awakening and delusion.
Viewed from the perspective of the single nature of the Dharma-body, there is no difference between sentient beings and Buddhas;

viewed from the perspective of delusion and awakening, or defilement and purity, there is no lack of distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas. It must be understood that while the nature of the Dharma-body is fundamentally identical, [the states of] defilement...

Is there not a difference between the characteristics of purity and delusion, awakening and ignorance? Therefore, speaking from the perspective of the *dharmakāya*, it is appropriate to say that sentient beings are themselves Buddhas;
it is also appropriate to say that Buddhas are themselves sentient beings.

However, speaking from the perspective of defilement and purity, delusion and awakening, the separation between the rising and sinking of sentient beings and Buddhas is no less than the vast distance between heaven and earth. This being so—
Those who revere and serve this Way—how could they not overturn delusion to achieve awakening, and wash away defilement to achieve purity?
Nevertheless, although one overturns delusion to achieve awakening, awakening does not exist apart from delusion; rather, it is through delusion itself that awakening is realized.
Likewise, in washing away defilement to achieve purity, purity does not exist as something distinct from defilement; rather, it is through defilement itself that purity is established.
It is as follows: the body that is the fruit of suffering for sentient beings arises from immeasurable bondage, ignorance, and delusion;
yet the Dharma-body of the Buddhas takes that very bondage, ignorance, and delusion and transforms them into merit and wisdom.
The body that is the retribution of suffering for sentient beings arises from the bondage of greed, desire, distraction, ignorance, and the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas is such that it takes even lustful desire as its purity and so forth.
The bodies of sentient beings, which are the retribution for suffering, arise from stinginess, violation of precepts, anger, laziness, distraction, and ignorance.
The Dharma-body of all Buddhas, however, takes even stinginess as the basis for the arising of giving and so forth. At the time of their delusion...
For the sake of sentient beings, they dwell on this shore of the six corruptions.
They regard stinginess, the violation of precepts, and so forth as one of the great objects of worldly pleasure, believing that without these, the affairs of the world could not be accomplished.

They do not realize that such pleasure is the cause of suffering and delusion is the root of defilement; there is nothing more extreme than this for sinking into the ocean of birth and death. Only when they attain awakening...
Yet, by reversing their delusions and regarding that which is defiled as pure, they become serene beyond the myriad burdens and attain liberation within the realm of the three emptinesses;
thus, they cannot contain their boundless joy. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said:
"Lust, anger, and ignorance are themselves liberation; do not seek liberation apart from lust, anger, and ignorance. Furthermore,
It is said: "The sixty-two views constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata; the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all the Pure Land;
birth-and-death is itself nirvāṇa; afflictions are themselves bodhi. All such scriptural passages represent awakening within delusion."
This is clear evidence that defilement itself is purity. Those who read this sutra should not fail to apply themselves to it with diligence.
Part Three: Explanation of the "Chapter on the Disciples. Section Two: First, explaining the title of the chapter.
The third chapter of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, titled "The Disciples" (*Śrāvaka-parivarta*), is named here according to its essential meaning.
In full, it should be entitled "The Chapter on the Disciples’ Inquiry into the Illness. This follows the precedent of the subsequent "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas" (*Bodhisattva-parivarta*).
One should also add the two characters "inquire after his illness" (*vyādhipṛcchā*). Their absence from the text is an abbreviation by the translator.

Regarding this inquiry after the illness, it would have been more appropriate for the Tathāgata to dispatch Mañjuśrī immediately, so that both guest and host might excel and their interaction be like the rhythmic clashing of a mallet upon a sounding block.
That he instead first dispatched a disciple, a Bodhisattva, was not only to manifest the superior eloquence and talent of Vimalakīrti, but also to highlight [the qualities of] Mañjuśrī.

This remote region is capable of receiving such a response. As for the "esoteric intent," it is precisely because this sutra is taught within the Vaipulya (fangděng) that it appropriately rebukes the partial and disparages the small, while extolling the Great and praising the Perfect.

Therefore, it describes how the Tathāgata first dispatched his disciples and bodhisattvas, causing them to recount their own words as they were being reprimanded; this serves to manifest that their eloquence and discernment are inconceivable. Thus, he proceeds to narrate the events.
The inclusion of the preaching of the Dharma interspersed therein is the ingenious artistry of those who compiled the sūtras.
○ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text has two parts. First, the elder’s reflection.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself as he lay ill upon his bed: "The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate; will he not deign to show me his pity? [Section Two:
The Tathāgata Sends Messengers to Inquire] [Part Three: The Initial Dispatching of Disciples, consisting of ten sections] [Section One: The Initial Dispatching of Śāriputra, the Honored One]
There are two [parts]. First, the Tathāgata’s command and dispatch:
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately told Śāriputra, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.

When the elder was manifesting his illness in Vaiśālī, he was simultaneously in a state of quiescence and illumination; likewise, while the Tathāgata was on the high seat in the Āmrapālī Grove, he was simultaneously [in that same state].

Illumination is quiescence. Furthermore, when the elder’s mind reflects, it is illumination that is eternally quiescent; when the Tathāgata knows his intent, it is quiescence that is eternally illuminating.
Although the functions of quiescence and illumination alternate between ceasing and arising, the nature of the *dharmakāya* is one suchness without a second suchness.
This is what is meant by "one body and one wisdom," and the same applies to the powers and fearlessnesses. Though they do not engage in conceptual thought—

If this is so when one merely intends to do so, how much more so when one contemplates it and strikes [the bell]? Having struck it, there is an immediate response. Therefore, as soon as one contemplates it, it is dispatched as swiftly as a drumstick striking a drum.
○ Second, the Venerable’s firm refusal, part two: first, a general refusal on account of incapacity.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Within the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, the untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of the various Arhats surpasses the mundane wisdom (*laukika-jñāna*) of Bodhisattvas.
Within the Mahāyāna Dharma, the Bodhisattvas excel in both matters. Now, using the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, [the Buddha] clarifies the greatness [of the Bodhisattva]."
Because [Śāriputra] was junior, he was summoned first. Among the disciples, Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom; therefore, he was summoned first.
That he was summoned despite knowing him to be incapable was intended to manifest Vimalakīrti’s extraordinary eloquence and to inspire the assembled multitude.
Furthermore, that others were also summoned was intended to allow each to demonstrate their own excellence.
Furthermore, it should be understood that his eloquence and wisdom were boundless.
II. A detailed explanation of the reasons for this, in two parts: first, an account of the event of his refutation.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, while I was sitting in meditation beneath a tree in a forest.
Master Sengzhao said: "As for the meditative seclusion of the Dharma-body, both form and spirit are extinguished. The Way transcends ordinary realms and lies beyond the reach of sight and hearing;
how could it again manifest within the triple world to cultivate the mind for the sake of concentration?
Śāriputra still possessed a physical body born of worldly retribution, as well as mental faculties resulting from worldly retribution; therefore, he regarded the human realm as a source of turmoil."

Yet you sit in meditation beneath a tree, unable to leave no trace of either spirit or body; thus, this censure was incurred. Generally, the purpose behind the arising of such censure is to bring about great benefit;
how could it be that the mind dwells upon "self" and "other," or on right and wrong?
II. Narrating His Refutation in Three Parts. First, the general refutation:
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "Śāriputra, it is not necessarily sitting in this manner that constitutes 'sitting in meditation'."
Now, as for the place where Śāriputra sat in tranquil meditation, it was truly the manifestation of body and mind within the triple world.
Why is this? For the triple world is the dwelling place of this body and the objective realm of this mind.
Sentient beings give rise to afflictions because of the six sense objects, and they summon birth and death because of those afflictions; the origins of these matters are ancient.
Therefore, those who wish to stem its current and block its source must first regulate the body so that it is neither too low nor too high;

regulate the breath so that it is neither too constricted nor too slippery; and regulate the mind so that it is neither too agitated nor too sunken. When entering, one begins with the coarse and proceeds to the subtle;

when emerging, one begins with the subtle and proceeds to the coarse. This is the primary gateway for entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and yet it is the sudden and perfect method of concentration.

Although one relies upon this gateway, one need not be restricted by it; rather, one manifests body and mind within the triple world precisely because a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching has first been able to awaken to the fact that the Dharma-body is inherently present as one's own nature.

If one can maintain this realization, then there is nowhere that is not the Dharma-body—whether one is in formal meditation is permissible, and whether one is not in formal meditation is also permissible. Regarding the three...
It is acceptable for the body and mind to manifest within the three realms; it is also acceptable for the body and mind not to manifest within the three realms, as Vimalakīrti has said:
"To manifest while not manifesting; to manifest without abandoning [the world]. Furthermore, there is no specific posture that is not itself *yǎnzà* (seated meditation).
Yet Śāriputra merely regards this very body as a burden; by explaining it away, one realizes it is not a burden at all. This is so.
This is because he was humbled by the Great Being.
II. A detailed explanation of the six [points]. First, showing through non-manifestation:
Now, as for "sitting in meditation," not manifesting body or mind within the three realms—this is sitting in meditation.
As for the meditative seclusion of the Dharma-body, it takes the serene light as its meditation bench.
At that moment, it extends vertically through the three periods of time and pervades horizontally throughout the ten directions. Body is mind; mind is body; body is the seat.
"Sitting" is the very body itself. It is the stilling of the traces of arising and ceasing; it is the severance of the footprints of coming and going.
It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness. This is what constitutes true sitting in meditation. Śāriputra has not yet awakened to this;

he merely regards his physical form as a burden and his mental consciousness as a vexation. To necessarily manifest one's body and mind within the three realms—this is what constitutes sitting in meditation.
This is not true sitting in meditation.
Second, to demonstrate that which is non-manifest yet manifest:
without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation, yet manifesting all dignified postures—this is true sitting in meditation.

Now, one who enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) possesses the mind; one who manifests various modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) possesses the body. In ordinary beings, body and mind are conflated into one;
thus, the body serves as the servant of the mind, while the mind grows weary for the sake of the body. Are not body and mind, within the three realms (*tridhātu*), truly laboring?
For the followers of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*), body and mind are extinguished and return to non-existence; therefore, their minds can indeed be made identical [to that of the Buddhas].
Like extinguished ashes, the physical form may indeed be likened to withered wood. Entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*), one becomes identical to empty space;
merging into this state, there is no further function. For those ancients who entered this absorption, body and mind were vast and open;

in the mere twinkling of an eye, they could pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of years, or even eighty-four thousand *kalpas*. While in such absorption, the body is sustained by the mind, and its blood—

The pulse is thereby regulated; the beard and hair grow therefrom. Upon emerging from meditative absorption, the mind does not unite with the body, and one necessarily manifests the eighteen supernatural transformations.
One then performs self-incineration by means of the fire of *samādhi*, after which one returns to emptiness and non-existence to enter the realm of no-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-dhātu*).
Only then does one attain the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*). Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas, together with all...
The Tathāgata realizes that the mind is the essence of the body, while the body is the manifestation of the mind. Although essence and manifestation differ, they are one in their inconceivability.
Because they are one in inconceivability, from the substance of the non-arising and non-ceasing samādhi, the function of manifold majestic deportment flourishes.
Now, the non-arising and non-ceasing samādhi is quiescence; yet, manifesting all forms of deportment is the arising of function from that very substance. Thus...
It is not precluded that within stillness there is constant movement; by realizing the function as returning to the essence, it is not precluded that within movement there is constant stillness.
Thus, essence and function share a single source, and stillness and movement are non-dual; in this way, meditative extinction and formal deportment have never been different.
Third, it is shown that one abandons without abandoning;
not abandoning the dharmas of the Path, yet manifesting the affairs of an ordinary person—this is "sitting in meditation" (*yàn-zuò*).

Master Zhaō said: "The followers of the Lesser Vehicle are obstructed by birth and death, and thus cannot harmonize with the light of the world. The Great Being [the Bodhisattva] regards the beautiful and the foul as equal."
The essential point is this: since the secular and the monastic are viewed as one, one may be an ordinary person all day long and yet abide in the Way all day long.
Vimalakīrti’s maintaining a household is precisely an instance of this.
4. Showing that dwelling is not dwelling:
the mind dwells neither within nor without; this is called sitting in meditation (*yansuo*).
For the true mind is all-pervasive and does not reside in either the internal or the external. Ordinary people are invariably deluded, thinking it resides within the physical body.

Yet the six faculties gallop about, inevitably攀缘 (pānyuán—clinging to and following) that which lies beyond the six sense-objects. This is what is meant by "the gathering of conditions causes internal agitation;
rushing outward, they flee in wild abandon. That these lead to afflictions and to birth-and-death is entirely due to this.

When those of the Two Vehicles shatter afflictions and transcend birth-and-death, they must necessarily close off the six emotions and withdraw the external into the internal; this is called "returning."
The delusory returns to the Real. Yet, does not the Bodhisattva likewise return from the delusory to the Real?

Because he is able to realize that it is neither internal nor external, and that both internal and external are entirely Real, when he darkens his mind within the Dharma-realm, he dwells in neither the internal nor the external.
He thus takes empty space as his meditation seat; to settle the mind in this way is what constitutes true sitting in meditation.
5. Showing cultivation while remaining unmoved:
To remain unmoved amidst all views while practicing the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*)—this is true sitting in meditation (*pratisaṃlayanam*).
Now, as for the sixty-two views, these are those held by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who, being deluded regarding the right path, practice a deviant path. Thirty...
Regarding the seven categories of the Path (mārga): the Tathāgata employs the Right Path to destroy the heterodox paths.

Nevertheless, the Path advances according to understanding, and as the four capacities differ, there are those who cultivate the category of the Path of Analytical Emptiness (*vibhāga-śūnyatā-mārga*) and, by shaking off and destroying all views within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), attain entry into *nirvāṇa*;
this is the understanding and practice of the Hīnayāna of the Tripiṭaka. Furthermore, there are those who cultivate the category of the Path of Immediate Emptiness (*sākṣāt-śūnyatā-mārga*) and yet...

To move without breaking through the various views within the realm and thereby attain entry into *nirvāṇa* is the understanding and practice (*jñāna-caryā*) common to the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

One cultivates the stages of emptiness first, the provisional next, and the Middle Way last; having broken [through delusions], one then realizes [the truth], and having realized it, one then fuses [with it].

To thus attain entry into Great *Nirvāṇa* is the understanding and practice that sequentially reveals the Middle Way of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*). One cultivates [the realization of] "immediacy" (*ji*).

The Chapter on Emptiness, the Provisional, and the Middle Way: To penetrate the sixty-two views, to fully employ inherent evil to give rise to cultivated evil, such that cultivated evil is itself inherent evil;

for inherent evil to be interfused so that there is no dharma that does not proceed toward it, spontaneously encompassing the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm without moving or breaking—this is the Perfect and Sudden Teaching that enables one to enter unsurpassed nirvana.

This is the most excellent stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā*). Now, for this reason, one may employ the *paryudāsa-pratiṣedha* (negation by way of exclusion) or the *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (negation by way of simple negation).
Regarding the teachings of the Vaipulya period, whether they lead to progress or not depends upon the capacities of sentient beings; they cannot be constrained by a single uniform standard.
6. To demonstrate severance through non-severance:
not severing afflictions (*kleśa*) while entering *nirvāṇa*—this is the practice of formal sitting (*pratisaṃlayana*).
Afflictions are the obstacles to awakening (*bodhi*), and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is the bondage to *nirvāṇa*. This has been so from of old.
Thus, it has long been the established tradition that one must sever afflictions (*kleśa*) to realize *bodhi*, and transcend birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to realize *nirvāṇa*.
Now, what Vimalakīrti teaches is that his Way differs from the common stream;
he says that one enters *nirvāṇa* without severing afflictions, because the nature of afflictions is empty, and the nature of *nirvāṇa* is likewise [empty].
Emptiness. Emptiness does not obstruct emptiness; therefore, there is no need to sever the emptiness of afflictions in order to enter the emptiness of nirvana.
This can be spoken of as the Way of Essential Emptiness (*tǐkōng*). As for what is called the Middle Way and Nirvana, it is like the moon beyond the clouds.
Birth-and-death cannot obstruct nirvāṇa, and bodhi cannot destroy birth-and-death. Bodhi and nirvāṇa lie far away in the stage of fruition;
they are realized through successive cultivation and are manifested distinctly. This may be spoken of as the path of sequential progression (*xingbu*).
Now, to say that one enters nirvāṇa without severing the afflictions (*kleśa*) must refer to the unchanging nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is able to adapt [to conditions].

When one cultivates evil afflictions through conditioned defilements, awakening to cultivation as being identical to nature means that afflictions following conditions are themselves the unchanging essence.
Pointing to this unchanging essence is what is called *nirvāṇa*; it is simply another name for the "evil of nature.
Thus, afflictions are themselves *nirvāṇa*, and there is no need to seek *nirvāṇa* apart from or outside of afflictions. This is...
This is true sitting in meditation. III.
Summary: If one can sit in this manner, it is approved by the Buddha.
The Buddha possesses five seals. Four seals characterize the Hīnayāna, wherein saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are distinct.

One seal characterizes the Mahāyāna, which is the single true reality (*ekalakṣaṇa*). What is now said—that the Buddha can use the seal of the true reality of all phenomena to seal all Mahāyāna teachings—refers precisely to "entering nirvāṇa without severing the afflictions."
Third, regarding the conclusion of his inability [to respond]:
At that time, World-Honored One, when I heard these words, I remained silent and ceased speaking; I was unable to offer a reply.
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.

Regarding the practitioner who resolves through contemplation (*guan-jie*): they contemplate that the mind is itself emptiness, such that not even the slightest trace of conceptual attachment remains; this is precisely what it means to "not manifest body or mind within the three realms.

Nevertheless, although it is emptiness, it does not preclude the provisional (*jia*); one does not lose the rules of conduct for the four modes of deportment, which is precisely what it means to "manifest majestic demeanor without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation.
Although it is provisional, one practices all the dharmas of the various paths, tracing the current back to its source. It does not...

That which obstructs is precisely the provisional (prajñapti); it manifests as the affairs of ordinary beings. This mind is precisely emptiness (śūnyatā); when sought within, without, or in between, it cannot be found.
Thus, this mind does not abide within, nor does it exist without. This mind is precisely the middle (madhyama);
by simultaneously negating both extremes, it is unmoved by any views. By simultaneously illuminating both extremes, one practices the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma).
Thus, by thoroughly comprehending the single thought-moment, one realizes that what is cultivated as evil is precisely inherent evil;
this is to enter nirvana without severing the afflictions.
○ Second, the dispatching of the Venerable Maudgalyāyana. Part One: The Tathāgata’s command to dispatch him.
The Buddha told Mahāmaudgalyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Master Shi [Kumārajīva] said: "Maudgalyāyana is a Brahmin surname; his personal name is Kolita. Kolita is the name of a tree deity;
because he was obtained through seeking that deity, he was named after it. He possessed great wisdom from birth, hence the name."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana was foremost in the power of supernatural faculties.
[Section Two: The Venerable’s Firm Refusal. First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I am not capable of going there to inquire after his illness."
II. Explaining the reason for this, in two parts. First, an account of the incident of his refutation.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, I entered the great city of Vaiśālī and, amidst the lanes and alleys, preached the Dharma for the lay devotees.
Generally, there are two meanings to the turning of the wheel of Dharma: first, to transfer the Dharma realized by oneself into the minds of others;
second, to skillfully manifest it to people according to their individual capacities and inclinations. Regarding the realization attained by Maudgalyāyana:

he had already destroyed the afflictions of views and thought, had already transcended the realm of birth and death, possessed all-encompassing wisdom, and had realized true emptiness. If one were to transfer this realization into the minds of others, although...
One cannot attain the emptiness of the Mahāyāna. Is it not because one’s own realization of the emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle has entered the minds of people?
Thus, one speaks according to the Dharma: "The Dharma has no sentient beings; it is the Dharma that is free from the defilements of sentient beings.

This must be shown to people through skillful means (*upāya*), according to their respective capacities and inclinations. That is, by means of the Dharma appropriate for a layperson's practice—whether it be a person who abides by the five precepts, or...

The ten wholesome actions lead to rebirth in the heavens; the giving that breaks through stinginess, the precepts that depart from desire, and the fundamental dhyānas—if one does not know that all these involve the failure to forget the various marks of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span, then not only can they not lead one toward the Mahāyāna, one will not even be able to escape the cycle of birth and death in the mundane world.
How could such things be sufficient to be called "teaching according to the capacity"?
"Are you preaching the Dharma?
[End of section]. II. Narrating his refutation, in two parts. First, the general refutation:
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Mahāmaudgalyāyana, when preaching the Dharma to lay householders..."
It should be as you, O virtuous one, have said.
Part Two: A Detailed Explanation has two sections. First, pointing to the essence of the Dharma taught:
"Now, those who preach the Dharma should preach it in accordance with the Dharma."
"According to the Dharma" refers to the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of that which is expressed. The essence of the Dharma is pure, as serene as empty space, free from all faults, and ineffable.
If one must speak of it, one should speak according to the Dharma; as it is said: "O you who preach the Dharma..."
There is no speaking and no showing; those who listen to the Dharma neither hear nor attain it—this statement is correct.
II. Clarifying that the Dharma is free from all faults (in four parts): A. Directly clarifying the various faults (in two parts): 1. Clarifying freedom by way of what is abandoned.
The Dharma has no sentient beings, for it is free from the defilement of sentient beings. The Dharma has no self, for it is free from the defilement of the self.
The Dharma has no life-span, for it is free from birth and death. The Dharma has no person, for its past and future limits are severed.

Sentient beings (*sattva*), self (*ātman*), life-span (*jīva*), and person (*pudgala*)—these are called the four marks. These constitute the root of the sixty-two views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
If one can be free from these four marks, then all views are abandoned. Sentient beings are formed by the defilement of five kinds of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
since phenomena (*dharma*) are already free from defilement, the mark of sentient beings is fundamentally non-existent. As for the "self," it is a master presided over by false conceptualization.
It is by name that it is so called. Since the Dharma is already free from the defilement of self, the delusive marks of a self are fundamentally non-existent.
"Life-span" is named for its abiding between one birth and one death; since the Dharma is already free from birth and death, the mark of life-span is fundamentally non-existent.

A "person" is named for the continuity between the two limits of before and after; since the Dharma has already severed the two limits of before and after, [the mark of personhood is fundamentally non-existent].
Thus, the personal characteristics of dharmas are fundamentally non-existent; this clarifies "detachment" by way of that which is detached from.
II. Clarifying detachment by way of that which detaches, in four parts. First, clarifying that dharmas lack all characteristics.
The Dharma is eternally quiescent, for it extinguishes all marks. The Dharma is free from marks, for it has no object of perception.
The Dharma has no names, for it transcends speech. The Dharma cannot be expounded, for it is free from applied and sustained thought. The Dharma has no form or appearance, for it is like empty space.
Dharmas are free from conceptual proliferation, for they are ultimately empty. Dharmas have no sense of "mine," for they are devoid of what belongs to a self.

Dharmas are without discrimination, for they are free from all consciousnesses. Dharmas have no counterpart, for they do not exist in mutual dependence. Dharmas do not belong to causes, for they do not abide within conditions.
The essence of the Dharma is fundamentally quiescent, profound, and wondrously luminous. It is like a mass of great flames that no phenomena can reach;

it is without subject and without object, severed from all conditions and sensory objects. It cannot be summoned by any names, for it has cut off all various forms of speech, thought, and observation.
Since false delusions are fundamentally non-existent, the source of verbal expression is primordially detached. Thus, the Dharma...

The nature is fundamentally empty; therefore, its essence is like space. All phenomena (*dharma*) are ultimately empty; therefore, they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). The dharma-nature transcends all relativity;
therefore, there is neither subject nor object. The dharma-nature is not consciousness; therefore, it is without discrimination. The dharma-nature is the sovereign;

therefore, it has no equal or counterpart. The wondrous nature is innate; therefore, it is not produced by causes and conditions. This explains "detachment" by way of that which is capable of detachment.
II. Clarifying the Reality of the Essence of Dharmas:

Dharmas are identical to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), for they enter into all phenomena. Dharmas accord with suchness (*tathatā*), for there is nothing to which they accord. Dharmas abide in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Because it is unmoved by any extremes, phenomena are identical to the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); this means that phenomena are themselves the dharma-nature. Regarding "entering all phenomena," "entering" means pervading;
it is like the entry of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*'s "dharma-realm body" into the thoughts and minds of all sentient beings. This refers to the dharma-nature.
That is all phenomena (*dharmas*). All phenomena are themselves the *dharmatā*. This is because phenomena accord with *tathatā* (suchness) by not acceding to anything.
This refers to true suchness and *dharmatā*, which can accord with defiled and pure conditions to fully produce the ten *dharmadhātus*.

Because it accords with conditions while remaining unchanging, and because it remains unchanged while acceding to conditions, phenomena always accord with suchness and do not change; they do not follow after defilement.
This is the transformation produced by pure conditions. As for "the reality-limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*), it refers to the true, eternal reality-limit of the Middle Way.
On the ground of the principle of the reality-limit, one is central while being at the extremes; since there are fundamentally no two extremes, it cannot be moved by any extremes.
Third, it further clarifies signlessness (*animitta*).
Phenomena (*dharma*) are without movement or agitation because they do not rely upon the six sense objects (*ṣadviṣaya*). Phenomena have no coming or going because they never abide.

This clarifies that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is eternally abiding. Indeed, where there is movement and agitation, there is arising and ceasing; where there is arising and ceasing, there is movement...
"Shaking" occurs because there is conceptual differentiation based on sense objects (*viṣaya*). Since [the mind] does not rely upon the six sense objects, how could there be any shaking?
"Coming and going" occurs because there is something in which to abide. Since dharmas fundamentally do not abide, how could there be any coming and going?
Fourth, it is directly stated that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*).
Phenomena accord with emptiness, follow signlessness, and correspond to wishlessness (*apranihita*). Phenomena are free from the beautiful and the ugly; phenomena are without increase or decrease;

phenomena are without arising or ceasing; phenomena have no place of return. Phenomena transcend the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind; phenomena are without high or low; phenomena are eternally abiding.
It is immovable. The Dharma is free from all modes of contemplation;
all characteristics such as beauty and ugliness, increase and decrease, and so forth, arise solely from false conceptualizations of signs.
Since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is true reality, how could there be any false signs at all?
Second, it is explained that the Dharma is ineffable.
Only Mahāmaudgalyāyana [understood this]: "The characteristics of dharmas are thus; how could they be expressed?
All dharmas are reality, free from all delusive marks. They have no names and no characters; the path of speech is cut off; there is no speaking and no..."
It is said: to speak while being free from all applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*)—if one wishes to speak of this, there is no way to set a word to it.
Part Two: Explaining that which is unspeakable yet spoken. First, the Dharma.
Now, as for those who preach the Dharma, there is no preaching and no demonstration; as for those who listen to the Dharma, there is no hearing and no attainment.
A Great Sūtra says: "Arising within arising cannot be described; non-arising within arising cannot be described; arising within non-arising cannot be described;
non-arising within non-arising cannot be described. Since these cannot be described, they also cannot be conceived. This is by means of the four...
The principles elucidated by the teachings are all ultimately inexpressible. Yet it is also said that because there are causes and conditions, they can nonetheless be expressed.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The Buddha-seed arises from conditions; for this reason, the One Vehicle is taught. Although it is inexpressible, [it is taught through such means].

One must speak in accordance with the Dharma. The Dharma is fundamentally without speech and without demonstration; therefore, the speaker should likewise take this absence of speech and demonstration as their speech and demonstration.
The Dharma is fundamentally without hearing and without attainment; therefore, the listener should likewise take this absence of hearing and attainment as their hearing and attainment.
In this way, although one speaks and demonstrates all day long, there is fundamentally no speaking or demonstrating. All day long...
One hears it daily, yet fundamentally there is no hearing. This is what is meant by "speaking when silent and being silent when speaking";
it is the absence of obstruction within the Great Gate of Giving.
II. The Parable.
It is as if a conjured person were to preach the Dharma for a conjured person. One should establish this intention when preaching the Dharma:
the conjured person represents the preacher, who fundamentally has nothing to show; the conjured person represents the listener, who fundamentally has nothing to hear or attain.
If one can establish such an intention regarding what is shown and what is heard and attained, then this exposition of the sutra will not fail to accord with reality.
Legitimacy. This constitutes speaking in accordance with the Dharma.
○ Fourth, showing the essentials of preaching the Dharma, in two parts. First, discerning capacities and exercising compassion:

One should understand that the faculties of sentient beings have both sharp and dull aspects; being skilled in knowledge and vision, one remains free from all obstructions and, with a heart of great compassion...
Praise the Mahāyāna.

Indeed, spiritual capacities vary between sharp and dull, and teachings may be either progressive or regressive. What is great should not be taught as small; what is small should not be taught as great.
What is extensive should not be taught as concise; what is concise should not be taught as extensive. First, one must be skilled in knowing and seeing without error; thereafter—

He employs great compassion without weariness; knowing the proper time and the opportune moment, whether his teaching is partial or complete, his skillful means ultimately lead all back to the Mahāyāna.
This is the great occasion and locus for the Tathāgata and Bodhisattvas to expound the Dharma.
Second, one should reflect upon repaying the Buddha’s kindness.
Reflecting upon repaying the Buddha’s kindness means not severing the Three Jewels, and only thereafter preaching the Dharma.

The Buddha’s kindness is difficult to repay; it can only be repaid by preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings, thereby ensuring that the Three Jewels flourish in the world and that sentient beings attain the Right [Path].
Faith is unbroken; it can be requited.
○ Third, the benefit gained from hearing the Dharma:
When Vimalakīrti spoke this Dharma, eight hundred lay devotees (gṛhapati) resolved their minds upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
I take heart.
Third, I conclude that I am incapable;
I lack such eloquence. Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
Regarding the Dharma spoken by the layman, it was established in response to his specific ailment;
thus, using Maudgalyāyana’s internal realization of the "lesser emptiness" (*parīttā-śūnyatā*) to refute the "lesser teachings" on humans and devas he had propounded was entirely appropriate.

Alternatively, whether one proceeds toward the Shared (*pāṭalā*), the Distinct (*bhinnā*), or the Perfect (*pariniṣpannā*) [teachings], there is likewise nothing that would not be appropriate. Now, this is discussed in relation to the eight hundred laymen.

Having heard the Dharma and obtained its benefit, one has already resolved upon the unsurpassed, perfect, and equal Bodhicitta; it is therefore appropriate that one be categorized as belonging to the Perfect and Sudden (Yuantun) teaching.

Regarding "contemplation through understanding": one contemplates that a single thought-moment is identical to the dharma-nature of the three truths, following along with True Suchness (Tathatā), which is neither changing nor...

He transmigrates [to enlightenment] and dwells in this true, eternal, and ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), unmoved by the two extremes. He is tranquil and motionless, transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations.

To contemplate in accordance with suchness and to speak in accordance with suchness—this is what it means to mindfully repay the Buddha’s kindness and to perpetuate the Three Jewels as a single essence.

Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Volume Four Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Volume Five Authored by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi, Mount Tiantai [The following is the beginning of the fifth volume: Furthermore, as for the statement that "the body is not-self," this refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Why? Because these five aggregates are subject to arising and ceasing; they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Therefore, it is said that the body is not-self. Moreover, the body is composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*): earth, water, fire, and wind. These four elements are each distinct and do not constitute a single, unified self. Since they are merely a collection of various conditions, there is no permanent, sovereign self to be found within them. For this reason, it is said that the body is not-self. Furthermore, the body is like a house constructed from various materials;

it has no inherent master or owner. It is merely a temporary aggregation of causes and conditions. Since it lacks a permanent essence, it is called non-self. Thus, one should contemplate the body as being devoid of a self. By contemplating the body as non-self, one can sever attachment to the physical form and give rise to the mind of renunciation. This is the meaning of the teaching that the body is not-self. [End of Volume Five]

"One should practice alms-gathering in successive order; it is not appropriate to avoid the wealthy and go only to the poor.

All these are for the purpose of abiding in the Dharma of equality.
Second, it is shown that one accepts by way of non-acceptance:
for the sake of not eating, one should practice begging for food; for the sake of destroying the mark of composite things, one should take morsel-food. For the sake of not... [text continues]
Because of this [reception], you should accept that food.
Now, the body of *dharmatā* is equal in measure to empty space and truly has no need for food; however, the form-body (*rūpakāya*) is dependent, and thus it must practice begging.
When one contemplates the true mark of the body, it is seen that although it is dependent, it is fundamentally without dependence; one views the dependent through non-dependence.

"Wait. Although he begged for food, he still did not eat it. Now, when one views those who have dependencies through the lens of non-dependency, then even urgency appears as leisure, and existence appears as non-existence;
one does not take greed and its like as the fundamental principle. Master Kumārajīva said:

"The characteristic of combination is *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food), which is one of the four kinds of nutriment. Dēng said: "Edible food is indeed formed by the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)."
This serves as its condition. The body depends upon this food; thus, through the harmony of the external four great elements, it sustains the harmony of the internal four great elements.
If one contemplates the true mark of the body, there is fundamentally no such harmony. That there is fundamentally no harmony is the meaning of "dissolving harmony.
To take food in this manner is to take it by means of non-acceptance, thereby making it an act of acceptance. Furthermore—
It does not take greed and the like as its primary principle. Thus, one begs for food precisely because of non-receiving;
this receiving of non-receiving is what constitutes right reception (*samyak-parigraha*). Within that which is truly unreceivable, I therefore receive it.
Hence it is said: "One should receive that food."
III. Showing the Method for Not Accepting [Gifts]. Part Two: First, showing the general characteristics.
One enters the village with the perception of it as an empty hamlet.
"Village" (聚落) refers to a rural settlement. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states: "Luo (落) means a dwelling; because people gather and reside there, it is called a village."

There are villages, hamlets, and settlements; furthermore, there are internal villages, which are the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and external villages, which are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
As the "Chapter on Emptiness" in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* states: "This body is false and deceptive, like an empty village."
The village of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) is where the bandits of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) dwell. Each remains in its own place, and none knows the others.

Now, it is said that one should contemplate them with the perception of an empty village (*śūnyagrāma-saṃjñā*). This means one should contemplate the six internal sense bases as being like an empty village.

Entering the village, one should contemplate the six external objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) as being like an empty village. This demonstrates the general characteristic of receiving what is not received. If [it continues] below...
The text states that "seeing forms is like being blind," which specifically demonstrates this point; within each and every phrase, both meanings are simultaneously present.
Second, the distinct characteristics are shown:
the forms seen are like those of the blind; the sounds heard are like echoes; the fragrances smelled are like the wind; and the food [eaten...]

One does not discriminate regarding flavors; one experiences all contacts as they are realized by wisdom. One knows that all phenomena are like illusory appearances, lacking intrinsic nature and lacking extrinsic nature;
they were originally non-arising, and thus now there is no cessation.
This specifically demonstrates how one enters a village by means of the characteristics of an empty village. The forms perceived are but a single speck within the village;
being like those who are blind and so forth refers to the individual sense organs within the characteristics of the empty village. The subsequent sections follow this pattern.

Having seen forms as those who are blind and so forth, hearing sounds and echoes, smelling fragrances and winds, tasting flavors without discrimination, and experiencing touch through wisdom and realization.

To know that the characteristics of dharmas are like illusions is to cause one to experience the various dharmas of the six sense-objects through non-reception, so that they all return to right reception (*samyak-samādhi*).
Why is this? It is because when entering a village to beg for food, the six faculties inevitably traverse the six sense-objects;
if one does not realize and penetrate that the village is an empty collection and thus enter the village, one will inevitably give rise to conceptual discrimination conditioned by those objects.
To take what is received as being truly received is to fall entirely into false reception;
how, then, can such a person be called a true mendicant (*bhikṣu*)? Therefore, when entering a village, one must regard forms as if one were blind.
For those with eyes naturally give rise to discrimination regarding forms; but since the blind do not see forms, what is there to discriminate? Nevertheless...
It is not said that one must block sight and hearing or sever all perception; rather, it means that when seeing forms, one should regard them as equal to the blind.

One must, while in the midst of seeing and hearing, realize and penetrate their essential emptiness. When one realizes and penetrates this essential emptiness, the eye does not enter into form, nor does form enter into the eye.
Furthermore, one can then be like what is described in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: realizing and penetrating that the nature of the eye is the faculty of seeing.
Illumination. When the spirit of awakening is clarified, one perceives that form is the nature of true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form;

each and every thing is pure and original, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. How could there be any further discrimination based on sense-objects, such that one would not return to right concentration? Master Zhaoluo said:
"Having attained the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows and the knowledge of non-arising, he realized the Way through self-attestation. With his whole body...
"Though there is softness and pleasure, one does not give rise to attachment. When the body experiences various tactile sensations, it should be like this.

Master Kumārajīva said: "Fingers joined together form a fist; therefore, they have no self-nature (*svabhāva*). Fingers are also like this, and thus they have no other-nature (*parabhāva*). Master Sengsheng said:
Because they arise from others, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since they lack intrinsic nature, how could they have extrinsic nature (*parabhāva*)?
Thus, they are fundamentally non-existent; what, then, is there to be extinguished? Therefore, they are like illusions. [The Master] Dēng said:
"One should also say that they lack a common nature (*sāmānyabhāva*) and lack a causeless nature (*ahetubhāva*). The text omits these for brevity.
○ Four: Showing the Method for Receiving [the Teaching], in three parts. First, showing that what is erroneous is itself correct:

III. Showing how to turn [the mind] toward reverence as the cause.
One should give a single meal to all beings, making offerings to all Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages, and only then may one eat.
The Venerable Fazhi said: "How far apart are the Buddha and Māra? What deficiency or surplus exists between the heterodox and the orthodox?
It is simply that the Dharma has no heterodoxy or orthodoxy; heterodoxy and orthodoxy arise from the mind. If the mind is heterodox, then all dharmas are heterodox."
When the mind is correct, all phenomena are correct. Therefore it is said: "If one observes sentient beings with true wisdom, sentient beings are all wondrous;

if one observes the Buddhas with deluded thoughts, even the Buddhas become deviant. Regarding the phenomena of the deviant and the correct, there are both their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
If one seeks the Dharma by relying solely on characteristics, then the paths of the deviant and the correct cannot but diverge accordingly. If...
If one observes the nature by means of its general characteristics, then the heterodox and the orthodox cannot fail to follow the same track.

Now, to cause one to enter liberation without abandoning the eight heterodoxies—that is, to enter the True Dharma by means of their very heterodox characteristics—is fundamentally based on the precedent of Kāśyapa, who first served heterodox teachers before entering the Right Path;
this is precisely the act of discarding the heterodox to return to the orthodox, just as one might sweep away waves to [reveal the water].
To seek [water] in this manner is not what is called the ultimate path of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun).

Therefore, the Layman exhorted him, causing him not to abandon the eight heterodoxies (*aṣṭa-mithyātva*) to enter the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*). By entering the correct state through the marks of heterodoxy, he was able to enter the Way by means of this;

furthermore, he was able to contemplate that all food is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and realize that food is nothing but mind. Thus, the seven types of food are all the Dharma-realm, down to a single grain.
One may take Mount Sumeru and offer it as millet; with this food of the Dharma-dhātu, one bestows upon all hungry sentient beings and likewise makes offerings to all Buddhas and worthy sages.
This is the practice of benefiting both self and others, wherein vows and deeds are inexhaustible.
Only when one is truly able to possess such conduct can one eat the food of others; otherwise, one receives it in vain.
Regarding "giving," Master Zhaolun said: "Unobstructed giving" means that whenever one obtains food, one must first form the intention to give it to all sentient beings before eating it oneself.
If one has attained the Dharma-body, one can truly satisfy all beings, as in the case of the single bowl of rice mentioned later.
If one has not yet attained the Dharma-body, simply forming the intention of equal giving is itself the unobstructed dharma.
This is also the wise counsel of former sages and the legacy bequeathed to beginners. II.
Concluding the accomplishment of merit in four parts: First, concluding the merit of the Middle Way by way of what is to be eliminated.
One who eats in this manner neither possesses afflictions nor is free from afflictions.
Master Zhao said: "Eating with afflictions is the way of ordinary beings; eating free from afflictions is the way of the Two Vehicles.
If one can eat as described above with equanimity, then it is the food of the Dharma-body; it is not eating while possessing afflictions."
"One eats while remaining free from afflictions.
Dēng said: "If one can contemplate food as the dharma-realm, its nature is the Middle Way;
therefore, it is neither the extreme of existence, which is identical to afflictions, nor the extreme of emptiness, which is separate from afflictions."
Second, regarding the cultivation [of practice], this establishes the merit of the Middle Way:
it is neither the state of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), nor the state of emerging from meditative concentration.
Master Zhaoseng said: "In the Lesser Vehicle, when one enters concentration, one does not eat; when one eats, one does not enter concentration. But for the Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body..."
One eats all day long, yet remains in meditative concentration all day long; therefore, there is no designation of "entering" or "exiting. Dēng said:
"Although this is so for the Dharmakāya, how could it not be so for the beginner's mind? One should likewise contemplate that the food is the Dharma-realm and that the mind is the Middle Way.
If one can contemplate in this way, then although one eats all day long, one does not eat all day long; and although one does not eat,"
And yet this does not hinder eating.
Third, by way of the dwelling place, the merit of the Middle Way is established:
it is neither dwelling in the world nor dwelling in nirvana.

Master Zhao said: "If one wishes to say he dwells in the mundane world, his Dharma-body transcends the ordinary and profane; if one wishes to say he dwells in Nirvana, he manifests eating food like an ordinary human.
(4) This section concludes the discussion on the merit of the Middle Way by way of the field of blessings (*puṇyakṣetra*).
For one who practices such giving, there is neither great merit nor small merit; it neither benefits nor harms.
To speak according to conventional characteristics, the field of the gift has its degrees of greatness or smallness, and the person receiving the gift experiences benefit or harm.
However, this present practice of begging for food takes the Middle Way of signlessness as its principle, transcending both extremes.

Regarding the two extremes, one should practice the Middle Way. As for those who give, if they truly understand this, then even if they give to the Triple Gem, their merit will not be considered great;
even if they give to the six realms of existence, their merit will not be considered small.
As for those who receive, whether they possess virtue or lack it, there is neither gain nor loss, because all are able to transcend [the duality].
Third, one attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
This is the correct entry into the Buddha-way, not relying on the Śrāvaka path.
Since the fruit of Buddhahood takes the Middle Way as its cause, once this cause is possessed, one correctly enters the Buddha-way. [This is distinct from] the Śrāvaka dharma.
In the midst [of these], one cannot possess such [qualities]; therefore, it is called "not relying.
○ Fourth, the conclusion establishing non-emptiness:
Kāśyapa, if one eats in this manner, it constitutes not eating the alms of people in vain.

Now, the method of begging for food is for the sake of benefit and not for the sake of loss. Therefore, if one does not contemplate the emptiness (*śūnyatā*) of food, it benefits existence (*bhava*) but does not benefit *nirvāṇa*.
If one does not contemplate the conventional nature (*prajñapti*) of food, it benefits the path of a Bodhisattva but does not benefit *nirvāṇa*.

If one does not contemplate the middle way (*madhyamā pratipad*) regarding food, it benefits the two extremes (*antadvaya*) but does not benefit the Buddha-way. To benefit existence is to sink [into saṃsāra].

To be submerged in birth and death while merely benefiting from the provisional and the empty is to be addicted to the partial vehicles. To practice only the Middle Way is neither to benefit nor to harm;
this benefit that is not a benefit constitutes the great benefit. Therefore, it is said that one does not eat the offerings of others in vain.
III. Conclusion on the Benefits.
At that time, World-Honored One, having heard these words, I attained what I had never experienced before and immediately conceived a profound sense of reverence for all bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, I thought: "How is it that one with such a name as a householder can possess eloquence and wisdom to such an extent? Who else could do so?"
They do not resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Since that time, I have no longer exhorted others to practice the paths of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
This concludes the section on the Venerable Kāśyapa: having heard this Great Dharma, he felt shame for his former small-mindedness and aspired to the Great;
