Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.

Regarding the explanation according to the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*): it is like the instruction that one should practice begging for food because of [the principle of] non-eating, and so forth. By applying the three meanings of the Shared (*tsū*), Distinct (*beppon*), and Perfect (*en*) teachings to interpret this, there is nothing that will not be appropriate.
As it is said: "One experiences all tactile sensations as the realization of wisdom, thereby attaining the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*)."
Regarding the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*): is it not the case that all three teachings are able to achieve this at the stage of the fruit where pervasive delusions are destroyed?
If one says that "without abandoning the eight perversions, one enters the eight liberations; entering through perverse characteristics into correct characteristics;
neither possessing afflictions nor being free from afflictions"—this is something that, were it not for the Perfect and Sudden teaching, could ultimately not be penetrated.
Regarding the interpretation through contemplating the mind: the eye takes form as its nutriment; the ear takes sound as its nutriment;

and so on, up to the body, which takes touch as its nutriment; and the mind, which takes dharmas as its nutriment. When taken as solid food (*kavalikāhāra*), it encompasses all five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).

When these enter the internal faculties, they become the object-field of dharmas (*dharma-āyatana*). By contemplating that the mind is empty, one sees forms as equal to blindness and hears sounds as... [equal to deafness].
Regarding echoes and the like: if one contemplates that the mind is *prajñapti* (provisional), then by offering a single meal, one makes offerings to all Buddhas and the assembly of worthy sages;

only then may one eat. If one contemplates that the mind is *madhyama* (the middle way), then there is neither affliction nor freedom from affliction, neither entering a state of meditative concentration nor arising from it, neither abiding in the world nor abiding in *nirvāṇa*. There is no [great...]
Merit. There is no such thing as small merit; it neither brings benefit nor causes harm.
○ Fourth, the dispatching of the Venerable Subhūti, part two. First, the Tathāgata’s command to dispatch him.
The Buddha told Subhūti, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness. Master Zao said:
"Subhūti means 'Good Fortune' (Śubhavyūha) in the language of Qin. Among the various disciples, he is foremost in understanding emptiness (*śūnyatā*)."
II. The Venerable One’s Firm Refusal (in three parts). First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the account of the incident of his rebuke.
Why is this so? I recall that once, when I entered his house to beg for alms, Vimalakīrti took my bowl and filled it completely with food.
Master Daosheng said: "Vimalakīrti’s traces reside in the status of a layman, and thus he is subject to the suspicion of being stingy.
If one were to interrogate him before even offering food, people might well say that such a thing is true. Therefore, he first filled his bowl to the brim but did not hand it over."
Fearing that Subhūti might take the bowl and depart, he did not exhaust the force of his discourse.
Part Two: Narrating His Refutation in Two Sections. First, a general refutation demonstrating their equality.
He said to me: "O Subhūti, if one can be equal toward food, then all dharmas are also equal; if all dharmas are equal, then one is also equal toward food.
It is by practicing alms-gathering in this way that one may accept food."
This provides a general demonstration of how the mind of equality contemplates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
For all the myriad phenomena of the world take the inconceivable, perfectly interfused true suchness (*tathatā*) as their substance.

It is precisely because true suchness possesses the capacity for both non-alteration and following conditions that every single phenomenon produced through following conditions is, in each and every instance, the non-altered state of true suchness.
In essence, all things—both the environment and its inhabitants—are nothing other than the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).

Therefore, it is said that the ocean of lands is the Dharma-realm, and even a single atom is the Dharma-realm. Since all are the Dharma-realm, what single phenomenon is not identical to the Dharma-realm?
Thus, the Dharma-realm of the ocean of lands is not large, and the Dharma-realm of a single atom is not small. Now, Vimalakīrti precisely demonstrates this through the Dharma-realm.
At that time, when Śubhavyūha was begging for food, [the Buddha] immediately used the food to demonstrate the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
He caused him to contemplate the equality of food with all dharmas; therefore it is said: "That which is equal regarding food is also equal regarding all dharmas;
that which is equal regarding all dharmas is also equal regarding food. One who practices such alms-seeking within the dharma-realm may thereafter receive the food of the dharma-realm.
This is still a general indication; the following text then demonstrates it through the equality of dharmas and so forth.
However, this also serves as the sublime medicine for Subhūti’s mental inequality—his abandonment of poverty to follow wealth.

It is like the nine-fold elixir of immortality used to treat the subtle ailment of imbalanced vital energies (*rō-ei*); when Subhūti takes it, it is fitting that he will not merely be able to cure his illness.
It will surely lead to the attainment of the Great Enlightenment of the Golden Immortal through this means.

○ Second, the specific analysis demonstrating its equality has three parts. First, the direct demonstration of equality has three parts. First, the demonstration based on the identity of the inverse and the compliant has two parts.
First, the demonstration based on the phenomena has two parts. First, the demonstration that the three paths are identical to the three virtues.
Subhūti, if one does not sever lust, anger, and delusion, yet is not associated with them; if one does not destroy the body, yet conforms to the single mark;

if one does not extinguish ignorance and craving, yet gives rise to clarity and liberation; if one attains liberation through the marks of the five heinous crimes; and if one is neither liberated nor bound—[this is the perfection of wisdom].
One does not sever lust, anger, and ignorance, yet does not dwell with them; one does not extinguish delusion and craving, yet gives rise to illumination and liberation.
To demonstrate the path of delusion is itself *prajñā*. Without destroying the body, one accords with the single mark (*ekalakṣaṇa*). To demonstrate the path of suffering is itself the *dharmakāya*.
By means of the marks of the five heinous crimes, one attains liberation; there is neither liberation nor bondage. To demonstrate the path of karma is itself liberation.
This is liberation. The general demonstration states: "That which is equal regarding food is also equal regarding dharmas;
that which is equal regarding dharmas is also equal regarding food. The reason for this lies precisely here.

Did we not say previously that the inconceivable essence of the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm constitutes my single thought-moment, and likewise manifests its entire essence as sentient beings and as Buddhas? It acts...
Regarding the practice of "acting as the correct" (sādhana): since it acts by means of the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), what single dharma could there be that does not possess all dharmas?

Nevertheless, one must know that there is inherent goodness (prakṛti-kuśala) and inherent evil (prakṛti-akuśala), as well as cultivated goodness (bhāvanā-kuśala) and cultivated evil (bhāvanā-akuśala). These are inherent goodness and inherent evil.
Suchness is the essence that does not change. Cultivating good and cultivating evil are the functions of Suchness as it accords with conditions.
In the beginning, it does not change while acceding to conditions; in the end, it accedes to conditions without changing. As the Sūtra says:

"Lust, anger, and ignorance" refer to the cultivation of defilement; "physical characteristics and the five heinous acts" refer to the cultivation of evil. It is precisely because one is able to comprehend this cultivation of defilement...

That which is defilement in its nature is evil in its cultivation; that which is evil in its nature is evil in its cultivation. The defilement and evil of nature and that purity and goodness of nature are fundamentally interfused in essence, being one and not two.
One need only observe that the evil of cultivation is precisely the evil of nature, and the characteristics of this cultivated evil are spontaneously the Way.
This correctly demonstrates that a practitioner of the Perfect Teaching need not sever the lust and anger of the nine realms.

The first is inherent nature (*xingju*); the second is accomplished through cultivation (*xiucheng*). Although these are inherent, cultivation arises entirely from nature; and although the second is accomplished through cultivation, [it is rooted in that nature].

Cultivation is perfected because cultivation is entirely present within the nature, and the nature entirely gives rise to cultivation. Therefore, all cultivated good and cultivated evil are themselves the inherent goodness and inherent evil of the nature.

From the perspective of cultivation, although one may distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, since the cultivation of both good and evil is entirely contained within the nature, there is nothing to be discussed in terms of heterodoxy versus orthodoxy or good versus evil. Now, Vimalakīrti, by means of...
Principle supersedes phenomena, and cultivation is extinguished within the nature. Thus, his unhindered eloquence is such as this.
Therefore, when one examines what he says, although it appears contrary, it is always compliant; although it appears to be a reversal, it is in fact correct.
If one does not understand this, then to speak in vain of "equality" is entirely without foundation.

Regarding "contemplative understanding": to realize that a single thought-moment is fully endowed with all phenomena—such that they are simultaneously the True, the Conventional, and the Middle—is called the "true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena," which is termed the equality of all phenomena.
To be able to contemplate this through the three types of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* is called "being equal toward all phenomena and equal even toward food.
One contemplates that cultivated evil is identical to inherent evil; thus, one does not sever lust, anger, or delusion.

To contemplate this as the perfection of nature is also not to be joined with it; likewise, below, the non-extinction of delusion and craving gives rise to clarity and liberation—this is to contemplate that a single thought of affliction is itself bodhi.
Without destroying the body, one accords with the single mark;
to contemplate a single thought of the path of suffering as the Dharma-body, and through the marks of the five heinous crimes to attain liberation, yet not to understand them [as such].

It is not liberation. To contemplate the path of karma within a single thought-moment is itself liberation. When the inherent evil of nature (*xing-è*) fully gives rise to the evil of cultivation (*xiu-è*), one does not perceive the Four Noble Truths;
yet when the evil of cultivation is fully identical to the inherent evil of nature, it is not that one fails to perceive the Truths.

If awakening (*bodhi*) were identical to afflictions (*kleśa*), then there would be neither the attainment of the fruit nor the state of a sage. If afflictions were identical to awakening, then there would be neither an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) nor a holy one.
To be apart from the dharmas of ordinary beings is not to be non-saintly; the ten realms remain distinct. Thus, although all dharmas are accomplished, the three thousand realms are entirely empty.
Consequently, one is apart from the characteristics of all dharmas; when there is no perceiving wisdom whatsoever, then one does not see the Buddha.

Furthermore, there is no dharma to be observed; thus, one does not "hear" the Dharma. To observe the sixty-two views as the lineage of the Tathāgata means that one need not seek the Tathāgata apart from these views.
If this were so, you would fall where your teacher fell, and you too would follow him in his fall;

you would likewise enter into various false views and fail to reach the other shore. By observing that the nature is replete with the twenty-five states of existence, one accomplishes the King Samādhi.
Abiding thus in the eight difficulties, one does not attain freedom from difficulty; being identical with afflictions, one is separated from pure dharmas.

Contemplating that a single thought-moment and the ten realms are all empty, one immediately attains the Samādhi of Non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*). At that moment, all sentient beings likewise attain this samādhi.
Thereupon, one awakens to the dharma-gate of the inherent evil of nature. Thus, those who bestow [offerings] upon you are not called fields of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). As for making offerings...
Those who raise you will fall into the three evil realms. You will act as one hand with the various Māras, becoming their companions in toil and labor.
Affliction is simply affliction; awakening is simply awakening. Affliction does not obstruct awakening, nor does awakening destroy affliction.
This is to slander the Buddha and disparage the Dharma; such a person shall not enter the ranks of the assembly and shall ultimately never attain nirvāṇa. The rest...
The meaning can be understood through contemplation.
V. Sending the Venerable Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra (in two parts). First, the Tathāgata’s command to send him:
The Buddha addressed Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra: "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
Master Shi said: "Pūrṇa is the name of the father; in the language of Qin, it means 'Full. Maitrāyaṇī is the name of the mother;
in the language of Qin, it means 'Good Knowledge' and is also called 'Compassionate Mother. Among all the disciples, he was the foremost in preaching the Dharma."
II. The Venerable One’s Firm Refusal (Part 3). First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Pūrṇa addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the narration of the incident of his refutation.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, while in a great forest, sitting beneath a tree, I was preaching the Dharma to several newly ordained bhikṣus.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Near the city of Vaiśālī there is a grove. Within the grove is water, and the water is called Monkey Pond.
In the grove there is a monastery cell; it is one of the three monasteries of Vaiśālī.
In that place, Pūrṇa was preaching the Dharma for the sake of those newly entered into the path."
II. Narrating His Refutation (in two parts). A. First, rebuking Pūrṇa (in two parts). 1. Rebuking him for failing to enter meditative absorption to observe the faculties of others.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "Pūrṇa, you should first enter meditative absorption and observe the minds of these people."
Thereafter, he preached the Dharma.
Master Sengzhao said: "In the Mahāyāna, from the stage of the Dharmakāya upward, one attains the unimpeded true mind.

The mental faculty is quiescent and has never been anything other than in a state of concentration. Because the mind is constantly concentrated, it can universally illumine all phenomena without the need for deliberate seeking."
This is known later. The mind of the Hīnayāna is limited and obstructed, and it cannot remain in constant concentration.

Whatever it observes, it sees while in concentration but does not see when emerging from concentration. Furthermore, even those Śrāvakas with deep power of concentration perceive the faculties of sentient beings for at most eighty thousand kalpas;
those with shallow power of concentration perceive only their own number of births. As for what the Mahāsattvas perceive, their vision reaches the unconditioned.
[The Buddha] sighed in pity. "This newly ordained bhikṣu possesses faculties suited for the Mahāyāna; he ought to hear the Great Way. Yet, you have taught him the Lesser Dharma.
Therefore, instruct him to enter meditative concentration."
II. The Sixfold Reprimand for Teaching the Dharma to Unsuitable Disciples. First, the reprimand for bestowing the Great upon the Small:
"Do not place foul food into a precious vessel.

The "precious vessel" is a metaphor for the faculties of the Mahāyāna. This vessel is fit to be filled with *amṛta* (the supreme essence); to place foul food therein is a metaphor for [bestowing the Lesser Vehicle upon such a person].
The Dharma does not accommodate the capacities of beings.
Second, the reprimand regarding "viewing as equal" is largely the same [as the previous one].
One should know the thoughts in the mind of this bhikṣu; do not equate lapis lazuli with common crystal.

Lapis lazuli is a metaphor for the great capacity of a bhikṣu; yet now, for his sake, the Small [Vehicle] is preached. This is why lapis lazuli, a precious object, is viewed as cheap and treated like crystal.
(3) The third point: rebuking the small because it harms the great.
You do not know the fundamental capacities of sentient beings; do not attempt to initiate them into the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).
They themselves have no wounds, so do not injure them.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle loathe birth and death as if they were a prison, and view afflictions (kleśa) as enemies; they will surely shatter [the fetters].
One realizes Bodhi only after being afflicted; one enters Nirvana only after severing birth and death. It is like having an abscess on the body:

one must necessarily apply needles and moxibustion to the skin to rot away the putrid flesh, so that there may eventually be healing. This applies to those of the highest faculties who follow the Perfect and Sudden teaching.
To realize that birth and death are identical to nirvana, and that afflictions are identical to bodhi, is like a body without sores.
Now, Pūrṇa has preached the Lesser Dharma for him, which is like a mediocre physician who forcibly applies acupuncture and moxibustion to a body that has no sores.
Yet this harms its fundamental essence.
○ Fourth, teach the great and do not show the small.
If one wishes to practice the Great Way, do not point out narrow paths. Do not attempt to fit the great ocean into the footprint of an ox.
Master Zhao said: "A great object should be placed in a great location. Why turn a dragon-elephant onto a rabbit’s path?
Why pour the great ocean into a cow’s footprint?
He did not employ minor teachings for those of the fifth stage.
Do not equate the light of the sun with the glow of a firefly.

A bhikṣu who has long set his mind upon the Mahāyāna possesses wisdom like the light of the sun; to instruct such a person now with the teachings of the Hīnayāna is to regard the light of the sun as equal to the glow of a firefly.
6. Reprimanding for Shallow Wisdom and Mismatching Capacities:
"Pūrṇa, this bhikṣu has long since resolved his mind upon the Mahāyāna, yet he has forgotten this intention midway.
How can you instruct him with the teachings of the Hīnayāna? I observe that the wisdom of the Hīnayāna is feeble and shallow, like that of a blind person who cannot distinguish [colors]."
He discerns the sharpness or dullness of the faculties of all sentient beings.
Part two: Subsequently preaching the Dharma for them, which has two sections. First, entering meditative absorption to bestow empowerment; second, initially attaining the knowledge of past lives.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered a samādhi, causing these bhikṣus to recognize their own past lives:
how they had planted the roots of various virtues under five hundred buddhas and dedicated them toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The faculties of sentient beings all possess past seeds—whether virtuous or non-virtuous, great or small—which are stored within the field of consciousness and will inevitably manifest after a long time.
Although the grace of Heaven is impartial, it must nevertheless select those that are strongest and bring them forth first.
This bhikṣu has planted the roots of virtue in past lives and is further able to dedicate them toward Bodhi;
therefore, the Great Being, employing his supernatural power, awakens his spiritual consciousness and enables him to know his past lives, thereby establishing the faculties for the Mahāyāna.
2. Sudden Enlightenment of the Original Mind:
At that moment, they were suddenly enlightened and regained their original minds. Thereupon, the bhikṣus bowed their heads at the feet of Vimalakīrti in prostration.
II. Preaching the Dharma for their Sake.
At that time, Vimalakīrti preached the Dharma for their sake. III.
Gaining Benefit from Hearing the Dharma.
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, one no longer regresses.

Among the three types of non-regression—of stage, of practice, and of mindfulness—although one initially resolves to attain enlightenment and practices, because the afflictions have not yet been severed, there may still be regression and the loss of memory across lifetimes.
Now, upon hearing the teaching of the Dharma, one again relies on past...
"Life. By relying on this, one cuts off delusions and ascends to the stage of non-retrogression.
"Third, the conclusion of incapacity:
I consider that Śrāvakas do not examine the faculties of others before preaching the Dharma; therefore, I am unfit to go to him to inquire about his illness."
Regarding the explanation by way of the provisional teachings (*yàojiào*), our school’s classification of Mahāyāna teachings consists of the Shared (*tōng*), Distinct (*bié*), and Perfect (*yuán*).

All of these are contrasted with the *piṭaka* of the Three Baskets (*sānzàng*), which they treat as Hīnayāna. Thus, this chapter applies to all three Mahāyāna teachings. However, one must not wound those who have no sores;

therefore, one must discuss whether there is injury or no injury based on the distinction between the internal realm (*jiè nèi*) and the external realm (*jiè wài*). As for the internal realm, it is by means of...
The Tripiṭaka masters analyze form to clarify emptiness; this is considered a clumsy method of deliverance, for it treats what is not a wound as a wound and has already inflicted injury.
Only the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) views form as emptiness, rather than asserting that emptiness arises from the extinction of form; this is called the skillful teaching.
It takes emptiness as the substance of the non-wound, and realizing this substance is itself the spirit—this is called being uninjured. Beyond the realms, there is the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

That which is expounded [in other teachings] is merely the Middle, yet it treats the three truths as distinct and sequential; practicing them one after another and entering them in succession is called "inflicting a wound.
Only the Perfect and Sudden Teaching expounds the Perfect Middle, wherein the true and the conventional are identical, and afflictions and birth-and-death are themselves Bodhi and Nirvana.
This is what is meant by "originally having no wound, so there is nothing to inflict."
Regarding contemplative understanding: one contemplates that within a single moment of mind, among the three poisons, it must belong to one poison; this is called the "afflicted mind.

To realize that this cultivated defilement is itself the innate defilement is called the "wisdom of the cause of realization. Since affliction is identical to bodhi, [the cause of realization is established].
There is no need to further destroy afflictions to separately seek bodhi; this is called "originally having no wound, so do not injure it.
Furthermore, this single thought belongs to the *vijñāna-skandha* acquired through retribution; it is the mind of birth and death.

To realize that cultivated evil is precisely inherent evil is termed the "conditioned cause for liberation. Since birth and death are themselves nirvana, there is no need to further destroy birth and death.
Seeking nirvana through parting from death is called "originally having no wound, so do not injure it.
(6) Sending the Venerable Kātyāyana away, part two. First, the Tathāgata’s command to dispatch him.
The Buddha said to Mahākātyāyana, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Master Shi [Kumārajīva] remarked: "This was the clan name of a Brahmin from South India who was well-versed in the sūtras."
II. The Venerable One’s Firm Refusal (in three parts). First, a general refusal of his incapacity.
Kātyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not capable of going to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the account of the refutation.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, the Buddha briefly taught the essential points of the Dharma to the bhikṣus.
Thereafter, I expounded upon their meaning—namely, the meaning of impermanence, the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of non-self, and the meaning of cessation.
When the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, there are two kinds of *udāna*. *Udāna* here is translated as "seal" (*mudrā*).
One seal seals the sūtras of the Hīnayāna and possesses five meanings. Four meanings seal the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), namely: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
The Buddha uses this seal to seal and determine birth and death as definitively impermanent, such that they cannot be made permanent;
and even definitively as selfless, such that they cannot be made to possess a self. This single meaning seals nirvāṇa as the seal of quiescent extinction.
The Buddha uses this seal to seal and determine nirvāṇa as definitively quiescent, devoid of afflictions and birth-and-death. This is in contrast to the Small [Vehicle].
Those who ride upon it explain the distinction between the mundane and the supramundane. A single seal stamps the Mahāyāna, proclaiming the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena:
it seals that birth-and-death and afflictions are definitively eternal, definitively blissful, definitively non-existent, and definitively neither self nor non-self—non-dual.
It seals that phenomena were originally not so, and now they are likewise non-existent.
[The teaching on] cessation. Now, Kātyāyana has subverted what the Buddha taught in the authentic Sūtras of the Hīnayāna.
For when the Buddha spoke this Dharma, he intended the meaning rather than the literal expression; though he spoke of impermanence, it was in reference to permanence and so forth.
Yet Kātyāyana did not understand the Buddha’s intention; while he indeed destroyed the ordinary person's attachment to permanence, he himself clung to impermanence. Thus, [this view] arises.
He preaches the Dharma of the true mark by extinguishing mental activities; therefore, the Great Being rebukes and instructs him therein.
Part Two: Narrating His Refutation, in two sections. First, a general rebuke of mental activities involving arising and ceasing.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "Kātyāyana, do not use a mind characterized by arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark.
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, teach the Dharma of the true mark with only a single seal; that is to say, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma."
There is neither two nor three; this present seal of the Hīnayāna is spoken of as a provisional expedient out of necessity, yet its intent does not reside in the Small Vehicle.
It is what is meant by "distinguishing and teaching three within the single Buddha-vehicle.

Is it not the case that the seal of the Hīnayāna is opened from within the single seal in order to dispel the emotional views of ordinary beings who cling to the impermanent as permanent? These emotional views—
Once these [delusions] are removed, the principle of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) is revealed; thus, the gate of expedient means (upāyamukha) is opened to demonstrate the true reality.

Therefore, one should know that the seals of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness originally reside in the Great [Vehicle], not in the Small. Now, Kātyāyanīputra ultimately relies upon the Small Vehicle to expound them;
thus, he uses a mind of arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of the true mark.
II. Specifically demonstrating the Dharma of the true mark has five parts. First, demonstrating the meaning of true impermanence:
"Kātyāyana, that all dharmas are ultimately neither produced nor extinguished—this is the meaning of impermanence."

When the Tathāgata speaks of the impermanence of all phenomena (*dharma*), he intends precisely to dispel the attachment of ordinary beings who grasp at the impermanence of arising and ceasing as being permanent.
Thus, "impermanence" refers to the permanence that is free from arising and ceasing.

If this emotional attachment to the permanence of arising and ceasing is eliminated, then the realization of the ultimate non-arising and non-ceasing of all phenomena will manifest. This is what the Tathāgata has taught.
The meaning of impermanence resides in this very point. How could it be explained through the mental activities of arising and ceasing?
○ Second, showing the meaning of true suffering:
To penetrate thoroughly the five aggregates of clinging as empty and non-arising—this is the meaning of suffering.
When the Tathāgata says that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) are suffering,

he intends to dispel the ordinary person’s attachment to these five aggregates as being the pleasure of enjoyment. Thus, the meaning of suffering is to demonstrate that while there is no pleasure for the ordinary person within the five aggregates,
there is nonetheless the pleasure of penetrating their emptiness and the non-arising of phenomena.
Now, once suffering and illness have been eliminated, the joy of the four virtues manifests.
Is it not, then, that the meaning of the suffering of ordinary beings constitutes the meaning of the joy of the sages?
○ Third, the demonstration of the meaning of true emptiness.
That all phenomena are ultimately non-existent is the meaning of emptiness.

The Buddhas teach the Dharma of emptiness in order to deliver those who are attached to existence. Although the followers of the Two Vehicles have destroyed attachment to existence, they nevertheless remain attached to emptiness.
It is not only existence that is fundamentally empty; this very emptiness is also empty. When both emptiness and existence are empty, this is called the Middle Way.

Regarding the Way and its Meaning: the essence of the Middle Way is also empty; this is called ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Within this ultimate emptiness, how could all phenomena ever be non-existent?

Yet these very phenomena are empty, and this is termed the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmāṇāṃ bhūtalakṣaṇam*). When the Tathāgata speaks of emptiness, he refers to the meaning of this true emptiness.
4. Showing the True Meaning of Non-Self:
That self and non-self are non-dual—this is the meaning of non-self.
"Self" refers to the true self realized by the Tathāgata; "non-self" refers to the absence of the attachment to a self held by ordinary beings.
Thus, this self is precisely non-self; non-self is the true self. How could the "refutation of self" of the Hīnayāna or the "forgetting of self" of the non-Buddhists ever hope to reach this?
5. To demonstrate the meaning of true quiescence:
phenomena were originally not ablaze; now they are not extinguished. This is the meaning of quiescence. Master Zhao said:
"The Hīnayāna [teaches] that the three realms are ablaze, and thus one seeks the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) by extinguishing them. Now, as for this blazing..."
However, since it has already manifested, the name "extinction" arises from its arising. In the contemplation of the Mahāyāna, things are fundamentally not so;
what, then, is there to extinguish? That which is neither so nor extinguished is true quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*).
III. Gaining Benefit from Hearing the Dharma.
While this Dharma was being taught, the minds of those bhikṣus were liberated.
III. Conclusion of the Inability [to Attain].
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
Regarding the provisional teachings, the five seals—impermanence and so forth—seal the sūtras of the Tripitaka and the Hīnayāna; their meaning is thus established.
Only the seal of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) can seal the three teachings of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect. If one explains the Mahāyāna by means of "mere emptiness" alone...

If one takes "vehicle" (yāna) as the basis, then the seal belongs to the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), which clarifies the Mahāyāna by means of the "sudden-middle" (danzhong). If one takes the "middle" of the Separate [Teaching] (biejiao) as the basis, then the seal belongs to the Separate Teaching, which clarifies the Mahāyāna by means of the "separate-middle.

If one takes the "middle" of the Perfect [Teaching] (yuanjiao) as the basis, then the seal belongs to the Perfect Teaching, which clarifies the Mahāyāna by means of the "perfect-middle. According to the capacities of beings and their progressive understanding, there is originally no fixed location for it.

Regarding contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*): one contemplates that a single moment of mind is replete with all phenomena, which is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Middle Way, encompassing both the conventional and the ultimate;
this is the meaning of impermanence as being neither arising nor ceasing. The five aggregates and the thousand dharmas are empty in their very place, realizing that nothing arises;
this is the meaning of suffering. Although all phenomena are present, they possess the characteristic of "possessing non-possession"; thus, all phenomena are ultimately non-existent.
This is the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). All dharmas within the single mind are both provisional and empty; that this self and non-self are non-dual is the meaning of non-self (*anātman*).

These dharmas of the mind are eternally of the nature of quiescent extinction; that these dharmas were originally not burning and now likewise have no extinction is the meaning of quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
7. Sending the Venerable Aniruddha (2). First, the Tathāgata’s command:
The Buddha addressed Aniruddha, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Master Zhao said: "Aniruddha—translated into the language of Qin as 'As One Wishes'—was of the Kṣatriya caste. Among the disciples, he was foremost in the divine eye.
[Section Two:
The Venerable's Firm Refusal (Part Three)] First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Aniruddha addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
[This section] explains the reason for this in two parts; first, it recounts the incident of his physical collapse.

Why is this? I recall that in the past, while I was walking back and forth in a certain place, a Brahmā King named Śuddhavimala, together with ten thousand Brahmās, emitted pure radiance and came to where I was. He prostrated himself in salutation and asked me:

“How far does the divine eye of Aniruddha see? I replied, “Virtuous one, I see this trichiliocosm, the buddha-field of Śākyamuni Buddha, as clearly as if I were looking at an āmalaka fruit in the palm of my hand.”
The Brahmā King also possesses the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Hearing of Nalakalīra’s divine eye, he did not know whether it was the same as his own or different;
thus, he raised this question. Nalakalīra then answered that while it was indeed different from his, it was also the same, saying:

"One is able to see the great trichiliocosm as if looking at a fruit in the palm of one's hand. This is because the Brahmā King’s divine eye arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and merit (*puṇya*), yet it is obstructed by the interval between lifetimes.
The divine eye of Aniruddha was obtained as a karmic retribution; because it was produced through the cultivation of causes and the severance of afflictions, it differs from the former.
However, if it penetrates and perceives the great trichiliocosm, then they are the same.
II. Narrating His Refutation of My Words, Part Two. A. First, Refuting the Two Extremes, Part Three. 1. Directly Questioning the Two Extremes:
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Aniruddha, is that which is seen by the divine eye characterized by signs?"
Is it the mark of non-action?
Second, showing the meaning of both ends:
if it were the mark of action, it would be equal to the five supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists; if it were the mark of non-action, it would be the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is not.
There should be seeing.

Regarding those with the characteristic of volitional activity (*abhisaṃskāra-lakṣaṇa*), there is seeing through mental attention (*manasikāra*). Regarding those without the characteristic of volitional activity, there is no mental attention.

To have seeing through mental attention is the same as the supernatural power of mental attention possessed by those non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*); it is not the divine eye power (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*).
Regarding the formation of mental images (*nimitta*): it is not necessary to apply intentional attention (*manasikāra*). Since one does not apply intentional attention, how could there be seeing?
To form an image is to fall into existence; to form an image is to fall into non-existence. Having fallen into existence and non-existence, how can this be the true divine eye?
This first refutes that Nārada’s [vision] is not the true divine eye, yet it is not that he lacks something resembling the divine eye.
[The Buddha] remained silent for a third time.
World-Honored One, at that time I remained silent.
[Section Two: Demonstrating the Middle Way. Part One: Brahmā’s Inquiry.]
Those Brahmās, hearing his words, attained what they had never experienced before; they immediately prostrated themselves in homage and asked:
"In this world, who possesses the true divine eye?"
The two Great Beings provide an exposition.

Vimalakīrti said: "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has attained the true divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). He constantly abides in samādhi and perceives all Buddha-lands without dualistic characteristics."
This text contains two points that are refuted and two points that are demonstrated. Regarding the two points refuted:

first, the view held by non-Buddhists that there is seeing when one applies mental attention (*manasikāra*), and the view of Nārada that there is seeing when one enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*);

second, the view that there is seeing when signs (*nimitta*) are produced, and no seeing when signs are not produced. Regarding the two points demonstrated: first, that all Buddhas always abide in *samādhi* and yet see; second, [that they see]...
One does not perceive this through dualistic marks; it is eternally within samādhi, and is thus the king of samādhis.

Because it is free from dualistic marks, it is the Middle Way and the Buddha-nature. This divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is identical in essence to the Buddha-eye (*buddhacakṣus*), though their functions differ.
Indeed, all Buddhas possess only this single eye; because it performs five functions, it is called the "five eyes."
III. Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Benefit:
Thereupon, the Brahma King Śuddhāvāsa and his retinue of five hundred Brahmās all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti, they suddenly vanished from sight.
Third, he concludes his inability [to go].
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.

Regarding the explanation according to the teachings (*yàojiào*), there are five kinds of seeing with the eye: first, the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*), which is possessed by ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) and is able to see the myriad phenomena of the phenomenal world.
The ten thousand phenomena: when separated by skin, one does not see the five viscera; when separated by paper or a membrane, one does not see external objects.

The second is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), possessed by the various devas, which can see through to distant and near things without obstruction, whether in the process of being forged or otherwise;

there are differences in its smallness and greatness. The Cāturmahārājakāyika devas see their own bodies clearly; the Trāyastriṃśa devas see clearly within the Lesser Iron Ring Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*); and so on upward, with increasing size and scope.
As their respective characteristics differ, when it comes to the Brahma King, he perceives the entire trichiliocosm.

However, the five supernormal powers (pañcābhijñā) of non-Buddhists, those within our own teachings, and spirits alike are all produced through deliberate mental effort; they are therefore not the same as the manifestations experienced by the various devas.

Third, the eye of wisdom (*prajñā-cakṣus*): possessed by Bodhisattvas of the two teachings and three vehicles, as well as those of the Separate and Perfect [teachings] who have destroyed both common and pervasive delusions;

it is manifested from the perspective of the True [Dharmadhātu], enabling them to awaken to the principle of true emptiness. Fourth, the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*): possessed by Bodhisattvas who have emerged into the provisional [world]; having already destroyed the common delusions, they further destroy the "delusions like grains of sand";

it is manifested from the perspective of the conventional, enabling them to illuminate and perceive the principle of conventional truth, thereby knowing the illness and identifying the medicine. Fifth, the Buddha-eye... [text continues].
The eye is possessed only by the Buddha. He destroys the delusions of ignorance and illuminates the principle of the Middle Truth.

Furthermore, while the four preceding individuals each possess but one eye, the Buddha alone is fully endowed with the five eyes. The fleshly eye is the same as that of ordinary beings, perceiving the myriad phenomena; it is obstructed yet unobstructed.
The heavenly eye penetrates beyond obstructions and does not hinder the perception of the myriad phenomena. Therefore, it is said: "not by means of duality."

They meet one another within the Buddha-land. With the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), one realizes both the conventional and the middle; with the Dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*), one realizes both emptiness and the middle.

The Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*) illuminates the Middle Way, which is simultaneously identical to both extremes. Now, as for the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) of Nandika, it was obtained through cultivation.
However, [the Buddha] appeared with only half a head. Had he been a Buddha who had attained the fruit of the Tripitaka, he would have appeared with a full head.
Thus, that which is possessed by ordinary beings is not the true flesh-eye; even that possessed by Nārada and the various devas is not the true heavenly eye.
Therefore, the Mahāsattva first refuted [the claim] by means of the "done" and "not done," and subsequently demonstrated that only the World-Honored Buddha does not [possess such a limited vision].
Second is the visualization of the various Buddha-lands.

Regarding the contemplative understanding (*guanjie*), the illumination of the five eyes does not transcend the three truths; now, one contemplates that a single thought-moment is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle.

Illuminating the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), one possesses the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus). Observing the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one possesses the fleshly eye (māṃsa-cakṣus), the divine eye (divya-cakṣus), and the dharma-eye (dharma-cakṣus).
Illuminating the middle truth (madhyama-satya), one then possesses the Buddha-eye (buddha-cakṣus).
8. Sending the Venerable Upāli (2): First, the Tathāgata’s command to dispatch him.
The Buddha said to Upāli, “Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness.”
II. The Venerable One’s Firm Refusal (in three parts). First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the account of the incident of their censure. Why is this so?
I recall that in the past, there were two bhikṣus who had violated the disciplinary rules.

Feeling ashamed, they did not dare to ask the Buddha; instead, they came and asked me, saying: "O Upāli, we have indeed violated the disciplinary rules and feel truly ashamed; we did not dare [to ask the Buddha]."
He asked the Buddha, "I pray that you resolve my doubts and regrets so that I may be spared this transgression. I then provided him with an explanation according to the Dharma.
Regarding the two bhikṣus who committed an offense against the Vinaya and felt ashamed, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-śāstra* by the Great Master Tiantai states:
"At that time, two bhikṣus were living together in an araṇya (hermitage). One had gone elsewhere, while the other was sleeping in the open air. A courtesan was gathering firewood..."
A man was committing an act of impurity when a companion bhikṣu arrived. Seeing him, the companion drove him away; the woman fled and fell into a pit, where she died.

The one who lay with her suspected he had committed an offense of sexual misconduct, while the one who chased him away suspected he had committed an offense of killing. Neither dared to ask the Buddha, so they came to report the matter to Upāli.
Upāli explained according to the Vinaya as a standard: if one has committed a root offense, he was made to undergo training and repentance;
if one has committed a preparatory offense, he was made to perform the *pāyantika* confession; if there was originally no intentional mind, he was told that confession was unnecessary.
II. Narrating his words of rebuke (7 sections). First, the instruction to directly eliminate [the offense].
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "O Upāli, do not further increase the guilt of these two bhikṣus."
One should directly eliminate it and not disturb their mind.
A person who has violated the precepts already harbors fear; if one further determines their guilt, it will cause the arrow of remorse to pierce their heart so firmly that it cannot be extracted.
This is to say that one is instead disturbing their mind. One should act as shown below: the nature of sin is fundamentally empty. The...
This means that all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can eliminate; therefore, it is said that one should "directly eradicate them.
II. Showing that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty (in three parts). First, showing this by way of the offenses themselves.
Why is this so? That nature of sin does not exist within, nor does it exist without, nor does it exist in between.
If one regards sin as sin, how could there be any trace to be found? If one briefly sets aside the sin to observe the nature of the one who commits it, then its measure is equal to empty space;
it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between. Thus, the sin is immediately extinguished.
II. Showing by way of the mind:
As the Buddha has taught, "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
The mind does not abide within, nor does it abide without, nor does it abide in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with sinful defilements.
The mind is the root of all phenomena; all defilement and purity arise because of it.

Since one knows that a pure mind gives rise to purity and a defiled mind gives rise to defilement, how could one not contemplate that the nature of offenses is fundamentally empty, whereby all offenses are extinguished?
Therefore, the conclusion states: "The mind is thus, and offenses are thus."
Third, the demonstration by way of phenomena (*dharma*):
All phenomena are likewise; they do not transcend suchness (*tathatā*).
How much more so for transgressions! Since the fundamental mind is pure, when one applies the analogy of transgressions to all phenomena, it is the same for everything. It does not.
Know that all things are thus. Their coming has a source; what is this source? It is that all dharmas do not transcend the great root of *tathatā* (suchness).
Now, since all dharmas do not transcend *tathatā*, how could there be a single dharma that is not *tathatā*?
Since the nature of sin is such as this, can one not know what it is that should be pursued?
And they are directly extinguished.
○ Third, he directly reveals it by means of himself.
For example, when Upāli attained liberation through the characteristics of the mind, did he still have any defilement? I said, "No. Vimalakīrti...
Māmakī said, "The mental characteristics of all sentient beings are likewise free from defilement.

Master Kumārajīva remarked, "'Mental characteristics' refers to the fact that even Arhats observe the true reality (dharmatā) of the minds and thoughts of sentient beings and thereby attain liberation.
Now, when asking about the time they achieve the Way—specifically during the ninth path of liberation (vimukti-mārga) when observing true reality—do they perceive [it]?"
In this regard, is there defilement? [Answer: Yes.
Fourth, he demonstrates its defilement and purity:
"Upāli alone, conceptualization is defilement; the absence of conceptualization is purity. Inversion is defilement; the absence of inversion is purity."
This is purity. Grasping at a self is defilement; not grasping at a self is purity.
Sentient beings, due to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), give rise to inversion (*viparyāsa*); because of this inversion, they become attached to a self.
Thus, these three—false conceptualization, inversion, and the self—are all defilements. If one can distance oneself from these three, the mind becomes pure. Furthermore...
There is no other purity to be found apart from this.
○ Fifth, showing the root of defilement, in two parts. First, showing that arising and ceasing do not abide, in three sections. First, the explanation by way of Dharma:
"Upāli, all dharmas arise and cease without abiding."
All deluded thoughts arise from the discrimination of sense objects.
This discrimination of sense objects, in turn, results from failing to realize that all phenomena are fundamentally empty. Therefore, one seeks to extinguish these thoughts.
One must investigate its root. When one realizes that all phenomena arise and perish without abiding, and that there is no dharma to be taken as an object, then the discrimination of objects ceases;
deluded thoughts and inverted views are eliminated, and the marks of all transgressions naturally extinguish themselves.
II. Explanation by analogy:
Like an illusion, like lightning.
III. Application to the dharma.
All dharmas do not wait for one another; they do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
This is because all dharmas are established based upon the ground of non-abiding; since the principle is non-abiding, phenomena are likewise non-abiding.
The dharma of non-abiding is ultimately difficult to comprehend; therefore, two metaphors—like an illusion and like lightning—are established to illustrate it.
The first metaphor illustrates that illusory phenomena are fundamentally empty, and thus do not abide. The second metaphor illustrates that they move with such rapidity that they do not abide.
"Waiting" means borrowing or relying upon; it is like worldly phenomena, where this depends on that for its formation, and the dependent relies on what is produced.

Because there are characteristics, there is mutual dependence. Now, when we observe all phenomena, they are like illusions and like lightning; that which arises is such, and that which passes away is likewise so.
Fundamentally, they do not depend upon one another. It is not only by means of months, years, and seasons that things may temporarily abide and thus be mutually dependent;
even within a single thought-moment there are sixty *kṣaṇas*, and within a single *kṣaṇa* there are sixty births.
Cessation. Thus, birth, duration, change, and cessation do not remain still for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). All phenomena (*dharma*) are like this;
how could they possess any [inherent] characteristics? As the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says: "That which arises is immediately subject to cessation; this is not taught for the sake of the foolish."
This is what is meant by that.
○ Second, showing that [all things] exist through false perception. This consists of the principle, the analogy, and the application.
All phenomena are false perceptions, like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon in water, and like a reflection in a mirror; they are produced by deluded thought.

All phenomena arise as false perceptions; this is the principle (*dharma*). The four examples, such as dreams and so forth, are the illustrations (*upamāna*). That they arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the application (*yukti*).
Just as seeing food and clothing in a dream cannot provide nourishment or warmth, and seeing a river of water in a mirage cannot quench the heat.
Thirsty, one sees the reflection of the moon in the water; it cannot be grasped by reaching for it.
The various forms and images in a mirror cannot be seized. All phenomena are likewise: born from deluded perception, they are said to exist where there is nothing;
ultimately, they cannot be grasped, and though one attempts to grasp them, they are not obtained. Because they cannot be obtained, one knows that the nature of transgression is fundamentally empty.
Sixth, the completion of the practice of the Vinaya.
One who understands this is said to revere the Vinaya; one who understands this is said to have a thorough understanding.
Now, precepts derive their name from preventing what is improper and ceasing evil. To merely cease [evil] within body, speech, and mind without not committing transgressions is not the truth.

This concerns the upholding of the Vinaya. Generally, there are three types of bodily misconduct, four types of verbal misconduct, and three types of mental misconduct; these are the branches. One must skillfully stem their flow by blocking their source.

The source is the mind. If one can realize that the nature of offenses is empty, that the mind is without self, that it is not inverted, and that it is free from deluded thoughts, then the mind will be pure and untainted.
Erroneous and non-virtuous states will not arise, and all evils will naturally cease.
"It is done. He is well-versed in the Vinaya;
is this not the case? ○ Seventh, he was intimidated by them.
Thereupon, the two bhikṣus said: 'How profound is his wisdom! This is beyond the reach of Upāli. He is the foremost among those who uphold the Vinaya.'"
Yet he was unable to speak. I replied: "Apart from the Tathāgata himself, there has never been any śrāvaka or bodhisattva capable of restraining his eloquence in joyful exposition.
Such is the clarity and penetration of his wisdom."
Third, the benefit gained from hearing the Dharma:
At that time, the two bhikṣus immediately had their doubts and regrets removed and gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, making this vow:
"May all sentient beings attain such eloquence as this."
Third, he concludes that he is incapable [of the task].
Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.
To explain this according to the provisional teachings (*yǎojiè*): Upāli explains the Dharma to two bhikṣus in accordance with the Vinaya; this is firmly established as the Tripiṭaka.

This is acceptable. However, as for those who are called *vinayadhara* (upholders of the Vinaya), there has never been one who did not take the five categories (*pañcāpatti*) and seven groups (*saptasaṃghāvaśeṣa*) as their fundamental basis.
Furthermore, one must not hastily abandon the concrete matters for the sake of abstract principle simply because they have been criticized by a Great Being (*mahāsattva*).
According to the original intent of the Great Being’s critique, one should instead integrate principle with matter and harmonize the minor rules so that they return to the ultimate.
"Great. As for "great," this refers to the three teachings of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) gate.

For the two monastic orders within the Shared, Distinct, and Complete [teachings], the five categories and seven groups of precepts constitute the precepts of phenomena (*dharma*), while non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned constitute the precepts of principle (*tattva*).
For Bodhisattvas, the ten grave and forty-eight light precepts of the Brahma Net Sūtra constitute the precepts of phenomena; one must maintain both phenomena and principle together.

To practice both the great and the small [precepts] simultaneously is the fundamental intention of the Tathāgata; it is the excellent model for which the Great Being (Mahāsattva) offered admonition and instruction.

Regarding those who understand through contemplation (*vipaśyanā*): when they give rise to a mind that discriminates based on sensory objects, they set in motion the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, thereby producing within them painful feelings, pleasant feelings, or neutral feelings.
This is called violating the precepts. Nevertheless, among these there are degrees of lightness and gravity.

Regarding the distinctions between the *vibhaṅgas* and *skandhas*, if one can turn back to investigate the source of the mind and realize that offenses and blessings are non-arising—what is called "seeking the mind throughout the three periods of time, yet the mind is not found;
where the mind is not found, the source of delusion is originally non-existent; where deluded mind is non-existent, that is bodhi;
birth-and-death and nirvana are fundamentally equal"—then since even blessings cannot be obtained, how could there be any offenses to be found?
Section. To be able to contemplate in this manner is called "skillful understanding.
○ Nine: Sending Venerable Rāhula. Part One: The Tathāgata’s Command to Send Him.
The Buddha addressed Rāhula: "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness."
Master Kumārajīva said: "When the asuras devour the moon, it is called Rāhula; in the language of Qin, this means 'obscuration,' referring to the obscuring of the light of the sun and moon.
This Venerable One dwelt in his mother’s womb for six years. Because he was obstructed by the womb, he was named accordingly.
Within the teachings of the Śrāvakas, he is foremost in secret conduct (*guhyacaryā*). The account of his causal origins is extensive; it is fully contained in Master Kumārajīva’s commentary."
I shall not cite further examples here.
II. The Venerable One’s Firm Refusal (in three parts). First, a general refusal on the grounds of being unable to bear it.
Rāhula addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not capable of going there to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the account of the incident of his being sent away.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī came to where I was, prostrated themselves in salutation, and asked me:
"O Rāhula, you are the son of the Buddha; having renounced the sovereignty of a universal monarch, you have gone forth..."
"The home is for the sake of the Way; what benefits are there for those who leave the home? I then explained to him, in accordance with the Dharma, the merits and benefits of leaving the home.
"If the Buddha had not left the home, he would have become a Golden-Wheel King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents. If Rāhula had not left the home, he would have..."
He became an Iron Wheel-Turning King, ruling over a single world-system. Master Kumārajīva said: "Rāhula missed the opportunity; there are four reasons for this.

First, he did not perceive the person's faculties and thus prescribed a medicine that was not appropriate for him. Second, the merit of leaving the household life is immeasurable, yet he described it as being limited.
Third, this is the true reality (*dharmatā*), yet he explained it in terms of signs. Fourth, the dharma of leaving the household life is fundamentally for..."
Regarding the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and *nirvāṇa*, Rāhula did not say that they would necessarily be attained at the end [of his life].
Therefore, he contradicted reason and deviated from the fundamental tenets, suffering defeat at that time.
○ Second, the narration of his refutation, in four parts. First, showing that although he left the household life, there was no benefit of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Part one.
I was censuring the benefits of speaking [of such things],
when Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Rāhula, you should not speak of the benefits of the merits of leaving the household life."
Third, it demonstrates the absence of benefit and virtue.
Why is this so? Because being without benefit and without merit is what constitutes leaving the household life.
Master Zhao said: "The intent of leaving the household life lies subtly in non-action (*wuwei*). How could the Way of non-action admit of [anything else]?"
Is it beneficial as a merit? Third, regarding the conclusion:
there is benefit and there is conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*).
As for conditioned phenomena, one may say they possess benefit and possess merit.
II. Showing the benefits of both the conditioned and the unconditioned. First, a general demonstration of the benefit of the unconditioned being without marks:
Now, one who has left the household life does so for the sake of the unconditioned dharma. Within the unconditioned dharma, there is neither benefit nor merit.
Master Zhao said: "Now, where there is the fruit of non-action, there must be the cause of non-action. That cause and fruit share the same characteristic is the Way of spontaneity (*ziran*).
To leave the household life for the sake of non-action is precisely the cause of non-action. Non-action—"
There is neither benefit nor merit; one should know that it is the same for those who have left the household life.
Part Two: Specifically showing the characteristics of the presence and absence of the benefit of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta). First, first showing the essence of the unconditioned.
Rāhula, as for those who have left the household life, there is neither "that" nor "this," nor is there anything in between.
Master Zao said: "Those who falsely leave the household life loathe this saṃsāra and revere that nirvāṇa; therefore, they perceive the distinctions between these three positions.
Those who truly leave the household life cast off all burdens and transcend both 'this' and 'that'; how could there be any such thing as right or wrong among these three?"
How extraordinary is this dwelling!
II. Furthermore, he demonstrates the ninefold function of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). First, he demonstrates that which is to be abandoned and that which is realized:
being free from the sixty-two views, one dwells in *nirvāṇa*.
That which is conditioned and possesses benefit all belongs to false views; that which is unconditioned and possesses no benefit abides in nirvana.
(2) This demonstrates the wisdom and practice undertaken by the noble ones.
That which is accepted by the wise and practiced by the noble ones is conditioned and beneficial;
this is the conduct of ignorant ordinary people. That which is unconditioned and without benefit is what the noble ones accept and practice.
Third, it demonstrates those who are subdued and those who are delivered.
He subdues the various māras and delivers those in the five realms of existence.
The term "bhikṣu" (home-leaver) contains three meanings: first, terrifying the māras; second, destroying evil; and third, a mendicant. The māras delight in...
Regarding birth and death: once one has left the household life, one further transforms others so that they all transcend the three realms and oppose the intent of Māra.
When Māra attempts to restrain them by force, they instead cause him to be bound by the five fetters; thus, having already terrified Māra as the cause, they will surely subdue him as the fruit.
Having subdued the enemy Māra, they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings—this is the capable task of one who has left the household life. The rest is as previously explained.
4. Showing what is purified and what is attained:
one purifies the five eyes, attains the five powers, and establishes the five faculties.

While those of the two vehicles attain only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the bodhisattva attains the dharma-eye (*dharma-cakṣus*); only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is fully endowed with the Buddha-eye (*buddha-cakṣus*).
The eye—this constitutes reaching directly to the attainment of Buddhahood, at which point one is truly called "one who has left the home life.

Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom are termed both "roots" (*indriya*) and "powers" (*bala*), because it is only when the roots for entering the Way are deep that power subsequently arises.

Now, having spoken of purifying the five eyes, the subsequent mention of the roots and powers means that these roots and powers may be distinguished according to the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-bhūmi*). Now...
This is ultimate suchness. 5.
Showing freedom from affliction and the abandonment of evil:
not afflicting others and remaining free from all various evils.
Those who dwell at home establish their own domains, each setting up boundaries; because they encroach upon one another, there is affliction and disorder.

Those who have left the home life dwell in leisure and vastness, like empty space; by reflecting back upon the source of the mind, the faculties and their objects are free from transgression, and thus they do not cause affliction to others.
That is to say, all various evils are likewise entirely abandoned.
(6) Showing the subduing and transcending:
subduing all non-Buddhists and transcending provisional designations.

Master Sengzhao said: "The sun and moon do not intend to dispel darkness, yet darkness is naturally eliminated; those who have left the household life do not intend to crush external views, yet external views naturally dissolve.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Conditions meet without substantiality; they are merely provisional names. If one attains their reality,"
Thus, one is not deluded regarding the conventional; hence it is called "transcendence.
(7) It demonstrates what has been emerged from and what is absent:
emerged from the mud, without attachment, without "mine-ness," without that which is received, and without disturbance.
One emerges from the mire of craving and views; there is no attachment to the three realms.
Since there is no deluded self that can receive, there are no sensations to be received. If one can be thus, what more could disturb or confuse them?
8. Showing inner cultivation and outer protection.
Internally cultivating joy, one protects the minds of others.
Master Zhao said: "Disturbance arises from excessive seeking; sorrow and suffering arise from insufficiency. Those who have left the household life [possess little...]"
Desire and agitation were thus absent, and the Dharma was fully realized within; hence, his joy was overflowing.
To "protect their minds" is what Master Kumārajīva meant by being able to encourage and accord with sentient beings, rather than acting in opposition to their hearts.
9. Showing what is followed and what is abandoned:
One follows meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and abandons all faults.
Among all faults, there is none that does not arise from distraction (*vikṣepa*). If one can follow meditative concentration, the mind will not [be distracted].
Through non-distraction, all faults will naturally be removed.
Third, this concludes the formation of true renunciation:
if one can act in this way, that is true renunciation.
IV. Exhorting the Sons of the Elders to Leave the Home Life (3). First, the Great Being exhorts them by noting that a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti said to the sons of the elders: "You all should together leave the home life within the True Dharma."
Why is this? Because a Buddha appears in the world but is difficult to encounter.
The two sons of the elder then took their leave, saying that their parents would not permit it.
The other sons of the elders said, "Householder, we have heard the words of the Buddha: if one's parents do not permit it, one cannot go forth into homelessness."
The three great bodhisattvas exhorted them by saying that one becomes a renunciant through the very arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment.
Vimalakīrti said, "Indeed, if you all arouse the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, that itself is renunciation;
that itself is full ordination."
There are three kinds of households from which one departs, and there are likewise three things esteemed in the Way. First is the household; second is the realm;

and third is the mind. Although one may have departed from the household of parents, wife, and children, if one has not departed from the household of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*), it is not true renunciation.
Although one may have departed from the household of the six sense-objects, if one has not departed from the household of the mind and consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*), it is not [true renunciation].
This is true renunciation. Only when all three aspects have emerged together is it truly renunciation. For one may have left the household life in body while the mind has not yet left it;
this is not true renunciation. Or, the mind may have left the household life while the body has not yet left it.
Nor is this true renunciation. Only when both body and mind have departed together is one truly a renunciant.
This is said in reference to those of middling and inferior faculties. As for those of superior faculties, even though their bodies remain in the secular world, [they are truly renunciant].
Yet the mind should always be that of one who has left the household life. That which the Great Being (Mahāsattva) pointed out—arousing the mind for the Unsurpassed Way—is true renunciation.

This is to transcend both emptiness and existence, and even to forget the Middle Way. It would be a pity to merely possess the name of "resolutely arousing the mind" without the practice of transcending the mundane world;
thus, one may hope not to辜负 (disappoint) the holy words of the Great Being.
III. Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Benefit:
At that time, the thirty-two sons of the elders all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
III. Conclusion on Incapability.
Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.

Regarding the explanation according to the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*): the renunciation demonstrated by the Great Being possesses no benefit of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), but possesses the merit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This can be spoken of within all four teachings; it depends solely on observing the nature of one’s progress and understanding. As for the conditioned...

That which "has" is existence; that which is "unconditioned" is emptiness. The three vehicles of the *Āgama* and *Vaipulya* [teachings] are all able to leave the house of marks and enter the house of marklessness;
though this is called "leaving home," it is not true leaving home. As for the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna-śāsana*),...
Although one may leave the houses of emptiness and existence to enter the house of the Middle Way, this is not true renunciation.
Only when a Bodhisattva of the Perfect and Sudden teaching has left the houses of both extremes does the house of the Middle Way itself become empty;
this is true renunciation.
Regarding contemplative understanding (*guanjie*): to contemplate that the single thought-moment of mind is empty is to depart from the house of signs;

to contemplate that the single thought-moment of mind is provisional is to depart from the house of signlessness; to contemplate the simultaneous negation of both extremes within the single thought-moment of mind is to depart from the house of the two extremes;
to simultaneously illumine both emptiness and existence is to depart from the house of the Middle Way. To contemplate the mind in this manner is true departure.
[This concludes] the chapter on the House.
○ Second, the dispatch of the Venerable Ānanda. First, the Tathāgata’s command to dispatch him:
The Buddha addressed Ānanda, "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
II. The Venerable One’s Firm Refusal (Part 3). First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Ānanda said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go to him to inquire about his illness.”
Master Shi said: "In Sanskrit it is called Ānanda; in the Qin language it means 'Joyful. Among the disciples, he was foremost in dhāraṇī-retention. [The interlocutor] asked:
'If Ānanda held the treasury of the Buddha's teachings, then what he heard should have been sufficient for him to know that [the Buddha] was not ill. Why did he fail to understand?'"
The answer is: Since both the ultimate truth and the skillful means are the words of the Buddha, both teachings are to be trusted.
Furthermore, it is said that Ānanda also participated in providing the skillful means.
II. Explaining the reason for this, in two parts. First, the narration of the incident of his rebuke.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, the World-Honored One suffered from a slight ailment that required cow’s milk.
I immediately took my bowl and went to stand at the gate of a great Brahmin’s house. At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "O..."
"Ānanda, why are you standing here at dawn holding your alms bowl? I replied, "Householder, the Blessed One has a slight ailment and requires cow's milk; that is why I have come here."
Master Daosheng said: "Dawn is not the time for begging for food; there must be a reason. Therefore, I questioned him. [Section Two:
Narrating His Refutation, Part Three. First, the Great Being’s Exhortation, Part Five. First, the Exhortation that the Tathāgata is Free from Illness.]
Vimalakīrti said, "Stop, stop, Ānanda! Do not speak such words. The body of the Tathāgata is of vajra-nature;
all evils have been severed, and all virtues are universally assembled. How could there be any illness? How could there be any affliction?"
Master Kumārajīva said: "In the Hīnayāna, the bones are adamantine, but the flesh is not adamantine. In the Mahāyāna, both the internal and external are adamantine;
everything is truly full, possessing great power because there is no place of illness."
Deng said: "The Tathāgata, the Bodhisattvas, and the *rishi* (powerful ones) of the Two Vehicles differ in substance, yet all are termed 'Vajra' because they are supremely firm and solid.
When ordinary people die, their flesh decays and their bones remain, yet these eventually disintegrate and fall apart.
Only the Vajra-body consists of *śarīra* (relic-bones), linked together like hooks and chains, as continuous as a chain of fine links; it never perishes."
[He was] distracted and bewildered.
○ Second, he instructed him to depart in silence and not slander [the Buddha]:
"Ānanda, go in silence; do not slander the Tathāgata. Do not let other people hear such coarse words; do not cause [the Buddha’s] great majesty..."
The virtuous devas and the bodhisattvas who have come from the pure lands of other directions heard these words.
Third, he instructed them by using the inferior to illustrate the superior:
"Ānanda, even a wheel-turning sage king, by virtue of his meager merit, still attains freedom from illness; how much more so the Tathāgata’s immeasurable [merit]!"
"How universally supreme is this assembly of merit!
Master Kumārajīva said: "There was an Arhat named Bakula. In the past, he was a pharmacist who told the monks observing the summer retreat:
'If any among you require medicine, come to me and take it. Throughout the entire period, the assembly had no need for anything, except for one [monk]."
A bhikṣu suffered from a minor illness and accepted a single harītakī fruit. Because of this, for ninety kalpas he was born among humans and devas, experiencing immeasurable happiness;
merely hearing the word "illness," his body was free from even the slightest ailment.
Even now, at the age of ninety, he has never been ill. How much more so for the Buddha, who has accumulated immeasurable merit—how could illness arise?
"Fourth, instructing them to cease slander:
'Go, Ānanda! Do not cause us to suffer this disgrace. If the heterodox Brahmans hear these words, they will think:
"What kind of teacher is this? Unable to save himself from his own illness, how can he save those who are ill? It is fitting [to prevent this]."
Depart quickly and secretly; do not let anyone hear this.
○ Fifth, regarding the Buddha’s body as supremely transcendent:
Ānanda, you should know that the bodies of all Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body, not a body of thought or desire. The Buddha is the World-Honored One.

He has transcended the three realms. The Buddha’s body is without outflows; all taints have been exhausted. The Buddha’s body is unconditioned and does not fall within the realm of numerical reckoning.
For such a body as this, how could there be any illness?
There are two kinds of triple realms: first, the triple realm within the world, wherein sentient beings cannot escape the affliction of birth-and-death (pariccheda);
second, the triple realm outside the world, wherein sentient beings cannot escape the affliction of transformation (pariṇāma).
The Buddha has transcended both of these triple realms; since he is free even from the affliction of transformation, how could he possibly have the affliction of birth-and-death?
The distinction between the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) may be understood by analogy. Thus, the Buddha’s body is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) body;
how could it fall within the numerical reckoning of mundane, segmented lifespans? Yet you say that his body has illness.
II. The Venerable One’s Remorse for His Error. First, the Venerable One feels shame:
"At that time, O World-Honored One, I was truly filled with shame; could it be that, being close to the Buddha, I have misunderstood?"
Second, a voice from the sky issued a proclamation.
Immediately, a voice was heard from the air saying: "Ānanda, it is as the householder has said; however, it is because the Buddha has appeared in this world of the five turbidities."
"Manifesting this Dharma, deliver sentient beings. Go, Ānanda, and take the milk; do not feel ashamed. Master Dayou of Wumen said:
