"As for the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*), the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: 'It is like clear water into which sand and soil are thrown;
the soil loses its solidity, the water loses its purity, and it becomes turbid and muddy. Due to these five turbidities, the principle..."
Water loses its clarity and is given five names for turbidity. First is the *kalpa-kṣaya* (劫濁). In Sanskrit, *kalpa* means "period of time.
From the time when human lifespan in the *apakarṣa-kalpa* (減劫) reaches twenty thousand years, one enters the *kalpa-kṣaya*; the four turbidities then increase and intensify.
Assembling at this time, hatred increases and weapons arise; greed increases and famine arises; delusion increases and pestilence arises.
Thus, the three calamities break out on a grand scale, and consequently, the afflictions flourish twofold and various views blaze even more fiercely.

The various turbidities converge like waters rushing into a dark torrent. Second, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) refers to the five sharp fetters—the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), attachment to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)—as well as the sixty-two views and so forth. Third, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

These refer to the five dull afflictions (*pañca-mṛdu-kleśa*)—greed, anger, ignorance, pride, and doubt—as well as the one hundred and eight afflictions and so forth. Regarding the fourth, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*):

this provisional designation is established based on the karmic retribution of grasping at the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), views, and pride. Regarding the fifth, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*):

it refers to the destruction of years and the shortening of life through momentary arising and ceasing. A detailed explanation is found in the *Yuánzhōngchāo*; those who require it should consult that text. [End of] fruit.
The *Bao yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Retribution) states:

The Tathāgata was free from illness, yet for the sake of transforming a certain brāhmaṇa—who prided himself on his own wisdom, extensively sought after heterodox paths, was stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous, and who held the Buddha-vehicle in contempt—the Tathāgata employed skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
Under the provisional name of being ill, the Three Sages manifested themselves by expedient means to guide the Brahmin.

First, they caused the Bodhisattva to go to the Brahmin’s house and transform a milch cow whose womb had given birth to two offspring; its nature was fierce and perverse, and it delighted in harming human life.
The Buddha dispatched Ānanda to go and beg for milk. The Brahmin, not yet understanding the Buddha’s intention, became angry when he saw Ānanda arrive.
A thought suddenly arose in his mind, and he said to his wife: "I now intend to have the ox trample and harm Ānanda;
that is why I called out, 'Venerable One! Venerable One! You may go to where the ox is and seek him out as you please.
When the ox saw Ānanda, it knelt down and said: "Venerable One, the Buddha wishes for my milk. You should milk the left udder and leave the right udder; milk the right udder and leave the left."
The left udder. For what reason? My two calves depend upon my milk for their very lives.
The two calves of the cow likewise crouched down and addressed the Venerable One: "We now willingly accept those waters and grass; this is our mother's milk."
"All should serve the Buddha. When the brahmin saw the ox in this manner, he felt deep reverence and admiration, exclaiming that it was unprecedented.
He immediately took various kinds of exquisite jewels and his retinue, went to the Buddha's dwelling, scattered flowers as an offering, and sought the Buddha’s forgiveness for his transgressions.
The Buddha preached the Dharma to him, and he realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). This is the fundamental account of how the Buddha converted the brahmin.

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the explanation according to the teachings (*yàojiào*): when discussing the Buddhas at the stage of fruition (*guótóu*) across the four teachings, and speaking in terms of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s transcendence of stages, they are all one and the same Buddha.
All their Dharma-body and Reward-body (*fǎbào-shēn*) are entirely free from illness. Here, we are merely discussing the manifested response-bodies (*yìngshēn*) that they manifest;
it is only in reference to these that we speak of having or not having illness. Since the fruit-stage of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching is an inferior response, [the Buddha] manifests as a king.
The Prince was born at the Twin Trees and entered parinirvāṇa there; how could this body of birth and extinction be free from illness? This is precisely what the various devas have now reported.
As for the body perceived by those of the Shared Teaching (Skt. *sāmānya-yāna*), it is a "conformity-body" (*anupraveśa-kāya*);

its manifested response is like the waves upon water, and since even that is said to be without illness, how much more so the Dharma-body and Reward-body of the Distinct and Perfect Teachings—how could they be said to have illness?
This is because what is manifested as a response is both the essence and the function.

For those who practice through contemplative understanding, the two observations of emptiness and provisional existence have not yet reached the Middle Way; thus, it can be said that they possess afflictions. However, the wondrous observation of the Middle Way—

When both are simultaneously negated and both are simultaneously illuminated, what illness could there be? Yet, when emptiness and the provisional are themselves the Middle Way, illness is itself no illness;
and when the Middle Way is itself emptiness and the provisional, it does not hinder their manifestation as illness.
“Venerable Lord, Vimalakīrti’s wisdom and eloquence are such as this. Therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness.”
II. Brief Account of the Five Hundred.
Thus, these five hundred great disciples each addressed the Buddha, recounting their own past causes and conditions and describing what Vimalakīrti had said;
they all declared that they were unable to go to him to inquire after his illness.
The Buddha’s great disciples numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty; those who manifested the acceptance of reprimand were surely more than this.
Herein, the foremost among the disciples have been cited; since these leaders have been rebuked, the rest may be understood accordingly.
Indeed, Śāriputra was foremost in wisdom, and Ānanda was foremost in erudition; these ten individuals possessed their respective long-standing excellences from former lives.
Vimalakīrti refuted them by challenging their positions. In doing so, he generally set aside their strengths to attack their weaknesses:

he refuted Śāriputra regarding his "seated meditation," Maudgalyāyana and Pūrṇa Kātyāyana regarding their "preaching of the Dharma," Mahākāśyapa and Subhūti regarding their "begging for alms," Aniruddha regarding his "divine eye," and Upāli regarding his "upholding of the Vinaya."

The Vinaya censures Rāhula for his ordination; it censures Ānanda for begging for milk. Generally, if one attacks what another excels at, one has already lost the ground of one’s own former advantage;
if one attacks what another is deficient in, it is easy to displace their new position. If one uses the small to attack the small, one will barely have time to keep one's mouth shut;
how much more so when using the great to attack the small, the sudden to attack the gradual, and the round to attack the partial? How could [the opponent] possibly...?
They met his sharp edge; thus, once they were struck down by him, few of his disciples were able to offer a word of rebuttal.

Nevertheless, there was a profound reason for what he did therein: it was precisely because the great disciples were attached in their hearts to minor practices, taking the conduct of the śrāvaka as foremost, the conduct of upholding the Vinaya as second, and the conduct of the mendicant (bhikṣu) as third.

The third is [the practice of] alms-gathering; the fourth is the practice of solitary meditation; the fifth is the practice of serving the teacher; and the sixth is the practice of preaching the Dharma.
These six practices are precisely the causes for cultivating the fruit of Arhatship and attaining the retribution of the six supernormal powers.

This constitutes the fruit [of the teaching]. The Sūtra enumerates ten individuals, which are consolidated into seven matters; thus, the noble practice (*ārya-caryā*) of Nirvāṇa is perfected, and the way for disciples to serve their teacher is established.

By means of censure, rejection, opening, and demonstration, it causes them to turn away from the Small Vehicle and head toward the Great Vehicle, thereby attaining the benefit of "fresh butter" (*navanīta*) and accomplishing the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the *Saṃdhinirmocana* assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Because the Sūtra is profound, its...
It is here that [the meaning] resides.
*The Commentary on the Non-Self in the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Scroll Five.
*The Commentary on the Non-Self in the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, Scroll Six.
Written by the Tiantai Mountain monk Youxi Chuandeng.
Section Two: Dispelling the Various Bodhisattvas. Part One: Explaining the Title of the Chapter.
*The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Four: The Bodhisattva.
The names of the Bodhisattvas and the titles of the chapters are omitted here, as they have already been explained in the "Chapter on Disciples.
II. Explanation of the Sūtra Text, in two parts. First, the extensive narration of the four great Bodhisattvas, in four sections. First, the dispatching of Maitreya Bodhisattva, in two parts.
First, the Tathāgata’s command to dispatch him.
Thereupon the Buddha said to Maitreya Bodhisattva, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.

Master Kumārajīva remarked: "Since Maitreya has already succeeded to the position of the Honored One and is destined to attain Buddhahood in this very land, he is the one venerated by the minds of the multitude;
therefore, the Buddha commanded him first. Whether Maitreya or Vimalakīrti is superior in stature cannot yet be definitively determined. Or—"
It is said: "Although Vimalakīrti was great, there were circumstances under which he did not attain Buddhahood. Or it is said:
"Although Maitreya is great, he willfully declined to proceed because of conditioned phenomena. Or it is said: "This is a manifested body of Maitreya, not his primary essence.
For these three reasons, there are records of his being summoned and constrained.
Deng said: "The karmic affinity between these two individuals should be determined by the *honji-suijaku* (original and manifested traces) of the sūtras.

Generally speaking in terms of their original status (*hon*), Vimalakīrti was once the Tathāgata Kanakamuni, while Maitreya currently occupies the rank of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) as the one who will succeed Śākyamuni in his final birth;
thus, the relative height of their original status can be known. Speaking in terms of their manifested traces (*sui*), Vimalakīrti’s rank resides in the Perfect [Teaching]."
He teaches the stage of the Dharma-body of the First Abode; it is only when Maitreya succeeds Śākyamuni’s birth-body that he does so.

According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, within the Hīnayāna teachings, this corresponds to the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), wherein the two delusions of views and thoughts are suppressed but not yet severed. Thus, the relative loftiness or lowness of their traces may also be known.
Furthermore, according to the main text, by means of non-arising (*anutpāda*), he refutes arising and ceasing, [addressing those of] the lowest of the low.
It is only fitting that he should receive the reprimand of a superior person.
II. The Bodhisattva’s Firm Refusal (in three parts). First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in three parts. First, the account of the incident of his refutation.
Why is this so? I recall that in the past, when I was the King of Tuṣita Heaven, I preached the practice of the stage of non-retrogression to him and his retinue.
Master Kumārajīva said, "This person preaches the Dharma among humans. This deva, regarding Maitreya—who is about to ascend as the Teacher of the Gods—conceives a sense of profound reverence;

therefore, he constantly comes to listen to the Dharma. Master Kumārajīva further said, "The stage of non-retrogression is precisely the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)."

Deng said: "The stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) begins at the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*) and ends at the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

According to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it begins at the first ground (*prathamā bhūmi*) and ends at the final mind. According to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), it begins at the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) and ends at the final mind.

According to the Treasury Teaching (*zangjiao*), it begins at the lower patience (*kṣānti*) and ends with the thirty-four moments of mind culminating in the Worldly Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*)."
According to the Concealed Teaching (Samdhinirmocana), the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment has already cultivated the practice of the six perfections for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;

he further dwells for one hundred kalpas planting the causes for the marks and signs of a Buddha before entering the stage of Middle Patience (*madhyakṣānti*), thereby becoming a Honored One in the position of succession and attaining the stage of non-retrogression.
II. Narrating His Refutation of My Words. 2. First, the refutation of my discriminative mind. 3. First, questioning him regarding the matter.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me: "Maitreya, the World-Honored One has bestowed upon you the prediction that in one more birth you shall attain [Buddhahood]."
Regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, Master Daosheng said: "*Anuttara* means 'unsurpassed. *Samyak* means 'correct and universal.
*Saṃbodhi* exists in that [Sanskrit] language, but it has no name here [in Chinese]. In reality, it is the wisdom that reaches the ultimate and dwells at the final limit."
Deng said: "There are four grades of bodhi. Śrāvakas cultivate it and attain the bodhi of inferior wisdom; pratyekabuddhas cultivate it and attain the bodhi of middling wisdom;
bodhisattvas cultivate it and attain the bodhi of superior wisdom; and Buddhas cultivate it and attain the bodhi of supreme-superior wisdom.
Now, when it says 'one shall attain,' this refers to the bodhi of a Buddha. However, there are four teachings, and now..."
This is merely a provisional manifestation, speaking only of the Buddha’s bodhi according to the Tripitaka teachings. Master Daosheng said:

"One life" means there are no longer immeasurable lives remaining; it refers to the single life that remains. This "single remaining life" refers solely to the one life of wondrous enlightenment (miao-jue).
Second, the refutation of the actual thesis has three parts. First, the refutation by means of [the analysis of] arising has three sections. First, the three positions are stated for determination:
By which kind of arising does one receive the prediction? Is it the past, the future, or the present?
If one says there is no arising, then there is no such thing as birth. Since it is said that there is "one birth," birth must necessarily have a world (time).

Therefore, the three periods of time are established as the means to dismantle the fundamental [view]. Indeed, the four truths of arising and ceasing are what those of the Tripiṭaka Teaching maintain.

Furthermore, let us speak in terms of the two truths of the Path and Cessation: the Path is easily subverted by its opposites, while Cessation involves the extinction of existence and the return to non-existence.
Then the arising and ceasing of the three periods of time would be manifestly real; this would constitute "having birth. How, then, can it be called "non-arising"? 2.
Refutation by way of the [three] positions:
If it is a birth of the past, that past birth has already ceased. If it is a birth of the future, that future birth has not yet arrived. If it is a [birth of the] present...
Regarding existence: in the present life, there is no abiding.
The Tripitaka Teaching is clumsy; it posits fixed determinations across the three periods of time. Therefore, those who receive this teaching take birth-and-extinction as their primary tenet.
They do not realize that within the three periods of time there are no three periods of time, nor that within birth-and-extinction there is the fundamental [nature].

There is no arising or ceasing. This is why this Great Being takes that which involves arising and ceasing according to the Tripitaka Teaching (Zangjiao) to break through its fundamental lack of arising and ceasing;
it may be said that he demonstrates this by means of the principle of non-arising according to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
It may also be said that he demonstrates this by means of the principles of the immeasurable and the unconditioned (wu zuo) according to the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (Biéyuán).
Third, citing the Buddha’s teaching as proof:
As the Buddha said, "O Bhikṣu, at this very moment you are born, you age, and you perish. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
"That which is born at the very first moment is subject to extinction; this is not taught for the sake of the ignorant. This refers to the nine temporal periods within a single kṣaṇa. One.

Contemplate the three thousand worlds: their essential natures mutually negate one another, such that arising is itself non-arising. Like sparks from a flint or flashes of lightning in the empty void, they shimmer and flicker;

if illusory cataracts are dispelled, the wild flowers of delusion vanish of their own accord—how could there be any "arising"? How then can it be said that one receives the prediction of a single lifetime?
With every new moment, arising and ceasing pass each other by; how could change wait until the onset of white hair? This is also the view of Sengzhao.
"You understand speech well.
(2) Second, refuting the two [positions] by means of non-arising. First, establishing their positions:
"If one were to receive the prediction of enlightenment through non-arising,"...
Second, refutation by means of the meaning:

Non-arising is itself the state of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). Within this state of true reality, there is neither the conferring of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) nor the attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
When a person has not yet attained the Way, their births are immeasurable. When they are about to attain the Way, there remains but one more birth.
Once the Way is attained, there is no further birth. The Great Being previously used "birth" to refute the notion of a single birth;
since there is no single birth, there is likewise no immeasurable number of births. Since there is neither a single birth nor an immeasurable number of births, there is no [birth].

The Way of birth is attained. Although birth is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), how could non-birth be indeterminate? If one does not know that even birth is indeterminate, how could non-birth be determinate?
Indeed, both "determinate" and "indeterminate" are merely conceptual constructs of the deluded mind. Since non-birth is free from such conceptual constructs, how could there be any determination?
Therefore, for the Bodhisattva’s station of non-birth, the conceptualizations of self and other—
"Death" refers to the extinction of birth; it is called "forgetting. At such a time, I do not know who is born, who is the Buddha, who has attained the Way, or who has not attained the Way.
Furthermore, who is it that receives a prediction (vyākaraṇa), and who is it that does not?
Therefore, it is said: "Within the state of ultimate reality (bhūtatathatā), there is also no receiving of a prediction," and so forth.
III. Refuting the two [positions] by means of True Suchness (*tathatā*). First, concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent:
"How is it, Maitreya, that you receive the prediction for one more birth?
This single phrase may serve to conclude the preceding; that is to say, since birth is already without prediction (*avyākṛta*), and non-birth likewise has no prediction. How?
Why is it that Maitreya receives the prediction of one more birth? If it refers to a birth in the future, then this sentence properly introduces the question:
"Why is it that Maitreya receives the prediction of one more birth? Is it because he received the prediction from suchness, and so forth?
II. The second section, the correct refutation by means of *tathatā* (suchness), has two parts. First, the refutation by means of the arising and ceasing of *tathatā*. First, the interrogation:
"Is it from the arising of *tathatā* that one receives the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), or is it from the ceasing of *tathatā* that one receives the prediction?"
Previously, the refutation of arising and ceasing led to entry into non-arising; non-arising is itself suchness (*tathatā*). Now, to further investigate and refute [the remaining misconceptions]:

the "non-arising" mentioned previously was the non-arising that enters into non-arising by means of refuting arising. What is clarified here as "suchness" is the non-arising that is the primordial nature of the fundamental reality (*dharmatā*).
Although their essence is non-dual, there is a distinction between them in terms of their doctrinal paths. Nevertheless, this is further discussed in relation to arising and ceasing.
The evidence for this is that the ultimate source has its root; it is because one has not yet forgotten the single lifetime.

For once it is said that one has received the prediction of a single lifetime, "life" must necessarily be contrasted with "extinction. This is also an inevitable condition of form; therefore, he first used this as a provisional means to express it.
2. Refutation:

If one were to receive the prediction of enlightenment through the arising of suchness, suchness would have no arising; if one were to receive the prediction of enlightenment through the cessation of suchness, suchness would have no cessation.
It is said that where there is a record (saṃskāra), there is arising and ceasing; if there were no arising and ceasing, how could there be a record?
Therefore, all that is called "having a record" is not suchness (tathatā).
II. Refuting Duality by Way of the Rational Nature of True Suchness. First, it is shown that all things are suchness:
all sentient beings are suchness; all phenomena are also suchness; all noble sages are also suchness; even Maitreya is suchness.

"All sentient beings" refers to the primary retributions (*pratyātmabhāva*) of the nine dharma-realms. "All phenomena" refers to the environmental retributions (*bhājanaloka*) of the ten dharma-realms.
"All sages and worthies" refers to the various stages of the sages and worthies of the three vehicles.
This is because, once it is called "True Thusness" (*tathatā*), then all things are thus; if there were even a single thing that was not, [it would not be True Thusness].
If it were thus, it could not be called True Suchness (tathatā).

He receives the prediction. Why is this? Because sentient beings are themselves the Buddha; there is no necessity for them to return to the source or revert to the origin.
Broken tiles and rubble are themselves the Buddha; there is no necessity to distinguish between the animate and the inanimate. Sages and worthies are themselves the Buddha;

II. Showing the Practice Without Discrimination (25 sections). First, the Practice of Quiescent Extinction:
Quiescent extinction is bodhi, because it extinguishes all marks.
Enlightenment is signless (*animitta*). One can only attain it by necessarily extinguishing all signs and conceptual discriminations.
○ Second, non-contemplation:
non-contemplation is enlightenment, because it is free from all conditions (*pratyaya*).
Awakening is free from all defiled conditions; it can only be attained by means of absolute non-reliance. III.
Non-practice as Practice:
Non-practice is awakening, because there is no recollection or thought.
Awakening is free from mental objects; it can only be attained when the mind-consciousness no longer functions.
(4) The Four Abandonments:
abandonment is awakening, because it relinquishes all views.
Bodhi is forever free from the sixty-two views and false attachments; one must sever all views before it can be attained.
○ Fifth, detachment from activity:
detachment is bodhi, because it is free from all deluded thoughts.
Awakening does not harmonize with delusive thoughts; it must be attained by remaining far removed from them.

these obstacles are themselves awakening, for they obstruct all vows.
Enlightenment is fundamentally inherent; it cannot be sought through aspiration or desire. Only by necessarily ceasing all aspiration and desire can it be attained.
○ Seven: Non-entry into Practice.
Non-entry is bodhi, because it is free from craving and attachment.
Bodhi is without craving and attachment; one can attain it only by having no entry whatsoever within the six sense bases.
○ Eighth, compliant practice.
Compliance is bodhi, for it accords with suchness (*tathatā*).
Bodhi accords with true suchness; one must not oppose the principle of reality (*yathābhūta*) in order to attain it.
○ Ninth, the dwelling of practice:
this dwelling is bodhi. Because one dwells in the dharma-nature (dharmatā), bodhi is itself the dharma-nature.
Only by constantly abiding in the dharma-nature can one attain it.
10. Reaching Practice (*prāpti-caryā*).
This refers to reaching Bodhi and reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Since Bodhi is the very limit of true reality, the mind must at all times reach this limit of reality; only then can one attain it.

non-duality is bodhi, because it is free from the mind and dharmas.

○ The twelve equal practices:
"equal" is bodhi, for it is equal to empty space.
Bodhi is equal, just like empty space; the mind must be equal in order to attain it.

the unconditioned is bodhi, because it is without arising, abiding, or ceasing.
Awakening is eternally abiding; its essence is not subject to the four marks of existence. Only when the mind is necessarily unconditioned can it be attained.

To know is awakening, for it thoroughly understands the mental conduct of sentient beings.

Enlightenment has no location, for it is devoid of form and color.

Provisional names are bodhi, because names are empty.

Awakening (*bodhi*) is like a magical creation because it is free from grasping and rejecting.

Twenty: The practice of an undisturbed mind.
Non-disturbance is bodhi, because it is eternally quiescent.
Bodhi is eternally quiescent; it cannot be attained by means of a disturbed mind.
21. The Practice of Serene Quiescence.
Serene quiescence is bodhi, for its nature is pure.
Since the nature of bodhi is fundamentally pure, one must bring the mind to serene quiescence in order to attain it.

Non-appropriation is bodhi, because it is free from objective reference (*ālambana*).
As soon as there is an objective reference, one is contrary to bodhi; only by not giving rise to grasping and attachment can one attain it.
23. Non-differentiation in practice.
Non-differentiation is bodhi, because all phenomena are equal.
Bodhi and the nature of all phenomena are equal and without difference; their characteristics are necessarily non-different. Only by this can one attain it.

Peerlessness is bodhi, for there is nothing with which it can be compared.

II. Answering by means of principle and practice, in two parts. First, the direct answer in eighteen sections. First, showing by means of the arousal of the four minds.

The answer is: The straightforward mind is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because it is free from hypocrisy. The practice of undertaking [virtuous deeds] is the site of enlightenment, because it is able to accomplish all tasks.
The profound mind is the site of enlightenment, because it increases merit and virtue. The bodhicitta is the site of enlightenment, because it is free from error.

II. Second, it is shown by means of the six practices of the other shore (*pāramitā*).
Giving is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because there is no expectation of recompense.

If one gives while demanding a reward, it constitutes a gift with signs (*nimitta-dāna*); such is a cause for rebirth as a human or deva, and is insufficient to constitute a practice of the site of enlightenment.
Furthermore, upholding the precepts is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because one thereby fulfills one's vows.
Although the characteristics of the Mahāyāna precepts are numerous, when stated in broad terms, they do not exceed the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*). First:
The first is the precept of restraining one's conduct; the second is the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas; and the third is the precept of benefiting sentient beings.
Having attained these three precepts, there is no aspiration that is not fulfilled.
Patience is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because the mind is free from obstruction toward all sentient beings.

Practicing the five perfections with such diligence that they are not mixed and with such progress that there is no retreat, one is therefore without regression.
Meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it renders the mind supple and gentle.
When the mind is distracted, one encounters all things with harshness; if one attains meditative concentration, everything becomes supple and gentle.
Wisdom is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because it directly perceives all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Third, it is demonstrated by means of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

Compassion is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it endures weariness and suffering.

Joy is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), because it delights in the Dharma.

(5) Second, the teaching on two methods for benefiting others:
Expedient means (*upāya*) is the *bodhimaṇḍa*, because it involves the transformation and education of sentient beings.
In teaching and transforming sentient beings, there are three kinds of skillful means, as explained in the "Expedient Means" chapter.
Only when each of these is fully perfected can one deliver others and lead them to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because they gather in sentient beings.
Master Kumārajīva said: First is giving (*dāna*). There are two kinds of giving: the inferior person gives material wealth, while the superior person gives the Dharma.
Second is kind speech (*priyavāditā*). Kind speech also has two kinds: toward inferior persons, one uses gentle words.
To bring joy: toward superior persons, one consoles them with Dharma-discourse; in all cases, one employs loving speech out of a heart of love.
Third, beneficial speech: beneficial speech also has two types. Toward inferior persons, one establishes skillful means to enable them to obtain worldly benefits;
toward superior persons, one establishes skillful means to enable them to obtain the benefit of the Dharma. Fourth, cooperation: cooperation also has... [text continues]
There are two types. If they associate with evil people, he entices them with wholesome dharmas; if they associate with virtuous people, he causes their roots of goodness to increase.
Entering according to their kind and acting in accordance with them is therefore called "sameness of purpose" (sābhoga).
6. This is shown by means of two methods of correct practice:
"Extensive learning is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for one acts according to what has been heard.
To hear without practicing is like counting sand, which only exhausts oneself; to practice without having heard is like being blind.
Walking. Abundant learning and true wisdom—these are what should be accepted as taught. Therefore, abundant learning is called the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Subduing the mind is the site of enlightenment, because it correctly contemplates all phenomena.
Though extensive learning and practice according to it constitute a site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one must necessarily achieve the cultivation of practice to subdue the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Only after subduing them can they be severed, whereby one is able to enter the site of enlightenment; at the outset, this is achieved by restraining the mind to a single point to effect such subdual.

Subsequently, being able to perfectly subdue [the afflictions] at the five stages constitutes "subduing"; this is the primary practice for a person of perfect capacity ascending to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
○ Seventh, it is shown by means of the Chapter on the Aids to the Path:
the thirty-seven factors are the site of enlightenment, because they involve relinquishing conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma).

One cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) because they enable the relinquishing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) notions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. One cultivates the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) because they enable the relinquishing within the conditioned:
the severing of evil that has already arisen, the non-arising of evil not yet arisen, the arising of goodness not yet arisen, and the increase of goodness already arisen.
This continues up to the cultivation of the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), and the seven factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*).
[The character] "branch" (*śākhā*). Because the Eightfold Noble Path can abandon the worldly functions of conditioned existence and enable entry into the Way.
○ Eighth, it is shown by means of the noble practice of the Four Truths.
The Truth is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for it does not deceive the world.

*Satya* (Truth) refers to the dharma that is examined and verified; therefore, it does not deceive the world. Nevertheless, there are four truths: suffering (*duḥkha*), accumulation (*samudaya*), cessation (*nirodha*), and the path (*mārga*).
There are three truths: the ultimate, the conventional, and the middle. There are two truths: the ultimate and the conventional. There is one truth: the single, real truth. There is no-truth:
the absence of the characteristics of the various truths mentioned above. To discuss only the Four Truths, first is suffering.
It is certain that this is suffering; it cannot be conjoined with pleasure and so forth, let alone with the subsequent truths.
If one correlates this with the following section on dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), then the intended meaning here is precisely to clarify the Four Noble Truths.
9. It is shown by means of the noble practice of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-ārya-caryā*).
Dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because everything from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) is inexhaustible.
The twelve links of dependent origination revolve through the three periods of time like a ring without beginning; therefore, they are inexhaustible. Furthermore,
The twelve links of dependent origination do not transcend the three paths; yet, the path of suffering is the Dharmakāya, the path of delusion is Prajñā, and the path of karma is Liberation.
How could the subtle and wondrous nature of dependent origination ever be exhausted?
10. It is shown by means of afflictions:
all afflictions are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because they are known as they truly are.
To know afflictions as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is because they are themselves awakening (*bodhi*).
Eleventh, it is manifested through sentient beings.
Sentient beings are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because they know there is no self.
The *Vajracchedikā* says: "Sentient beings, sentient beings—these are not sentient beings; they are called 'sentient beings'. This is the thorough understanding of sentient beings.

Emptiness is itself the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Furthermore, because they arise through the provisional combination of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), they are called "sentient beings.
When each and every one returns to its fundamental dharma, then fundamentally no self can be found.
Twelfth, it is demonstrated by means of all dharmas:
all dharmas are the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because one knows that all dharmas are empty.
Sentient beings cling to all dharmas as being existent; this is the source from which afflictions arise. The Bodhisattva penetrates the emptiness of all dharmas; this is the Path.
The reason a site (dojō) is established is because of inversion and because of arising; how could there be any other dharma?
○ From verse thirteen onwards, it is shown that subduing demons is the site of practice (dōjō), for it is unshakable.
The Bodhisattva realizes that the suchness of the realm of Māra and the suchness of the realm of the Buddha are one suchness, not two suchnesses;
being unmoved by the magical arts of Māra is itself the subduing of Māra.
14. It is revealed by means of the three realms.
The three realms are the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), for there is nowhere to go.
Sentient beings have six destinies: three destinies lead toward goodness, and three destinies lead toward evil; thus, there is the rising and sinking within the three realms.

The Bodhisattva does not ascend toward the good, nor does he descend toward evil. He thoroughly realizes that the triple world is like flowers in the sky, fundamentally being the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi;
therefore, he takes the triple world itself as the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Fifteenth, it is demonstrated by means of preaching the Dharma:
the lion’s roar is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) because of fearlessness.
The Bodhisattva acts in accordance with what he preaches; he expounds the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, which is to say, he proclaims it with a single voice.
He speaks, attaining understanding according to the capacities of beings; therefore, he has no fear.

(16) He demonstrates through the practice of the fruit that power, the fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) constitute the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), for they are free from all faults.
The ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth, are all the meritorious virtues of the bodhisattva’s myriad practices.

Because they are merits (*guṇa*), they possess power (*bala*) capable of extinguishing evil; because they are virtues (*guṇa*), they possess utility capable of generating goodness. Therefore, they are free from all faults.
Seventeenth, it is demonstrated by means of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).
The three types of supernormal knowledge are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), because there are no remaining obstructions.
Master Zhaolun said: "This is precisely what the Buddha has attained. Taken collectively, it is called 'Buddha. The Buddha is itself the Way. Above.
Taking the bodhisattva practices as the field, he now takes the Buddha as the path within the fruit, and all phenomena as the field.
He subdues the armies of Māra without being moved by them; he wanders through the three realms without following their courses; he proclaims the fearless sound of the Dharma without difficulty;
he possesses the thirty-two marks of a Buddha without a single deficiency; and he has attained mastery in the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Unimpeded. All these are the ways from which the Great Way arises.
○ Eighteenth: To know all dharmas in a single thought-moment is demonstrated.
Knowing all dharmas in a single thought-moment is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), because it accomplishes all-knowledge.

When the causal practices for the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) are fully prepared, then at the time of attaining Buddhahood and sitting upon that site, one thoroughly exhausts the true reality (dharmatā) of all phenomena.
The ten realms, both the primary and secondary retributions, and the nature and characteristics, as well as the beginning and end of the sacred and the mundane, are entirely the Buddha-mind;
this is known in a single thought-moment. This is no mere hyperbole.
II. Conclusion:

Thus, noble son, if a bodhisattva, in accordance with the various pāramitās, teaches and transforms sentient beings, you should know that all their actions—whether lifting or lowering a foot—are derived from the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and abide within the Buddha-dharma.
To summarize what has been explained: all phenomena of cause and effect are none other than that which the Bodhisattva constantly establishes.

Thus, whether lifting or setting down the feet, or in every action, word, or silence, there is nothing that is not the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), wherein the causal stage is perfected as the fruit of Buddhahood.

While this Dharma was being taught, five hundred devas and humans all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
III. Conclusion on the Inability [to Understand].
Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire about his illness.
Regarding the explanation through the provisional teachings (*yōkyō*): if one speaks of the six practices for reaching the other shore and so forth, all four teachings may be employed.

However, as for the arousal of the four minds, this must be a matter within the Mahāyāna gate. If one discusses the crookedness or straightforwardness of the mind, then it pertains to the realm within [the triple world].

Those who conceal their faults are considered crooked, while those who are transparent are considered straightforward. Regarding those outside the boundaries, those who remain separate are considered crooked, while those who are perfectly integrated are considered straightforward.

If one discusses crookedness and straightforwardness through successive stages of transmission, even the transparent person is still somewhat crooked, whereas the separate person is considered straightforward;
yet even the separate person is still somewhat crooked—it is only the single, perfectly integrated person who may be called ultimately straightforward.

Regarding contemplative understanding: the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way, which accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*), is the straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*). The wondrous contemplation of ultimate emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the profound mind (*gambhīracitta*).
Delighting in the practice of all wholesome deeds through the wondrous contemplation of the wondrous provisional (*upāya*) is the mind of initiating action that can accomplish tasks.
Because one contemplates these minds, one gives rise to the Four Great Vows; benefiting oneself and others is the Bodhisattva mind.
There is no error. The remaining seventeen sections may be understood by analogy with this observation.

The term "Bodhisattva" is a general designation for the seven classes of followers. If one has not yet received the bodhisattva precepts, one retains one's original name;

...such is the bodhisattva. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "Do not offer such unlawful things to us, the śramaṇas and sons of the Śākyas.
II. Holding the World Firmly Refuses. III. First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
The World-Upholder (Dhṛtarāṣṭra) addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.
[Section Two: Explaining the Reasons for This, Part Two. First, the account of the incident of his defeat, Part Six. First, the arrival of Māra to pay homage.]

Why is this? I recall that in the past, while I was dwelling in a quiet chamber, Māra Pāpīyas approached me accompanied by twelve thousand celestial maidens who appeared like Śakra, playing music and singing with stringed instruments.
Together with his retinue, he bowed his head at my feet, joined his palms in reverence, and stood to one side.
Second, the confusion of Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
He thought to himself, "I believe this is Śakra.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Pāpīyan means 'the slayer' in the language of Qin. Because he constantly seeks to sever the life-force of wisdom (prajñājīvita) of others, he is called 'the slayer.'"
It is also called "the worst among evils. There are three kinds of evil: first, evil; second, great evil; and third, the worst among evils.

If someone treats one with evil and one returns evil for evil, this is called "evil. If a person does not encroach upon oneself yet one gratuitously inflicts evil upon them, this is called "great evil.
If a person comes to provide offerings and show respect, yet one does not think of returning the favor—this is called "the worst among evils."
To return harm for kindness is called the worst among evils; of all such evils, the Māra-king is the most extreme.
Although the Buddhas always desire to bring peace and security to all sentient beings, he instead brings about their ruin and disorder; therefore, he is said to be "extreme. Master Zhao said:
"Māra maintains the tranquility of the world and seeks to disturb the minds of beings. If he were to manifest his true form, they would likely be too afraid to speak with him."
Therefore, he transformed himself into the appearance of Śakra. At that time, Dhṛtarāṣṭra did not perceive him through his supernormal vision, and thus he thought, "This is Śakra.
[The Buddha] then admonished him not to be self-indulgent, saying to him: "Welcome, Kauśika! Although you possess the fruits of merit, you ought not to be self-indulgent."
Master Shi said: "Kauśika" is a clan name; "Māgadha" is his personal name. Master Sheng said: "Because he has come for the sake of making offerings, it is well that he does so.
To follow the music of the female lute is a practice of self-indulgence (*svairinī*). One who possesses merit yet indulges in such things [is at fault]."
Furthermore, it is the root of transgression. Fourth,
when preaching the Dharma for them,

Master Sengzhao said: "The three steadfast things are the three dharmas of steadfastness: body, life, and wealth. If one forgets the body and life, discards wealth, and abandons worldly attachments..."
Furthermore, those who cultivate the Way will inevitably attain an infinite body, an inexhaustible life, and imperishable wealth.
These three are not burned even when heaven and earth are incinerated; they do not end even when the kalpas reach their conclusion. Therefore, they are called the "Dharma of Firmness."
Because the Lord of Devas was deeply attached to the five desires and did not contemplate impermanence, he exhorted him to cultivate the firm Dharma.

V. Preaching the Dharma to the Five Hundred Maidens (in four parts). First, causing them to resolve upon the Way.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to the maidens: "Māra gave you to me;
now you must all resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. He then preached the Dharma to them according to their individual capacities, causing them to resolve [upon enlightenment].

Regarding the "intention for the Way" (the aspiration for enlightenment), Master Zao said: "Since he is currently under the influence of Māra, he must follow the teachings of desire; since he is now with me, he should follow the teachings of the Way. Master Sheng said:
"Since it has already been given to me, it belongs to me; he cannot help but follow my teachings."
Second, causing them to delight in the joy of the Dharma:

He further said, "You have already resolved upon the path; there is the joy of the Dharma with which you may find self-delight, and you should no longer take pleasure in the joys of the five desires."
Master Kumārajīva said: "The nature of fish is such that they rely solely upon water; the nature of women is such that they desire only pleasure.
When one first resolves to seek the Way and exerts oneself in cultivating goodness, one has not yet attained true joy. Once the accumulation of virtue becomes pure, one’s delight becomes ever deeper.
Unchanged by hardships and even more earnest in the midst of suffering, there is genuine love within the heart and no other source of joy without."
Causing them to find delight therein, they will grow weary of celestial pleasures.
From this point downward, the enumeration of the myriad dharmas intends to capture the joy within the dharmas, rather than the dharmas themselves.
The three daughters asked about the joy of the Dharma.
The celestial maiden then asked, "What is meant by the joy of the Dharma?
The four great beings explained eighteen [types of joy]; the first is rejoicing in the Three Jewels.
He replied: "I delight in constant faith in the Buddha; I delight in wishing to hear the Dharma; I delight in making offerings to the Saṅgha.
Entering the Path begins with taking refuge in the Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics and the Three Jewels of Sustained Maintenance.
Otherwise, one's life would have no place of return and the mind would have no basis of reliance. Therefore, I take refuge in the Three Jewels of Essential Unity as my primary guide."
Otherwise, fundamental awakening (mūla-bodhi) would have nothing to manifest, and initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) would have nowhere to return.
If these two were not in harmony, the Great Way could not be realized. Therefore, taking refuge in the Triple Gem is the fundamental basis for the bliss of the Dharma.
2. Delighting in Renunciation of the Five Desires.
To delight in renouncing the five desires:
the female demons delight in the five desires and do not renounce them; how, then, can one leave the Māras?
Third, the root of delighting in detachment from desire:
one should contemplate the five aggregates as enemies and thieves; contemplate the four great elements as venomous snakes; and contemplate the internal sense bases as an empty village.
One desires to possess a precious body, yet delights in not knowing that the five aggregates (*skandhas*) are like hostile bandits,

the four great elements (*mahābhūtas*) are like venomous snakes, and the six sense bases (*āyatana*) are like an empty village. Since this body is as unreal as these— being like an enemy, like poison,
and like that [empty village]— if one can contemplate deeply, one will naturally become detached from desire, and Māra will naturally stay far away.
Fourth, one delights in protecting the resolve for the Way and delights in following and protecting that resolve;
only then can one take refuge in the Triple Gem and further distance oneself from the five desires. By contemplating the root of desire, one becomes fully endowed [with these qualities].
This is the intention for the Path (mārga-citta). This intention for the Path should indeed be protected so as not to be lost.
○ Fifth, delighting in benefiting sentient beings;
delighting in providing abundant benefit to sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva’s resolve is set upon delivering others. Since one has attained personal progress and benefit, it is appropriate to broaden that which benefits oneself in order to benefit others.
(6) Joyfully honoring and supporting the teacher.
One should delight in reverently supporting one's teacher.
The teacher is like a king of physicians; when a serious illness has been well-cured, one ought to contemplate repaying that kindness.
How much more so when the illness is only slightly improved—one cannot yet depart from the physician. Therefore, it is fitting to delight in revering the teacher.
○ Seventh, the cultivation of the six perfections with joy:
joy in the extensive practice of giving; joy in the steadfast maintenance of the precepts; joy in patience and gentleness; joy in the diligent accumulation of roots of goodness;
joy in meditative concentration without distraction; and joy in stainless, luminous wisdom.
As shown in the preceding text, this is the initial arousal of the mind. To reach the other shore, one must cultivate the six perfections.
○ To delight in expanding the path-mind;
to delight in expanding the bodhicitta.
Previously, while following and protecting the bodhicitta, one first germinated its seed; now, one causes it to be expounded and expanded through the four great vows.
Ninth: Delighting in the subduing of all māras.
One delights in subduing the various māras and delights in severing all afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are many kinds of māras; for now, let us speak of them briefly in terms of cause and effect.
The various māras are the fruit summoned by afflictions, while afflictions are the cause created by the various māras. Indeed, if there were no afflictions, then there would be no [māras].
This is because there is Māra.
○ Tenth, delighting in purifying Buddha-lands.
Delighting in purifying Buddha-lands.
Only by severing delusions and subduing demons can one transcend birth and death and achieve the Buddha-way; one must certainly cultivate the causes for purifying the Buddha-lands.
(11) The eleventh is the mark of delighting in the accomplishment of the primary and secondary physical characteristics.
Because one desires to achieve the marks and signs of excellence (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), one cultivates all manner of meritorious virtues.
Only when the Buddha-land is purified does it become the true environment; the Buddha’s primary retribution consists in being fully endowed with all the marks and signs.
Desiring to bring the fruit of these marks to completion, one must necessarily cultivate the karma that produces them.
Twelfth: Adorning the Site of Enlightenment with Music.

To adorn the site of enlightenment with music means to broaden the bodhicitta above; this is called the "Path" (mārga). Since every path must have a site (kṣetra), the Buddha’s Dharma-body is that site.
Furthermore, having first realized the pure *dharmakāya*, it is as yet without adornment; one should therefore adorn it with the myriad practices of merit.
(13) Joyfully hearing the Dharma without fear.

To delight in hearing the profound Dharma and not fear it means that one does not dread the profound Dharma, which is the method for attaining ultimate Buddhahood. This Dharma is exceedingly deep and immeasurable, inconceivable;
it is what is called "profound, firm, remote, and far-reaching," such that no one can reach it. When those with a beginner's mind hear this Dharma, few do not give rise to fear.
To be fearless in this regard is to be one who truly delights in the Dharma.
(14) When delighting in the three liberations, one delights in the three gates of liberation at the proper time, and does not delight in them at an improper time.
Master Zhao said: "The three liberations are emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. To be bound and thereby released is what is meant by 'liberation.

That which serves as the means for accomplishing the Way is called a 'gate. When those of the Two Vehicles enter these, they do not exhaust their ultimate limit, but instead attain realization midway."
This is called an improper time; it is what this Great Being does not delight in.
Fifteenth, he delights in associating with fellow students.
Delighting in associating with fellow students, his mind harbors no resentment or obstruction toward those who are not fellow students.
Master Kumārajīva said: "I study the Mahāyāna, and he does likewise; this is called 'studying together. If what is practiced differs, it is called 'studying differently.
When our circumstances are the same, we rejoice; when they differ, we remain equanimous. Our minds are impartial, without increase or decrease."
Sixteenth, delighting in protecting and associating with [the right],
yet delighting in protecting against evil associates and delighting in associating with virtuous associates—
loving the good and detesting the evil— one is a solitary practitioner, not one possessing the mind of the Mahāyāna. Although...

When encountering those who are evil, one should still guide and protect them, causing them to reform their wickedness and turn toward goodness; only then does one truly belong to the Bodhisattva Vehicle.
(17) Joyful Mind Delights in Purity.
The mind delights in purity.
Possessing the aforementioned joys, the mind becomes joyful; if it were not pure, the demon of delight would enter the mind.
(18) Joyfully cultivating the various factors of enlightenment.
To delight in cultivating the dharmas of the immeasurable *mārga-pakṣya* (factors of the path) is what constitutes the Dharma-joy of a bodhisattva.
Although the categories of the path number only thirty-six, they are called "immeasurable" because this refers to them as encompassing the four teachings.
Thus, when the Separate Teaching speaks of the immeasurable Four Truths, Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, Six Perfections, and factors of the path, it is precisely [this].
For the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattva's Dharma are infinite.
○ The Six Māras and their Daughters Return.
Thereupon, Pāpīyān said to his daughters, "I wish to return with you all to the celestial palace."
The seven women did not comply.
The women said, "We have been given this householder; we possess the joy of the Dharma and find it most delightful.
We no longer take pleasure in the delights of the five senses."
All these women possessed innate spiritual faculties; having heard the joy of the Dharma but once, they immediately found it sweet.
Therefore, they did not follow Māra nor take pleasure again in the five desires.
Māra, the eighth, instead begged them [to return].
The Māra said, "Householder, you should relinquish this woman. One who gives away all that they possess to others is a bodhisattva.
[9] The householder returned her to him.
Vimalakīrti said, "I have already relinquished her; you may take her away so that all sentient beings may have their aspirations for the Dharma fulfilled.
Master Kumārajīva remarked: "By returning the daughter to Māra, the layman fulfills Māra’s aspiration; therefore, he made this vow."
"May all sentient beings attain the fulfillment of their aspirations for the Dharma. This is the vow of Vimalakīrti. Master Zhaolun said:
"To grant a wish based on a specific circumstance is the constant practice of a Bodhisattva. By returning the woman to Māra, Māra’s own wish was fully satisfied;
therefore, he gave rise to a vow that all sentient beings might attain the fulfillment of their aspirations for the Dharma, just as Māra’s wish was fulfilled."
Deng said: "The layman was begging for a girl on behalf of Māra, his intention being to convert him. Once the conversion was complete, the layman had no further need for her.
Nevertheless, although she was returned to him, she still belonged to him, because his mind was identical to that of a Great Being."
