Thereupon, the daughters questioned Vimalakīrti, "How do we abide in the palace of Māra?"

Master Zhao said: "In the past, when you were in the palace of Māra, you took the five desires as your pleasure; now that you are among the Bodhisattvas, you take the joy of the Dharma as your pleasure.
When you return to the heavens of Māra, what practice will you undertake?"
II. Showing the Three [Dharma Doors]. First, the illustrative explanation. Vimalakīrti said:
"Sisters, there is a dharma door called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp. You should study it. As for the Inexhaustible Lamp:
it is like a single lamp lighting hundreds of thousands of lamps; all that was dark becomes bright, and that brightness is never exhausted."

A lamp takes the dispelling of darkness as its purpose; therefore it is said that "all who are in darkness shall be enlightened. Beginning with a single lamp, one lamp is transmitted to another, and this transmission is inexhaustible;
hence it is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (*akṣaya-dīpa*). This is still expressed through metaphor.
II. The Convergence of the Two Dharmas.
"Sisters, it is like this: suppose a single bodhisattva were to instruct and lead hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Yet, his own resolve for that path would not be extinguished; rather, in accordance with the Dharma he teaches, he himself..."
It increases all wholesome dharmas; this is called the "inexhaustible lamp.
Now, a single bodhisattva may be compared to a single lamp. To guide and lead hundreds of thousands of sentient beings is like one lamp igniting hundreds of thousands of lamps.
In this way, their resolve for the Way is neither extinguished nor exhausted. This is why [it is so called].
This is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp. III. Conclusion.
Although you are currently in the palace of Māra, by means of this Inexhaustible Lamp, cause countless sons and daughters of the gods to resolve upon [enlightenment].
As for the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, it is to repay the Buddha’s kindness and to bring great benefit to all sentient beings.
While the previous metaphors and teachings were still general in their indication, they are now concluded and brought home, specifically commanding the demoness to abide in the realm of Māra.

In the palace, he transmits the lamp of the Dharma that is inexhaustible, thereby expanding the mind of Bodhi. This is precisely because human beings are easy to transform, whereas those of demonic nature are difficult to subdue;
thus, by identifying with the demon as being identical to the Buddha, he causes the demonic mind to be transformed.

This is what constitutes the true repayment of the Buddha’s grace and the bringing of benefit to sentient beings. Now, this Dharma-gate possesses two meanings: the horizontal and the vertical. First, regarding the horizontal:

Regarding the meaning of the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (akṣayapradīpa): it refers to how, within this very world, various individuals transmit [the teachings] to one another, each person illuminating the next.
It is like the practice of setting up an inexhaustible lamp today, where a single lamp is lit in the center and ten mirrors are suspended around it;

the light and reflections multiply and interpenetrate one another. The thousand lamps within a single mirror pervade all the other mirrors, and the [lamps] within those many mirrors likewise pervade all.
A thousand lamps enter entirely into a single mirror; therefore, it is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (*akṣayapradīpa*).
Regarding the vertical dimension, the Inexhaustible Lamp refers to the successive transmission from generation to generation, illuminating without end.

It is like one lamp that, as it is about to be extinguished, transmits its light to a subsequent lamp; the transmission of this subsequent lamp is infinite, and its continuous circulation never ceases.
Therefore, it is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp.
11. The Woman Follows Māra Back.
At that time, the goddess bowed her head at the feet of Vimalakīrti and followed Māra back to his palace, where she suddenly vanished from sight.
"Third, I conclude that I am incapable.
World-Honored One, Vimalakīrti possesses such sovereign supernormal powers, wisdom, and eloquence;
therefore, I am not fit to go to him to inquire after his illness."

Regarding the classification according to the provisional teachings: although it is difficult to definitively categorize the *Lokadhātu-parigraha-bodhisattva-sūtra* as either Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna, or as partial or perfect, if one says that entering meditative concentration allows one to recognize a māra while failing to do so when not in concentration, this clearly refers to a *Tripiṭaka* bodhisattva. Were it otherwise, [the case would differ].

This refers to a bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [on enlightenment]. It should be understood that such a person not only does not immediately recognize Māra, but is also as yet unable to subdue him.

Yet it can also be known that when a Mahāsattva preaches the Dharma to Māra, and regarding the Dharma-joy he delights in, and the inexhaustible lamp he transmits—all of these belong to the realm of Māra which is itself the Buddha.
This is the Way of the Single Suchness and Non-dual Suchness, which is judged to be of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
There is no doubt regarding this teaching.

As for "resolving through contemplation," one contemplates that a single thought-moment contains the hundred realms and the thousand suchnesses; every mind is the true mark of reality (*dharmatā*), and every phenomenon is truly eternal.
This is the horizontal elucidation of the meaning of the "inexhaustible lamp. If the mind flows forth and enters the three periods of time, then in every thought-moment...
To awaken and realize this, every moment of mind illuminates and examines itself; thus, the beginning and the source accord with one another, luminous and inexhaustible.

This is precisely the meaning of the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (wujinding): "to illuminate it again and again. As the Patriarch said: "Nine ages in a single kṣaṇa; three thousand worlds in one thought-moment.
Regarding the essential principles of Chan and the Teachings, what doctrine could be deemed inadequate? This is what is meant.
IV. Sending the Elder’s Son Sudatta (in two parts). First, the Tathāgata commands him to go:
The Buddha addressed the elder Sudatta, saying, "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
II. The Elder’s Firm Refusal (in three parts): First, a general refusal on the grounds of incapacity.
Śubhavyūha addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, I am not capable of going there to inquire after his illness.”
II. Explaining the reason for this in four parts. First, the narration of the incident of the refutation.

Why is this so? I recall that in the past, within my own father’s house, I established a great assembly of almsgiving to provide offerings to all śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and various non-Buddhists, as well as to the poor, the lowly, the destitute, and beggars, for a period of seven full days.
Master Daosheng said: "According to the Dharma of the Brahmins, one performs a great sacrifice to Brahmā on the seventh day, practicing extensive giving with the hope of being reborn there.
He [the donor] says that he has inherited his father’s legacy and continues his ancestral vocation; by entrusting himself to this practice, he can bring about the illumination of the Dharma-giving."

"This is truly great. Dīpaṃkara said, "In the customs of the Western Heavens, when a Great Almsgiving Assembly is established in Sukhāvatī, from the sovereign and ministers down to the elders, householders, and those of great wealth, all follow one another’s example.
This is the virtue of governance through which wealth is dispersed and the people are gathered. Kumārajīva said, "There are three kinds of beggars: first, śramaṇas; second, noble persons."
Third, the lowly and base. All those who follow their own desires are called beggars.
Second, recording his words of rebuke, in two parts. First, the general refutation of the matter.
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered the assembly and said to me: "O son of a householder, a great sacrificial feast (*mahā-dāna-pūjā*) should not be..."
"As you have proposed, we shall hold an assembly for the gift of Dharma; what need is there for this assembly of material gifts? Master Kumārajīva said:
"When one sees another practicing giving, rather than rejoicing in it (anumodanā), they instead criticize and disparage them.

There are three kinds of giving: first, the gift of material wealth; second, the gift of the mind; and third, the gift of Dharma. To give material wealth to others is called the gift of material wealth. [The gift of] compassion..."

To equalize one’s own mind and bestow happiness upon others is called the gift of the mind (*cittadāna*). To preach the Dharma for the benefit of others is called the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Furthermore, all the various virtues practiced by a bodhisattva are intended solely to bring benefit to sentient beings. There are two kinds of such benefit to sentient beings.
First, there is immediate benefit; second, there is future benefit. Because of these two, both are called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).
Now, because one wishes to cause those of virtuous conduct to practice the mind of giving the Dharma, material giving is set aside.
II. The second section uses the sudden to supersede the gradual, consisting of two parts. First, the question:
"I said, 'Householder, what is meant by the assembly for the gift of Dharma?
Second, the answer, which has two parts. First, a general explanation of the sudden gift from the perspective of the fruition."
The Dharma-giving assembly has no beginning and no end; it simultaneously makes offerings to all sentient beings. This is called the assembly of Dharma-giving.
Master Zhaoluo said: "To assemble people through fixed forms cannot be expected for even a single moment; to relieve things with material wealth cannot..."
In a single moment, it pervades all. Thus, that which unifies and penetrates without corners encompasses everything without omission;

that which silently bestows the moisture of the Dharma covers all simultaneously without waiting for the proper time. Therefore, it can take the boundless as a single assembly, such that there is no place where the Way does not provide nourishment.
Dwelling in the heart while harboring virtue, the myriad things naturally submit. Why then persist in the petty kindness of moistening one another with droplets, while abandoning [the greater good]?
Now, the greatness and benefit of the rivers and seas lies in establishing a single occasion of offering while instituting the conventional practices for both preceding and succeeding periods.
Dēng said: "What you, Layman, call a 'Dharma-giving assembly' (dharmadāna-pūjā) generally clarifies the great giving upon the fruition of Buddhahood.
However, since the fruit must necessarily arise from its cause, the intention is to lead those of virtuous character to aspire toward the fruit so as to cultivate the cause; therefore, it is sudden."

It is a matter of "taking away" by degrees: taking away wealth by means of the Dharma, and taking away traces by means of the mind. If one reaches the state of Buddhahood, then wealth, Dharma, and mind are without distinction.
One is thus able to bestow a single wealth upon immeasurable people, guide immeasurable multitudes with a single Dharma, and harmonize immeasurable categories within a single mind.
This does not mean that the general practice of giving away one's wealth is rendered ineffective.
II. A detailed explanation of how the fruit arises from the cause, in three parts. First, the question:
What is meant by this? II.
The demonstration, in twenty-two sections. First, the causes for giving rise to the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*).
That is to say: one gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness by means of bodhi; one gives rise to a mind of great compassion by means of rescuing sentient beings;
one gives rise to a mind of sympathetic joy by means of upholding the true Dharma; and one practices a mind of equanimity by means of gathering wisdom.

The four immeasurable minds can be possessed by both Brahmā and those of the three vehicles. However, for some they result in the merit of Brahmā, while for others they lead to the three types of enlightenment.
Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, acts for the sake of the fruit of Buddhahood—enlightenment—to rescue suffering sentient beings, to protect and uphold the True Dharma, and to embrace wisdom;
therefore, he alone is able to practice the great gift of the Dharma.
Second, the arising of the causes for the six *pāramitās*:
by gathering in those who are stingy and greedy, one gives rise to the *dāna-pāramitā*; by transforming those who violate the precepts, one gives rise to the *śīla-pāramitā*;
by means of the dharma of non-self, one gives rise to the *kṣānti-pāramitā*; and by being detached from the marks of body and mind, one gives rise to the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
Through the characteristic of bodhi, one gives rise to the dhyāna-pāramitā; through omniscience (sarvajñatā), one gives rise to the prajñā-pāramitā.

The Tripiṭaka Bodhisattvas also practice the six perfections; however, they give rise to the perfection of giving to transcend stinginess, the perfection of precepts to transcend greed, the perfection of patience to transcend insult, the perfection of vigor to transcend indolence, the perfection of meditation to transcend distraction, and the perfection of wisdom to transcend delusion—doing so for their own sake rather than [for others].

As for human beings, although they have crossed to the other shore of the *pariccheda* (segmented) birth-and-death, they have not yet crossed to the other shore of the *pariṇāma* (transformative) birth-and-death;

thus, they are insufficient to accomplish the Dharma-giving of the six *pāramitās*. Therefore, we now initiate the Buddha’s sixfold *pāramitā*-giving, which encompasses everything from stinginess up to *prajñā*, and through omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), this is able to achieve the great Dharma-giving.
Third, they give rise to the causes of the three gates of liberation:
they give rise to emptiness while teaching and transforming sentient beings; they give rise to signlessness without abandoning conditioned phenomena;
and they give rise to wishlessness while manifesting birth.
Master Sengzhao said: "To dwell upon sentient beings is to deviate from the meaning of emptiness; to dwell upon the meaning of emptiness is to abandon sentient beings.
One who skillfully penetrates the characteristics of dharmas and leaves their mind empty of attachments will, throughout the day, transform sentient beings while never deviating from emptiness.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The signless cuts off all conditioned existence; therefore, he instructs that one must not abandon [sentient beings]. Master Sengzhao further said: "To act..."
This refers to the fabrication of birth and death. For those who undergo rebirth, it is not the case that they are born through the act of creating birth.

Therefore, when a Mahāsattva undergoes rebirth, they constantly give rise to non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Master Deng said: "Those of the Hīnayāna enter the three gates of liberation and inevitably sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence.
The Buddha, having realized this essence, gives rise to great function; he is born from non-birth, and his birth and transformation are two aspects of one reality."
Profoundly dark. It is signless yet possesses signs; signs are themselves signlessness. It is unconditioned yet performs action; action is itself non-action.
○ Fourth, the arising of the causes of skillful means.
To uphold the True Dharma, one must exert the power of skillful means.
To uphold the True Dharma, one requires both the provisional and the ultimate gates: internally, one practices according to the ultimate path;

externally, one gathers and nurtures sentient beings through *upāya-kauśalya*. Thus, being in accord with principle while not contravening the nature of things, one is truly capable of protecting the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
To maintain [the practice].
○ Fifth, to give rise to the causes for the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) in order to deliver sentient beings; that is, to give rise to the four means of integration.
To deliver sentient beings, one does not fail to practice the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*);
therefore, one should give rise to them. (6) To give rise to the cause for eliminating the dharma of pride, one eliminates the dharma of pride by serving all with reverence.
Or, though one may respect those above, if one does not respect those below, then negligence and arrogance will arise because of it.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings, they may view them equally through the lens of Buddha-nature, or they may regard them universally with compassion and reverence.
If one possesses the mind of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, how could there be any arrogance?
(7) Arising the causes for the three steadfast dharmas:
regarding body, life, and wealth, one gives rise to the three steadfast dharmas.
See the previous note.
○ Eighth, the cause for giving rise to the recollection of the Dharma:
among the six recollections, one gives rise to the recollection of the Dharma.
Who among humans is without thought? What is precious is that they attain its correctness. On one hand, contemplate the Three Jewels as one body;
on the other hand, contemplate giving, precepts, and the devas. There is no state of mind that will not thereby become correct.
○ Ninth, the cause for giving rise to sincerity and straightforwardness:
regarding the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-ābhiprāya-samagra-vinaya*), one gives rise to a sincere and straightforward mind.
Master Kumārajīva said: "If one wishes to bring harmony to the assembly, it must depend on these six dharmas: first, to initiate physical action with a heart of loving-kindness; second..."
First, one initiates verbal karma with a mind of loving-kindness. Second, one initiates mental karma with a mind of loving-kindness.

Third, when receiving food, one sets aside a portion of the rice from one's bowl to offer it to one senior monk and two junior monks. Fourth, one maintains pure ethical discipline. Fifth, one possesses the wisdom of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*).
Sixth, if one practices these six dharmas, the community will always be harmonious and compliant, free from discord or contention. In the past...
There were two assemblies engaged in a common dispute; the Buddha, on account of this, taught the six points of harmonious respect (*ṣaḍ-ābhisamācārikāḥ*).
○ Tenth: giving rise to the causes of pure livelihood.
By correctly practicing wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to pure livelihood.
There are two kinds of purity of livelihood (*ājīva*). First, the external, which is to constantly practice begging for food, as in Śāriputra’s response to Viśākhā.
Second, the internal, which holds that if there is even a single instance of unwholesomeness within the three types of action (*trikarma*), one cannot be considered pure.
○ Eleventh: Giving rise to the causes for pure joy.
When the mind is pure and joyful, one draws near to the noble ones (*ārya*).
How could the noble ones of the Three Vehicles be easily approached? It is only when the mind is pure and joyful that one can draw near to them. Thus it is said:
One is able to draw near [to them].
○ Twelve: The cause for giving rise to subduing.
One does not harbor hatred toward others, but gives rise to a mind of subduing.
The failure to tame the human mind has two maladies, namely: attachment and aversion.
For one who studies the Way, even if they themselves lack attachment, should they harbor aversion, the mind remains untamed.
○ Thirteenth, it arises from the cause of the profound mind (*adhyāśaya*).
By means of the dharma of renunciation, one gives rise to the profound mind;
the profound mind is the mind directed toward the fruit of Buddhahood. Only when one has definitely departed from the two kinds of houses within the triple world can one be so called.
Only when one has attained depth may one enter the abode of the various jewels.
(14) Arising the cause of much learning:
by practicing according to what is taught, one gives rise to much learning.
If one merely possesses extensive learning, it is like a blind man hearing of the Way; to hear but not practice is like having eyes but no feet.
Only when the blind and the lame assist one another can they reach their destination. This is the ultimate point.
○ Fifteenth, the cause for arising in a secluded place.
One arises in a secluded place by means of the dharma of non-contention (*araṇā*).
Master Zhao said: "Enmity and rivalry arise from the gathering of crowds; non-contention emerges from seclusion. Master Deng said: "Emptiness..."
Seclusion is true *araṇya*. In the Hīnayāna, it is defined by emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
In the Mahāyāna, it is the state where the nature of awakening is wondrously luminous and original awakening is luminously wondrous; this is the true site of practice for *araṇya*.
16. Arising from the cause of meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*), one proceeds toward the wisdom of the Buddha. One arises in meditative seclusion;
however, the meditative seclusion of the Hīnayāna has no such destination, because in that system, concentration is not identical to wisdom. In the Mahāyāna, concentration is indeed wisdom.
Because of wisdom, one approaches the Buddha’s wisdom; thus, one engages in meditative seclusion (*pratisaṃlayana*).
○ Seventeenth: The cause for initiating practice.
It is to untie the bonds of sentient beings and to initiate the stages of practice (*bhūmi*).

The Bodhisattva’s Four Great Vows take the salvation of sentient beings as their foundation. Yet, if one has not yet attained liberation oneself and hastily attempts to save others, one not only sinks oneself but also causes others to sink.
Therefore, one vows to sever all afflictions and vows to study the Dharma-gates, taking these as the correct means for delivering others and untying their bonds.
18. Arising the Causes of Merit:
Through the possession of the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the purification of the Buddha-field (*buddhakṣetra*), one gives rise to meritorious karma.
In the bodhisattva’s practice, all merit is for the sake of attaining the Buddha’s marks and purifying the Buddha-field; otherwise, it would be merely provisional.
This vehicle is not the practice of the incomplete path.
○ Nineteenth: It arises from the cause of the karma of wisdom;
it knows the mental inclinations of all sentient beings and preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate. Thus it arises from the karma of wisdom.

Master Zhao said: "The myriad practices of the Mahāyāna are divided into two types of karma. Because wisdom serves as the standard for practice, the karma of wisdom (*jñāna-karma*) is established separately.
Since all other practices follow from it, the karma of merit (*puṇya-karma*) is established collectively. Whatever is cultivated and established is not accomplished by a single type of karma;

yet, in various sūtras, the cultivation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) and the pure land is linked to the karma of merit, while mindfulness of the Dharma and the preaching of the Dharma are linked to [the karma of wisdom]."
The karma of wisdom. This refers primarily to the abundance of its functional activity; it has never been devoid of mutual correspondence.
Twenty: arising from the cause of Brahma-karma, one knows all dharmas, neither grasping nor rejecting, entering the gate of the single characteristic, and giving rise to the karma of insight.
Master Zhao said: "To decisively and thoroughly examine the principles is called *jñāna* (wisdom); to direct the mind toward discernment is called *prajñā* (insight).
First one resolves the thoughts of sentient beings and determines the characteristics of all phenomena, and only then does one preach the Dharma; therefore, this is linked with *jñāna*.
Now, one directs the mind to discern the characteristics of phenomena, causing them to enter through a single gate; therefore, this is linked with *prajñā*. As for 'lamp,' it means knowing all."
The Dharma is neither grasped nor abandoned; it is to contemplate the middle within the middle. To enter the gate of the single characteristic is to realize the principle of the middle.
Is this not where the Dharma-gate of the Buddhas and the wise vocation of the great man reside?
Twenty-one: It gives rise to the causes for all wholesome karmas;
it severs all afflictions, all obstacles, and all unwholesome dharmas, and brings forth all wholesome karmas.

Within the three wholesome paths of existence, how could there not be wholesome karma? Nevertheless, as all such karma belongs to the three obstructions, it is insufficient to be considered truly wholesome karma.

Only by severing all afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), all retributive obstructions (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and all karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), and practicing in this manner, can it be called true goodness.
Twenty-second: The cause for giving rise to the factors that assist the path to Buddhahood.
By attaining all wisdom and all wholesome dharmas, one gives rise to all factors that assist the path to Buddhahood.
Master Zhao said: "All wisdom is the activity of knowledge (*jñāna-karman*); all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) are the activity of virtue (*guṇa-karman*);
and the dharmas that assist the Buddha-way are the various untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas of the Mahāyāna. Daoping said: "All dharmas that assist the Buddha-way..."
It is not that the adornments of merit and wisdom are not accomplished; therefore, one must give rise to them by means of these two dharmas.
III. Conclusion:
"In this way, son of good family, this is the assembly for the gift of Dharma. If a bodhisattva abides in this assembly for the gift of Dharma..."
He is a great donor and also a field of merit for all the world.
Now, as for this assembly: although things are divided by their natures, they must gather according to their kind. Previously, matters were used to illustrate matters;
now, matters are likewise used to illustrate the Dharma. Since matters involve the gathering of wealth and the gathering of people, the Dharma likewise involves the gathering of types.

From the illumination of the Dharma and the gathering of those who illuminate the Dharma, they have already formed a Dharma assembly; how much more so when reaching the fruit of Buddhahood, where there is neither before nor after.
Through wealth, through the Dharma, and through the mind, they simultaneously make offerings to all sentient beings.
This is why they are called the Great Dharma Assembly, the Great Donor, and the Great Field of Merit.
III. Gaining Benefit by Hearing the Dharma.
World-Honored One, when Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma, two hundred people from among the assembly of brahmins all resolved their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
IV. The Four Causes for Beneficial Giving (2). First, regarding the prior practice of giving material wealth:
At that time, my mind attained purity, and I marveled at this unprecedented occurrence.

I prostrated at the feet of Vimalakīrti and immediately untied a necklace worth hundreds of thousands [of gold pieces] to offer him. He was unwilling to accept it. I said, "Householder, please, you must certainly accept it. Following...
That which is given according to one's intention.
II. Transforming [the gift] into the Dharma-gift has four parts. First, practicing inconceivable giving.
Vimalakīrti then accepted the necklace and divided it into two portions. Taking one portion, he offered it to the foremost person in this assembly.
He gave one portion to the beggar below and offered it to that Sugata Duṣprasaha;

this clearly illustrates impartial giving (*sama-dāna*). If one were to discuss the superiority or inferiority based on the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), there would be a vast difference between the two.
Now, by means of the equality of mind and the equality of dharmas, one practices the equality of wealth and so forth.

This demonstrates that the assembly for the gift of Dharma is truly the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, the subsequent passage manifests wondrous responses to verify that this is not in vain.
Second, the manifestation of inconceivable response:
All those in the assembly saw the Tathāgata Duṣpradharṣa in the land of Prabhāsa;
they also saw the pearl necklace above that Buddha transform into a jeweled pavilion with four pillars, its four sides exquisitely adorned, yet without obstructing one another.
The assembly seeing that Tathāgata signifies turning the inconceivable cause toward the ultimate fruit.
Furthermore, the sight of the pearl necklace upon that Buddha’s head signifies that the cause of this Dharma-gift will necessarily result in the fruit of the unsurpassed path of awakening.
The four-pillared jeweled platform is the seat upon which one sits when attaining the path of Buddhahood.
It must be thus. That the four sides are solemnly adorned without mutual obstruction signifies the land of true retribution, which is free from all hindrances.
○ The third layer clearly illustrates impartial bestowal.

At that time, Vimalakīrti, having manifested these supernatural transformations, spoke again as follows: "If a donor gives with an impartial mind to even the lowliest beggar as if they were the Tathāgata—
regarding the field of merit as being without discrimination, equalizing it with great compassion, and seeking no karmic reward—
this is called the fulfillment of the gift of Dharma."

Master Zhao said: "If one can equalize the honorable and the humble, and practice giving with impartial compassion as the singular retribution for one's actions, then one possesses the perfection of the gift of Dharma."
Fourth, the recipients obtain benefit.
A most lowly beggar within the city, having witnessed this supernatural power and heard what was spoken,
immediately resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The lowest of beggars are the field of compassion (*karuṇā-kṣetra*). When people had not yet heard the Dharma of equality, they regarded compassion as something base.
Now that they have heard the Dharma, they not only realize that the mind of giving is equal, but they also know for themselves that the essence of reverence and compassion are identical.
Since the essence of reverence and compassion is identical, how could one allow others to give with an impartial mind while being unable to do so oneself?
Since one’s own field [of merit] is merely equal [to others], why not give rise to the unsurpassed mind of enlightenment—the field of respect?
○ Third, concluding the inability [to go].
Therefore, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.

Regarding the explanation according to the provisional teachings: since the elder’s son Sudāna has already joined the ranks of the bodhisattvas, the fact that he convened a great assembly can be understood through the *Tripiṭaka* (the teaching of phenomena and practice).

Furthermore, if one understands that the Great Being, through this assembly of Dharma-giving, practiced impartial compassion to reveal and instruct [others], then it can also be known that the teaching belongs to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*).
Regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guan-jie*): other meanings may be understood by analogy with what precedes.

If one contemplates that the gift of Dharma (*dharma-dāna*) is equal, then one contemplates that a single thought-moment is equal to the Buddha-mind; this constitutes an assembly for the equal Dharma.

By practicing the gift of the equal Dharma, if one contemplates separately, observing that a single thought-moment is replete with the ten realms (*daśa-dhātu*), then contemplating the Buddha-realm (*buddha-dharmadhātu*) is called the "Difficult-to-Conquer" (*Durjayā*).

Come! Observe the dharma-realm of hell as the lowest of beggars; yet this birth of the Buddha and that [birth in hell] are identical within a single thought-moment, all being simultaneously the True, the Conventional, and the Middle.

Since one no longer perceives the superiority of the Buddha-realm above, nor the inferiority of the hell-realm below—such contemplation as this is called the "Assembly for Contemplating the Equality of Mind."
II. A Brief Account of the Bodhisattvas.
Thus, each of these bodhisattvas spoke to the Buddha regarding their own past causes and conditions, recounting the words spoken by Vimalakīrti.
They all said, "We are not fit to go there to inquire after his illness.

The sutra’s account of the bodhisattvas mentions only four individuals by way of brief illustration. The listing of these four matters is intended precisely to reveal the Dharma-gate for the realization of Buddhahood by bodhisattvas;
if one can possess these four, it is sufficient. How is this made clear? It is because these constitute the fundamental principle for attaining Buddhahood.

The essential point lies in the cause and effect of the true nature (*dharmatā*). Maitreya’s reception of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to attain Buddhahood in a single lifetime corresponds precisely to that fruit;
his teaching of the Dharma to the three youths, including Prabhāvyūha, likewise corresponds precisely to that cause.

It is precisely because at the time of attaining Buddhahood, one must sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) to subdue demonic adversaries and transmit the inexhaustible lamp, and only thereafter extensively practice the gift of Dharma.
However, this does not mean that the site of enlightenment is only constituted at the moment of sitting there;

it must essentially exist within the causal stage. In every action, whether lifting or setting down the foot, everything is none other than the site of enlightenment. Such are the designations of cause and effect.
This is what is meant by "correspondence. As for the subduing of Māra, one must further realize that the realm of Māra is itself the Buddha-realm.

If Māra were not identical to the Buddha, how could countless sons and daughters of heaven all hear the Dharma, resolve their minds upon the Unsurpassed Way, and transmit the Dharma-gate of the Inexhaustible Lamp?
Thus, since the Dharma of the Inexhaustible Lamp can be transmitted within the realm of Māra, it can likewise be transmitted elsewhere.
Is it not fitting that this alone should accord with the Dharma-realm? Furthermore, this is the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate, which is present everywhere without exception.
As for the Dharma-assembly of equality regarding the gift of Dharma, it is precisely what those Bodhisattvas of great resolve ought to practice.
To demonstrate this at the end is also to reveal the beginning and end of the causes and effects of the Buddha-way. Moreover, one must...
One must understand that for a bodhisattva, the path lies in the mind and not in outward traces.

If one seeks a bodhisattva solely by means of external traces, then only those who wear crowns upon their heads and whose bodies are adorned with necklaces and various ornaments would be considered bodhisattvas, while all others would not be of their kind.
Now, if one seeks them by way of the mind, then although the traces differ, the fundamental essence does not differ. Therefore, the Dharma...
Among the bodhisattvas, there are bodhisattvas who are [themselves] bodhisattvas; there are bodhisattvas who are śrāvakas;
there are bodhisattvas who are elders (gṛhapati) and lay devotees (upāsaka); and there are bodhisattvas who are sons and daughters of good family.
If Maitreya, as described in the present text, has received the prediction of one more birth, he is certainly a bodhisattva among bodhisattvas. Dhṛtarāṣṭra, however, is a śrāvaka.
Xiang was a bodhisattva among monks; Guangyan was a bodhisattva among youths; and Shande was a bodhisattva among elders.
Therefore, if one seeks the bodhisattva through the mind, the path of the bodhisattva is vast;
if one seeks the bodhisattva through outward traces, the path of the bodhisattva is narrow. As for bodhi, although what is designated by that name is one, the path—
It varies according to the person. Furthermore, there are four grades: those of inferior intelligence who practice it attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;

those of middling intelligence who practice it attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha—this is not what is being discussed here; only those of superior intelligence who practice it attain the enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
This is precisely the dharma-gate practiced by the four individuals including Maitreya, yet the Great Being Vimalakīrti...
As for those who cultivate this with the highest of superior wisdom to attain the Bodhi of the Buddha, it is here that [the teachings] are struck, broken, opened, and revealed.

Sometimes the *zang* (storehouse/hidden) is integrated to return to the *tong* (common), the partial is separated to return to the perfect (*yuan*), and the gradual is integrated to return to the sudden (*dun*).

This was precisely appropriate for the time of the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*) period, when the four gates were universally opened and the three faculties were equally benefited. This, moreover, is the universal approach.
The teaching and the principle are naturally so.

Part Two: Dispatching Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. First, explaining the title of the chapter:
*The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Five: "Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Illness."
This may be understood by reference to the preceding section.
II. Explanation of the Sūtra Text, in three parts. First, the Tathāgata’s command and dispatch:
At that time, the Buddha addressed Mañjuśrī, saying: "Go to Vimalakīrti and inquire after his illness."
Master Zhaolun said: "Mañjuśrī" means "Wondrous Virtue" in the language of Qin. The Sūtra states that he has already attained Buddhahood in the past, named "Dragon-Lineage Supreme Honored King.
[Section Two: The Humility of the Two Bodhisattvas, Part One: Humility in Refusing to Respond.]
Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, that superior person is difficult to respond to. Master Zhao said:

Mañjuśrī, intending to satisfy the minds of the assembly and to fulfill his mission, first praised the virtues of Vimalakīrti so as to generate in the multitude the thought that such a person is difficult to encounter;
thus he praised that man’s path as supreme and difficult to respond to.
Deng said: "The Dharma assembly of Vimalakīrti is vast and inconceivable. When host and guest engage in their profound discourse, they must face one another like a wooden block and a mallet.
To fashion a vessel of the Dharma, how could it be through mere minor conditions? Thus, without Vimalakīrti, there would be no one fit to be the host;
without Mañjuśrī, there would be no one fit to be the guest. First, the others were found to be inadequate; subsequently, Wondrous Virtue (Mañjuśrī) appeared."
It is difficult to repay [your kindness]. I must certainly comply with your command to deliver these words, so as to bring about this auspicious assembly of our time.
II. Praising His Merit:

He has profoundly realized the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*). He skillfully expounds the essential points of the Dharma; his eloquence is unimpeded, and his wisdom is unhindered. All bodhisattvas...
He fully understands all ritual methods and penetrates the secret treasury of all Buddhas without exception. He subdues all demons and sports with supernatural powers;
his wisdom and skillful means have both reached the further shore.
Profoundly penetrating the true reality (*tathatā*), the essence realized is profound. Skillfully expounding the essentials of the Dharma and so forth, the function arising from it is great.
Fully knowing all the ritual methods of the bodhisattvas as the causes for practice, the wisdom that emerges into the provisional is matured.

There is nothing among the secret treasuries of the Buddhas that one does not enter; the fruit carried therein is fulfilled. As for the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) for subduing Māra, they are wisdom.
Skillful means. These three [qualities] reach the other shore without exception. As for such a person, how could they be easily answered?
○ Third, the Bodhisattva accepts the command, in two parts: first, the formal narration of accepting the command.
Nevertheless, I must comply with the Buddha’s sacred command and go to inquire after his illness.
Although it will be difficult for me to respond appropriately, I may perhaps go once I have received the command;
for when one inquires after the illness by imperial decree, the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power will surely bestow its protection, and thus there may be some success.
II. Narrating His Dignified Manner (Vīrya), Part Five. First, the Great Assembly’s Reflection on the Past.
Thereupon, within that assembly, the various bodhisattvas, great disciples, Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings all had this thought:
"Now these two great beings, Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, are conversing together; they will surely discourse on the wondrous Dharma.
At that moment, eight thousand bodhisattvas, five hundred śrāvakas, and hundreds of thousands of devas and humans all desired to follow them.
The assembly at the Āmra Garden consisted of eight thousand śrāvakas in common with the Buddha, and the Buddha’s constant retinue also numbered one thousand two hundred and fifty people.

As for those who did not go along, there are two possible reasons: first, five hundred among them had their faculties matured and were fit to receive the benefit of the "raw butter" (amṛta) from this assembly, and thus they all went together; the others had not yet received such benefit, and therefore did not go.
Second, he preaches the Dharma from the Buddha’s seat. The empty space cannot be exhausted; the remaining assembly does not go there, but remains to attend upon the Buddha.
Second, the arrival and demeanor of the bodhisattvas.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, surrounded by a respectful retinue of bodhisattvas, great disciples, and gods and humans,
entered the great city of Vaiśālī.
○ The Three Great Beings Prepare for the Ceremony.
At that time, the elder Vimalakīrti thought to himself: "Now Mañjuśrī is coming together with a great assembly.
He immediately employed his supernatural powers to empty the interior of his room, removing all furnishings as well as his attendants, leaving behind nothing but a single couch.

He fell ill and lay down. Master Sengsheng said: "I contemplate this as an empty room; this demonstrates a disposition of vast receptivity. Because there is 'coming,' there is 'going,' and thus it is empty;

its subtle application serves to mark the fundamental principle. Master Sengzhao said: "The manifestation of this illness arose because of current events. The empty room and the departure of attendants [serve this purpose]."
To initiate the discourse on "arising," he simply placed a single bed; this is the origin of the practice of borrowing a seat. He said:

"The room is empty, which symbolizes the fundamental land of quiescent light (*jiguang-tu*). The empty room symbolizes the traces of phenomenal application (*yòngjí*). While objects have coming and going, emptiness has no arrival or departure.
Thus, by relinquishing old traces to bring forth new responses, the room accommodates a vast seat; this is the manifestation of a Buddha-land within the midst of dust. It is not... [text ends].
That which has a basis for its functioning through deliberation is thus.
4. The Bodhisattvas enter and see.
When Mañjuśrī had entered the house, he saw that the room was empty, devoid of all things, with only a single bed where one lay alone.
V. The Mutual Exchange between Guest and Host (2). First, the Great Being praises his arrival.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said: "Welcome, Mañjuśrī! You come with the characteristic of non-coming; you see with the characteristic of non-seeing."
This virtuous Mañjuśrī arises from the essence to manifest its function; relying on the fundamental, he descends as a trace-manifestation.

The subtlety of these two aspects—essence and manifestation—as function is such that how could there be coming or going in the essence of the Dharmakāya? Yet, visible manifestations do not hinder the descent of response from the Dharma;
relying on the essence to give rise to function, this is precisely "coming with the aspect of non-coming" and "seeing with the aspect of non-seeing."
The two bodhisattvas responded with polite greetings.
Mañjuśrī said, “It is so, householder. If one has come, there is no further coming; if one has gone, there is no further going. Why is this?
That which comes comes from nowhere, and that which goes goes nowhere. This is what can be seen.”

Furthermore, that which has already come does not come again; this means there is no characteristic of coming. That which has already gone does not go again; this means there is no characteristic of going.
The same applies to the characteristic of seeing. Indeed, when the Sage manifests his traces, they are like waves upon water; though the waves may be a thousandfold...

The differences are merely provisional. The nature of water is eternally one; it does not become different through a thousand variations. Arising as a response from the Dharma, the whole body is itself the Dharma.
Since the Dharma has no coming or going, how could its response be anything other than identical? Thus, Mañjuśrī answered in this manner.
I. First, the formal inquiry regarding his illness. 2. First, he first conveys his own words:
"Setting aside this matter for now, Householder, can this illness be endured? Is there improvement from medical treatment? Has it not worsened?"
This is because his illness is the same as that of ordinary people; thus, he asks in a general manner, using the common expressions for inquiring after one's health.
Second, [the Buddha] then poses his question.
The World-Honored One has sent his inquiries most earnestly and repeatedly.
To say that the Buddha’s inquiry after the householder’s illness was "extremely long" means that it was exceedingly protracted.

In the Confucian texts, the causes of illness are explained through the five elements (*pañca-mahābhūta*) and their mutual generation and overcoming; in the Buddha-dharma, the causes of illness are explained through the increase or decrease of the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*). Although the words differ—
On the surface they appear different, but in principle they are actually the same. Recently, the non-Buddhist teacher Li Madou (Rimadu) of the Western Heavens refuted the Buddha-dharma, saying:
"The human body does not receive the earth element; it consists of only three elements. Illness likewise consists of only three elements.

This is indeed the general doctrine of the non-Buddhists of the Western Heavens. They do not realize that each of the four great elements possesses both a collective and a specific meaning. Collectively, they all pervade; specifically, [they function differently].
Thus, it follows the aggregation of sentient beings to form their bodies. When the four great elements are in harmony, the person is free from illness;
when one element is out of harmony, one hundred and one illnesses arise; when all four elements are out of harmony, four hundred and four illnesses arise simultaneously.
This lack of harmony is merely a matter of increase and decrease.
III. The Threefold Personal Inquiry. Part Two: First, the three general questions.
"Householder, from what cause does this illness arise? How long has it been present? And how shall it be extinguished?"
II. Regarding the three responses given to the two [questions], the first response concerns the duration of the illness.
Vimalakīrti said: "From ignorance and craving, my illness arises."
Master Zhao said: "The answer concerns the duration [of the illness]. Why does the Bodhisattva suffer from this ailment? It is simply because he gives rise to illness out of compassion for others.
The illness of sentient beings has ignorance and craving as its root; the illness of the Bodhisattva has great compassion as its source. Indeed, the high arises from the low."

This cause is not birth. Therefore, the arising of compassionate distress originates from ignorance and craving; yet ignorance and craving have no fixed sequence, and their source cannot be identified.
My own long-standing illness shares the same root as theirs. This clarifies that the beginning of compassionate distress need not be discussed solely in terms of oneself.
II. Answering the second question: "How should this illness be extinguished? This has two parts: first, the explanation by way of Dharma; second, the initial statement. [The Buddha said:
"Because all sentient beings are ill, therefore I am ill. If all sentient beings were to attain freedom from illness..."
"Then my illness will be extinguished.
Master Zhaowang said: "The answer is 'extinguished. The illness of a Mahāsattva arises because of others. Since their illness has been extinguished, what cause for affliction remains for me?
Nevertheless, because sentient beings are infinite and their delusion and craving are boundless, he is moved by great compassion and bestows it upon them."
Because their measure is equal, the former compassion is inexhaustible, taking delusion and craving as its limit; the latter compassion is boundless, perishing together with all living beings.
This is because compassion reaches [all things]; it is used to clarify that the cessation of compassion is not something remote.
II. Explanation. Why is this so?
It is because the Bodhisattva enters into birth and death for the sake of sentient beings. Where there is birth and death, there is illness.
If sentient beings can become free from illness, then the Bodhisattva will no longer have illness.
Master Zhaolun said: "The Dharma-body is without birth; how much more so, then, can it have form? Since it has no form, from what source could illness arise?
Nevertheless, because he undergoes birth for the sake of others, he cannot remain without form. Since he possesses form, he cannot be without affliction;
therefore, according to the duration [of his stay], he shares in their illnesses. If they are freed from illness, then the Bodhisattva likewise has no further illness."
Furthermore, there is a parable:
Suppose an elder has an only son. When the son falls ill, the parents also fall ill; yet when the son recovers from his illness, [the parents likewise recover].
The parents also recovered.
○ Third, the analogy of the correspondence:
The Bodhisattva is likewise; toward all sentient beings, he loves them as his own children. When sentient beings are ill, the Bodhisattva is ill. When sentient beings...
When the illness is cured, the Bodhisattva is also cured.
(3) Answering regarding the cause of the illness:
He further asks, "From what cause does this illness arise? The illness of a Bodhisattva arises from great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
III. Three Questions Regarding the Emptiness of the Room and the Absence of Attendants. Part Two: The Initial Two Questions.
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder, why is this room empty and devoid of attendants?"
One asks whether the room is empty; one asks whether there is no attendant.
○ Second, answering the two questions with two [points]. First, answering the question regarding the emptiness of the room. 2. First, directly answering that question.
Vimalakīrti said: "The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty.

The emptiness of Vimalakīrti’s room was originally intended to represent the wondrous land of *śāntaprabhāsa* (the Land of Tranquil Light). Now, when he speaks of the lands of all Buddhas, he refers to this very *śāntaprabhāsa*.
Although it is *śāntaprabhāsa*, it also encompasses the three lower lands; it is like one who dwells within golden grain. Thus...
The Land of Tranquil Light is where the various Bodhisattvas dwell; this is the Land of Real Reward (*vipākabhūmi*). The Land of Expedient Means is where those of the Two Vehicles dwell.

The Land of Common Residence is where elders and laypeople dwell together; this is the land of ordinary beings and sages. What is now called "land" encompasses all four lands. Where they are empty, all are equally empty.

What is now called "Quiescent Light" (Jigō) is the ultimate, supreme grade. It possesses exclusively the virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, and is entirely devoid of the characteristics of the three delusions and two deaths;
therefore, it is described as "emptiness. This is not like the emptiness of the first gate of the three liberations in the Hīnayāna, which regards emptiness as the absence of even a single thing.
As will be seen in the subsequent passages, [the Buddha] borrows his seat from King Dīpaṃkara and begs for alms at the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) world.
The non-obstruction of the one and the many, and the mutual containment of the small and the large—these inconceivable liberations all originate from this.
This is what the Great Master called "true and pure liberation."
II. Answering the Counter-Question in Two Parts. A. The First Three Questions and Answers Clarify the Emptiness of the Merits of the Fruit. 1.
The First Question and Answer Concerns That by Which It Is Empty. A. The Question.
He asked again, "By what is emptiness defined?

Master Zhao replied, "In a room, it is by the absence of objects that it is considered empty. [The questioner asked,] "By what is a Buddha-field empty? This was intended to clarify the meaning of ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).
II. The Response.
He replied: "By means of the emptiness of emptiness.

Regarding "emptiness above," it refers to the emptiness of the Tathāgata’s wisdom of realized fruition (*pratyātma-jñāna*). Regarding "emptiness below," it refers to the emptiness of the *dharmakāya* realized by the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, the emptiness of the *dharmakāya* is inherently possessed by all living beings; yet because they lack the wisdom of retribution (*vipākajñāna*), the *dharmakāya* does not manifest.
Therefore, regarding the emptiness of the empty room, one must further employ the wisdom of retribution of Vimalakīrti to empty that very emptiness of the room and remove the existence of the room.
This is the intended meaning. When Mañjuśrī asks, "By what is it made empty? he is precisely questioning wisdom. Vimalakīrti’s profound realization [is the answer].
Therefore, he answered with "emptiness of emptiness.
○ Third, the question and answer regarding what is the use of emptiness. Part two: First, the question.
He asked again: "What is the use of emptiness?"
The intent of Mañjuśrī’s question is: Since the principle of the Dharma-body is fundamentally empty, what need is there to employ the wisdom of retribution (vipākajñāna) to empty it?
2. The Answer:
It is said that it is empty because of non-discriminative emptiness.
This answer rests upon two points of meaning. First, the Dharma-body is fundamentally without discrimination;
if one does not realize emptiness, one falls into discrimination. Therefore, non-discrimination is emptiness, and thus it is appropriate to empty it.
Second, sentient beings fall into discrimination and fail to accord with emptiness, thereby giving rise to the afflictions of birth and death. For this reason, one desires to realize this.
Emptiness. One should accord with the principle of non-discriminative emptiness by means of emptiness itself. ○ Section 31:
Question and Answer on Whether Emptiness Can Be Discriminated (2). First, the question:
Furthermore, can emptiness be discriminated?
II. The Answer.
He replied: "Even discrimination is empty.
Now, wisdom is the antithesis of ignorance; that which is called ignorance exists precisely because of the absence of discrimination. Since [discrimination] is absent...

Discrimination constitutes ignorance; thus, it can be known that wisdom also possesses discrimination. However, there is a distinction between that which takes objects as its conditions (*ālambana*) and that which does not.
Ordinary beings turn their backs on original enlightenment (*mūlapratibodha*) and fall into taking objects as conditions; therefore, their discrimination becomes consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Bodhisattvas illuminate the *dharmakāya* and do not fall into taking objects as conditions; therefore, their discrimination becomes wisdom (*jñāna*). Thus, ordinary beings possess discrimination [that is consciousness].

Both having discrimination and being without discrimination result in delusion; for a Bodhisattva, both having discrimination and being without discrimination result in wisdom. Generally speaking, for a Bodhisattva, that which possesses discrimination is "quiescent yet constantly illuminating," and that which is without discrimination is "illuminating yet constantly quiescent.

Because it is illuminating yet constantly quiescent, it is said that even discrimination is empty. Master Sengzhao also stated: [The original Chinese text continues: "Discrimination is precisely non-discrimination; non-discrimination is precisely discrimination. Therefore, though there is discrimination, it is not dualistic; though there is no discrimination, it is not non-dualistic. This is because the essence of the mind is originally pure and luminous. It is only due to the adventitious defilements of ignorance that one fails to realize this. Once ignorance is extinguished, the nature of the mind is revealed. Since the nature of the mind is originally luminous, it is called "wisdom" when it is free from delusion. Thus, the Bodhisattva’s practice consists in maintaining this luminosity while remaining in a state of non-attachment. This is why it is said that although there is discrimination, it is ultimately empty. This is the profound meaning of the Middle Way.

It is not that one must first eliminate all thoughts and then claim to have attained enlightenment; rather, it is through the very presence of thought that one realizes its emptiness. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "To dwell in the midst of all phenomena without being stained by them—this is the dwelling of a Bodhisattva. This is the true path of liberation. One who understands this is called a true follower of the Buddha. Those who otherwise cling to the duality of existence and non-existence merely increase their own confusion. May all beings awaken to this truth. (Note: The final sentence regarding Master Sengzhao is an interpretive summary based on the provided fragment.)
It is said: "What was previously called 'discrimination' is merely the discrimination of non-discrimination.
If one can be without a mind toward discrimination while discriminating within non-discrimination, then even though one discriminates all day long, one has never actually discriminated.
Therefore it is said that discrimination is also empty. Although Master Zhao’s words are beautiful, as for their ultimate aim—

It would not be manifest; it simply cannot provide people with a point of entry. All the preceding questions and answers should be understood as clarifying [the truth] by means of immediate phenomena.
For example, within a chamber, the room is empty and fundamentally void. Being void, there is no obstruction; yet when objects are present, they create obstruction.
This is a metaphor for how the Buddha-land is fundamentally empty, but sentient beings create obstruction through their attachments. Through wisdom, the Bodhisattva...

"Empties its contents; this is precisely what is meant by 'emptiness of emptiness. Mañjuśrī asked again: 'If the room is empty and that emptiness is itself empty, why is it necessary to further employ emptiness?
He answered: 'Because the room is empty, there is no discrimination; because there is no discrimination, it is empty. Therefore, it is appropriate to empty it.

Precisely because it is empty, it is of a single characteristic and without discrimination; because there is no discrimination, it is empty. Were there even a single thing present, [discrimination would arise]. "

Thus, it arises in dependence upon objects. Therefore, it is said that it is empty because of non-conceptual emptiness. Mañjuśrī asked again: "If there were objects within the room, there would be conceptualization;
could emptiness itself not be conceptually distinguished? He replied: "Conceptualization, too, is empty."
The meaning is this: if one belongs to the realm of common sentiment, then there are both things and conceptual discrimination.
However, when viewed through principle, it is not only that things are empty; even conceptual discrimination itself is empty. Thus it is said, "discrimination is also empty.
This chapter originally uses phenomena to clarify principle; therefore, I have explained it again here.
Section Three: Clarifying the Emptiness of the Person through Two or Three Questions and Answers. First, a question and answer concerning where emptiness should be sought.
First, the question:
Furthermore, it is asked, "Where should emptiness be sought?"
The preceding section elucidated the emptiness of the virtues of the fruition, clarifying the relationship between the objective realm and wisdom by means of the Dharma-body and Reward-body.

Those who do not understand this will mistakenly believe that Vimalakīrti’s room is empty; thus, those at the initial stage of the path are excluded from participation, and the heterodox and the orthodox become utterly separated.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī initiates the inquiry, hoping that Vimalakīrti will provide a definitive resolution.
II. The Response.
He replied: "One should seek it among the sixty-two views (*dvāṣaṣṭi-dṛṣṭi*).

The sixty-two views are the false interpretations adhered to by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) whose mental activities lie outside the [Buddhist] principle. Among the two types of latent tendencies (*anuśaya*):"

The sharp edge of a blade belongs to the active afflictions (*kleśa*); being sharp, it belongs to discrimination (*vikalpa*). Its efficacy surpasses that of the dull back of the blade, which, when discussed in terms of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), belongs to the afflictions of cultivation.
Tracing the flow back to its source, it belongs to the afflictions of nature (*prakṛti-kleśa*). The afflictions of nature and the purity of nature share the same essence.
When one practices while deluded, although the defiled and the pure appear distinct, upon awakening to them as the very nature, the defiled and the pure are non-dual.
Thus we know that "nature-defilement" is merely another name for Buddha-nature. For the essence of True Suchness inherently possesses the ten realms.
Its essence is unchanging, yet it can accord with conditions of defilement and purity. Following pure conditions, it can manifest as Buddha, as purity, as goodness, and as correctness;
following defiled conditions, it can manifest as the nine [realms], as defilement, as evil, and as deviation.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Able to follow along with defiled and pure conditions, it fully creates the ten dharma-realms.

What is now said—seeking the fruit of Buddhahood, the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, the objective realm, and wisdom, within the midst of the sixty-two views—is precisely to cause one to contemplate and cultivate that defilement is itself the nature of defilement.
When the nature of defilement is interfused, there is no phenomenon that does not tend toward it; one spontaneously encompasses and attains the nature-purity of the Buddha-realm.
II. The Second: A Question and Answer on Where the Sixty-two Views Should Be Sought. 1. The Question.
Furthermore, it is asked: "Where should the sixty-two views be sought?
2. The Answer.
The answer is: One should seek it within the liberation of all Buddhas.
Master Zhao said: "Abandoning false views is called liberation; turning one's back on liberation is called false view.
Thus, false views and liberation are mutually exclusive; which of them is the source? That which is their source is but one. Therefore, one seeks it within liberation.

"Regarding 'when it is based on wrong views' (邪見): the lamp [of wisdom] is the pure aspect within the nature of *tathatā* (true suchness), while wrong views are the defiled aspect within the nature of *tathatā*.
Since both are *tathatā*, there is no distinction between the false and the correct.
If one follows defiled conditions and flows along with the current, one becomes false. Now, it is said that wrong views should be regarded as the Buddhas."
Seeking within liberation causes one to flow upstream back to the source; it is to set aside differences and seek the underlying unity.
○ Question and Answer 31: What is sought in liberation? Part 2: First, the question.
He asked again: "Where should one seek the liberation of all Buddhas?
The second answer:
He replied, "One should seek it within the mental activities of all sentient beings."
Now, false views are delusion; liberation is awakening. Both are matters of cultivation, not of inherent nature (*prakṛti*); they are derivative, not fundamental.
If one follows the current, a thousand differences arise, such that one cannot help but perceive them as distinct.
If one traces back to the source, the One Way is equal, such that one cannot help but perceive them as identical. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The mind is like a skilled painter."
They construct the various five aggregates. Within all worlds, there is no dharma that they do not construct.
This is precisely because the mental activities of sentient beings, in a single thought-moment, inherently possess the nature and characteristics of the ten realms, complete in every respect.
They may be made deviant, they may be made correct; they may become ordinary beings, they may become Buddhas. Therefore, the liberation of all Buddhas causes [beings] among the multitudes...
One seeks it by giving rise to mental activity within the sphere of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*). This is the liberation of false views; both are fundamentally rooted in mental activity.

Non-Buddhists seek it by contravening the nature of reality through unwholesome means, and thus they fall into false views. The Buddhas seek it by following the nature of reality through wholesome means, and thus they achieve liberation.
What is this liberation? It is precisely that the lands previously shown are all empty; they are empty even of emptiness, and there is nothing [to be grasped].
The various classifications of emptiness are all matters of this same principle.
The fundamental framework and great tenets elucidated in the sutras, as well as the great function of liberation, all originate herein. It is for this reason that Vimalakīrti lay ill.

Regarding the interpretation through contemplation (*guanjie*): one contemplates a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*), even that which is as brief as a finger-snap, and realizes it is the chamber of ten feet square (*fangzhang shi*).

Using the wisdom of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) to contemplate this single thought-moment, one sees that it is both still and moving, both luminous and obscured; this is precisely Vimalakīrti manifesting the appearance of illness.
To fully realize its total emptiness is to remove everything from within the chamber; the Buddha-land is likewise empty. Thus it is.
By means of the wisdom of the contemplation of emptiness, one empties the objects of that contemplation; this is "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
Realizing that neither subject nor object can be apprehended, one is empty by virtue of non-discriminative emptiness; thus, even discrimination is empty.

One contemplates that within the nature of this single mind, the five aggregates are each and every one the *dharmadhātu*, like the jewels in Indra’s net—layer upon layer, inexhaustible, and mutually interpenetrating.
Regarding the relationship of host and guest, or whether the form is large while the self is small, or that the self is within the form, and so forth—these are the emptiness of emptiness and so on;
they should be sought among the sixty-two views. Such views are equal to the Buddha-dharma realm;
thus, the sixty-two views should be sought within the liberation of all Buddhas. The ocean of infinite lands is not separated from it.
The tip of a hair: this means that the liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings.
○ Second, the answer to the question regarding having no attendants, in two parts: first, the direct answer.
Furthermore, regarding what you have asked concerning why there is no attendant: all Māras and all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are my attendants.
Now, to revere oneself while following one’s mandate, providing whatever is required for service—this is called being an attendant. To act contrary to this is not so.

If one takes that which is right to be right and that which is contrary to be wrong, then the objective realm becomes subject to discrimination and the principle will reside in falsehood; thus, right and wrong become entangled.
When mixed within the divine breast, the heterodox and the orthodox become entangled in the contemplation of the Way. It is not only that which is contrary that is considered contrary;
even that which is compliant becomes contrary in turn. Now, the Mahāsattva realizes that Māras are like Buddhas;
seeking liberation amidst all views, there is nothing heterodox that is not orthodox, and nothing contrary that is not compliant. How much more so in the realm of desire!
All are the realm of Māra; the objects of desire are all the realms of Māra. To realize the true mark (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, then everything is Buddha;
to follow along with conditions and discriminate among sensory objects, then everything is heterodox.

Therefore, one who skillfully masters the Way may allow the Jing and Wei rivers to remain distinct yet not separate them, and may distinguish between incense and rancid herbs yet not differentiate between them.
II. The interrogation and explanation:
Why is this so? Because the various māras delight in birth and death, yet the bodhisattva does not abandon birth and death.
Because externalists delight in various views, yet the bodhisattva remains unmoved by those views.
Master Zhaolun said: "Māras delight in attachment to the five desires and do not seek transcendence from the world; therefore, they are bound by birth and death.
Those of heterodox paths, though seeking transcendence, cling to their own doctrines; therefore, they are bound by false views.

The Great Being perceives that birth and death are identical to nirvāṇa, and thus is able not to abandon them. He perceives that false views are identical to right view, and thus is able to remain unmoved."
Because they are immovable and do not abandon [the world], they are able to serve as attendants by means of this very [reality].
As for those who understand through contemplation, they eliminate the afflictions of views and thoughts along with birth and death; thus, they take the śrāvaka saṃgha as their attendants.
That which is affliction and birth-and-death is, when contemplated, taken to be bodhi and nirvana; thus, even the various māras and non-Buddhists become one's attendants.
○ Third, the inquiry into the causes and conditions of this illness has three parts. First, the inquiry into the characteristics of the illness. Second, the initial inquiry.
Mañjuśrī said: "As for the illness of the householder, what are its characteristics?
By asking about the characteristics of his illness, he intends to reveal that the illnesses of sentient beings are likewise without characteristics."
II. The Response.
Vimalakīrti said: "My illness is formless and invisible.
This need not necessarily mean that because Great Compassion is free from affliction it is formless and invisible; rather, one should address it directly in relation to sentient beings.
This illness is likewise fundamentally formless, just as the illness of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) is formless and invisible.
If one were to refer to the Great Being alone, it would be devoid of meaning.
II. Questioning this illness: Part Two. First, the initial question. Furthermore, he asks:
"Is this illness associated with the body, or is it associated with the mind? Mañjuśrī asked this three times;
these questions should naturally follow one another. Since he has asked what the characteristics of the ailment are, it must necessarily be related to either the body or the mind.
[They] coincide. If [the illness] were conjoined with body and mind, then among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it would certainly belong to one specific element;
thus, the three answers of Vimalakīrti would also have to follow in succession. Now, since the questions and answers are interspersed, it is sufficient that my illness is formless and invisible;
with this single answer, all [objections] are dispelled, leaving no room for further interjection. Therefore, between the questions and answers—
He spoke with a pause. [Section Two: The Answer] He replied:
"It is not a union of the body, because the characteristics of the body are separate. Nor is it a union of the mind, because the mind is like an illusion."
Master Zhao said: "When the marks of the body are detached, it is no longer the body; when the mind is like an illusion, it is no longer the mind.
Since both body and mind are non-existent, with whom would the illness conjoin? Because there is no conjunction, there is no illness; because there is no illness, it cannot be perceived."
III. Questioning Which of the Great Elements is Ill. 2. First Question.
Furthermore, he asks: "Regarding the four great elements—the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element—which of these great elements is ill?"
Master Shi said: "This is intended to clarify the origin from which illness arises. That from which illness arises is not due to a single factor;

it must arise from the provisional conjunction of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Since it arises from a provisional conjunction, illness has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Having no intrinsic nature,"
Thus, the aforementioned [state] is invisible. Although this clarifies the causes from which illness arises, it also clarifies why there is no illness.
Part Two: The Response, in two sections. First, clarifying that one is both identical to and separate from the Great [Dharma].
The answer is: This illness is not the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*), yet it is not separate from the earth element; the water, fire, and wind elements are likewise so. Master Zhaowang said:

"The intrinsic nature of the four great elements is itself free from affliction. It is only when various conditions assemble that they undergo increase and decrease, and mutually overcome one another."

It is only through this that affliction arises. If one wishes to say there is illness, its fundamental nature is inherently non-existent; if one wishes to say there is no illness, it exists by way of mutual dependence.
Therefore, the illness is not the earth-element, yet it is not separate from the earth-element. The other great elements are likewise so.
Second, explaining the sicknesses of the multitude and my own sickness:
the sicknesses of sentient beings arise from the four great elements. Because they have sickness, I likewise have sickness.
The sicknesses of the four great elements of sentient beings exist where there was originally nothing; my sickness of great compassion likewise arises because of them.
Regarding the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that a single moment of mind arises through the mutual encounter of the sense faculties and their objects.
I say that these phenomena born of causes and conditions are themselves emptiness; this refers to the illness itself, not the four great elements.

It is also called a provisional designation, yet it does not exist apart from the four great elements. It is also called the Middle Way, which simultaneously illuminates both emptiness and existence. This is because sentient beings possess this illness.
Therefore, I am ill.
○ Fourth, the question on how to console and encourage [the sick] has three parts. First, the question:
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti, "How should a bodhisattva console one who is ill?"

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates five practices for bodhisattvas: first, noble practice (*āryacaryā*); second, Brahma practice (*brahmacaryā*); third, celestial practice (*devacaryā*). These three constitute the methods for the bodhisattva’s own cultivation.
Fourth, the practice of illness (*vyādhi-caryā*); fifth, the practice of an infant (*bālacaryā*). These two constitute the bodhisattva’s [benefit for others].

This is the nature of birth. Now, that the Great Being manifests illness is precisely the practice of illness. Nevertheless, there are differences between the beginning and the end, and between cause and effect.

Since he has already manifested being ill in common with all sentient beings, those who are not ill ought to console and encourage those who are ill, just as the Tathāgata sent his disciples to inquire after Vimalakīrti’s illness and likewise offered consolation.

This is but one aspect. This may be a case of using a person who has attained the fruit to console another who has attained the fruit, or using a person who has attained the fruit to console one still on the path of cause.
What Mañjuśrī now asks concerns the matter of using the final mind to console the initial mind, thereby demonstrating the method for dwelling amidst illness.
II. The second part consists of six sections. First, the four seals are presented without partiality to provide consolation and instruction.

Vimalakīrti concludes by saying: "One speaks of the impermanence of the body, but does not speak of revulsion toward the body; one speaks of the suffering of the body, but does not speak of delighting in nirvāṇa;
one speaks of the non-self of the body, yet speaks of teaching and guiding sentient beings; one speaks of the emptiness and stillness of the body, but does not [speak of...]"
"Ultimately quiescent.
Master Zhao said: "The method of consolation and encouragement should involve explaining to the sick person that the body is impermanent in order to remove their greedy attachment;
one should not speak of revulsion and renunciation so as to cause them to seek realization. Those who do not contemplate impermanence and do not feel revulsion are ordinary people."
Those who contemplate impermanence and feel weary detachment are followers of the Two Vehicles. Those who contemplate impermanence yet do not feel weary detachment are Bodhisattvas.
Therefore, one should console and encourage the beginner, causing them to settle their mind within illness to rescue all sentient beings—neither wearying of birth and death nor delighting in Nirvana.
This is the method of consolation for the Great Being (Mahāsattva). Master Kumārajīva said:
According to their varying degrees of acuity, the teachings are presented in either extensive or abbreviated forms. For example, a great tree cannot be toppled by a single blow of an axe;
