since its roots run deep, it cannot be removed by a single dharma. Some, though hearing of impermanence, claim it is not suffering; for them, one teaches suffering.
Once they have heard of suffering, they may then claim there is a master of suffering and pleasure; for them, one teaches non-self and emptiness.
Master Zhao said: "Although he perceives the suffering of the body, he does not take pleasure in the bliss of Nirvana.
Although he knows there is no self, he does not omit instruction because sentient beings are empty. Although he perceives the emptiness of the body, he does not grasp at the ultimate path of Nirvana.
Therefore, he is able to dwell peacefully within birth and death, sharing the same ailments as sentient beings; it is for this reason that he consoles and exhorts them."
In the household, one should speak of what ought to be practiced; one should not speak of what ought not to be practiced.
Second, not entering the three periods of time as a means of consolation:
one speaks of repenting for past transgressions, but does not speak of entering the past.
Master Shi said: "The events of today must stem from past transgressions; therefore, the teaching commands one to repent for those past transgressions.
Since it has already been stated that there are past transgressions, this might imply that transgressions possess a fixed nature that enters into the past.

Thus, he explains that they do not enter the past, in order to eliminate the notion of their permanence. Master Zhao said: "The teaching instructs the sick bodhisattva to repent for what has passed..."
Regarding sin: although past sins bind a person, it is not said that sin possesses a permanent nature;
rather, it proceeds from the future to the present, and from the present into the past.
Third, one should reflect upon oneself and take pity on others, showing them consolation and encouragement.

By means of one's own illness, one should take pity on the illnesses of others; one should recognize the suffering of countless kalpas in past lives and keep in mind the benefit of all sentient beings.

Master Shi said: "This causes one to extend [one's own feelings] to others and feel compassion for all beings. One should reflect and say: 'I am currently afflicted by a slight illness, yet my suffering is already so great;
how much more so must it be for sentient beings in the evil realms who undergo immeasurable suffering! For countless eons, they have endured boundless pain without ever having practiced the Way.
If one undergoes suffering for the sake of the Way, one will surely obtain great benefit. Having used this as a metaphor for oneself,"
Furthermore, one should contemplate bringing benefit to sentient beings so that they may obtain profit. Master Zhaoluo said: "One should seek out how one suffered immeasurably in past lives;
compared to this, the present suffering is but a moment—how could it be worth causing such anxiety? One should simply exert oneself to rescue others from their suffering."
4. Cultivating Merit and Purifying One’s Livelihood through Consolation and Encouragement.
This involves recollecting the merit one has cultivated and reflecting upon a pure livelihood.
Master Kumārajīva said: "According to the customs of foreign lands, from birth until death, every meritorious deed performed is recorded individually."
At the time of death, those nearby should speak for them, causing them to rely on their merit so that their hearts are free from sorrow and fear.
"Pure livelihood" (*śuddhājīva*) refers precisely to right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). One should reflect: "From birth until now, I have always practiced pure livelihood;

I shall surely go to a good destination. What, then, should I fear? Master Zhao said: "Do not give rise to wrong livelihood (*mithyā-ājīva*) out of a desire to save your body. Wrong livelihood means..."
To command flattery and adornment for the sake of profit and survival.
○ Fifth, "Do not grieve" means to demonstrate encouragement through diligence:
do not give rise to sorrow or affliction, but always arouse diligent effort.
Master Shi said: "Though his body has passed away and his life has ended, his intention does not abandon them.
[6] He shall manifest as a King of Physicians to provide consolation;
he shall act as a King of Physicians to treat and cure all illnesses.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Let him, on account of his illness, give rise to a great vow:
'Since there is no one who can cure such various illnesses, I shall employ the Dharma as medicine to heal all diseases.'"
II. Conclusion.
A bodhisattva should console a sick bodhisattva in this manner, causing them to rejoice.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that the nature of a single moment of mind is replete with the ten realms. Although one contemplates the six mundane states as impermanent, suffering, and empty, [the ultimate nature remains].

Selflessness and quiescence constitute the six ordinary realms; yet the four virtues of the four noble stages are perfectly manifest therein. This shows that one does not deviate from the four seals, thereby providing consolation and encouragement.

Contemplating this mind as the eternally abiding true mind, it does not enter the three periods of time; this shows that one does not deviate from the four seals, thereby providing consolation and encouragement.

Contemplating within this mind that the nature of sin is fundamentally empty, one performs repentance; this shows that one does not deviate from the four seals, thereby providing consolation and encouragement.

Thus it is. First, one contemplates that within a single mind, the three delusions are vast and boundless; then, one contemplates that within the subsequent single mind, the three delusions are likewise so.
Because one is mindful of one's own suffering, one takes pity on the suffering of others; thus, by being mindful of oneself and taking pity on others, one provides consolation and encouragement.
To contemplate the mind as being Buddha is of the utmost merit. Relying upon this right livelihood, one dwells in peace; this is to cultivate merit and purify one’s livelihood.

This is to provide consolation and encouragement. Contemplate this mind-nature as eternally blissful, self, and pure; by observing it with diligence and without regression, one will not grieve over their own vigor—this is to provide consolation and encouragement.
Contemplate that this mind is the Buddha-mind, wherein the Middle Way both negates and illuminates, capable of curing the maladies of dullness and agitation;
thus one should become a King of Physicians—this is to provide consolation and encouragement.
Sixth, the question: How does one tame [the mind]? Part two. First, the question.
Mañjuśrī said: "Householder, how does a sick bodhisattva tame his own mind?"
Master Sengzhao said: "The previous question concerned the propriety of consolation; the present question concerns the method for regulating the mind.
When there is skillful analogy externally and skillful regulation internally, one can endure the cycle of birth and death, sharing the same ailments as all living beings.

Having experienced every kind of bitterness and sorrow, one does not regard them as suffering. This is precisely the reason why Vimalakīrti dwelt amidst illness. It is intended to instruct those who are beginners."
The path for dwelling amidst illness; thus this question arises.
II. In the response to the question on subduing [afflictions], the text consists of three sections, whose meanings correspond to the three contemplations in the *Śrī-mālā-siṃhanāda-sūtra*.

First, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional, also called the contemplation of the two truths. Second, the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness, also called the [contemplation of] equality...
Equal contemplation. Taking the contemplation of the two emptinesses as the skillful means, one attains entry into the contemplation of the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Mind after mind is quiescently extinguished, naturally flowing into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Master Tiantai explained its meaning as follows: "First, the contemplation of entering emptiness from the provisional:

the 'provisional' refers to that which is false and illusory; it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). 'Emptiness' refers to that which is examined and real; it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."

Furthermore, because one desires to leave the mundane and return to the True, it is called the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*prajñapti*). "The conventional" is the designation for entering emptiness;

first, one must contemplate the conventional and realize that the conventional is illusory and false, thereby attaining union with the True. Therefore, it is called the contemplation of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).

When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*). This is consistent with this sutra’s sequence of first emptying the person and the conventional, and subsequently emptying phenomena (*dharma*).
"Conventional. To tame the mind is the same [for all]. Now, first, regarding the entry from the conventional into emptiness, we clarify the two aspects of taming.
First, the three stages of breaking through the conventional self to enter emptiness. First, examining who it is that suffers from the illness.
Vimalakīrti said: "A bodhisattva who is ill should reflect thus: 'This illness of mine arises entirely from the delusions, inversions, and various afflictions of past lives;
it has no substantial reality. Who is there to suffer this illness?'"
Master Zhao said: "The method for dealing with illness requires that one first understand the root cause of the disease.
The arising of disease is entirely due to the delusions and inversions of past lives. Because of these delusions and inversions, afflictions arise; once afflictions have arisen..."
One cannot be without a body; since there is a body, one cannot be without affliction. If one traces back to its source, it is found to be empty, false, and unreal.
Since the source is not real, who is it that suffers from illness? This clarifies how a beginner first practices the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*).
Second, the body is likewise without a master. Why is this?
Because it is a combination of the four great elements, it is conventionally designated as a "body. Since the four great elements have no master, the body likewise has no self.
Master Zhao said: "This explains the meaning of non-self (*anātman*). The four great elements (*mahābhūta*) combine and aggregate, and are merely designated by the provisional name 'body.
Since the four great elements have no master, how could a self of the body arise? It is like a single grain of sand having no oil; the same is true for a collection of sand.
The 'master' and the 'self' are merely different names for the same thing."
Third, it demonstrates that one should not give rise to attachment.
Furthermore, these illnesses arise entirely from attachment to a self; therefore, one should not give rise to attachment toward the self.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The arising of illness has two causes: first, due to past attachment to a self, one extensively produced karmic fetters and afflictions."

When the fruits of karmic bonds ripen, one undergoes suffering. Second, due to the mental affliction of attachment to a self in the present, and because of this mental affliction of attachment to a self, the illness increases.
Master Daosheng said: "To restore the source of this illness, one must realize it is fundamentally empty; yet there is still that which is ill."
All arise from attachment to the self (*ātman*). If one can remain unattached to the self, how could illness exist?
II. Refuting the provisional nature of dharmas to enter emptiness, in two parts: A. Causing the thought of dharmas to arise. 1. Concluding the preceding and introducing the subsequent.

Once the root of the disease is known, one immediately eliminates the notion of a self (*ātman*) and the notion of sentient beings (*sattva*), and should instead give rise to the notion of dharmas (*dharma*).
Master Zhaoluo said: "The notion of a self is the most grievous of afflictions; therefore, one eliminates the notion of a self and gives rise to the notion of dharmas. This is the notion of dharmas.
To [cling to] emptiness is a disease; to [cling to] self is the medicine. Since the low and the high are mutually dependent, one employs them provisionally for the sake of treatment.
II. Correctly elucidating the perception of dharmas (dharmasaṃjñā) has two parts. First, elucidating the arising and ceasing based on dharmas.
One should form this thought: "This body is merely composed of a multitude of dharmas; its arising is solely the arising of dharmas, and its cessation is solely the cessation of dharmas.
Master Zhao said: "This explains the notion of dharmas. The various dharmas of the five aggregates assemble provisionally to form the body;

their arising is solely the collective arising of these dharmas, and their cessation is solely the collective cessation of these dharmas. There is no separate, true sovereign that presides over their arising and cessation.
Having eliminated the notion of a self (*ātma-saṃjñā*), one perceives only the various phenomena of dependent origination; therefore, this is called the "notion of phenomena" (*dharma-saṃjñā*).
Second, it clarifies that they do not know one another:
furthermore, these phenomena do not know one another; when arising, they do not say, "I am arising," and when ceasing, they do not say, "I am ceasing."
Master Zhao said: "The myriad things are in a state of chaotic profusion; who causes their gathering and dispersal? When conditions combine, they arise; when conditions disperse, they separate.
Since gathering and dispersal have no prior appointment, phenomena do not know one another."
II. Second, one should eliminate the notion of phenomena (dharmasaṃjñā). First, that which is inverted should be abandoned.
That sick bodhisattva, in order to eliminate the notion of phenomena, should form this thought:
"This notion of phenomena is itself an inversion; inversion is precisely a great affliction. I should abandon it."

Master Zhao said: "Although the conceptualization of dharmas has been eliminated, the self still constitutes an inversion with respect to the Truth; since one has not yet escaped from affliction, one must therefore transcend it.
Master Shi said: "Up to this point, the self was dispelled by means of dharmas; from here on, dharmas themselves are dispelled by means of emptiness."
II. The second section, the correct elucidation of the extinction of dharmas, has five parts.
First is the elucidation of detachment from dharmas. What is meant by detachment?

It is detachment from "self" and "what belongs to self. Master Zhao said: "The self is the master of all things; all things belong to the self. If one detaches from 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' then..."
There is no dharma that is not free [from self]. II. Explaining freedom from "self" and "what belongs to self. How is one free from "self" and "what belongs to self"?
It means being free from two dharmas. How is one free from these two dharmas? It means not giving rise to thoughts regarding the internal or the external.
"All dharmas proceed in equality.
Master Zao said: "When there is 'self' and 'what belongs to self,' then dualistic dharmas arise spontaneously. Once dualistic dharmas have arisen, then the internal and external take form.
Once the internal and external have taken form, then all dharmas acquire distinct names. When all dharmas have distinct names, then the characteristics of right and wrong appear."
They lean toward one another; when they lean toward each other in terms of right and wrong, then manifold afflictions are produced.

If one can refrain from thinking about internal and external dharmas and practice with a mind of equanimity, then one enters the practice of emptiness. Regarding the affliction of conceptualizing dharmas as "internal" or "external," these are the objects of the sensory passions.
III. The Equality of the Two Emptinesses. First, the heading:
"What is meant by equality? It means that the self is equal to nirvana.
Master Zhao said: "From the ultimate heights to the lowest depths, to view them all as identical—this accords with equality."
II. Explanation.
Why is this so? Both "self" and "nirvana" are empty. Master Zhao said:
"In terms of phenomena (*dharma*), there is nothing that is not different; in terms of principle (*li*), there is nothing that is not one."
○ Fourth, both of these are empty. By what are they empty?
They are empty merely by virtue of being names. These two dharmas lack any determinate nature.
Master Zhao said: Because one turns away from Nirvana, it is called "self"; because one abandons the self, it is called "Nirvana."
The two phenomena are mutually dependent; thus, names arise. If one traces them back to their own nature, that nature has no fixed determination;
therefore, both are empty.
○ Fifth, one should eliminate the illness of emptiness itself.
Having attained this equanimity, there is no other illness remaining; there is only the illness of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and even that illness of emptiness is empty. Master Kumārajīva said:
"The preceding [passage] clarifies the absence of self (*anātman*) and the absence of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), yet it has not yet eliminated emptiness.

As long as emptiness is not eliminated, emptiness becomes a burden; being a burden is itself an illness. Therefore, he clarifies that even the illness of emptiness is empty. Master Sengzhao said: "Sentient beings are bound by attachments and burdens."
Being profound and deep-seated, it cannot be abandoned all at once; therefore, one gradually eliminates it through successive stages until there is nothing left to eliminate.

Above, one removes the self by means of dharmas, and removes dharmas by means of emptiness; now, by means of ultimate emptiness, one empties even that emptiness—this is the very pinnacle of being free from affliction.

Second, regarding the demonstration of subduing by entering the provisional from emptiness: Master Tiantai, in his commentary on the second [chapter] of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* concerning the contemplation of the provisional, states:
"As for the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness, if one were to abide in emptiness, how would this differ from that of the two vehicles?"

The Buddha-dharma would not be accomplished, nor would sentient beings be benefited. Therefore, one contemplates emptiness (*śūnyatā*) but does not abide in emptiness; instead, one enters into the provisional (*prajñapti*).

Knowing the illness and identifying the medicine, one administers the medicine according to the illness so that it may be taken and practiced. This is called the contemplation of entering the provisional from emptiness.
As for the term "equality," it is called equality in comparison to what preceded it: previously, one used emptiness to shatter the provisional; now, one shatters emptiness itself.

Because the application of the provisional and the application of the refutation are equal, it is called "equal contemplation. When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the Knowledge of the Paths (mārgajñatā).
This is identical to the present practice of contemplating sentient beings in the evil realms when one’s own body experiences suffering, thereby giving rise to great compassion;
once I have been tamed, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings. Now, based on this, the explanation of the sūtra is divided into nine parts. First, [it] causes...
To receive while there is no receiving—this is the sick Bodhisattva. By means of non-receiving, he receives all sensations (*vedanā*).
Master Kumārajīva said: "Receiving" refers to the three sensations of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. If one can understand that sensation is non-sensation, then one can...
For the sake of sentient beings, one undergoes birth and endures the three types of sensation.
Second, regarding not extinguishing [sensation] to realize [enlightenment]:
as long as the Buddha-dharmas are not yet complete, one likewise does not extinguish sensation to realize [enlightenment].
Master Zhao said: "One who is skillfully self-subdued is unstained by existence while dwelling in existence, and unstained by emptiness while abiding in emptiness.
This is the ultimate state of non-reception. Because the mind is without reception, there is nothing it does not receive.

Because there is nothing it does not receive, it is able to eternally share in all sensations with all sentient beings. 'All sensations' refers to painful sensations, pleasant sensations, and sensations that are neither painful nor pleasant."

This is pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*). Since the Buddha-dharma is not yet complete and sentient beings have not yet been delivered, one does not alone extinguish the three sensations to attain realization.
○ Third, instructing them to contemplate suffering so as to give rise to compassion.
Even if one experiences physical suffering, one should contemplate sentient beings in the evil realms and give rise to great compassion, thinking:
"Since I have been tamed, I shall likewise tame all sentient beings."
Master Kumārajīva said, "If even this body of mine, composed of merit and wisdom, suffers such pain, how much more so for the sentient beings of the evil realms who endure immeasurable suffering?
Thereupon, he gave rise to a heart of compassion, vowing to uproot all sufferings and to share equally with all living beings in both their pain and their joy.
"Fourth, it causes one to eliminate the illness but not the dharma;
it eliminates only the illness, without eliminating the dharma.
Master Kumārajīva said: "This refers to the 'dharmas of permanence, bliss, purity, and self' as perceived by those with false views. Therefore, it is said:"

Regarding "non-existence": it is not that one uses the non-existence of dharmas such as pleasure and purity to eliminate them; rather, it is simply for the purpose of eliminating the disease of deluded conceptualization.
Since there is no dharma that can be eliminated, one is thus able to abide within it, without eliminating the dharma itself.
V. Causing the Severance of the Root: Two Parts. First, the introduction:
To sever the root of the ailment, he instructs them.
Master Zhaolun said: "All dharmas arise through conditions; their aggregation and dispersal are not of themselves. When they assemble, they take form; when they disperse, they leave no trace."
The Dharma is simply natural. What cause for concern could there be for me? That which gives rise to concern arises from my own deluded thoughts;

it is these thoughts that create affliction within the Dharma itself. How could the Dharma ever cause me to give rise to deluded thoughts? Thus, deluded thoughts are the root of illness, while the Dharma is not my affliction.
Therefore, when instruction and guidance arise, they merely eliminate the root of the illness; they do not eliminate the Dharma.
II. The second section, the fourfold sequential explanation, begins with the first sequential explanation:
the root of illness. What is meant by the root of illness? It is the presence of objective grasping (*ālambana*). From the presence of objective grasping, there arises the root of illness.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The previous discourse explained how a bodhisattva seeks out the root of their own illness and dwells in the mind with principle;

thus, they can remain undisturbed while dwelling amidst illness. Now, it clarifies that for the sake of severing the illnesses of sentient beings, one must investigate the source of those illnesses, and only then respond according to what is appropriate.
When the spiritual faculty (*indriya*) subtly moves, movement implies that the mind has an object of attachment. When the mind has an object of attachment, this is called 'clinging' (*ālambana*)."
Conditions. To grasp at signs through攀緣 (pān-yuán, objective clinging) is the beginning of deluded movement; it is the root of affliction.
○ Second, to further explain攀緣:
what is it that is攀緣ed? It refers to the three realms.
Master Zhao said: "This clarifies the realm of objective conditions (*ālambana*). Dharmas beyond the three realms are untainted (*anāsrava*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
these dharmas are without marks (*animitta*) and cannot be grasped as objects by deluded thoughts. That which can be grasped as an object consists only of the three realms."
The third turning explains the severing of objective referents (*ālambana*).
How does one sever objective referents? By means of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). If there is no apprehension, then there is no objective referent. Master Zhao says:
"The reason for objective referents is that the mind harbors the intent to grasp; the reason for grasping is that the mind harbors the intent to acquire."
If one can know that all phenomena are empty and deceptive, such that there is neither grasping nor attainment, then the攀緣 (pān-yuán; clinging to objects) will naturally cease.
○ Fourth, an alternative explanation of "non-attainment":
What is meant by non-attainment? It means being free from the two views. What are the two views? They are the view of the internal and the view of the external. This is non-attainment.

Regarding "that which is attained," Master Zhaoming said: "Internally there are deluded thoughts; externally there are all phenomena. These two are false and illusory; in the end, nothing is attained.
(6) Elucidating Merits and Faults, Part Three. First, the Dharma, Part Two. First, concluding the merits and virtues.
Mañjuśrī, this is how a sick bodhisattva disciplines his mind to sever the suffering of old age, illness, and death;
this is the bodhi of that bodhisattva.
[Omission] Two: the lack of wisdom and benefit.
If it were not thus, that which one has cultivated and refined would be devoid of wisdom and benefit.

Master Zhaoluo said: "If one can skillfully regulate the mind, harbor no divergent thoughts, and dwell eternally within birth and death while severing that suffering—this is the path to Bodhi for a Bodhisattva.
If one cannot do so, then whatever practice one performs internally..."
This alone does not constitute having wisdom; externally, this alone does not constitute having benefit.
II. An illustrative analogy:
Only when one has conquered an enemy can one be considered brave.
To abide in non-subduing is to treat birth-and-death as an enemy; to abide in subduing is to treat nirvana as an enemy.
The enemy of birth-and-death drowns one in existence (*bhava*); the enemy of nirvana sinks one into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
One who abides neither in non-subduing nor in subduing, and is thus able to overcome these enemies, may truly be called brave.
Third, the method of combining practices.
To thus simultaneously eliminate old age, sickness, and death is what is meant by a Bodhisattva.
To eliminate them simultaneously means not to focus on only one; if one focuses exclusively on one, one's practice will become biased.
○ Seventh, instructing them to contemplate that illness is not real:
That bodhisattva who is ill should further form this thought: "Just as my own illness is neither real nor existent, so too the illnesses of all sentient beings are neither real nor existent."
Master Kumārajīva said: "The understanding that illness is not real enables one to remain undisturbed in its midst.

If one were to regard illness as truly existent, then the illness could never be eliminated. Sentient beings are infinite, and thus illness would likewise be inexhaustible. As for such inexhaustible illness—"
If its nature were truly existent, how could it be transcended? At that moment, one would become confused and the mind would turn back in retreat.
If the illness were not real, it would be easy to eliminate; then compassion would arise, and one would give rise to great vows to save all beings.
8. Causing Love and Views Not to Arise, Part Four. First, the explicit clarification:
When performing this contemplation, if love or views of great compassion arise toward sentient beings, one should immediately abandon them.

Master Shi said: "If one has not yet deeply penetrated the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) and perceives the existence of sentient beings, giving rise to attachment in the mind, compassion born from this is called 'great compassion based on attachment and views' (aijian dabe). Great compassion based on attachment and views is false and impure;
because it can cause people to give rise to thoughts of weariness and exhaustion, it should be abandoned. Master Zhao said: "If one is to discipline oneself, one should first..."
One contemplates that one’s own illness and the illnesses of sentient beings are formed by causes and conditions; they are false and devoid of reality.

One simply gives rise to compassion based on this mind. If this contemplation is not yet pure, and one perceives sentient beings through attachment and gives rise to compassion, it is called "compassion born of attachment and views.
Although this compassion is wholesome, because it is mixed with attachment and views, it remains within the realm of the dualistic mind and cannot escape [the cycle].
It should be accumulated; therefore, it should be relinquished.
Second, the manifestation of what it is:
Why is this so? Because the Bodhisattva eliminates adventitious afflictions and gives rise to great compassion.
Master Sengzhao said: "When the mind encounters external conditions, afflictions arise abruptly; therefore, they are called 'guest-dust.

The dharma of a Bodhisattva requires the removal of this guest-dust and the arousal of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). If love and views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi*) are not yet severed, then afflictions will proliferate all the more;
therefore, one should abandon them."
Deng said: "In the teachings of the Hīnayāna, the afflictions of view (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) are compared to guests, because the meaning of 'guest' is coarse;
the afflictions of thought (bhāvanā-kleśa) are compared to dust, because the meaning of 'dust' is subtle."
III. Refuting errors:
Those who possess compassion based on attachment and views will harbor weariness and aversion toward birth and death.
IV. Clarifying the merit.
If one can distance oneself from these, there will be no weariness or fatigue; wherever one is born, one will not be shrouded by craving or views.

Master Kumārajīva said: "If one can eliminate craving and views, one immediately abandons the karma of fetters and undergoes birth through transformation by the Dharma, becoming sovereign and unimpeded.
Master Sengzhao said: "That which has an object of perception must have an obstruction; that which has an object of attachment must necessarily..."
That which is loathed is this path of extremes; how could it possibly lead to the function of the infinite?
If one can depart from this, then the Dharma-body is born through transformation, being neither present nor absent. Birth and death are endless, yet one does not perceive them as distant.
How, then, could there be the obscuration of attachment and views, or the exhaustion of weariness?
IX. Distinguishing Right from Wrong (2): First, clarifying only what is right.
That which is produced is without bondage, and it is able to preach the Dharma for sentient beings to liberate them from their bonds.
Master Zhao said: "When attachment and views are naturally eliminated and the Dharma-body is established, then that which is produced is without bondage, and one is likewise able to liberate others."
That is bondage.
Second, establishing the validity of this point:
as the Buddha has said, it is impossible for one who is themselves bound to be able to release another from their bondage; whereas it is possible for one who is themselves unbound [to do so].
It is possible that one can untie those bonds.

Third, regarding the clarification of subduing [the mind] by entering the Middle Way from Emptiness and Provisionality: Master Tiantai, in his commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, explains the contemplation of emptiness as follows:
"Taking the two kinds of emptiness as the skillful means" means first contemplating the emptiness of saṃsāra, and subsequently contemplating the emptiness of nirvāṇa.

These two emptinesses serve as the skillful means for simultaneous negation (*dvaya-pratiṣedha*): first one contemplates the emptiness of function, and next one contemplates the conventionality of function.
These two functions serve as the skillful means for simultaneous illumination (*dvaya-avabhāsa*). With every thought, one turns toward and enters the ocean of *sarvajñatā*.
This refers to the simultaneous illumination of the two truths (*satyadvaya*). When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

This is equivalent to the present practice where wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*) are exercised concurrently; it carries the sense of simultaneously illuminating both emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*). The subsequent thirty-one sections clarify that the Bodhisattva is "neither" of the two extremes;
this carries the sense of simultaneously negating both emptiness and the conventional. This current explanation is divided into two parts. First, the simultaneous identity with emptiness.
The provisional explanation of subduing is divided into three parts. First, connecting the preceding with the following:
"Therefore, a bodhisattva should not give rise to bondage.
Second, raising the inquiry regarding bondage and liberation.
What is called bondage? What is called liberation? [Section Three:
Explaining Bondage and Liberation] Part One: The Direct Explanation. First, an initial clarification of bondage and liberation:
Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna is the bondage of a bodhisattva; arising through skillful means is the liberation of a bodhisattva.
Master Shi said: "Attachment to the flavor of dhyāna presents two obstacles: it obstructs both nirvāṇa and the bodhisattva path. Master Zhao said:
"Taking birth within the three realms and the realization attained by the two vehicles are both due to attachment to the flavor of dhyāna; this is why it constitutes a bondage. He further said:
"Since one has personally transcended birth, yet employs skillful means to take birth for the sake of sentient beings, then there is no bondage between self and other."
This is considered the explanation. Part Two:
Explaining the liberation through wisdom has two sections. First, the initial presentation of the two meanings:
"Wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation. Skillful means without wisdom is bondage; skillful means with wisdom [is liberation]."
Regarding "liberation" (jie):
Master Zhao said, "The skillful accumulation of manifold virtues is called *upāya* (expedient means); directly penetrating the characteristics of dharmas is called *prajñā* (wisdom).
Only when both practices are fully possessed does one attain liberation. If one possesses wisdom but lacks expedient means, one cannot avoid being bound."
If one possesses skillful means but lacks wisdom, one likewise cannot escape bondage.
[Section Two: Explaining the two meanings in two parts. First, the explanation taking skillful means as primary. Part One: Clarifying that wisdom without skillful means is bondage.]

What is called "the bondage of wisdom lacking skillful means"? It refers to a bodhisattva who, with a mind of attachment and views, adorns buddha-fields and brings sentient beings to maturity, while seeking to discipline themselves within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. This is called "the bondage of wisdom lacking skillful means."
Master Kumārajīva said: "To contemplate emptiness without grasping, and to engage with existence without attachment—this is called skillful means (*upāya*).
Now, it is clarified that from the sixth stage (*bhūmi*) downward, one has not yet attained unimpededness. When contemplating emptiness, there is nothing to grasp or attach to;

yet when emerging from contemplation to manifest in pure lands and transform beings, one gives rise to a mind that perceives signs and becomes attached through views. This is clumsy in engaging with the realm of movement; [only those above this level are] subtle."

In the context of tranquil contemplation (*śamatha*), the wisdom that contemplates emptiness does not grasp at signs; although this is a skillful means (*upāya*), it receives its name from wisdom (*prajñā*).
Here, one takes only the non-attachment while engaging with existence as the skillful means; therefore, it is said that "there is no skillful means, but there is wisdom.

From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) upward, the mind is constantly in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), such that movement and stillness are no different; therefore, it is said that "there is both skillful means and wisdom."
Deng said: "Regarding these two meanings, if they are discussed in terms of the stages of the gradual teaching (*jiàojiào*), one may speak as Master Kumārajīva did.

However, if they are discussed in terms of the sudden teaching (*dùnjiào*), then even those at the initial stage of a person of the Perfect Teaching (*yuánrén*) are able to possess both simultaneously.
As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* says: 'One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. This refers to not abiding in the six sense-objects while practicing."
Generosity and the other perfections are wisdom that abides nowhere. The arising of the mind and the practice of the paramitas are skillful means.
When these two are both present from the very beginning, the perfect practice is brilliantly clear. In the following explanation of gain and loss: when bound, one is bound by both;

it is not only a bondage to existence, but also a bondage to emptiness. When liberated, one is liberated by both; it is not only through existence that liberation is attained, but through emptiness as well.

It is understood. Prior to the Six Dynasties, those who judged the characteristics of the teachings knew only the principle of the "expedient Mahāyāna" (he-tong jiao da-cheng), which clarifies emptiness through form (*jise mingkong*) and its harmonious integration.

Now, although Kumārajīva and Sengzhao frequently speak of the sixth and seventh stages (*bhūmi*), they did not realize that these were positions established by the Tathāgata to clarify the "expedient" (tong) through the "distinctive" (bie).
This is comparable to the teaching of universal penetration (*tongfang*) discussed in this sutra.
This is one stage removed. Now, let us clarify this according to the Tiantai teachings.

When Bodhisattvas adorn Buddha-lands and bring sentient beings to maturity with a mind of attachment and views (*sneha-dṛṣṭi*), they are Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭaka (Tripiṭaka) Teaching who practice the six *pāramitās*.
Although they subdue their afflictions, they have not yet severed them; therefore, they still involve themselves in attachment and views. Regarding emptiness, signlessness, and...
Within the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), one self-subdues. Regarding those bound by wisdom lacking skillful means (*upāya*):

although such Bodhisattvas practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) during the stages of the three provisions (*saṃbhāra*) and four applications (*prayoga*), and suppress afflictions through the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), they pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* while practicing the six perfections during the stages of lower and middle patience (*kṣānti*), and plant the causes for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over the course of a hundred eons.
II. Explaining liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
What is meant by liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means? It refers to not adorning buddha-fields or bringing sentient beings to maturity with a mind of attachment or biased views;

rather, within the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one disciplines oneself without weariness or fatigue. This is called [liberation through wisdom accompanied by skillful means].
"Skillful means and the wisdom of liberation. Master Zhao said:
"From the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one is fully endowed with both types of practice; though one traverses the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one does not grow weary.

This is why it is called 'liberation'. Master Deng said: "This refers to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared (*pāryāya*) Teaching who have mastered the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); they possess the faculty of skillful liberation."

Great! Therefore, one is able to know that all phenomena are the crossing over [of suffering] which is itself principle; form is emptiness, yet it is not through the extinction of form that there is emptiness.

One is thus able to give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere. Furthermore, one knows that although one has severed the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), this does not hinder following along with the cycle of birth and death while performing the practice of delivering sentient beings.
For this reason, one adorns the Buddha-lands. Among the three samādhis, these two wheels are yoked together side by side.
It soars high upon its wings; therefore, it is called "liberation through skillful means and wisdom.
II. Explaining by taking wisdom as primary has two parts. First, clarifying that lack of wisdom constitutes bondage despite having skillful means.

What is called "bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means"? It refers to a bodhisattva who, while dwelling amidst afflictions such as desire, hatred, and wrong views, plants the roots of various virtues.
This is called "bondage through lack of wisdom and skillful means."
In the former case, skillful means come first and wisdom follows; in this case, wisdom comes first and skillful means follow.
Both are the practices of Bodhisattvas in the Tripiṭaka Teaching who possess inferior faculties and clumsy understanding. This may be understood by analogy with what was stated above.
II. Explaining liberation through wisdom and skillful means.
What is meant by liberation through wisdom and skillful means? It refers to being free from all afflictions, such as greed, hatred, and wrong views.
Yet they cultivate the roots of all virtues and dedicate them toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This is called "liberation through wisdom and skillful means.

In the former case, skillful means come first and wisdom follows; in the present case, skillful means come later and wisdom comes first. Both are the same in being the Bodhisattva path of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-śāsana*).
The practice of the Great Skillful Means of the Bodhisattvas can also be understood by analogy with what was stated above.

This has been explained thus according to the two teachings within the realm (the Tripiṭaka and Shared Teachings). If explained according to the two teachings outside the realm, then the previous statements would be incorrect; they should instead belong to the Distinct Teaching.

The statement that "attainment comes later" must pertain to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Alternatively, the phrase "attainment comes later" may apply equally to the latter three teachings, which, when contrasted with the former Three Baskets (*sanzang*), are collectively termed "inept.
Their textual category belongs to the Vaipulya (*fangdeng*), and this is consistent with their doctrinal principles.
One who can understand the rules for Tiantai’s classification of the teachings will comprehend how the one thousand [teachings] derive from this source.
II. Conclusion:
Mañjuśrī, that sick bodhisattva should contemplate all dharmas in this manner.

Since he is called a "sick bodhisattva," this should be explained specifically in reference to the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*). If one says his rank has already ascended...
Only upon reaching the seventh stage is one truly said to have attained it; such a person is the Bodhisattva Free from Illness.
○ The second part consists of three layers of explanation. First is the primary explanation:
Furthermore, contemplating that the body is impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self is called wisdom. Although the body possesses illness, [the practitioner] constantly remains...
To benefit all beings within birth and death without weariness—this is called skillful means.
(2) Second interpretation:
Furthermore, one contemplates the body; the body is not separate from illness, and illness is not separate from the body. This illness and this body are neither new nor old.
This is called wisdom (*prajñā*). Even if the body is afflicted by illness, it does not undergo ultimate extinction; this is called skillful means (*upāya*). Master Sengzhao said:
"The designations 'new' and 'old' arise from 'before' and 'after. Yet, apart from the body there is no illness, and apart from illness there is no body.
Since both are produced by a multitude of conditions, which is before and which is after? Since there is neither before nor after, there is neither new nor old. New and old...
Since they are non-existent, one immediately enters the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*); therefore, it is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*).

Possessing this wisdom, yet proceeding with the same speed as others without grasping at *nirvāṇa*, is termed "skillful means" (*upāya*) for self-discipline. Dēng said: "According to my current re-explanation, both wisdom and skillful means are present from the very first moment;
it is not necessary to speak of them in terms of entering specific stages. If one were actually to enter such stages, only then would [the term] be so named."
If [one thinks] it is for the sake of attainment, then those who have newly begun their studies are utterly excluded from this sutra.

II. Clarifying subduing by means of the dual negation of both emptiness and the provisional. This has two parts: A. First, the dual application of emptiness and existence to conclude the preceding and introduce the subsequent.
This has two parts: 1. The heading.
Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should thus discipline his mind; he should not abide within it, nor should he abide in an undisciplined mind.
One should tame [the mind] in this manner: thus one does not abide in existence, nor does one abide within it; consequently, one does not abide in emptiness.
The latter phrase simply means that one also does not abide in existence. The meaning of the Middle Way is thereby revealed.
In the preceding chapter, the taming of the mind was clarified precisely through the non-abiding in both emptiness and existence.
II. Explanation. Why is this so?
If one dwells in an undisciplined mind, that is the way of fools. If one dwells in a disciplined mind, that is the way of the śrāvakas.
Second, the dual negation of emptiness and the provisional clearly elucidates the practice of the Middle Way: ordinary beings are fundamentally Buddhas;
that which they possess in excess is the discrimination of conditioned objects. Those of the Two Vehicles are also fundamentally Buddhas;

that which they possess in excess is their attachment to quiescence and sinking into emptiness. Bodhisattvas are also fundamentally Buddhas; that which they possess in excess is fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Now, this clarifies the Bodhisattva’s practice of the Middle Way. It must differ from that of ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles.
Abiding in discipline and abiding in non-discipline, one correctly practices the Middle Way; thus, one destroys fundamental ignorance.

For this reason, the following thirty-one practices are all explained in terms of the Middle Way as "neither of the two extremes. By cultivating the perfect cause, one realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. [Text]
This constitutes the thirty-first [point]. First, by means of taming and not taming, one clarifies the Middle Way.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abide in a mind of either taming or not taming; to be free from these two dharmas is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Abiding in discipline leads to sinking into emptiness; abiding in non-discipline leads to stagnation in existence.
To be free from these two extremes is to correctly practice the Middle Way; therefore, this is the Dharma of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas.
Second, the Middle Way is elucidated by way of transcending both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa:
to remain within saṃsāra without being defiled by its conduct, and to abide in nirvāṇa without entering final extinction—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Because he does not abide in non-subduing, he is not defiled while remaining in birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Because he does not abide in subduing, although he dwells in *nirvāṇa*, he does not undergo eternal extinction.
(3) Third, the Middle Way is elucidated by way of departing from both ordinary beings and sages.
This is not the practice of ordinary beings, nor is it the practice of noble sages; it is the practice of Bodhisattvas.
Because they are not defiled while remaining within birth and death, they are not ordinary beings; because they abide in nirvana without undergoing eternal extinction, they are not noble sages.
Fourth, the Middle Way is elucidated by way of the practice of freedom from defilement and the practice of purity:
it is neither a practice of defilement nor a practice of purity; it is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Because it is not the practice of ordinary worldlings, it is not defiled; because it is not the practice of noble sages, it is not pure.
○ Fifth, explaining the Middle Way by means of transcending Māra and subduing Māra:
although one has transcended the conduct of Māra, manifesting the subjugation of Māra is the practice of a Bodhisattva.
Whenever there is a Māra to be subdued, it occurs at the juncture when one is about to transcend the realm of Māra but has not yet fully transcended it.
Māra comes to disturb him, seeking to prevent him from leaving his realm; therefore, there is the matter of the Bodhisattva subduing Māra.
If one has already transcended the conduct of the realm of Māra, then Māra cannot cause disturbance; how, then, could there be a Māra to be subdued?

Now, although the Bodhisattva has transcended the conduct of Māra, it does not preclude his manifesting the subduing of Māra. Thus, he is not hindered by existence, nor is he hindered [by non-existence].
Regarding emptiness, this is precisely the practice of the Middle Way.
○ Sixth, explaining the Middle Way by way of departing from both the timely and the untimely:
to seek all-knowledge without seeking at an improper time is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
There are two types of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). First is the omniscience of the two vehicles, which takes emptiness as its fruit.
Second is the omniscience of the Buddha-fruit, which takes the perfection of the Middle Way as its fruit. The followers of the two vehicles hasten toward realization.
This is called "seeking at the improper time.
7. Regarding the elucidation of the Middle Way through detachment from non-arising and non-entry:
although one contemplates that all phenomena are unarisen, one does not enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*); this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

The principle of all dharmas is fundamentally non-arising; the Bodhisattva accords with this principle and constantly contemplates it. Yet, while they are non-arising, they have never failed to arise.

When the Bodhisattva contemplates them, arising and non-arising are both darkly merged (mysterious and indistinguishable). Therefore, this differs from the contemplation of non-arising by the followers of the Two Vehicles, who enter the stage of the correct position of partial emptiness.
8. Clarifying the Middle Way by way of distancing oneself from views concerning dependent origination:
Although one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination, yet enters into all manner of false views—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Non-Buddhists are deluded regarding the fact that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and thus they cling to them as being spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

One who can contemplate dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) does not fall into false views. Nevertheless, the Bodhisattva realizes that the sixty-two views constitute the lineage of the Tathāgata;
he enters into them with fervor in order to seek the liberation of all Buddhas. Therefore, it is said that he "enters into all false views. Indeed, one who contemplates conditions...
Rising and entering [the assembly], how could he be the same as those with false views?
Ninth, regarding the abandonment of attachment to sentient beings and views to clarify the Middle Way:
although one embraces all sentient beings, one does not harbor attachment; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva gathers and sustains sentient beings through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
While this may appear similar to attachment and false views, it ultimately does not fall into attachment or false views; thus, it constitutes the practice of the Middle Way.
10. Explaining the Middle Way by means of detachment, seclusion, and exhaustion:
Although one delights in seclusion, not relying on the exhaustion of body and mind is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The followers of the Two Vehicles loathe this body and mind as a great burden of birth and death;

therefore, they cultivate the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness to distance themselves from them, seeking ultimate liberation through such detachment. How could the Bodhisattva not differ from ordinary beings in his cultivation of detachment?
Yet, while reaching the ultimate limit of body and mind, he ardently seeks birth in order to deliver sentient beings. Thus it is said:
By extinguishing ignorance, one attains the blazing lamp of *sambodhi*.
(11) This clarifies the Middle Way by means of the *dharmatā* of the triple world itself:
though one traverses the triple world, one does not destroy its *dharmatā*; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Ordinary beings wander through the three realms and thereby destroy the dharma-nature; those of the two vehicles realize the dharma-nature and thus no longer wander through the three realms.
The bodhisattva differs from these; therefore, they practice the path of the Middle Way.
Twelfth, by means of practicing emptiness while planting all virtues, the Middle Way is elucidated.
Although one practices within emptiness, planting the roots of all virtues is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
To "practice in emptiness" means to enter emptiness from the conventional; to "plant the roots of virtue" means to emerge from emptiness into the conventional.

Thus, one enters emptiness while emerging from the conventional, and emerges from the conventional while entering emptiness. Having already been able to negate both simultaneously, one further illuminates both simultaneously.
Thirteen: To clarify the Middle Way by means of saving sentient beings while abiding in signlessness—though practicing signlessness, one saves sentient beings; this is the conduct of a bodhisattva.
The meaning is the same as before; the only difference is that the former plants merit exclusively within oneself, while the latter focuses exclusively on saving sentient beings.
When these are combined and brought back to their source, they are different yet the same.
14. The fourteenth section clarifies the Middle Way by showing that one takes birth precisely through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Although one practices non-action, manifesting the reception of a body is the practice of a bodhisattva.

The practitioners of the Two Vehicles practice the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and thus never again undergo rebirth. The Bodhisattva, however, practices the unconditioned for the sake of delivering sentient beings;
therefore, he brings his own births to an end. Once his own births are exhausted, it is precisely at that time that he should undergo rebirth to fulfill his vows.
He must certainly not hasten prematurely to enter the state of certainty (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
Fifteenth, by means of non-arising while practicing wholesome conduct, the Middle Way is elucidated.
Although one practices non-arising, yet one gives rise to all wholesome conduct; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
If one practices non-arising and the mind never arises at all, one sinks into emptiness. Now, the Bodhisattva arises from non-arising, which distinguishes them from the followers of the Two Vehicles;
they arise from arising yet remain without arising, which distinguishes them from ordinary beings. Therefore, this constitutes the practice of a Bodhisattva.
16. Regarding the sixteen [aspects], one knows that while practicing the perfections, mental factors (*citta-saṃskāra*) arise, thereby clarifying the Middle Way.
Although one practices the six *pāramitās*, to universally know the minds and mental factors of sentient beings is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Master Shi said: "The six perfections are the dharmas for one's own practice. Once one's own practice is complete, one then transforms others.
In transforming others, one comes to know the minds of sentient beings. Although one is currently practicing them oneself, one is already able to know the minds of others.

Furthermore, the sixth perfection contemplates the signlessness of all phenomena; because it does not take signlessness as an obstruction, it is also able to know the minds of sentient beings."—Master Zhao.

It is said: "The six perfections are the practice of signlessness (*animitta*). Being signless, there is no cognition; yet one simultaneously and universally knows the mental activities of sentient beings.
(17) This section clarifies the Middle Way by means of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the non-exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava*).
Although they practice the six supernormal powers, they do not exhaust their outflows; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

Although those of the two vehicles attain the six supernormal powers, they necessarily exhaust all outflows and transcend the three realms, yet they do not manifest their bodies to deliver sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva is different from this. Therefore, although he practices the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), he does not exhaust his outflows (*āsrava*).

To say that he does not exhaust them is not like the non-exhaustion of ordinary beings; it is merely a manifestation of taking birth so as to lead those who do not know to believe that the Bodhisattva truly possesses outflows.
18. Regarding the four minds in terms of practice, not being born in the Brahma Heaven clarifies the Middle Way.
Although one practices the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), not being greedily attached to birth in the Brahma world is the practice of a bodhisattva.
There are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa-citta*) of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the four immeasurable minds of bodhisattvas, and the four immeasurable minds of Tathāgatas.
The four immeasurable minds of ordinary beings necessarily result in rebirth in the Brahma heavens.
Now, these four immeasurable minds of the bodhisattva have their fruition in the attainment of Buddhahood; therefore, they do not crave or cling to birth in the Brahma worlds.
19. Practicing dhyāna and so forth, yet not following after dhyāna to clarify the Middle Way:
although one practices meditative concentration, liberation, and samādhi, one is not reborn according to those states of dhyāna; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Master Shi said: "Dhyāna refers to the four dhyānas; Samādhi refers to the four formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti); Vimokṣa refers to the eight liberations (aṣṭa-vimokṣa);
and Samādhi refers to emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Daoping said: "The general characteristics of the Dharma, whether great or small, are for the most part the same;

one need only observe how the mind is applied. For this reason, the names and categories employed in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) of Tiantai are not restricted to the [four] truths or the [twelve] causal links."
The Dharma of deliverance encompasses all things; it is like a person of great merit for whom even tiles, rubble, grass, and wood, when held with a faithful hand, are nothing but treasures.
This is in perfect accord with the bodhisattva practices elucidated in this sutra.
If one must distance oneself from these [practices] to be considered "sudden and complete" (yuantun), how does this differ from merely labeling the "ordinary middle" (danzhong) as Buddha-nature?

Twenty: To clarify the Middle Way by means of both conjunction and separation regarding the four foundations of mindfulness—though one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, one does not ultimately and permanently abandon body, sensation, mind, and phenomena; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists cling to the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena, regarding them as permanent, pleasurable, self, and pure;

therefore, the Tathāgata calls these the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*). Furthermore, the followers of the Two Vehicles observe these same four and regard them as impure, impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self;
although this is considered correct from their perspective, it is likewise called an inversion by the Tathāgata. This is because ordinary worldlings and...
The two vehicles take the four types of flourishing as inversions; the Two Vehicles take the four types of withering as inversions.
Only the Tathāgata’s wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way is neither flourishing nor withering, transcending the eight inversions and attaining parinirvāṇa therein.

Now it is said that although one practices the four foundations of mindfulness, this differs from flourishing yet is not ultimate, demonstrating the departure from body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
The Dharma is thus different from witheredness; it is neither flourishing nor withered—this is the practice of the Bodhisattva.
(21) This section clarifies the Middle Way by means of the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), which do not abandon physical and mental diligence.
Although they practice the four right efforts, they do not abandon physical and mental diligence; this is the conduct of a bodhisattva.

As for the followers of the two vehicles, although they are courageous in their right efforts regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they lack even a single thought of delight in the bodhisattvas’ playful mastery of supernatural powers and the purification of buddha-fields; thus, they are still termed indolent.
The Bodhisattva is different from this; therefore, this is the Middle Way.
(22) Regarding the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the Middle Way is clarified by attaining sovereign supernormal powers (*abhijñā*):
although one practices the four bases of psychic power, to attain sovereign supernormal powers is the practice of a Bodhisattva.

The practitioners of the Two Vehicles cultivate the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and are indeed able to attain the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) associated with the mental application of the Lesser Vehicle;
how could these compare to the Bodhisattvas who cultivate the Mahāyāna bases of psychic power to attain the sovereign supernatural powers that transcend mental application?
23. Distinguishing sentient beings by means of the five faculties to clarify the Middle Way:
Although one practices the five faculties, yet distinguishing whether the various faculties of sentient beings are sharp or dull is the practice of a bodhisattva.

The cultivation of the five faculties by those of the two vehicles is directed toward non-discrimination; thus, faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom all converge in non-discrimination.
Should one involve oneself in discrimination, then faith cannot attain its truth and mindfulness cannot achieve its unity.
Now, because the wondrous practice of the Bodhisattva lies in the Middle Way, although the activity of these five faculties remains detached from all sensory objects and conditions, yet...
Regarding the wondrous Dharma-gate for sentient beings, one is able to ardently and analytically discern it; therefore, this is the Middle Way.
(24) Explaining the Middle Way by means of the five powers to clarify the power of the Buddha.
Although they practice the five powers (*pañcabala*), they joyfully seek the ten powers (*daśabala*) of a Buddha; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

The practitioners of the two vehicles practice the five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and give rise to the five powers, merely extracting themselves from birth-and-death within the realm of fragmentation (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*), opening the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*)—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and securing the fruit of the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). As for the bodhisattva’s practice of the five powers, they joyfully...
Seeking the ten powers of a Buddha, uprooting the two kinds of birth-and-death, opening the flower of the Tathāgata’s seven factors of enlightenment,
and binding the fruit of the Sugata’s eightfold noble path— this is the practice of the Middle Way.
Twenty-five: Clarifying the Middle Way by means of the Buddha’s wisdom regarding the factors of enlightenment.
Although one practices the seven factors of enlightenment, to discern the Buddha’s wisdom is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The practitioners of the Two Vehicles cultivate the seven factors of enlightenment, yet they do not transcend the analytical contemplation of a partial emptiness.
The seven factors of enlightenment of a Bodhisattva, however, differ from this; they are the analytical contemplation of the Buddha’s wisdom of the Middle Way.
26. Explaining the Middle Way by means of practicing the Buddha-way through the Eightfold Noble Path:
Although one practices the Eightfold Noble Path, to joyfully practice the immeasurable Buddha-way is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva likewise practices the Eightfold Noble Path; yet, although the names of these "right" [factors] are the same, the path they practice is different.
This is because they differ in being empty or non-empty, and distinct in being ultimate or non-ultimate.
Twenty-seven: Clarifying the Middle Way by means of not falling into quiescent extinction through the integration of cessation and contemplation.
Although one practices the dharmas of cessation and contemplation that assist the path, one does not ultimately fall into quiescent extinction; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.

To restrain the mind at a single point so that it is tranquil and unmoving is called *śamatha* (calm abiding). To have wisdom illuminate clearly so that everything is distinct and not obscured is called *vipaśyanā* (insight).
The followers of the Two Vehicles also cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* as aids to the Path;

however, they merely bring to rest the movement of discrimination regarding *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, and through insight, they observe the darkness of ignorance regarding *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, ultimately returning to quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). As for Bodhisattvas...
In the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of śamatha and vipaśyanā, there is no movement of the three delusions and their conceptual discriminations that is not stilled;
there is no darkness of ignorance within the three delusions that is not illuminated by contemplation. Therefore, he does not fall into [the one-sided state of] quiescent extinction.
28. Clarifying the Middle Way by means of the marks and signs of adornment through which all dharmas do not arise:
although one practices such that all dharmas neither arise nor cease, yet adorning one’s body with the marks and signs of excellence—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
The practice of all phenomena as neither arising nor ceasing is the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Adornment with the marks and signs is the Reward-body (saṃbhogakāya).

Without the Reward-body, the Dharma-body would not be adorned; without the Dharma-body, the Reward-body would not be established. Only when the Dharma-body and Reward-body support one another does one realize the Buddha-way.
29. Clarifying the Middle Way by means of manifesting as followers of the Two Vehicles while not abandoning the Buddha-dharma:
Although they manifest the deportment of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they do not abandon the Buddha-dharma; this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Whether it be the practice of a bodhisattva or a manifestation of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), how could one discard and fail to practice it because of its smallness relative to the two vehicles?
Therefore, although his form is that of a bhikṣu, his mind is ever fixed on the Buddha-way;
this is what is meant by "using the sound of the Buddha-way to let all hear it."
30. Explaining the Middle Way by means of the ultimate *saṃbhogakāya*:
although it accords with the ultimately pure characteristics of all phenomena, it manifests its body according to what is appropriate; this is the practice of the Bodhisattva.
Master Zhao said: "The ultimate mark of purity is, in principle, devoid of form; yet, according to what is appropriate for each, it manifests various images.
(31) This section clarifies the Middle Way by showing how lands manifest through emptiness and quiescence.
Although one contemplates that all Buddha-lands are eternally quiescent like space, yet manifests various kinds of pure Buddha-lands—this is the practice of a bodhisattva.
Since the Buddha-lands are fundamentally free from defilement and pure, they are eternally quiescent like space; it is precisely because they are pure [that they appear as such].
Thus, the land of inherent nature manifests with brilliant clarity; accordingly, it can manifest various dharmas as appropriate for the capacities of beings, thereby purifying the Buddha-land.
32. Regarding the practice of the cause while possessing the fruit to clarify the Middle Way:
although one has attained the Buddha-way, turns the wheel of Dharma, and enters nirvana, one does not abandon the path of the bodhisattva.
This is the practice of the bodhisattva.

Attaining the Way, preaching the Dharma, and entering into quiescence constitute the ultimate great fruit of the bodhisattva; it is here that the cultivation of causes by the bodhisattva reaches its completion.
Nevertheless, sentient beings are inexhaustible, and the *saṃnāha* (armor of resolve) is likewise inexhaustible. How could it be otherwise?
One attains nirvana through this; one must necessarily carry out the cause while bearing the fruit, practicing the path of the bodhisattva as did Avalokiteśvara and Mañjuśrī.
Otherwise, it is not the path of the bodhisattva.
IV. Gaining Benefit through Hearing the Dharma.
When these words were spoken, among the great assembly led by Mañjuśrī, eight thousand devaputras all resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Regarding the classification of the teachings (*panjiao*), this sutra is said to belong to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/ Fangdeng) period. Although it is said to "rebuke the partial, reject the small, praise the Great, and extol the Perfect," its primary intent lies mostly in the rejection of the Small Vehicle.
Thus, it specifically rebukes those who lack wisdom in their skillful means, those who lack skillful means in their wisdom, and those whose great compassion arises from attachment and views.
It also rebukes the practitioners of the Tripiṭaka and the Six Perfections Bodhisattvas who, without severing delusions, attempt to save sentient beings.

It is the wisdom of the "ashes" resulting from the severance of delusions. If one speaks of "rebuking the partial," this applies not only to the Small Vehicle, but can also be said of both the Shared and Distinct Teachings;
it even applies to those in the stage of names and words within the Perfect Teaching whose contemplative practice has not yet been perfected and who have not yet subdued the five abodes of ignorance.
How could one immediately escape the lack of wisdom in skillful means, the lack of skillful means in wisdom, and the great compassion of attachment and views?
Therefore, for a person of the Perfect Teaching, the two practices of skillful means and wisdom must not be abandoned for even a moment from the very first thought of the path.

When speaking of skillful means, it refers not only to the skillfulness in saving sentient beings and the practice of the six perfections, but also to the [discipline] within the four modes of deportment.

Whether turning or looking up and down, there is nothing that is not a skillful means (*upāya*) for perfecting the person. Yet these skillful means cannot exist without being governed by the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Sometimes wisdom comes first and skillful means assists it; sometimes skillful means comes first and wisdom assists it.
Such practices are none other than the skillful means of the Middle Way, which both negates and illuminates simultaneously. I entrust this to your practice.

One should diligently practice this. However, after the Great Master explained the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*) of the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, he further clarified the three contemplations within a single mind (*ekacitta*).
He cited the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states: "The three wisdoms (*trijñāna*) are actually attained within a single mind;

it is but a single contemplation that constitutes the three contemplations, and it contemplates a single truth (*satya*) as the three truths. Therefore, it is called the 'three contemplations in one mind' (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*). This is analogous to a single mind.
Yet there are arising, abiding, and ceasing; these three marks exist within a single mind. When this contemplation is perfected, one realizes the three wisdoms within the single mind.
This is also called the "mark of the extinction of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*), meaning that one knows all various types of activities and characteristics.
The "mark of extinction" is the power of dual negation. As for "knowing all various characteristics," it is [the power of] duality...
This is the power of illumination. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle.
The *Madhyamaka-śāstra-vṛtti* explains: "The three wisdoms are in reality attained within a single mind. This is precisely that meaning. This contemplation is subtle and wondrous:
it is three while being one, and one while being three. One contemplation is all contemplations; all contemplations are one contemplation. It is neither one nor many.
It is not that all [contemplations] are so; rather, such contemplation subsumes all contemplations. One must understand that the method of contemplation shown in this chapter contains two gates:
the sudden and the gradual. The first exchange of questions and answers between Mañjuśrī and Vimalakīrti, which clarifies the principle of the room being empty, is the sudden contemplation.
The three subsequent exchanges, which clarify the taming of the mind, are the gradual contemplation. However, it is not...

The sudden cannot be used to harmonize the gradual, nor can the gradual be used to open the way for the sudden. When the sudden and gradual are practiced in unison, this constitutes the present "Perfect Contemplation" (*yuan guan*).
This, moreover, accords spontaneously with what was shown by the Great Master. Someone may raise a doubt, saying: "Although the Sudden Contemplation is perfect..."
It appears as if there are three characteristics. Yet, that which is shown by Vimalakīrti is solely this one emptiness (*śūnyatā*). How, then, are they reconciled? The answer is:

this is precisely the principle of the "one emptiness, all things are empty" within the perfectly sudden (*yuan-dun*) threefold contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). For example, when one engages in the contemplation of emptiness, it is not merely that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is empty;
rather, the middle and the true [truths] are also empty. This is called the "Great Contemplation of Emptiness" (*mahā-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*). This is what is indicated in the present text.

This is precisely the Great Emptiness; it is also called Sudden Emptiness and Perfect Emptiness. Were it not for this emptiness, how could a room accommodate such a vast assembly and be termed inconceivable?
If the wise understand that the one arises from the thousand, there is no need for further deliberation.

Regarding the practitioner who resolves through contemplation: the three minds are themselves empty. One by one, they investigate which of the five aggregates possessed therein is the one that suffers from illness.
Within this interval, the body likewise lacks a self; therefore, one should not give rise to attachment toward the mind.

Thus, one breaks through the provisional person and enters emptiness, thereby subduing the mind. Furthermore, within the five aggregates, one contemplates that arising is merely the arising of dharmas, and ceasing is...

Only dharmas cease. Furthermore, these dharmas do not know one another; they do not say, "I arise" or "I cease. Moreover, observing these dharmas, one sees that they are also inverted; I should abandon them.
Abandoning both self and what belongs to the self, one does not dwell on the internal or external, practicing equanimity.
Both "self" and "nirvāṇa" are empty. There is only the sickness of emptiness, yet even the sickness of emptiness is empty.
This is to break through the provisional nature of phenomena and enter the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) to subdue the mind. Furthermore, one contemplates this mind:

although it is emptiness, it is also provisionality; all phenomena remain distinct. Because they are provisional, it does not hinder the experience of various sensations within a state of non-appropriation;
nor does one extinguish sensation to realize emptiness. Thus, one takes pity on one's own mind as it sinks and drifts in birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Out of compassion for others, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). Although he eliminates provisional illnesses, he does not eliminate phenomena;

thus, mind after mind arises. By contemplating and teaching them, he causes them to sever suffering. He instructs them to sever their objective attachments (*ālambana*) and employs various skillful means (*upāya*) to transform their remaining minds.

Although he transforms these remaining minds, he does not depart from the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*); he immediately emerges from emptiness to practice the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-darśana*).
It is the subduing of that mind. Furthermore, one contemplates the Middle Way within this mind, which is simultaneously both emptiness and the provisional.

Therein, skillful means and wisdom are like two cheeks that constantly assist one another and never depart. This is neither [the duality of] emptiness and existence, nor is it a state of mere subduing.
