III. Extensively Enumerating Manifestations of the Body to Clarify the Threefold Inconceivability. First, the manifestation of the body through supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).
Furthermore, Śāriputra, a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation can, by means of supernormal powers, manifest the body of a Buddha;
or manifest the body of a *pratyekabuddha*; or manifest the body of a *śrāvaka*; or manifest the body of Śakra; or manifest the body of Brahmā.
He manifests as the body of a king, or the body of a world-ruler, or the body of a wheel-turning sage-king.

By nature, he is fully endowed with the ten realms, which are ultimately present before him. According to the stimulus of sentient beings' capacities, these realms appear like reflections in a mirror;
such is the natural law of the universal gate of his enlightened activity.
Second, transforming sounds to expound the Dharma: Furthermore,
all sounds existing throughout the worlds of the ten directions— whether superior, middling, or inferior tones— he is able to transform them all, causing them to become the voice of the Buddha,
producing the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the various teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions.
All these dharmas are universally made available for hearing within it.
By manifesting through the Universal Gate, [the Bodhisattva] appears in whatever form is necessary to deliver beings, and therein preaches the Dharma.
Now, it transforms all manner of sounds into the voice of the Buddha, producing the sound of the Dharma so that all may hear it everywhere,
thereby manifesting the inconceivable nature of liberation.
III. Summary of the Power of the Inconceivable.
Śāriputra, I have now briefly explained the power of the bodhisattva’s inconceivable liberation.
Were it to be explained in detail, it would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.
IV. A General Explanation of the Gates of Wisdom and Skillful Means (4 sections). First, Kāśyapa’s Praise of Himself and His Humility (5 sections).
First, Praising the Rarity of the Dharma Gate:
At that time, Mahākāśyapa, having heard the teaching on the inconceivable liberation gate of the bodhisattvas, marveled at it as something unprecedented.
It is so, Śāriputra. It is as if someone were to display various forms and images before a blind person;
they would not see them. In the same way, all śrāvakas who hear this inconceivable Dharma-gate of liberation are unable to understand it.
When the wise hear this, who among them would not resolve to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
II. To show that the Hīnayāna is excluded from this [path]:
"Why have we eternally severed our roots? Regarding this Mahāyāna, we are like withered seeds.
III. To manifest that the Śrāvakas ought to weep.
All śrāvakas, upon hearing this inconceivable Dharma-door of liberation, should weep aloud,
their voices shaking the trichiliocosm.
Master Zhao said: "Because that which is discordant is grave, one must resort to words to express weeping and wailing. For those of the Two Vehicles, sorrow and grief are eternally eliminated;
they do not even have a trace of weeping, let alone cause the three thousand worlds to tremble. Master Deng said: "That is not so.

One must know that although the Two Vehicles have severed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) regarding the internal realm, they are not without the sorrow and grief of views and thoughts regarding the external realm. As it says below: 'The fetters...'"
Because their habitual tendencies are not yet exhausted, the flowers will still cling to their bodies. This is because they fear birth and death; thus, they obtain the five desires.
The followers of the Two Vehicles despise themselves as having no share [in this], yet during these twelve years, they have not yet forgotten their attachment to the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle.

They claim that by severing the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), they are already like withered seeds. They do not realize that even if views and thought were exhausted, the seeds would still sprout. Such is the Dharma rain for the Great Beings (*mahāsattva*).
He was just beginning to open its roots; his wailing for three thousand days marked the very inception of its sprouting.
○ Fourth, to manifest the sovereignty of the Bodhisattvas:
all Bodhisattvas should rejoice greatly and receive this Dharma upon the crown of their heads.
Master Zhao said: "Kāśyapa intended to clarify the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles and to uplift the audience of his time;
therefore, those for whom it was not their lot should shed tears of despair, while those for whom it was their lot should harbor joy at receiving it upon the crown of their heads."
Fifth, it is shown that the māras can do nothing about this:
If there is a bodhisattva who has faith and understanding in this inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, all the hosts of māras can do nothing against them.
When the two devaputras heard this praise,
they resolved their minds on enlightenment. As Mahākāśyapa was speaking these words, thirty-two thousand devaputras all resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
III. The Three Great Beings’ Praise and Manifestation of the Bodhisattva. Part One: Clarifying that Bodhisattvas Frequently Act as Māras.

At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Mahākāśyapa: "O Virtuous One, those who act as Māras in the immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya worlds of the ten directions are for the most part bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*), who employ the power of skillful means (*upāya-śakti*)."
Therefore, in order to teach and transform sentient beings, he manifests as a Mara king.
Master Zhao said: "According to Kāśyapa, those who possess faith and understanding of the inconceivable cannot be disturbed by Māra.
Yet, there are also Bodhisattvas in the ten directions who possess faith and understanding yet are disturbed by Māra; this is intended to clarify the greatness of the inconceivable."
The actions of a Bodhisattva are sovereign. Because he wishes to encourage those who have newly begun their study, he manifests as the Māra King;
this is not something that can be accomplished by the power of Māra. This also clarifies the inconceivable and fulfills the intended meaning of Kāśyapa’s words.
II. Explaining that Bodhisattvas frequently manifest as those who beg for evil things.
Furthermore, Kāśyapa, there are immeasurable bodhisattvas in the ten directions;

some may encounter people who beg from them for their hands, feet, ears, noses, heads, eyes, marrow, brain, blood, flesh, skin, or bones, or for villages, cities, wives, children, male and female slaves, elephants, horses, carriages, or gold and silver.
Lapis lazuli, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, pearls, and conch shells; clothing, food, and drink—
those who beg for such things are mostly bodhisattvas dwelling in the inconceivable liberation who, through the power of skillful means,
go to test them so as to make their resolve firm.

Master Kumārajīva said: "For a Bodhisattva whose karmic activities have been exhausted through the perfection of giving, yet who has not yet reached its ultimate limit, an inconceivable Bodhisattva forcibly solicits from him so that his lack of stinginess may be fully perfected and made firm.
This also causes sentient beings to know of his firmness, and enables him himself to realize his own firmness."
II. The Bodhisattva’s Expedient Means and Original Mind. First, it clarifies that he possesses the power of majestic virtue (*prabhāva*).
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva who dwells in inconceivable liberation possesses the power of majestic virtue;
therefore, he employs coercion to demonstrate [the truth] to all sentient beings.
II. Praising this as a difficult feat, in two parts. First, the explanation by way of Dharma:
Such a difficult feat is one that ordinary, inferior beings, lacking power and influence, cannot thus coerce a bodhisattva.
II. The Parable: It is like the trampling of a dragon-elephant, which a donkey cannot endure. Master Zhao said:
"To amputate a person's hands and feet, to separate them from their wife and children, and to forcibly seize their national wealth—these things give rise to sorrow and grief."

Although there may be slight suffering in the present moment, it brings about great peace for eternal kalpas. This is because one deeply contemplates the faculties of people and weighs their relative gravity;
it is not within the capacity of those who see the near but fail to perceive the far-reaching. Master Kumārajīva said:
"If sentient beings possessed a truly fixed nature, then the inconceivable Great Being would not need to travel in vain to transform them."
He attempts to cause them to experience suffering; because it is not real, it is easily accomplished, and thus he practices tormenting and oppression.
○ Fourth, the conclusion forming the Dharma-gate of liberation.
This is called the gateway of the wisdom and skillful means of a bodhisattva who dwells in the inconceivable liberation.
Master Zhaò said: "Wisdom reaches far and penetrates deeply; skillful means guides from nearby. It is through these that diverse traces are manifested and various obstacles are overcome.
There is nothing that does not proceed by way of them, yet none can fathom them. Therefore, the two gateways of provisional and ultimate wisdom constitute the inconceivable."
This is the foundation of our deliberation.

Regarding the classification of the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation according to the provisional teachings, it specifically pertains to the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect Teaching who have ascended to the first stage (bhūmi).

From there up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), they gradually shatter ignorance and partially realize the threefold virtue, drawing near to Subtle Enlightenment (wonderful enlightenment). Only then can they...

This is ultimately so; it also includes Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching who have ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*). However, once they have separately ascended to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), they are already identical to those of the Perfect Teaching at the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).
Although it is said that this "includes the Separate," it is in fact purely Perfect. This is as explained by Master Kumārajīva, Sengzhao, and other masters.
This refers to a Bodhisattva in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) who is able to possess this power. However, it is not known what kind of teaching’s sequence of stages this "seventh stage" represents.
If it refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), then this power would have already been attained at the first stage; it would not wait until the seventh.

If it refers to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*), it is only at the seventh stage that one exhausts the delusions of thought (*si-huo*) and begins to learn how to emerge into the provisional world (*chu-jia*); yet even then, such a realization has not yet occurred. According to the commentaries from Guanzhong, [this] mostly accords with the Separate Teaching.

Regarding the "penetrating principle" (tōri): that which it refers to is the seventh stage (*saptamī-bhūmi*). This should be understood as the stages in various Mahāyāna sūtras where the specific is used to clarify the universal;

it is equivalent to the "Stage of Those Who Have Accomplished Their Task" (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*). Although one can sport with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and purify Buddha-fields at this level, one has not yet attained such inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*).
Regarding "contemplative understanding": one contemplates that within a single thought-moment, the nature is replete with the three thousand [realms].

This refers to the essence and magnitude of the nature itself: while one realm manifests, nine realms lie latent; when one dharma manifests, two thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine dharmas lie latent.

Alternatively, whether it be the faculties and objects, or the primary and secondary bodies, each manifests while the others remain latent. One acts as the host and the rest as guests; the host is able to encompass them all.
The guest returns to the host; or the small appears within the large, and the large appears within the small.
This is the inconceivable dharma-gate of liberation, which is fully present within a single mind.

Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Scroll Seven Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Scroll Eight Authored by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi, Mount Tiantai [Scroll Eight] The Buddha addressed the assembly: "If there were a self, it would not be subject to birth and death; it would be permanent and unchanging. Because there is no self, one undergoes birth and death, experiencing suffering and joy, and is subject to increase and decrease. Vimalakīrti said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if there were a self, it would not be subject to birth and death. Why? Because the nature of the self is originally quiescent and eternally abiding. If it were subject to birth and death, it would be impermanent and changing. Therefore, we know that because there is no self, one undergoes birth and death, experiences suffering and joy, and is subject to increase and decrease. The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent! Vimalakīrti, you have spoken well. This is indeed the true teaching of the Buddhas. If there were a self, it would be impossible for sentient beings to attain liberation. It is precisely because there is no self that they can transcend birth and death and realize nirvana. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there were a self, it would be identical to space. Why? Because space has no self, yet it pervades all places. If the self were like space, it would be omnipresent and could not be said to be born or die. Since it is not so, we know there is no self. Furthermore, if there were a self, it would be subject to defilement and purity. But since the nature of the self is fundamentally pure and free from defilement, we know there is no self. Moreover, if there were a self, it would be subject to grasping and attachment. But since the nature of the self is non-grasping and non-attached, we know there is no self. The Buddha said: "Vimalakīrti, you have skillfully expounded the profound meaning of non-self. All Bodhisattvas who wish to realize the Dharma of the Buddhas should first cultivate this understanding of non-self. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, what is meant by 'non-self'? The Buddha replied: 'Non-self means that all dharmas are empty and devoid of substantiality. They arise through causes and conditions and have no inherent essence. Because they are empty and without substance, they are called non-self. Vimalakīrti said: 'World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-self, then who is it that attains enlightenment? The Buddha replied: 'Enlightenment is attained by the mind that is free from grasping and delusion. When the mind realizes that all dharmas are empty and without self, it is called the attainment of enlightenment. Furthermore, non-self means that the five aggregates are empty and have no master. Form, sensation, perception, formation, and consciousness are all like illusions and dreams; they have no fixed substance and are ultimately non-existent. Because they are non-existent, they are called non-self. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if the five aggregates are non-self, then who is it that performs wholesome and unwholesome deeds? The Buddha replied: 'Deeds are performed by the mind. The mind, driven by ignorance and craving, creates karma. Although the mind is non-self, its power of conditioning gives rise to various fruits. Just as an echo arises from sound and an image appears from a mirror, though both the sound and the object are non-self, their effects are nonetheless produced.

Thus, although the five aggregates are non-self, the retribution of karma is not lost. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-self, how can one speak of the distinction between ordinary beings and sages? The Buddha replied: 'Ordinary beings cling to the notion of self and give rise to various afflictions, while sages realize the truth of non-self and abide in wisdom and liberation. Though both are non-self, their states of mind differ, and thus the distinction between ordinary beings and sages is established. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is truly no self, then who is it that receives the teachings of the Buddhas and practices the path? The Buddha replied: 'Receiving the teachings and practicing the path is the function of the mind. The mind, through hearing the Dharma, gives rise to faith and understanding, and through cultivation, realizes the fruit. Although the mind is non-self, its capacity for transformation and realization is inexhaustible. Therefore, one should not seek a self within the dharmas, but should instead rely on the power of non-self to transcend birth and death. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, why do sentient beings suffer? The Buddha replied: 'Suffering arises from the delusion of grasping at a self. Because they grasp at a self, they give rise to craving and aversion, which lead to the cycle of birth and death and all manner of suffering. If one realizes that there is no self, then craving and aversion will cease, and suffering will be extinguished. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, then who is it that attains the fruit of Arhatship? The Buddha replied: 'Arhatship is attained when the mind is completely free from the outflows of desire, existence, and ignorance. It is not a person who attains it, but rather the cessation of all delusions and the realization of the emptiness of all dharmas. Therefore, one should understand that the fruit of Arhatship is also non-self. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if all dharmas are non-self, then what is the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching on the Three Jewels? The Buddha replied: 'The Three Jewels are established based on the principle of non-self. The Buddha is the one who has realized the truth of non-self; the Dharma is the teaching of non-self; and the Sangha is the community of those who practice the path of non-self. Because they take refuge in these three non-self principles, they are able to transcend the world and attain ultimate peace. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, then who is it that makes offerings to the Buddhas? The Buddha replied: 'Offerings are made by the mind of devotion. Although the mind is non-self, when it encounters a field of merit such as the Buddha, it naturally gives rise to respect and generosity. This is the power of karmic conditions, not the action of a self. Therefore, one should offer with a mind free from attachment, knowing that both the giver and the gift are ultimately non-self. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, then who is it that experiences the bliss of Nirvana? The Buddha replied: 'Nirvana is the extinction of all suffering and the cessation of all conceptualization. It is experienced by the mind that has reached ultimate tranquility and is free from all grasping. Although the mind is non-self, when it realizes the emptiness of all dharmas, it attains the bliss of liberation. Therefore, one should know that the bliss of Nirvana is also non-self. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, then what is the meaning of the Buddha’s teaching on the Six Paramitas? The Buddha replied: 'The Six Paramitas are the path of non-self. Generosity is the giving away of the notion of self; discipline is the restraint of the mind from grasping at a self; patience is the endurance of the insults of others without anger; vigor is the effort to cultivate non-self wisdom; meditation is the concentration of the mind on the emptiness of all dharmas; and wisdom is the clear realization of the non-self nature of all things. By practicing these six, one transcends the world and realizes the ultimate truth. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, then who is it that becomes a Buddha? The Buddha replied: 'One becomes a Buddha by realizing the non-self nature of all dharmas. Through countless eons of cultivation, one perfects the wisdom of non-self and manifests the Dharmakaya. Although the Buddha is non-self, his compassionate vows and powers are inexhaustible, enabling him to transform and save all sentient beings. Therefore, one should aspire to Buddhahood by relying on the path of non-self. Vimalakīrti said: "World-Honored One, if there is no self, then why do sentient beings create karma? The Buddha replied: 'Karma is created by the mind. The mind, driven by ignorance, gives rise to thoughts of good and evil, which then manifest as physical and verbal actions. Although the mind is non-self, its power of conditioning is real and produces results. Therefore, one should be careful in one's thoughts and actions, knowing that even though there is no
○ Seven: Commentary on the Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings (2). First, the commentary on the chapter title.
*The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Seven: Contemplating Sentient Beings.

The objects of contemplation for the Two Vehicles largely involve emptiness (*śūnyatā*); the objects of contemplation for Bodhisattvas largely involve existence (*bhava*). Since [the former] involves emptiness...

One incurs the criticism of seeking self-liberation; yet to engage with existence again falls into the error of becoming a person. Only when the Buddha practices the Way do emptiness and existence proceed with ease.
As it is said: "Wisdom without skillful means is bondage; wisdom with skillful means is liberation; skillful means without wisdom is bondage."

There is liberation through wisdom and skillful means. Are skillful means not the engagement with existence (*saṃsāra*)? Is wisdom not the engagement with emptiness (*śūnyatā*)? This has already been fully prepared in the preceding chapter.
Mañjuśrī again feared that those guests who were stuck on words had not yet attained the principle of returning to the One;
therefore, he asked this question once more. Vimalakīrti’s response, however, reaches both emptiness and existence simultaneously, remaining ever in the Middle Way.
To dwell [in this way], there are indeed sentient beings who may be delivered; how could one forget the emotions involved in engaging with existence?
To observe through various metaphors, how could one negate wisdom to observe emptiness? Moreover, by exercising true compassion, one extensively refutes the thirty errors.

Thus, one simultaneously rescues those bound by the conditions of birth and those bound by the conditions of dharmas, soaring alone upon the Middle Way of non-conditionality. This is the Bodhisattva’s path for delivering sentient beings.
Beyond this, I do not know how to proceed.

○ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text has two parts. First, the direct clarification of the contemplation of sentient beings has four sections. First, clarifying the sentient beings who are the objects of contemplation has two parts.
First, Mañjuśrī asks, "How does one contemplate sentient beings?
At that time, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "How does a bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings?"
Those sentient beings who are to be saved are the object; the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of them is the contemplation.
Since it is not known how the Bodhisattva contemplates them to practice their deliverance, this question was asked.
Second, Vimalakīrti answers with twenty-nine similes. Vimalakīrti said:
"For example, just as a magician perceives the illusory person he has conjured, so does a bodhisattva perceive sentient beings."
Master Zhao said: "When a magician observes his illusions, he knows they are not real; the Bodhisattva’s observation of sentient beings is just like this.
It is like a wise person seeing the moon in water, like seeing the reflection of one's own face in a mirror, like a mirage in the heat, like an echo."

Sounds are like clouds in the sky, like a mass of foam on water, like bubbles on the surface of water, like the solidity of a plantain tree, like lightning remaining for long, like a fifth great element, like a sixth aggregate, like a seventh sense-faculty, like the thirteenth base, and like the nineteenth realm.
Thus does the Bodhisattva contemplate sentient beings: they are like form in the formless realm, like sprouts from parched grain.
The view of a self in the body of a *srotāpanna* is like the entry into a womb by an *anāgāmin*.
Master Zhaò said: "Although an *anāgāmin* may temporarily regress, they certainly do not undergo rebirth."
It is like the three poisons of an arhat.
Although an arhat may still possess the three poisons pertaining to the supramundane realm, what is meant here is that they have already eliminated the three poisons pertaining to the mundane realm.
Just as a bodhisattva who has attained the stage of patience (kṣānti) is free from greed, anger, and the violation of precepts,

so too for a bodhisattva at the stage of the realization of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), fundamental ignorance has already been shattered and the fetters of the mind have forever subsided; how much more so, then,
regarding the coarse matter of violating precepts?
Regarding "the Buddha’s habit-energies of affliction," Master Zao said: "Only the Tathāgata has completely exhausted all fetters and habit-energies;
it is like a blind person seeing colors, or like the inhalation and exhalation of one who has entered the meditative absorption of cessation."
Master Zhao said: "The mind races and stirs within; the breath enters and exits without. Once mental conceptions have ceased, there is no entering or exiting of the breath.
It is like the tracks of a bird in the sky, like the son of a barren woman, like the afflictions of a conjured person, or like what is seen in a dream once one has awakened."
Regarding the manner in which one who has entered parinirvāṇa receives a body, Master Zhaowu said: "There has never been anyone who enters nirvana and yet again receives a body;
it is like a fire without smoke. Thus do Bodhisattvas contemplate sentient beings.
The sentient beings to be delivered exist; yet when one contemplates them as fundamentally empty—as in the various metaphors—they are empty.
Thus, existence is immediately emptiness, and emptiness is immediately existence. Riding upon the twin wheels, they move directly forward; with both wings spread, they soar high.
When a Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings in this manner, it may be said that he abides in their fundamental nature.
II. Clarifying the Four Immeasurable Minds that Can Be Cultivated. First, the Immeasurable Mind of Loving-kindness (maitrī).
First, Mañjuśrī asks how one practices loving-kindness.
Mañjuśrī said: "If a bodhisattva makes this contemplation, how does he practice loving-kindness?"

The intent of the question is as follows: to contemplate in such a manner involves the realm of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), whereas to practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and bestow happiness involves the realm of existence (*bhava*).

This raises an objection based on the distinction between the object-condition of dharmas (*dharmālambana*) and the object-condition of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*), thereby opening the way to the Vimalakīrti’s doctrine of non-duality (*advaya*).

II. Vimalakīrti’s Response by Teaching the Dharma for the Sake of Birth. This has two parts. First, the actual explanation, which has two sections. First, a general presentation of true compassion. Vimalakīrti said:
"After a bodhisattva has made this contemplation, he reflects to himself: 'I shall preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.'"
The Dharma is itself true compassion. Master Zhao said:
"Sentient beings are fundamentally empty, yet they are unable to realize this for themselves; therefore, he preaches this Dharma to enable them to awaken on their own.
How could there be 'self' and 'other'? If one can contemplate the emptiness of sentient beings, then mental activity is likewise empty. By means of this...
This is the mind of emptiness; to practice compassion within this emptiness is what is called "true compassion of signlessness. Dēng said:
"Now, 'compassion' (maitrī) means bestowing happiness, and 'pity' (karuṇā) means extracting suffering. However, at the time of bestowing happiness, one has already extracted one's own suffering;

and at the time of extracting suffering, one has already bestowed happiness upon oneself. This is because the two dharmas of suffering and happiness are in essence like ice and fire—they do not belong to the same category."
The suffering of sentient beings arises from attachment to existence. The Bodhisattva contemplates emptiness and has already crossed to the other shore.
When the Bodhisattva delivers sentient beings, they likewise contemplate this realm. Having made this contemplation, they reflect:

"I shall preach this Dharma of emptiness for the sake of sentient beings, so that they may cross over the suffering of existence and the bliss of the unconditioned may spontaneously arrive. Thus, taking what they themselves desire, they turn it around to bestow it upon others.
Because it is for all people, it is called "true compassion.
Second, the specific opening of thirty types of compassion:
one practices the compassion of quiescence, because there is nothing that arises.
Although the varieties of the delusion of ignorance are numerous, when generally described, they do not exceed four: namely, arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "How much more so regarding the specific measures and enumerations of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing within this [mind]! This is precisely what is meant.

Regarding the characteristics of the arising of delusions, the characteristic of birth (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) stands at the beginning and the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*) stands at the end.
Regarding the characteristics of their elimination, the characteristic of birth stands at the beginning and the characteristic of cessation stands at the end.

Therefore, among the five patiences (*kṣānti*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) occupies the head of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), while the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*) occupies the end of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). Now, speaking generally from the perspective of the final stage, therefore—

Regarding what is called "the compassion of quiescence" (*śānti-maitrī*): on the surface, it does not exhaustively reach the ultimate principle. It is also said that it is "because there is nothing produced.

However, as for the efficacy of quiescence, if it can bring about the cessation of extinction (*nirodha*), how could it not be able to bring about the cessation of arising? Therefore, it can be said that it is "because there is nothing produced.
This compassion belongs to the objectless (*anālambana*), taking the Middle Way—where both emptiness and existence are empty—as its essence.
He practices the "unheated" compassion because he is free from afflictions.
A remarkable man of the world who harbors a sense of righteous indignation in his breast, he is able to dispel difficulties and resolve conflicts for others.
He must repay even the kindness of a single meal and will surely avenge even the grudge of a mere squint. This is called having a "hot heart," because—
This is because [ordinary beings] possess the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion. Now, the compassion of a Bodhisattva regards enemies and kin with equanimity;

it bestows and uproots through the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Although this may appear to be the clearing of difficulties and the resolving of entanglements, sentient beings who share a karmic affinity with them do not feel it as "warm," and those with whom they have no such affinity do not feel it as "cold. This is because it is free from the afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion.
This is because it eliminates affliction. This loving-kindness belongs to the category of dharma-conditions; its essence consists in accord with the fact that both enemies and kin are equally empty.
Loving-kindness such as that of practice and so forth is equal because it encompasses the three periods of time.
The compassion of a bodhisattva accords with the substance of the Four Great Vows and its principle pervades the entire Dharma-realm. Although sentient beings are boundless, he vows to deliver them;
though countless *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas have already passed in the past, his mind has not ceased;
though countless *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas lie ahead in the future, his mind will not rest; and as he dwells rightly within the ten directions for countless *gaṅgā*-sands of kalpas...
Even across realms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, their minds never experience weariness; this is called "the compassion of equal practice.

Because it accords with the principle of eternal abiding and is equal throughout the three periods of time, this compassion belongs to the objectless (*anālambana*); its essence consists in accordance with equality.
One practices the compassion of non-contention because there is nothing that arises.
When the human mind contends with phenomena, it is because the mind has arisen in relation to sense objects and conditions.

When a Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind to deliver sentient beings, they have already established themselves in non-abiding. Their current practice of loving-kindness (maitrī) thus accords with the teaching:
"one should give rise to the mind by abiding nowhere. This is called the loving-kindness of non-contention (araṇā-maitrī).

Furthermore, it is explained that because there is nothing that arises, this loving-kindness belongs to the category of the object-condition of dharmas (dharmālambana), as it accords with non-contention and non-arising.
Practice non-dual compassion, for there is no union between the internal and external.

Practice compassion that contemplates arising; once the internal and external have been distinguished, if one takes them as objects and gives rise to discrimination, then the sense organs and their objects will unite, and birth and death will be endless.
To realize them as being like illusions and transformations, then self and others are not two, and things and I are all [one].
Emptiness. This loving-kindness belongs to both [categories], yet it does not belong to the non-dual; it does not belong to the objectless, nor is it conjoined with the dharma-object.
One practices indestructible loving-kindness because it is ultimately exhausted.
As long as even a single existence of birth-and-death and afflictions is not exhausted, there will be a dharma that can be destroyed; only because it is ultimately exhausted is this so.
Therefore, the essence of this compassion is indestructible. This compassion belongs to the category of dharma-ālambana (objectless) because it accords with the characteristic of exhaustion.
One practices firm and steadfast compassion because the mind is beyond impairment.
The Middle Way is without conditions; it is as firm as a diamond and sharp enough to destroy delusions; therefore, the mind is indestructible.
One practices pure compassion because the nature of all phenomena is inherently pure.
Master Sengzhao said: "True compassion is signless; it is as pure as the dharma-nature. This compassion belongs to the objectless (anālambana).
One practices boundless compassion because it is like empty space."
The Middle Way is without conditions; its essence is like empty space, fundamentally without boundaries.
One practices the compassion of an arhat because it destroys the thieves of the fetters.
In Sanskrit, *arhat* means "one who has destroyed the thieves"; this compassion belongs to the category of dharma-conditions, which is to say, it does not involve the mind grasping at objects.
Taking sentient beings as the object, benefit spontaneously manifests.
This is the practice of the Bodhisattva’s compassion, for the sake of settling sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva has no [fixed] mind; rather, they take the settling of sentient beings as their mind. This compassion belongs to the category of "object-conditioned" (sattvālambana); therefore, it is so described.
One practices the Tathāgata’s compassion because one has attained the mark of suchness (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*).
Compassion is divided into three types according to its objects: that which takes sentient beings as its object belongs to Bodhisattvas; that which takes phenomena as its object belongs to Arhats;
and now, that which takes no object as its condition (*anālambana*) should belong to the Tathāgata. Because its essence accords with the Middle Way, it is said that one attains the mark of suchness.
One practices the compassion of a Buddha because of awakening sentient beings.
In Sanskrit, *buddha* means "awakened. There are three types of awakening: first, self-awakening, which pertains to the object-condition (*dharmālambana*);

second, awakening others, which pertains to the sentient-being-condition (*sattvālambana*); and third, perfected awakening, which pertains to the non-object-condition (*anālambana*). Since it is said here that one awakens sentient beings, it is categorized accordingly.
This is the condition for birth.
One practices spontaneous compassion because it is not obtained through causes.
Master Zhaoluo said: "The Way of the Mahāyāna is accomplished without a teacher; this is called 'spontaneous' (zìrán). Such is the true compassion of the Bodhisattva."
Furthermore, it does not arise from causes; therefore, it is called "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*). This compassion belongs to the objectless (*anālambana*).
One practices the compassion of *bodhi* because it is of one equal flavor.
Master Sengzhao said: "The path of equality, one flavor, and signlessness is called *bodhi*; it is true compassion free of signs."
It is also of equal, single flavor, and may be called bodhi. This compassion belongs to the objectless (anālambana);
it practices peerless compassion because it severs all craving. Compassion is close to love;
love is equal toward all sentient beings. The Bodhisattva cultivates compassion with the Dharma as its object (*dharmālambana*) and has already severed all [craving].
Although their love may be equal throughout the day, it does not truly equal theirs. This compassion belongs to the object-conditioned (dharmālambana) type;
they practice great compassionate love because they guide others by means of the Mahāyāna.
If one does not first uproot suffering, the happiness bestowed will ultimately not be ultimate. Therefore, compassion (*karuṇā*) and kindness (*maitrī*) are one in meaning but different in name.
To guide [beings] with the bliss of the Mahāyāna in order to liberate them from the suffering of the two deaths is called "great compassionate kindness.
This kindness belongs to the objectless (*anālambana*), because it guides [beings] toward the Mahāyāna.
One practices compassion without weariness because one contemplates emptiness and non-self.

Master Zhao said: "The sentiment of fatigue and weariness arises from the preservation of a self. One who practices compassion with a mind of emptiness and non-self will reach the end of birth and death;
there will be no further fatigue or weariness. This compassion belongs to the category of compassion based on dharmas (dharmālambana-maitrī).
One practices the compassion of the gift of Dharma because there is nothing left to regret.

Material gifts are exhaustible, and thus involve regret; the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, and thus involves no regret. This compassion gives rise to both [material and spiritual] dharmas, belonging to both categories.
One practices the compassion of observing the precepts (*śīla-karuṇā*).

Because it transforms those who violate the prohibitions, the Bodhisattva’s observance of the precepts does not merely consist of personally refraining from violating them; rather, it simultaneously seeks to transform others who violate them, so that people may see the virtuous and aspire to emulate them.
Bestowing happiness through this, there is no compassion greater than this. This belongs to the category of "compassion based on sentient beings" (*sattvālambana-karuṇā*).
One practices the compassion of patience (*kṣānti*) because it protects both others and oneself.

Master Kumārajīva said: "If one can practice patience, then internally one does not weary oneself, and externally one does not harm others; therefore, it is said that it protects both others and oneself.
This also belongs to the category of the compassion of conditioned arising (*upapatti-saṃvartanīya-karuṇā*).
One practices the compassion of diligence (*vīrya-maitrī*) because of bearing the burden of sentient beings.
Although a person may possess strength, if they are further subject to regression, they will be unable to carry any load.

Therefore, when a Bodhisattva bears the burden of sentient beings, it is appropriate that diligence serves as their strength. This, too, belongs to the category of conditions related to sentient beings (*sattvālambana*).
One practices the compassion of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), because one does not relish its flavor.
Those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), having attained meditative concentration through cultivation, mostly give rise to attachment to its flavor.

When a Bodhisattva attains meditative concentration, they should properly rely upon that concentration to practice compassion. By practicing compassion, they transcend the mundane to benefit sentient beings, rather than craving the flavor of concentration. This...
This is also subsumed under the category of the compassion based on dharmas.
One practices the compassion of wisdom because there is nothing for which one does not know the proper time.
Master Kumārajīva said: "To seek the fruit before one's practice is complete is called 'not knowing the time. Master Dēng said: "It is not merely this."
To seek to deliver others while one has not yet delivered oneself; to have attained deliverance for oneself yet fail to deliver others;

to claim that all sentient beings are brought to extinction while believing there are actually sentient beings who attain extinction; or to dwell nowhere yet fail to give rise to the mind [of compassion], or to give rise to the mind while not dwelling [in non-attachment]—all these are called "not knowing the proper time.
This is also subsumed within the compassion based on dharmas (*dharmālambana-maitrī*).
It is the practice of expedient compassion (*upāya-maitrī*), because it manifests in all ways.

Beyond the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), there is a perfection of expedients; compassion is likewise so. When a bodhisattva manifests in all ways according to the capacities of sentient beings, this is called expedient compassion.
This belongs to the category of compassion based on living beings (*sattvālambana-maitrī*).
One practices unhidden compassion because of the purity of the straightforward mind.
There are three kinds of being unhidden: first, being unhidden in teaching, because the mind and speech are straightforward; second, being unhidden in practice, because there are no devious paths;
third, being unhidden in principle, because the mind accords with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If there is anything hidden, it cannot be called pure.

It is pure. It is subsumed under the loving-kindness that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana-maitrī*). One practices the loving-kindness of the profound mind (*gambhīracitta-maitrī*), because there is no admixture in one's practice.
Whatever actions are performed, if they are mixed, they are not profound; now, this loving-kindness of the profound mind is profound, and therefore it is not mixed. This, too, is the Dharma.
It is encompassed by the condition of loving-kindness.
One practices non-deceptive loving-kindness because it is not false or artificial.
Since a bodhisattva is free from even the slightest falsehood at all times, how much more so when practicing loving-kindness? Would one do so through falsehood? No.
And thus they deceive sentient beings; this too is subsumed under the *maitrī* (loving-kindness) that takes phenomena as its object (*dharmālambana*).
They practice the *maitrī* of bestowing peace and happiness, because they cause [beings] to attain the bliss of Buddhahood.
Because the great *maitrī* of the Bodhisattvas constantly desires to grant sentient beings the bliss of the Buddha’s wisdom so that they may realize the four virtues, therefore...
To practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*) is called "bestowing peace and happiness. This belongs to the category of objectless loving-kindness (*apraṇihita-maitrī*).
○ Second, the conclusion:
Such is the nature of the bodhisattva’s loving-kindness.
II. The Immeasurable Mind of Compassion (Karunā). Part 1: The Question.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "What is meant by compassion?
Part 2: The Answer.
The answer is: "Whatever merits a bodhisattva has performed, he shares them all with all sentient beings.
Master Zhaoluo said: "Compassionate toward those who suffer long-term afflictions, he does not regard his own person; whatever multitude of virtues he possesses, he vows to bestow upon all."
To put others first and oneself last is the practice of great compassion.
Section Three: The Immeasurable Mind of Sympathetic Joy (Muditā). Part One: The Question.
What is meant by sympathetic joy?
II. The Response. The response states: "There is that which benefits others; one rejoices without regret.
Master Zhao says: "Having personally attained the benefit of the Dharma, one shares the joy with the multitude. One rejoices because both self and others have attained the bliss of the Dharma."
This is called joy.
○ Second, the immeasurable mind of equanimity (upekṣā). Part one: the question.
What is meant by equanimity?
[The second] answer:
He replied, "In the merit and blessings one performs, there is no expectation.
Master Kumārajīva said, "This means not seeking favor in the present life, nor seeking retribution in the future."
Regarding the provisional teachings: the Bodhisattva contemplates sentient beings as being like illusions and transformations, yet is able to practice loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
This can be spoken of according to all three teachings—Shared, Distinct, and Perfect—but the primary intent lies in the Perfect Teaching.
This is because the thirty types of loving-kindness revealed within true loving-kindness encompass the three kinds of compassion (*karuṇā*).
Regarding the practitioner of contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*): they contemplate that a single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) encompasses the ten dharma-realms (*daśa-dharmadhātu*).

Although one remains within delusion, by contemplating through the twenty-nine similes such as "like an illusion" and so forth, within this state of non-apprehensibility (*anupalabdhi*), I therefore employ the thirty kinds of compassion of the true reality-mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-karuṇā*) to bestow the bliss of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and extract the suffering of inherent virtue. This constitutes the skillful means and wisdom of contemplating the mind.
The second is practicing both together. Just as with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), one should likewise observe the third [immeasurable].
○ Third, clarifying the virtues upon which one relies, in six parts: first, clarifying that there is fear within birth and death, and what one should rely upon.
Second, the initial question.
Mañjuśrī asked again: "In the cycle of birth and death there is fear; upon what should a bodhisattva rely? Master Zhao said:
"Birth and death constitute fear—there is nothing greater than this fear. For a Great Being who is moved by compassion, upon what can he rely?"
And yet he is able to dwell eternally within birth and death; does he not take fear as his object of fear?
[The second answer:
Vimalakīrti said, "When a bodhisattva is amidst the fear of birth and death, he should rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits."
The Bodhisattva Karuṇācintin acts as a compassionate vessel upon the ocean of suffering. He should rely on two kinds of power from the Buddha’s merits:
first, the power of the merits of other Buddhas—namely, the power of the merits cultivated by all Buddhas of the ten directions—which secretly perfumes and supports him so that he does not regress;
second, the power of the merits of the Buddha cultivated by himself, which is what is addressed in the following question.
Regarding the Dharma shown in the response, if one practices in accordance with it, there will be the merit of producing goodness and extinguishing evil.
If one relies solely on the text of the response, it appears to be merely one's own power; yet it is also called the merit of the Tathāgata when explained according to its underlying meaning.
Two kinds are required. II.
Clarifying upon what the Tathāgata’s merits should rely for their abiding. This has two parts. First, the question:
Mañjuśrī asked again, "If a bodhisattva wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits, upon what should they abide?"
2. The Response.
He replied: "A bodhisattva who wishes to rely on the power of the Tathāgata’s merits should abide in the liberation of all sentient beings.
There is no other power of the Tathāgata’s merits; it consists solely in making the liberation of sentient beings one's task. The bodhisattva...
If one can abide in this state to deliver sentient beings, then one accords with the Buddha-mind; the Buddha will surely bestow his empowerment through the power of his merit.
Thus, in a single act, one attains both goals.
III. The Threefold Knowledge: Regarding what should be eliminated when one desires to deliver sentient beings. Part One: The Questions.
Furthermore, it is asked: "When one desires to deliver sentient beings, what should be eliminated?
Part Two: The Answer.
The answer is: One wishes to deliver sentient beings and eliminate their afflictions;
yet, if one has not first eliminated one's own afflictions while hastily attempting to deliver others, both self and other will surely sink together—this principle is inevitable.
IV. Regarding the desire to eliminate afflictions, what should one practice? Part Two: First, the question;
second, the inquiry: "Furthermore, one asks: 'Desiring to eliminate afflictions, what should one practice?
Second, the answer.
The answer is: One should practice right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*).
As for the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are the five dull underlying tendencies (*pañca-anuśaya*) of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, and doubt; all arise from incorrect mindfulness.
Therefore, if one wishes to eliminate the afflictions, one should practice right mindfulness.
V. Five Questions. How does one practice right mindfulness? Part 1: The initial question;
Part 2: The further question. How does one practice right mindfulness?
Part 2: The answer.
The answer is: One should practice non-arising and non-ceasing.
[Section Six] Question: What dharma does not arise? What dharma does not cease? Part Two: First Question. Furthermore, it is asked:
What dharma does not arise? What dharma does not cease?
II. The Response.
He replied: "The unwholesome does not arise; wholesome dharmas do not cease.
These five preceding questions and answers have been explained progressively until this point, where it is established that the unwholesome does not arise and wholesome dharmas do not cease.
The essential path for practicing the bodhisattva conduct is this: if unwholesome states do not arise, one can thereby benefit oneself;
if wholesome dharmas are not extinguished, one can thereby benefit sentient beings. Thus, when "unwholesome" is mentioned, all obscurations and afflictions are included therein;
when "wholesome dharmas" are mentioned, the six perfections and the myriad practices are included therein. The following six questions address these points.
First, this response serves as the fundamental basis. Section Four:

Clarifying the Roots of the Wholesome and the Unwholesome (2). Part One: The Response Clarifies Six Points. First: A Question and Answer concerning what constitutes the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
He asked again: "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome? He replied: "The body is the root.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Body refers to the five aggregates (pañca-skandha).
[Question 21: "What is the root of the body?"
He asked again, "What is the root of the body? He replied, "Desire and greed are its root.
Master Kumārajīva said, "Because the depth of attachment to desire is profound, one extensively generates fetters and karma;
furthermore, it is through the moisture of craving that one undergoes rebirth. Therefore, among all the fetters, desire and greed are singled out for mention."
Question 31: What is the root of craving?
Furthermore, it was asked: What is the root of that which follows craving? He replied: False conceptualization is the root.
Craving arises from conceptualizing based on sensory objects; by discriminating between the beautiful and the foul, craving is produced.
○ Fourth, one question and answer: What is the root of false discrimination?
Again, it is asked: What is the root of false discrimination? The answer is: Perverted perception is its root.
The seer and the objects of seeing, along with the perceived characteristics, are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally they do not exist at all.
Yet sentient beings, through false conceptualization, claim they exist. In the world of flowers in the sky, there is fundamentally no beauty or ugliness;

yet sentient beings, through false conceptualization, designate them as beautiful or ugly—all such instances are termed "inversions. They are like those who are crazed or intoxicated, [confusing] head and tail.
They are exchanged; thus one calls the head the tail—is this not a perversion?
○ Question fifty-one: What is the root of perverted perceptions? Again he asked:
"What is the root of perverted perceptions? He replied: "Non-abiding is the root."
61. Question and Answer: "What is the basis of non-abiding?
He asked again, "What is the basis of non-abiding? The answer was: "Non-abiding has no basis.
2. Conclusion.
Mañjuśrī, all dharmas are established from the root of non-abiding.
Master Zhao said: "The mind is like water; when still, it reflects; when stirred, it lacks clarity. It is turbid with the defilements of ignorance and craving."
Stirred by perverse winds, surging and overflowing, it never remains still for even a moment. Observing phenomena through this lens, where could one go without falling into error?
It is like facing a gushing spring and demanding that it maintain its original state; such a thing has never occurred.
The arising of perverted perceptions is rooted in instability—is not this the very point of the teaching? All phenomena arise from the convergence of manifold conditions.
The body is formed. When conditions have not yet met, phenomena have no locus; having no locus, there is no abiding; having no abiding, there are no phenomena.

Because taking the absence of phenomena as the fundamental, one is able to establish all phenomena. If one takes the movement of the mind as the fundamental, then the characteristics of existence arise;
this principle reaches its limit at the initial movement, beyond which there is no further foundation. If one takes the absence of phenomena as the fundamental, then...

There is arising because there are causes; there is no non-arising without causes. Thus, there is nothing further that serves as a fundamental basis. Because there is no abiding, there is perverted perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).
Because of perverted perception, there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Because of conceptual discrimination, there is craving (*rāga*). Because of craving, there is the body (*ātmabhāva*).

Once there is a body, then good and evil are presented together. Once good and evil are presented, then all phenomena (*dharmas*) arise. From this point onward, the enumeration of terms [is as follows].
It cannot be fully exhausted. If one properly grasps its fundamental source, then the multitude [of afflictions] cannot be eliminated.
Daoping said: "There is delusion without abiding; there is truth without abiding. The current text specifically speaks of delusive dharmas, taking non-abiding as their fundamental source.
Master Sengzhao has explained this in detail. As for true non-abiding, it is like the Prajñāpāramitā, which, by means of non-abiding...

This is established as the primary tenet. Taking the *prajñā* of ultimate reality (*dharmatā*) as the principle and the *prajñā* of contemplative observation as the practice—namely, abiding in the *prajñā-pāramitā* by means of the dharma of non-abiding—the *Vajracchedikā* states: "One should generate the mind without abiding anywhere.
All of these clarify this meaning. One should know that the *prajñā* of ultimate reality is the essence of the unchanging *tathatā*; although...
Unchanging yet following conditions: this means that all the myriad phenomena of the world arise entirely from True Suchness (tathatā).
It is unchanging while following conditions, and it follows conditions while remaining unchanging. Based upon the ground of non-abiding, all dharmas are established.
This, moreover, is the external purport of this sutra.
○ Second, a comprehensive clarification of other meanings, in two parts. First, the manifestation of the heavenly maiden, in five sections. First, her manifestation and the scattering of flowers.
At that time, in the room of Vimalakīrti, there was a celestial maiden who, seeing the devas and humans and hearing the Dharma being preached,
manifested her form and immediately scattered celestial flowers over the bodhisattvas and great disciples.
Master Zhao said: "The heavenly maiden is a Mahāsattva of the Dharma-body who constantly propagates the inconceivable Way of the Mahāyāna together with Vimalakīrti.

Therefore, she manifested as a household deity and shared his room; seeing the great assembly gather and hearing the Dharma being preached, she manifested her form and scattered flowers, desiring thereby to provoke a discussion."
Second, as for whether the flowers adhered or did not adhere:
when the flowers reached the various Bodhisattvas, they all fell away; but when they reached the Great Disciples, they adhered and did not fall.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The heavens used this unprecedented chamber to show that this chamber contains no mixed teachings, and therefore disparages and deprecates the Hinayana."

This is to manifest the Great Way; thus, we act as mutual echoes and shadows to illuminate its supreme significance. Dēng said: "The heavenly maiden’s desire to manifest the Great Teaching is precisely this.
As for disparaging and deprecating the Hīnayāna, how could that be her intention?

One must know that there are two causes and conditions for the basis of such disparagement of the Hīnayāna: first, because their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, they remain attached to the "flowers" [of illusory phenomena].

As for the body: first, one attempts to remove the flowers by means of supernatural power, yet they cannot be made to depart. Once the flowers have already adhered to the body, this is the first affliction.
To then command them to depart is the affliction of afflictions. The initial affliction is the affliction of inherent existence.
Later, he fell ill; this was an illness caused by his previous illness. These two ailments weighed upon his mind, which led to his passing away.
○ Third, regarding the disciples removing the flowers:
all the disciples, even with their supernatural powers, were unable to remove them.
Master Zhao said: "In order to distinguish between the Great and the Small [vehicles], he caused the flowers to appear thus.

When the gods asked why, at that time they questioned Śāriputra: "For what reason have you removed these flowers? He replied: "These flowers are not in accordance with the Dharma; for this reason [I have removed them]."
Discard them.
To have incense and flowers clinging to one's body is already contrary to the dharma of a śrāmaṇera, let alone that of a bhikṣu. For this reason, discard them.
○ Fifth: The Five Heavenly Maidens Preach the Dharma. First, it is shown that wearing flowers constitutes a distinction from what is not in accordance with the dharma.
The deva said: "Do not say that these flowers are improper. Why is this? These flowers have no discrimination.
Being insentient, they possess no discrimination between what is proper and what is improper."
2. To show that because the Venerable One generates conceptual discrimination himself, he does not act in accordance with the Dharma:
"The Venerable One merely generates conceptual notions himself.
There are two meanings of conceptual discrimination: first, when an ordinary person discriminates by taking sense objects as conditions, they fall into existence; second, [when one discriminates]..."
To discriminate based on conditions and emptiness is to fall into non-existence;

ordinary beings discriminate and fall into existence, regarding flowers as being in accordance with the Dharma, using them for pleasure and enjoyment, and using them for clothing and adornment—thereby perpetuating birth and death.

Those of the Two Vehicles discriminate and fall into non-existence, regarding flowers as not being in accordance with the Dharma, viewing them with revulsion, and employing supernatural powers [to destroy them].
And thus one departs from it. That which accomplishes nirvana is entirely due to the arising of one's own discrimination; what has this to do with flowers?
Third, [the Buddha] shows that if there is no such discrimination, then one is in accordance with the Dharma.

If one who has gone forth in the Buddha-dharma engages in conceptual discrimination, it is contrary to the Dharma; if there is no conceptual discrimination, it is in accordance with the Dharma. Regarding what is "in accordance with the Dharma through the absence of conceptual discrimination":
first, one does not take objects as conditions for discrimination that falls into existence; second, [one does not take objects as conditions for discrimination that falls into non-existence].
Not conceptualizing based on emptiness, one does not fall into non-existence; this is precisely like the reality of the Middle Way.
[This] fourth point establishes that all Bodhisattvas do not cling [to these views] as proof.
As for observing that no flowers adhere to the various bodhisattvas, it is because they have already severed all conceptual discriminations (*vikalpa-saṃjñā*).
The term "all" (*sarva*), as previously explained, encompasses two types of meaning.
2. Because the five fingers fear birth and death, the five desires find their opportunity. First, the analogy:
It is like when a person is afraid, a non-human being finds their opportunity.
Master Shi said: "It is as if there were a rākṣasa who transformed his form into that of a horse; a certain man mounted it without suspicion."
The horse of the Middle Way asked the man, "Is this horse good? The man drew his sword and showed it to him. The horse asked, "Is this sword good?
The rākṣasa, knowing that the man’s mind was upright and fearless, did not dare to harm him at all.
II. Correlating with the Dharma.
Thus, because this disciple fears birth and death, form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch gain the advantage over him. For one who has already abandoned fear, all five desires are powerless.
While the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted, the flowers merely cling to the body; once the habitual tendencies are exhausted, they do not.
This means that the flower does not adhere.
Within the realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), there are two kinds of illnesses: first, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); second, birth and death itself.

As for "habitual tendencies," this is a general term for afflictions such as views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā-kleśa*); it does not refer to specific fetters (*saṃyojana*) practiced in past lives that one is currently unable to forget. For example:

When Kāśyapa heard the lute, he rose in agitation and began to dance. This refers generally to the fetters of afflictions and habitual tendencies existing outside the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
To claim that Kāśyapa once served in the musical department is a distorted and exaggerated fabrication. How base such a statement is! People today are ignorant of the meaning of the teachings.

Most cases are like this: habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) serve as the cause, and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) serves as the effect. Furthermore, there are two types: first, birth-and-death through habitual tendencies within the realms;

second, birth-and-death through habitual tendencies outside the realms. Within the realms, the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *vicikitsā-kleśa*) constitute the habitual tendencies, while the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-ātmabhāva*) constitutes the result.
Outside the realms, the "dust-sands" of ignorance (*avidyā*) constitute the habitual tendencies, while [the birth-and-death of] transformation...
Birth and death are easily undergone. Regarding these two dharmas, the practitioners of the Three Vehicles differ in their fear and attainment.
For those of the Two Vehicles, birth-and-death with distinct segments (*bhavasaṃdhi*) is like a prison;
although they find no opportunity for the five desires within the realm, they readily find opportunity for the pure and wondrous five desires outside the realm. Nevertheless, they still fear birth.
The "dead" refers to the mind of the Two Vehicles that has realized *nirvāṇa*.

Not realizing that such *nirvāṇa* is precisely the residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*) outside the [true] realm, how could it not be a state of fearing birth and death? This is precisely the cause that allows the five desires to gain the upper hand.
By analogy, just as ordinary beings do not fear birth and death, they likewise allow the five desires within the realm to gain the upper hand, just like ordinary people today.

Those who fear birth and death yet remain greedily attached to the five desires are such people. Therefore it is said: "As long as the habitual tendencies of the fetters are not exhausted, the flowers will cling to the body;
when the habitual tendencies of the fetters are exhausted, the flowers do not cling."

Regarding "contemplative understanding": within a single mind, the *prathama-artha* (ultimate) heaven manifests; this is the entirety of nature giving rise to cultivation, which is like the heavenly maidens scattering flowers.
If one contemplates this mind, although it is identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is not identical to the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).

When the flowers touch the body, they are identical to emptiness, identical to the conventional, and identical to the middle (*madhyamā*). Not only do the flowers within the realm of desire not adhere, but even the two kinds [of flowers] outside the realm do not adhere.
The flowers do not even cling to her body, for she is able to thoroughly understand the characteristics of both cultivation and non-cultivation.
II. Question and Answer Based on the Occasion (in two parts). A. The Goddess Manifests Her Eloquence (in six parts). 1.

Poison. Yet, the more one desires it, the purer it becomes; the more one kills, the more compassionate one is; the more perverse one is, the more upright one becomes. This is the supreme Dharma of the sages.

Folly. One should not dwell with it either. These are clear and manifest words of principle;

Is eloquence indeed like this? II.
The Two Goddesses Answer that There is Neither Attainment nor Realization. First, establishing the principle:
The goddesses said, "We have neither attainment nor realization; therefore, our eloquence is such as this."

"It is not realized. From this, eloquence arises; therefore, there is nothing that is not eloquently explained.

Why is this so? If there were anyone who had attained or realized [anything], they would be considered one of overweening pride regarding the Buddha-dharma.

The Way is fundamentally natural; originally there is nothing to be attained. To claim that there is something to be attained is not in accord with the Great Way—is this not the arrogance of overestimation (*adhimāna*)?

As for those who practice through contemplative understanding, if they merely contemplate this mind as empty, signless, and effortless, they will attain it immediately upon departing from verbal expression. However, to engage in...

While being identical to verbal expression, it is fundamentally without verbal expression;
thus, one speaks of liberation through very words themselves. Even when contemplating a single thought-moment, all dharmas, and even the three poisons, they are all Bodhi.

[Section 31: Questions and Answers Clarifying What Each of the Three Vehicles Aims to Seek. Part 1: Śāriputra’s Question.

Third, demonstrating the capacity for the Mahāyāna:

The Dharma of the Five Constant Virtues. In this chamber, the music of the Dharma is constantly performed;

in this room are Śākyamuni Buddha, Amitābha Buddha, Akṣobhya Buddha, Ratnaguṇa, Ratnārcis, and Ratnacandra.

Ratnavyūha, Durjayā, Siṃhaghoṣa, Sarvārthasiddha, and other such immeasurable Buddhas of the ten directions—when this superior person brings them to mind, they all immediately come and extensively expound the secret and essential Dharma-treasures of the Buddhas;
having finished speaking, they depart. This is the seventh unprecedented and rare dharma.

This is the eighth unprecedented and rare dharma.
These eight kinds of sublime merits, when read again, are not without their symbolic significance.

The first two represent the essence of the Land of Constant Quiescent Light (*nitya-śānta-prabhāsa-kṣetra*): the golden light represents illumination within the essence; "not being defiled by afflictions" represents quiescence within the essence.
The latter six represent the function of the Land of Constant Quiescent Light: the arrival of the Mahāyāna assembly represents the capacity of that function.

He gathers the assembly. He constantly expounds the Six Perfections. He preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings. He perpetually performs the music of the Dharma, enabling them to cultivate and attain the fruit of eternal bliss.
His jewel-treasury provides universal relief; his mind that gathers all things is impartial. The teachings of all Buddhas reach him to their ultimate conclusion.
He manifests various pure lands so that the multitude may have a refuge. Through these manifestations throughout his career, his essence is all-pervasive.
This is sufficient.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: observe how the sense organs and their objects correspond; when a single thought-moment arises, it necessarily belongs to one realm, whether mundane or supramundane.

These ten realms, when fully understood, are none other than emptiness, the provisional, and the middle—solely the One Buddha Vehicle, with no other vehicles.
This is precisely the pursuit of the Buddha Vehicle alone, like entering a campaka grove and smelling no other fragrance.

In this way, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, one hears only the Buddha-Dharma, fully possessing the great essence and great function, wherein stillness and illumination are fused as one; this is also what is meant by "twelve years."
The eight [qualities] within are marvelous and rare dharmas. III. Conclusion:
Śāriputra, these eight marvelous and rare dharmas are constantly manifested in this room. Who would see this and not [be moved]?

Section Four: One Question and Answer Clarifying that All Dharmas Lack Fixed Characteristics (in four parts). First:
Śāriputra asks why the goddess does not transform her female body into a male.
Śāriputra said, "Why do you not transform this female body?

It has already been twelve years, yet the heavenly maidens have served as attendants for this same length of time.

It is not that for all these years he has constantly sought the appearance of a woman; rather, because what is difficult to find in the present, he turned back and sought it in the past, yet truly found nothing at all.
Someone asked: "Regarding the two characteristics of male and female, which is truly superior and which inferior? He replied: "The teaching of the Tathāgata generally consists of two schools.

Which is superior? Second is the School of the Destruction of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-vināśa*). Briefly, it is as the heavenly maiden answered in this sutra:
fundamentally, there are no characteristics of male or female; who then can distinguish between superiority and inferiority?

Such discussions are all conducted because the Tathāgata manifested birth within the desire realm and, in accordance with worldly conventions, distinguished between male and female. One must know that within the Buddha-way, these do not fundamentally exist.

In the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī), one is born through transformation within a lotus flower rather than entering a womb; all people possess the marks of excellence.

One should know that the distinction between male and female forms exists merely to conform to the vulgar and defiled beings for the sake of teaching them. In the World of Ultimate Bliss, however, there is neither the negation nor the establishment of such distinctions.

6. To demonstrate that all dharmas neither exist nor do not exist, the Deva said:

That which neither exists nor does not exist is the natural principle of all phenomena (*dharmas*). Though the Dharma resides within people, they do not realize it through awakening.
In this world, there are those of brilliant intelligence and profound wisdom who have expanded [this principle] into a marvelous tale:

by means of eight individuals, they suddenly transform into hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of people—noble and base, rich and poor, male and female, master and servant, virtuous and wicked.

To be a man: alert and tranquil. This does not hinder a man from transforming into a woman.

It is thus. There is neither death nor birth.
This is the contemplative understanding: contemplating that all phenomena are the mind, eternally abiding in wondrous clarity, immovable and all-pervading;
fundamentally without arising or ceasing, and likewise without coming or going. This is what is meant by "neither death nor birth."
61. Question and Answer Clarifying that the Great Way is Unattainable (9). First, Śāriputra asks after how long he shall attain the Great Way.
Śāriputra asks the goddess: "After how long will you attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?"
Śāriputra’s question was intended to ask: although the goddess possesses wondrous eloquence and supernormal powers, she still dwells in the causal stage of a bodhisattva;
since a cause must inevitably yield its fruit, he did not yet know how long it would take, and therefore he questioned her.
The second heavenly maiden replied, "If you return to being an ordinary person, I shall attain the Way.
The deity said, "If Śāriputra returns to being an ordinary person, I shall then realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The three sons of Śāriputra replied, "It is unreasonable for me to return to being an ordinary person.
Śāriputra said, "It is impossible for me to become an ordinary person."
The four heavenly maidens replied, "Our attainment of the fruits of the path is also like this.
The deva said, "That I could attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is likewise impossible. Why is this?
Because *bodhi* has no place of abiding; therefore, there is no one who attains it."
Generally, among worldly things, there must first be characteristics for there to be a place of abiding; and only when there is a place of abiding can there be something obtained.
Since bodhi is without characteristics, how could it have a place of abiding? How then can it be said to be obtainable?
○ Fifth, Śāriputra asked about the realization of the Way by all Buddhas:
"Śāriputra said: 'Regarding all the Buddhas of the present who have attained, or will attain, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—what is meant by this?'"
The six goddesses replied, "In conventional terminology, there are past, future, and present.
The goddess said, "It is because they are reckoned by means of conventional terminology that one speaks of the three periods of time; it does not mean that bodhi has past, future, or present."
The Buddha-dharma has two aspects. First is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is precisely bodhi;

it is vertically exhaustive and horizontally pervasive, incapable of being altered by the three periods of time. Second is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which consists of all phenomena (*dharma*).

Ordinary beings, with their conventional eyes, perceive coming and going. The Buddha, in accordance with ordinary beings, manifests the attainment of the Way; therefore, there are the past, future, and present.
