8. Śāriputra replied: "One attains by means of non-attainment;
it is because there is nothing to be attained that one attains. 9.
The goddess replied: "The same is true for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
The Deva said: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are also like this. They attain through non-attainment;
by means of the small they realize the great, yet there is no attainment to be known.
Regarding contemplative understanding: contemplate a single moment of mind, which is the eternally abiding true mind. Because it is identical with emptiness, it resides in non-attainment.

Because it is precisely the provisional, it is also said to be "attainable. When emptiness and the provisional are mutually identical, there is attainment through non-attainment, and non-attainment within attainment.
○ Second, Vimalakīrti praises his merit.
At that time, Vimalakīrti said to Śāriputra, "This goddess has already made offerings to ninety-two billion buddhas.

She is able to sport with the supernormal powers of a bodhisattva; her vows are fulfilled, she has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and dwells in the stage of non-retrogression.
By virtue of her original vow, she can manifest herself at will to teach and transform sentient beings."
The stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is specifically located in the First Ground (*bhūmi*), while its perfection is attained in the First Dwelling (*vihāra*).

These three types of non-retrogression constitute "non-retrogression through mindfulness. Considering the structural flow of this chapter’s text, it cannot be subsumed under the *Parivarta on Contemplating Sentient Beings*;

rather, it should be established as the *Parivarta on the Questions and Answers of the Heavenly Maiden*, beginning from the point where the heavenly maiden scatters flowers. Indeed, such is the nature of the chapters of this sutra.
Furthermore, as for the translator An, it is not even known whether he has lost the sequence of the meaning. I have humbly examined the dialogue between the heavenly maidens;

its phrasing is vast and expansive, while its principles are subtle and profound. Among these, there are three general points revealed: first, to manifest the subtle and wondrous realization attained by Vimalakīrti;
second, to manifest the deep and mysterious state in which he dwells in his room; and third, to manifest the eloquence of his realized realization.

The Unobstructed Eloquence (Pratibhāna-asaṅga) is, in its entirety, the orthodox core of this sutra that critiques the partial and disparages the small, while extolling the Great and praising the Perfect.

Part Eight: Explaining the Chapter on the Buddha-Way, Section Two. First, explaining the chapter title:
*The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Eight: "The Buddha-Way."
The Buddha-way (*buddhamārga*) is the ultimate Great Way of Bodhi realized at the fruit-stage of all Buddhas;
it is the wondrous enlightenment in which the three delusions are utterly exhausted and the two deaths are forever forgotten. When Mañjuśrī asks below, "How does one penetrate the Buddha-way?
he is specifically asking what the causes of this way are and how one should cultivate them so as to achieve such penetration.
II. Explanation of the Scriptural Text, in three parts. First, clarifying how one penetrates the Buddha-way. 2. First, Mañjuśrī’s question:
At that time, Mañjuśrī addressed Vimalakīrti, saying, "How does a bodhisattva penetrate the Buddha-way?"
Master Zhao said: "Regarding the Way of the Buddhas as described above, it takes non-attainment as attainment. This Way is void and profound;
it is not something that can be traversed by ordinary conduct. There must be a means by which it is traversed; therefore, I ask about it."
II. Vimalakīrti’s Response (in two parts). First, the general response:
Vimalakīrti said, "If a bodhisattva practices what is not the path, this constitutes the thorough penetration of the Buddha-way."
There are non-Buddha paths and there is the Buddha path. As for the non-Buddha paths, these are the paths of the nine dharma realms.
By means of the ten evil paths, one reaches the paths of the three miserable realms; by means of the ten good paths, one reaches the paths of the three happy realms.
By means of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, one thoroughly penetrates the path of the Two Vehicles;
by means of the Six Perfections and the myriad practices, one thoroughly penetrates the path of the Bodhisattvas. These are all cases of penetrating the non-path by means of the non-path.
If one follows such scriptures as the *Three Minds and Nine Practices*, the *Dharmapada* adorned by the power of concentration and wisdom,
the *Avataṃsaka* where the single mind and the dharma-realm are like space, the *Śūraṅgama* as the locus of correct practice, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* with its great dhāraṇī—
these are those who attain the Buddha-way through the Buddha-way. Both of these types constitute the sūtras.

The Way of the Constant: For those of initial resolve in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, to turn their backs on what is non-true and cultivate what is true, and to accord with the sutras while practicing the constant—this is the unchanging Way of the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Thus, if one now practices through the non-way to penetrate the Buddha-way, although the words seem contrary, the principle is in fact correct; although the traces seem inverse, the fundamental essence is eternally compliant. It is like...
It is said that by practicing the five acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya) without malice or anger, one reaches the hells free from all defilements of sin;
how much more so for a path that is not non-Buddhist? Yet, this path was also adopted out of necessity.
If one attains its cessation, then by being single-mindedly devoted to this path, one will penetrate the Buddha-way. Why must one necessarily contravene the scriptures and go against [the teachings]?
Is it not so? Did we not say previously: "The trampling of dragons and elephants is not something a donkey can endure; how could those who are vulgar, base, and inferior hope for this?

As for those whose initial resolve involves practice that is not the Way yet leads to the penetration of the Buddha-way, there is furthermore the chapter on Vimalakīrti’s inquiry, wherein the sixty-two views are said to be the seeds of the Tathāgata—this constitutes contemplating what is not the Way.
To penetrate the Buddha-way, one must distinguish between ore and dross and refined gold. [This concludes the first section. Part Two:
A Specific Response, which has two parts. First: the question regarding practicing on what is not the Way.
He asked again: "How does a bodhisattva practice what is not the Way?
[The answer] consists of sixteen points on practicing what is not the Way. First, three are shown by way of the retributive fruits of the three evil realms;
first, the path of hell.
The answer is: If a bodhisattva commits the five acts of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) yet remains free from malice and anger, they will enter hell without the defilements of sin.
Master Zhao said: "The five heinous crimes necessarily arise from malice and anger; once these sins are committed, one will inevitably enter hell upon casting off the body."
He undergoes suffering without interruption. Although the Bodhisattva manifests the performance of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), he is free from affliction and anger.
This is because he does not regard these crimes as crimes; thus, he is able to "conform" to them. If one regarded these crimes as crimes, who would dare to conform to them?
Furthermore, it is said that the ground of sinful defilement is the cause of hell. He manifests the receiving of its retribution, yet in reality, there is no such cause.
II. The Realm of Animals.
Regarding those who fall into the animal realm, they lack such faults as ignorance (*avidyā*) and arrogance (*māna*).
Master Zhao said: "When delusion and arrogance predominate, one mostly falls into the animal realm."
Third is the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
As for these hungry ghosts, they may nonetheless be fully endowed with merit.

Master Zao said: "Those who are stingy and greedy lack blessings and frequently fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. Master Deng said: "Even those who have committed the five deeds of immediate retribution..."
From the hells, through the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, they practice what is not the Way.
Yet, being free from the defilement of anger and affliction, and devoid of ignorance and pride, they possess the merit of the "jeweled hand"—this is the Buddha-way.
These are all those who, by means of the ten unwholesome paths, have attained penetration into the Buddha-way.
Second, the demonstration concerning the realms of form and formlessness:
Practicing the paths of the realms of form and formlessness, they do not regard them as supreme.

Ordinary beings, failing to understand this, are born into the realms of form and formlessness; relying on the extreme excellence of their karmic retribution, even though they are now shown to have been born there [for a purpose], they remain deluded.

Transforming [beings] to be identical with the heavens, he does not initially regard this as superior; this is because practicing the ten wholesome deeds and mundane dhyāna is not the Way, yet it leads to the penetration of the Buddha-way.
○ Third, showing by way of the causes of the three evil realms.
They manifest the practice of desire, yet remain free from all defiled attachments; they manifest the practice of anger, yet harbor no resentment or obstruction toward sentient beings;
they manifest the practice of delusion, yet subdue their minds with wisdom.

The preceding section clarified this by demonstrating the retribution for practicing the three evil paths, such as when Devadatta manifested the commission of the five heinous crimes and fell into hell while still in his physical body.
The Buddha then dispatched his own younger brother, Ānanda, to the prison to inquire after him, asking, "Is your elder brother suffering now?

He replied, "I am in hell, yet it is as if I were experiencing the bliss of the third dhyāna. This demonstrates that although he was actually performing the five acts of immediate retribution, he remained free from affliction.
This refers to anger (*dveṣa*). The current practice of the causes for the three miserable realms is similar in its textual structure; thus, the meaning is not considered redundant.
○ Fourth, showing by way of the six obscurations (*ṣaḍ-āvaraṇa*):

it shows the practice of stinginess and greed, yet one relinquishes all internal and external possessions without sparing even one's own body or life; it shows the practice of violating the precepts, yet one remains...
Abiding in pure precepts, they feel great dread even toward minor transgressions; they manifest anger, yet are always compassionate and patient;
they manifest laziness, yet diligently cultivate merit; they manifest distracted thoughts, yet are constantly mindful of meditative concentration; they manifest ignorance.

While they have thoroughly mastered mundane and supramundane wisdom, they manifest the practice of the six obscurations, thereby appearing to walk upon non-paths; yet they do not deviate from the six perfections, thereby attaining thorough mastery of the Buddha-way.
5. An exposition based on flattery (*śāṭhya*) and arrogance (*mada*).
This demonstrates the practice of flattery and hypocrisy; yet, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one follows the meaning of the sūtras.

Flattery and hypocrisy represent the heterodox path, whereas the meaning of the sūtras represents the orthodox path. Although one outwardly displays the practice of the heterodox, the mind follows the orthodox. Orthodox.
Therefore, one is able to penetrate and realize the Buddha-way.
(6) Sixth, showing by way of pride:
although manifesting the practice of pride, toward sentient beings one remains like a bridge.

He manifests the practice of arrogance, yet his outward appearance may seem as lofty as a high mountain; however, in his humility and radiance while delivering sentient beings, he is as lowly as a bridge.
Thus it is said that when a Bodhisattva blends with the light and accords with the dust of the world to benefit others and assist all things, it is like this.
○ Seventh, it is shown by way of the various afflictions (*kleśa*).
Although one manifests the practice of various afflictions, the mind is always pure.
That the mind is defiled by afflictions is not the Way. Because the mind is always pure, one is able to penetrate the Buddha-way.
8. Exposition by way of the demonic path (*māra-mārga*).
This demonstrates entering the demonic path while yet conforming to the Buddha’s wisdom and not following the teachings of others.

The demonic path is characterized by delusion because it follows the teachings of others; thus, it runs contrary to the principle that accords with the Buddha’s wisdom. Now, regarding the Bodhisattva:
Although he manifests entry into the heterodox paths of Māra, in reality he accords with the Buddha’s wisdom and penetrates the Buddha-way.
[Section Nine: Manifestation in Terms of the Two Vehicles] He manifests entry among the Śrāvakas, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma they have not previously heard.
The śrāvaka can only understand for himself by hearing the sound of the Four Noble Truths preached by the Buddha;

he cannot cause all beings to hear it through the sound of the Buddha-way. Now, the bodhisattva’s outward trace is the same while his fundamental essence is different; therefore, he is able to attain thorough penetration herein.
○ Tenth, it is shown by way of the pratyekabuddha.
It shows entering the state of a pratyekabuddha while yet accomplishing great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) to transform sentient beings.
The śrāvaka is like a wild sheep leaping alone, not looking back at the herd; the pratyekabuddha is like a deer in a village—how could he truly possess compassion?
In this regard, although one may say that a śrāvaka possesses compassion, it does not yet constitute the compassion of a bodhisattva.
Now, although a bodhisattva manifests the minor compassion of a pratyekabuddha, they actually accomplish the great compassion of a bodhisattva;
therefore, they are able to penetrate the path of the Buddha.
Eleventh, it is shown by way of entering into poverty and lowliness:
though he enters into poverty, he possesses the merit of an inexhaustible jewel-hand; though he enters into physical deformity, he is adorned with all the primary and secondary marks;
though he enters into low birth, he is born into the lineage of the Buddhas and is endowed with all virtues. Thus it is shown.
He enters into the state of being weak, inferior, and ugly, yet attains a body like that of Nārāyaṇa, which all sentient beings delight to behold;
he manifests the onset of old age and illness, yet has forever severed the root of disease and transcended the fear of death.
Those who are impoverished, physically impaired, or of low station are not on the Way; yet those who possess the merit of the "jeweled hand" and so forth are on the Buddha-way.
Their outward conduct may not be the Way, but their fundamental nature penetrates the Buddha-way. Thus, the merits of a bodhisattva are truly inconceivable.
Twelfth, it is shown by way of the necessities of life and retinue:

though he displays the possession of such necessities, he constantly contemplates their impermanence and truly has nothing for which he craves; though he displays the presence of wives, concubines, and female attendants, he always delights in remaining far removed from the mire of the five desires.
13. Regarding the demonstration of dullness:
although he manifests as dull-witted, he achieves eloquence and possesses perfect retention (*dhāraṇī*) without loss.
Master Kumārajīva said, "He may be compared to Prince Mūrdhaja."
14. Showing the Demonstration of the False Ferry:
This demonstrates entering the false ferry while using the true ferry to deliver all sentient beings.
Master Zhaolun said: "A place where a river or ford can be crossed is called a 'true ferry'; a place of peril, difficulty, and deception is called a 'false ferry. The Buddha..."
The Way is called the "Right Crossing," while external paths are called the "Deviant Crossing.
Fifteenth, showing the manifestation of entering all paths universally, thereby severing their causal conditions.
Sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms because they are bound by the twelve links of dependent origination.
The Bodhisattva has already severed these causal links, yet manifests entry into them; it is for this reason that he is able to penetrate the Buddha-way.
16. Explained in terms of parinirvāṇa:
To manifest in nirvāṇa while not severing birth-and-death;
sentient beings turn their backs on nirvāṇa and follow birth-and-death, while those of the two vehicles turn their backs on birth-and-death and follow nirvāṇa. Bodhi...
In this, the Bodhisattva is neither partial nor biased; he abides in the Middle Way.

He does not sever birth and death, and is thus able to enter the six realms of existence to transform and deliver beings according to their forms. He manifests nirvana, just as a lotus flower emerges from the water, remaining free from the mud.
III. Conclusion.
Mañjuśrī, when a bodhisattva is able to practice in this way upon what is not the Path, this is called penetrating the Buddha-path.

According to the teaching, these are all bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages of the Distinct and Perfect [teachings] who are able to practice this; they do not enter the Tripitaka or Shared [teachings].
This is the hand of the Bodhisattva.
As for the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that a single thought-moment is fully endowed with the ten realms; the Buddha-realm is inherently present within it, perfect and pure.
This is itself the Buddha-way. When the minds of the nine realms manifest, they are all termed "non-ways.
The practitioner does not reject these non-ways to separately contemplate the Buddha-way;

rather, they realize that the minds of the nine realms are nothing other than cultivated evil (*shūaku*), and that this cultivated evil is entirely the water of the Dharma-realm forming the waves of the nine dharmas. To be able to contemplate cultivated evil in this manner is itself...
Inherent evil. When inherent evil is interfused, there is no dharma that does not flow toward it;

it spontaneously encompasses the inherent goodness of the Buddha-realm, just as waves are entirely water and there is no water apart from waves. This is what is meant by "observing the mind to practice on non-paths and thereby penetrating the Buddha-path."
II. Explaining what constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata. First, Vimalakīrti’s question:
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī, "What is the lineage of the Tathāgata?"
Someone asked: "The previous inquiry concerned the Buddha-way, while the present inquiry concerns the lineage of the Tathāgata.

How do these two compare in terms of their similarities and differences? I replied: "They are the same yet not the same; they are different yet the same. "Why are they the same? Because the Buddha is the Tathāgata, and the Tathāgata is the Buddha.

How could there be two distinct entities? Therefore, they are the same. Why are they different? Because the gates of cultivation and nature, as well as cause and effect, are each distinct. Therefore, they are different."
For the Buddha-way belongs to the fruit, whereas the Bodhisattva practices within non-ways; thus, the cause can lead to the realization of the fruit.

Now, the "lineage of the Tathāgata" is discussed here in terms of the causal stage of sentient beings—this is the first point of difference. Furthermore, was it not the case that the previous answer discussed cultivation while the present answer speaks of nature?
This is the second point of difference. Therefore, it is said that they are the same yet different. As for saying they are different yet the same:
The previous answer—that a bodhisattva practices on non-paths and thereby penetrates the Buddha-path—concerns entirely matters within the dharma-gate of the inherent evil of nature (*prakṛti-pāpa*).
People know only that a bodhisattva can practice on non-paths and penetrate the Buddha-path, but they do not know that this dharma-gate has its origin in a fundamental source.
This was precisely what Mañjuśrī answered: the sixty-two views and all afflictions...
Afflictions are all seeds of the Buddha; because they are thus, even that which is not the Way is all seeds of the Buddha.
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas realize this Dharma-gate within its fruition, they transform and guide according to the capacities of beings and act in accordance with their true nature.
Thus, they do not contradict the Buddha-way, but are able to penetrate and master it. Hence it is said: "They are different, yet they are the same. Therefore...
In my treatise, *On the Innate Goodness and Evil of Nature*, I clarify the dharma-gate of the innate evil of nature by means of the six identities; this is precisely its core purpose.
II. Wenshu’s Response has two parts. First, clarifying the seeds by means of the conditioned has two parts. First, elucidating the seeds through the successive dharmas has five parts.
At the outset, it is indicated in general that the path of suffering is itself the Dharmakāya.
Mañjuśrī said: "The body serves as the seed.
The body is the path of suffering, because where there is a body, there is suffering. When one is deluded regarding this, the Dharmakāya becomes the path of suffering.

To realize this, the path of suffering is itself the Dharma-body; therefore, it constitutes the lineage of the Tathāgata. This indicates that the Buddha-nature as the correct cause serves as the seed.
(1) Second, the path of delusion is itself Prajñā.
Ignorance and craving are their seeds; greed, hatred, and delusion are their seeds; the four inversions are their seeds; and the five hindrances are their seeds.
These four categories of phenomena are all subsumed within the path of affliction. When one is deluded by them, one takes that which is wisdom and clarity to be the darkness of ignorance.
To awaken to this is to take very delusion and darkness as wisdom and illumination; thus, one becomes a seed of the Tathāgata.
This refers to the Buddha-nature as the "cause of realization" (yōin) being taken as the seed.
○ The third layer indicates that the path of suffering is itself the Dharma-body.
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) constitute the seeds.
As it was previously stated that the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind are all the Pure Land, the six sense bases are therefore all seeds.
This also refers specifically to the primary causes as being the seeds.
The four heavy fetters are the delusions of the path, which are none other than Prajñā.
The seven stations of consciousness serve as seeds; the eight wrong paths serve as seeds; the nine bases of affliction serve as seeds.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Within the first dhyāna, excluding the Brahmā King at the beginning of the kalpa and the various minor Brahmās of the kalpa's inception, from that point onward..."
These are combined into a single station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). At the beginning of the kalpa, there was only the Brahmā King; no other Brahmās yet existed.

The Brahmā King thought of desiring other Brahmās to exist, and at that time, other Brahmās encountered the conditions for birth. Consequently, the Brahmā King gave rise to a false view, claiming that he himself had created them.

The other Brahmās also claimed for themselves that they were born from the Brahmā King. Although there were differences in their refinement or coarseness, their false conceptions were not [different].
This is called "different bodies with one perception," the second station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).

In the second dhyāna, there is no superiority or inferiority in form, yet the mind possesses various [states], including the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and diverse thoughts. This is called "one form with different perceptions," the third station of consciousness.
In the third dhyāna, there is no coarseness or refinement in form, and the mind is free from diverse perceptions; this is what is meant by "one bliss."

Perception (*saṃjñā*). This is the fourth station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*). Together with the first three stages of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), these are called the seven stations of consciousness.
"Station" means that consciousness attains a state of secure dwelling; its mindfulness is clear and distinct, free from affliction or distress, and indestructible—this is what is meant by "dwelling.

In the miserable destinies (*apāya*), one is destroyed by suffering and pain; in the four dhyānas, one is destroyed by non-perception (*asaṃjñā*); and in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), one is destroyed by the extinction of perception.

It is destroyed. Furthermore, because the mental images (*saṃjñā*) and thoughts (*citta*) of that stage are faint and indistinct, and mindfulness (*smṛti*) is not clear, consciousness does not abide securely there.

Question: The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is also destroyed by the miserable destinies (*apāya*); why, then, is it established as a station of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*)? Answer: It is because one grasps the destruction of the stage [itself].

The realms do not perish through non-appropriation. The evil destinies and the auspicious destinies of the desire realm differ in their courses and vary in their levels; suffering and pleasure lead to distinct outcomes, and thus their meanings do not intersect.
Therefore, they do not perish one another. The Lamp says: Although the seven consciousnesses abide, as long as the afflictions have not been destroyed, they all constitute the path of affliction.
Since affliction is itself bodhi, they serve as the seeds of the Tathāgata. The eight heterodoxies are explained according to the usual teachings.
These also belong to the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*). Regarding the nine bases of resentment (*navāghāta-vastūni*), Master Kumārajīva said:

"To love my enemies, to hate my friends, and to resent my own person—these constitute three in one lifetime; across the three periods of time, they become nine. Furthermore, another interpretation states that the nine fetters (*nava-saṃyojana*) are also subsumed within the path of afflictions.
The five paths of action of the fingers are themselves liberation;
the ten unwholesome paths serve as their seeds.
These ten unwholesome acts are the paths of evil karma. To be deluded by them is to be bound in fetters, yet to awaken to them is liberation.
To be liberated from the fetters is thus to become the seed of the Tathāgata; this refers to taking the *pratyaya-buddha-dhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the conditional cause) as the seed.
II. Citing the essentials to clarify the seed.
To state it briefly: the sixty-two views and all afflictions are the seeds of the Buddha.
These sixty-two views and all afflictions are subsumed within the deluded path.

What Mañjuśrī has shown as the seed of the Tathāgata does not, in total, go beyond the three paths—that is, the three Buddha-natures. Furthermore, the three paths he describes do not, in turn, go beyond...
The twelve links of dependent origination throughout the three periods of time encompass all phenomena; these are, in essence, the nature of the three virtues.

Because sentient beings have been deluded since beginningless time, they perceive them as the defilement of the three paths. Furthermore, this defilement of the three paths is further differentiated into the twelve links of dependent origination.
As indicated in the sutra, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and the seven stations of consciousness (*sapta-vijñāna-sthiti*) serve as the seeds;

that is, among the twelve links, the present links of consciousness, name-and-form (*nāma-rūpa*), the six sense bases, contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*), along with the two future links of birth and the conditions for aging-and-death (*jarā-maraṇa*), all constitute the path of suffering.

Furthermore, the ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), greed, hatred, and delusion, the four inversions (*catur-viparyāsa*), and the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) are what is being referred to.

The eight wrong paths, the nine afflictions, the sixty-two views, and all defilements are, within the twelve links of dependent origination, the link of past ignorance and the two present links of craving and grasping—all of which constitute the path of delusion. These refer to the ten unwholesome courses of action.
Among the twelve links of dependent origination, the two links of past *saṃskāra* (formative forces) and present *bhava* (existence) are both paths of karma.

This is because one is deluded regarding the *dharmakāya*, taking it to be the path of suffering; thus, this *dharmakāya*, due to being within delusion, is designated by the alternative name "the causal true nature of Buddhahood" (*tathāgatagarbha*).
One is likewise deluded regarding *prajñā*, taking it to be the path of affliction; therefore, this *prajñā*, for this reason...
Because it is deluded, it is further termed the "enlightening cause" (了因) Buddha-nature.

Because one mistakes liberation for the path of karma, this cause of liberation exists within delusion and is therefore further termed the "conditioning cause" (緣因) Buddha-nature. These three causes of Buddha-nature are precisely the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The twelve links of dependent origination are called Buddha-nature. —Tiantai.

The Great Master’s commentary states: Ignorance, craving, and grasping are afflictions (*kleśa*). Since afflictions are themselves bodhi, when bodhi is fully realized, there are no longer any afflictions.
When afflictions are absent, this is ultimate purity—the *bodhi-nimitta-buddhadhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the cause of awakening).

Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) are the path of karma; these are themselves liberation (*vimukti*). This liberation is sovereign freedom—the *pratyaya-nimitta-buddhadhātu* (the Buddha-nature as the causal condition).
Name-and-form, old age, and death constitute the path of suffering; this is precisely the Dharma-body. The Dharma-body is without suffering and without pleasure;
this is called Great Bliss. It is neither born nor dies; it is eternal. It is the true cause of Buddha-nature.
Therefore, the Sūtra says that between ignorance and craving is the Middle Way. Ignorance belongs to the past; craving belongs to the present. If [one falls into] extremes...
If one is of middling capacity, there is nothing that is not Buddha-nature; all is eternal, blissful, self, and pure. Ignorance neither arises nor ceases;
this is called the inconceivable twelvefold chain of dependent origination as non-arising and non-ceasing.

Therefore, sentient beings are deluded regarding this, taking it to be the three paths, the three consciousnesses, and the three causes of Buddha-nature. When Bodhisattvas cultivate it, they transform it into these three aspects.

If one considers the three types of enlightenment and the three Great Vehicles, at the stage of the fruition of all Buddhas, they achieve the three bodies, the three nirvāṇas, the three jewels, and the three virtues;
therefore, Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva points to these as the "seed of the Tathāgata."
II. Refuting that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is not a seed. Part one: The initial inquiry. It asks: "What does this mean?

The intent of the question is as follows: Since dharmas consist of both the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned, if they are seeds, then both should be seeds; if they are not, then both should be non-seeds. Why is it that [only the conditioned] alone...?
This refers to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*); why then does it not mention the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)?
2. Explanation and Clarification (in two parts). First, a singular refutation of the faults of the unconditioned.
Answer: If one were to see the unconditioned and enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), they would be unable to again resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Third is the bodhicitta.
There are two types of contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination: first, origination; second, cessation. Regarding the contemplation of origination:

it refers to ignorance conditioning volitional formations, volitional formations conditioning consciousness, and so forth, up to birth conditioning aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
Regarding the contemplation of cessation: with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;
and so on, until with the cessation of birth, old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair cease. When a Bodhisattva cultivates this, they take cessation as their own cessation.

By contemplating the characteristics of the three paths as being devoid of the intrinsic nature of the three paths, they are able to perceive that the path of suffering is itself the Dharmakāya, and the path of afflictions is itself...

Prajñā: The path of karma is itself liberation. For those of the Two Vehicles, extinction consists in the total cessation [of existence]. They must destroy the three paths to accomplish the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Upon once realizing the unconditioned, they immediately enter the stage of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*).

By reducing the body to ashes and extinguishing wisdom, they take this as ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Having realized this *nirvāṇa*, they no longer receive further bodies within the triple world. [They] give rise to bodhi...
He controls his mind and thereby transforms and guides sentient beings.

○ Second, the double analogy of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). First, the repeated analogy of the Dharma clarifies the merits and faults of the conditioned and the unconditioned. First, the parable.
For example, lotus flowers do not grow on high ground or dry land; they grow only in low-lying, damp mud.
(2) The application of the analogy:

likewise, those who have seen the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and entered the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) can never again give rise to the afflictions (*kleśa*) that produce the Buddha-dharma.
It is only from within the mud that sentient beings can give rise to the Buddha-dharma.

This is precisely a metaphor for those of the Two Vehicles who, seeing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*); they are like the high plateaus and dry lands where lotuses do not grow.
Conversely, if this were used as a metaphor for Bodhisattvas who see the unconditioned yet do not enter the stage of right determination, it would be like [the following]:
High plateaus and dry land can produce fine, firm [grain]. Thus, the Bodhisattva attains two metaphors: there is no ground that is not suitable.
The followers of the Two Vehicles attain one metaphor: they can only be compared to high plateaus and dry land where lotus flowers do not grow.
II. The Analogy for the Two Kinds of Dharmas: Clarifying the Merits and Faults of the Conditioned and the Unconditioned.
First, the analogy: Furthermore, it is like planting seeds in the air; they will never sprout. Only in soil enriched with manure can they flourish and grow.
II. Correlating the Dharma.

Thus, for one who has entered the correct position of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), even if they do not give rise to the Buddha-dharmas, yet can produce the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* despite having a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru, they will give rise to the Buddha-dharmas. Therefore—
One should know that all afflictions are the seeds of the Tathāgata.
This is also a direct analogy for those of the two vehicles who, seeing the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), enter the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*);

it is just as planting seeds in the air can never result in growth. Conversely, this serves as an analogy for Bodhisattvas: at first, while still ordinary beings, they plant the seeds of bodhi within the fertile soil of the defilements.
Thus they attain flourishing growth. Next, the Bodhi tree grows long, spreading through space to provide shade and cover for all.
This constitutes the Bodhisattva attaining two metaphors; there is nothing that is not suitable. The followers of the Two Vehicles attain one metaphor;
they can only take the metaphor of planting seeds in the sky, which ultimately cannot sprout.
II. The Threefold Dharma and Parable Uniquely Revealing the Merit of the Conditioned (saṃskṛta). 1. The First: The Parable.
For example, if one does not descend into the great ocean, one cannot obtain a priceless jewel.
II. Correlating with the Dharma.
Thus, if one does not enter the great ocean of afflictions, one cannot obtain the jewel of omniscience.

Master Zhao said: "Since those of the Two Vehicles have already perceived the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and dwell securely in the stage of correctness, their minds are empty and tranquil, abiding in profound stillness."
Tranquil and joyful, they are free from the fear of birth and death and possess the bliss of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Content in their simplicity, they have no hopes and no desires.
Who, then, would begrudge dedicating their mind to the Mahāyāna? Ordinary beings, however, remain submerged and wandering through the five realms of existence.
Obscured by afflictions (*kleśa*), they lack the joy of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) when advancing, yet harbor the fear of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) when retreating.

Furthermore, their own minds are naturally haughty, and they aspire only to superiority. Thus, they are able to set out from the midst of worldly toil (*kleśa*) and direct their minds toward the Unsurpassed.

Taking root in birth and death, they cause the flowers of Perfect Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) to bloom. This is far removed from ordinary beings who perish in the swirling abyss of life, merely swimming amidst the dust of the world.

As for the ocean, how could it produce such unsurpassed treasures? For this reason, ordinary beings bear the reputation of being fickle and unstable, while those of the Two Vehicles suffer the shame of having their spiritual faculties impaired.
Deng said: "In the great ocean of afflictions, although the jewel of wisdom is present, one may drift away and lose one's life; there is no greater harm than this.
Were it not for a courageous man who firmly holds a floating bag and, through the skillful means of wisdom, dives deep into the abyss, how could the great treasure of wisdom be easily obtained?
Therefore it is said: 'The seeds of fish and the *āmra* fruit—so too is the Bodhisattva’s initial resolve. (Third)
In the midst of causal conditions, things are many; yet when the fruit is realized, they are few. The difficulty of achieving success is such that it is not easily accomplished.

Furthermore, the words of Master Zhaogong mentioned previously are certainly one perspective; I do not know if there might be another perspective, which lies simply in clinging to the teachings and being obstructed by emotional attachments.
Indeed, clinging to the teachings arises because of being obstructed by emotional attachments, and being obstructed by emotional attachments, in turn, arises because of clinging to the teachings.

It has been twelve years since he first arose [in this practice]. Yet, upon hearing the rebukes of Vimalakīrti and the reprimands of Mañjuśrī, he accepted his defeat with a willing heart and humbled himself to remain where he was.
Others called him "one who follows the Dharma of the ignorant," and indeed, he believed in that Dharma of the ignorant.

How can this be known? It is precisely because those of the two vehicles, from the time they first regressed from the Great [Vehicle] to practice the Small, have become addicted to the five desires and sunk into the cycle of birth and death;
not only have they regressed from the Great, but they have also lost the Small.

Consequently, they come to loathe the oppression of the three realms as if it were a prison, and long for the vast tranquility of *nirvāṇa* as if it were empty space; thus, they seek to save themselves.

There was no leisure; how could there have been leisure to assist others? When the Buddha first appeared in the world, he conformed to these stagnant sentiments and established this crude teaching, causing them to recognize suffering so as to sever its origin (*samudaya*), and to aspire toward cessation (*nirodha*) so as to cultivate the path (*mārga*).

They took the severing of the twelve links of dependent origination as their merit and the realization of partial emptiness and *nirvāṇa* as their goal, first extinguishing the mental afflictions and the burdens of the intellect.

This is the cause. Later, there is the fruit of the grayish body bound by birth and death; that is to say, one does not experience further birth in the fragmented realm (*vipaṅka-jāti*), nor does one again recognize the existence of transformation-birth (*pariṇāma-jāti*).
Furthermore, although one has realized true non-arising (*bhūta-anutpāda*), one is unaware that there is still the birth of skillful means (*upāya-jāti*).
Moreover, having once realized non-arising, one erroneously receives the seal of being a true son [of the Buddha] and falsely compares oneself to a Bodhisattva.
The fruit is merely a designation for the child; one should willingly undergo transformation and guidance while yielding to others, and maintain firm resolve to practice alone through solitary leaps.
Though the root is not destroyed, one deems it destroyed; though the sprout is not scorched, one harms it by scorching it.
One seals off the provisional city of the *pūrva-yāna* teachings and does not advance, guarding the thatched hut of attachment and refusing to return. This is self-...
It is not merely that this sutra rebukes and restrains them, nor that they must further rely on the wisdom of the emptiness of Prajñā to wash and cleanse themselves;
only after this can they receive the Buddha-wisdom of the Lotus Sutra to wash away, shatter, open, and reveal it to them.
Such people of deluded dharma are truly deluded for as long as they live—how can this be adequately described?
III. The Third Section: The Two Vehicles’ Self-Contempt for Lacking a Share and Their Benefit from Receiving Rebuke.
Part One: The Dharma Explanation. At that time, Mahākāśyapa exclaimed: “Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! You have spoken these words most skillfully. It is truly as you have said:
the host of afflictions (*kleśa*) constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata. As for us now, we are no longer capable of generating [the aspiration for enlightenment].”

Even those who have committed the five sins of immediate retribution are still able to give rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and be born into the Buddha-dharma; yet now we are utterly unable to do so.
II. The Explanation by Analogy:
It is like a man whose sense organs have been destroyed; he can no longer derive benefit from the five desires. III.
The Application to the Dharma (in two parts): First, the single application concerning the Two Vehicles.
Thus, for those śrāvakas who have severed all fetters, there is no further benefit within the Buddha-dharma; they never again aspire to it.
(2) Second, the dual integration of the noble and the ordinary. First, the establishment of the thesis.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, ordinary persons may turn back from the Buddha-dharma, but the śrāvakas do not.
(2) Explanation of the accomplishment:
Why is this so? Because when ordinary persons hear the Buddha-dharma, they are able to give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment and do not sever the Three Jewels.

If one were to cause a śrāvaka to hear of the Buddha’s powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth for the rest of their life, they would never be able to give rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Regarding the judgment according to the teachings, it should be understood that the principle belongs to the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) teaching.

If judged according to contemplative understanding, contemplating the present single mind as belonging to the twelve links of dependent origination is as follows: for example, when love arises from seeing a form with the eyes, this is the link of ignorance (*avidyā*).

The karma created by craving is called the link of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*). Single-minded and focused mindfulness is called the link of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness together with formative forces and matter is called the link of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
The arising of desire within the six sense bases is called the link of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Seeking craving through the sense bases is called the link of contact (*sparśa*).

The mind of greedy attachment is the link of feeling (*vedanā*). Clinging tenaciously without letting go is the link of craving (*tṛṣṇā*). Seeking after these various phenomena is the link of grasping (*upādāna*). As...

The arising of these dharmas is called the *bhava-aṅga* (existence link). Their uninterrupted succession is called the *jāti-aṅga* (birth link). Because this succession eventually ceases, it is called the *jarāmaraṇa-aṅga* (aging-and-death link).
Among these twelve links, three—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*)—belong to the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*).

Ignorance is itself illumination; it is the seed of the Buddha-nature as the discerning cause (*prajñā-vijñapti-hetu*). The two links of formative action (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*) belong to the path of karma (*karma-mārga*). [The five...]
The paths of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) are all characterized by liberation; they are the seeds of the Buddha-nature as the condition-cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

The seven links—consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death—belong to the path of suffering. There is no nirvana apart from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
That which is neither suffering nor pleasure is called Great Nirvana (*mahā-parinirvāṇa*); it is the seed of the Buddha-nature as the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*). These three virtues are thus...
The seeds of these [qualities] are fully present within the single thought-moment of the mind of an ordinary person.
○ Second, the Dharma-gate of the Three Clarities is categorized into two parts. First, the inquiry initiated by the Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation of Physical Form.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana who asked Vimalakīrti:
"Householder, who are your father, mother, wife, children, relatives, kinsmen, officials, subjects, and friends?
Where are your slaves, servants, elephants, horses, and carriages?"

This chapter begins with the inquiry of the Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation of Form (Samantavabhāsa-rūpakāya) because everything manifested by the layman Vimalakīrti is none other than a matter pertaining to the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Universal Manifestation of Form.
Since Vimalakīrti has manifested the body of a layman through the Samādhi of Universal Manifestation of Form, and since one who dwells at home must necessarily have parents, a wife, and so forth—
My son, as for the elephants, horses, carriages, and mounts—would they not all be manifested one by one?
The Bodhisattva Universal Manifestation of Form (Samantavabhāsa-rūpakāya) feared that those who do not understand might see only the traces while neglecting the source;

therefore, he has initiated this teaching to clarify it, hoping that those who awaken will find the source through the traces. Someone asked: "The principle of the Bodhisattva descending from the source to manifest traces—"
This is indeed so. It is simply that, based upon a single fundamental principle (*li-ben*), various manifestations (*zhong-ji*) are displayed.

Thus, although these manifestations may be numerous, the fundamental principle is originally not manifold. What you have now replied to suggests that there is one manifestation in the world and a separate fundamental principle within the Dharma-gate;
if the manifestations and the fundamental principle were thus distinct, where would the principle itself reside? The answer is: Now, as for...

The "Root" (ben) is the root of the "Trace" (ji); the "Trace" is the trace of the "Root. There has never been a case where the Root is non-existent while the Trace exists, nor where the Root exists while the Trace is non-existent.
Thus, the Root of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is like form and sound; the traces of phenomenal appearances (samskāra) are like shadows and echoes.
Therefore, for every single trace of a worldly phenomenon, there must necessarily also be the principle of the Dharma-realm.
There is one fundamental source: True Suchness (Tathatā). By its very nature, it is replete with all phenomena;

its essence remains forever unchanging while responding to conditions, and it remains forever responding to conditions without ever changing. Since time immemorial, the sentient beings of the six realms have stirred and struck this source through defiled conditions;
thus, the form and voice of True Suchness respond to them like echoes and shadows, becoming their parents.
For the sake of wife and children, it is said that True Suchness has one root and the world has one trace.
If the sound is not harmonious, the resonance will not follow; if the form is not straight, the shadow will not be upright. This is the natural principle, requiring no further argument.
Now, as for what the Great Being Vimalakīrti has manifested: he strikes the Dharma-realm with pure conditions; therefore, each and every [manifestation]—
This refers to the fundamental principle: taking true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) as the mother and expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) as the father.
Just as a form is upright when its shadow is straight, and a resonance is harmonious when the sound is concordant, this is likewise the law of nature. Furthermore, it may be asked:

"It may be acceptable that a Bodhisattva currently manifests as a layperson (*gṛhapati*), possessing family ties, a wife, and children in every respect; however, upon attaining Buddhahood, there are no such traces of these affairs."

The principle is rooted in all phenomena; there is nothing that is not empty. The answer is: regarding the traces of attaining Buddhahood, whether they exist or do not exist, they have no fixed location from the outset.
If we consider the attainment of Buddhahood by Amitābha, it need hardly be discussed whether his parents or wife existed;
yet, as for the attainment of Buddhahood by Śākyamuni, those matters did indeed exist. In general, as for their existence, they universally respond according to conditions. As for the phenomena...
All matters are fundamentally rooted in the Dharma-gate. In its absence, one withdraws their traces to return to the source. Every phenomenon returns to the ultimate reality.

Whether it be the *prajñāpāramitā*, skillful means (*upāya*), the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*), or compassion (*karuṇā*), there is nothing that does not return to the inconceivable great foundation of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Why, then, must one necessarily speak only of parents, wives, and children?
II. Vimalakīrti’s Response, in Four Parts. First, clarifying the Dharma through a sequential account of affairs, in two sections.
First, the complete realization of the great essence, in eighteen parts. First, the response regarding parents.
Thereupon, Vimalakīrti replied with a verse: "The Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Expedient Means (Upāya) is their father.
Here, "Wisdom" refers to ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), while "Expedient Means" refers to provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).

This is precisely what is meant in the *Lotus Sūtra* when it says that the wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable, and that the gateway to this wisdom is difficult to understand and difficult to enter. Indeed, these two types of wisdom are fundamentally what gives birth to all [Buddhas].
The Buddha is the fundamental guide of all. Furthermore, these two types of wisdom arise from the two principles of the provisional and the real.

Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Only Buddhas and Buddhas can fully exhaust the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena. Here, "all phenomena" refers to the provisional principle, while "the true aspect" refers to the real principle.
By investigating the real principle, one gives rise to real wisdom; by investigating the provisional principle, one gives rise to provisional wisdom. Real...
Only through the union of wisdom and means can all Buddhas be brought forth; therefore it is said: "There are no guides of the multitudes who are not born from this.
Second, the answer concerning one's own person.
All guides of the multitudes arise from this. III.
Answering the question regarding wife and children:
Taking the joy of the Dharma as one’s wife, the mind of compassion as one’s daughter, and a virtuous, sincere heart as one’s son.

The two wisdoms of provisional and ultimate give birth to the Teacher. Having completed his enlightened tasks, he realizes the Dharma with joy, much like a gentleman who finds delight upon obtaining a virtuous lady.
The female form is gentle and supple, and her mind abounds in compassion; thus, she is represented as a woman through her compassion.
A man possesses a nature of steadfast integrity and is able to accomplish the affairs of a household; thus, the wholesome mind—
To be sincere is what constitutes a man.
(4) Answering the question of dwellings:
the dwelling of ultimate emptiness and stillness.
"Shé" (舍) means "to abandon. It refers to one who abandons the multitude to dwell in solitude.

The Bodhisattva takes ultimate emptiness and quiescence as his dwelling, making it a place of rest for the myriad practices. What excellence of cessation could be more wondrous than this? What excellence could surpass it?
5. Answering the Disciples:
The various afflictions of the disciples are turned according to their will.
When a teacher takes on disciples, he causes them to follow his own turning, employing them in service and causing them to advance in cultivation.
It is simply to enable them to attain the fruit of the Way.
Now, for a Bodhisattva, it is appropriate to take the eighty-four thousand afflictions as disciples, transforming birth and death to rely upon nirvana, and transforming affliction to rely upon bodhi;
it is likewise appropriate to bring to fulfillment the gates of dhāraṇī and the gates of pāramitā. It is by means of these that they serve as disciples.
How wondrous it is! ○ Sixth, answering the question regarding spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*):
The factors of the path (*mārga-aṅga*) are the spiritual friends; through them, one achieves perfect enlightenment.
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "A good spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) is a great causal condition; that is to say, they transform and guide others so that they may attain the vision of the Buddha.
Now, a bodhisattva takes the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*) as their good spiritual friend;

it is appropriate to regard these as their instruction, as their companions in practice, and as their external protection. Is it not through this that the realization of perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) is achieved?
7. Answering on the Dharma Companions:

Regarding the companions of the various pāramitās and dharmas, when a bodhisattva practices the Way, they require dharma companions. Now, one takes the six pāramitās and the myriad practices as these companions; this is the truth.
He was a superior friend.
○ Eighth, responding to courtesans:
he gathered the assembly of courtesans through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), and used the chanting and recitation of Dharma words as their music.
When courtesans perform music, people follow it with delight; yet when a Bodhisattva gathers people through the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*),
causing them to hear the joy of the Dharma and realize the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa*, then no music can surpass this, and no joy can be greater than this.
9. Answering regarding the Garden:
The garden and grove of dhāraṇī; the forest trees of untainted dharmas; the pure and wondrous flowers of the factors of enlightenment; and the fruits of liberation and wisdom.
Just as a garden in this world can sustain flowering trees, so too does the Bodhisattva take the Great Dharani-gate of Perfect Enlightenment as a garden.
Within a single mind, they encompass the three virtues; within the nature-endowed, they sustain the myriad dharmas.
Thus, they enable the trees of the forest of untainted dharmas to have their roots and sprouts reach the ground of ultimate suchness, their spreading branches extending throughout the dharma-realm.
O Heavenly One! You have blossomed the wondrous flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment and bound the supreme fruit of the eight liberations and wisdom.
Your emotions are no longer dissipated; your principles have a definitive destination. To find delight in daily engagement—what joy could compare to this?
10. Answering the question on the bathing pool:

The bathing pool of the eight liberations is filled to the brim with the water of meditative concentration. It is strewn with the flowers of the seven purities; therein bathe those people who are free from defilement.
Master Shi said: "The utility of water is to remove dirt and dispel heat; the nature of liberation likewise removes heat and eliminates obstructions.
Master Sengsheng said: "To be still so as to be able to reflect is the significance of water. Once the mind of wisdom is settled and sufficient, it becomes profoundly tranquil and full.
Regarding the "Flowers of the Seven Purities," Master Shi said: "First is purity of precepts (*śīla-viśuddhi*), which is purity from beginning to end. [This pertains to] body and speech..."
In all that they do, there is not the slightest evil; their minds do not give rise to defilement, nor do they grasp at signs, nor do they aspire for rebirth.
They bestow fearlessness upon others without limiting it to any sentient beings. This is the purity of the two types of mind:

the mind that subdues afflictions through the three vehicles, the mind that severs the fetters, and even the mind of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) through the three vehicles—this is called purity of mind. As for the purity of the three views: it is the vision of the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Not giving rise to false conceptualization is called purity of vision (*dṛṣṭi-viśuddhi*). Fourth is purity of transcending doubt (*kāṅkṣā-vi-taraṇa-viśuddhi*):

if one's vision is not yet deep, although one may understand at that time, doubt may later arise; if doubt is severed through deep vision, it is called purity of transcending doubt. Fifth is purity of discerning the path (*mārga-prativedha-viśuddhi*).

If one can perceive that this is the path and should be practiced, and that this is not the path and should be abandoned, this is called the purification through discernment of the path (*mārga-vibhāga-śuddhi*).

Sixth is the purification through knowledge and vision of abandonment (*prahāṇa-jñāna-darśana-śuddhi*). "Practice" refers to the four modes of progress: difficult with slow fruit, difficult with quick fruit, easy with slow fruit, and easy with quick fruit.

"Abandonment" refers to the severing of all fetters (*saṃyojana*). Within the stage of training (*śaikṣa-bhūmi*), although one has exhausted [defilements], one is as yet unable to know for oneself what has been practiced and what has been abandoned; once [the stage of no-more-learning] is attained...

One studies the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Fully knowing and seeing for oneself what has been practiced and what has been abandoned, one attains clear penetration.

This is called the purification of the knowledge and vision of the abandonment of conduct. It is the seventh, the purification of nirvāṇa. When those stainless persons bathe in this, they bathe in stainlessness;
it is for the purpose of removing heat and attaining comfort. When a Bodhisattva, free from fetters, enters the eight liberations, externally...
It is for the sake of sentient beings, to bring joy to one's own inner mind. Master Zhao said: "Dhāraṇī and powerful memory are the garden of the myriad virtues.
In this garden, one plants the forest of outflows-free [wisdom], spreads the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment, and bears the fruit of liberation."

They adorn the ponds of the eight liberations and accumulate the waters of meditative concentration until they are profoundly full. They spread the flowers of the seven purities, arrayed across the surface of the water.
Thereafter, the stainless practitioners roam within these groves and bathe in these lotus ponds;
they relax, rest, and sport therein—this is the ultimate joy. How could it be compared to the pleasures of the groves and waters of the mundane world?
11. Answering the question of the elephant and horse:
The elephant and horse gallop with the five supernormal powers; the Mahāyāna serves as the chariot; one is tamed by a single mind and travels upon the Eightfold Noble Path.

Master Kumārajīva said: "It is like mounting a Great Vehicle to travel throughout the ten directions with sovereign ease and without obstruction, while simultaneously carrying sentient beings to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
Regarding 'one-pointedness of mind' (*ekacitta*): the Sanskrit original calls it the 'mind of the factors of enlightenment in harmony' (*samprayukta-bodhipakṣya-citta*).

Within this, there are three phases: first, arousal; second, gathering the mind; and third, equanimity (*upekṣā*). If the arousal is excessive, the mind becomes distracted; when distracted, one must gather it back."

If the fault of over-exertion (*pragraha*) occurs, one must subside; once subsided, one applies diligence (*vīrya*) to arouse the mind. If movement and stillness reach a state of equilibrium, one allows them to proceed naturally.
To remain poised in the center with composure is called equanimity (*upekṣā*). Equanimity is itself mastery; mastery is harmony. It is like a skilled charioteer:
if [the vehicle] is slow, he prods it forward; if it is fast, he restrains it. When speed and slowness are appropriate, he lets it go.
Then he releases them to depart, letting them stride freely upon level ground; wherever they go is certain. Master Zhaolun said: "The five supernatural powers are the elephants and horses;
the Mahāyāna is the superior carriage; and the single mind is the charioteer, traveling upon the Eightfold Noble Path."
12. Answer concerning the Marks and Subtle Features:
The primary marks adorn the countenance, while the various subtle features embellish the physical form.
The Tathāgata’s rūpakāya is fully endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor features; such is generally the case for Bodhisattvas.
It is the same. Only regarding the mark of the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head, it is slightly inferior.
○ Thirteenth, the answer concerning clothing and adornments:
Modesty is the upper garment; the profound mind serves as the flower garland.
The clothing of people is for the purpose of concealing shame and warding off wind and cold.
Although the Bodhisattva has no wind or cold to ward off, he likewise possesses shame that must be concealed; thus, he takes his own sense of shame and remorse as his supreme garment.
There is no adornment that surpasses this. The upper garment adorns the body, while the flower garland adorns the head; these two complement one another, and neither may be lacking.
Thus, with a profound mind of faith and joy, one cultivates various wholesome dharmas to adorn oneself—such that no worldly finery can equal it.
14. Answer concerning Material Wealth:
There are seven kinds of wealth; increase them through instruction. Practice according to what has been taught, and dedicate [the merit] for the sake of great benefit.
Master Kumārajīva said: "The seven treasures are faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and remorse. When one remains at home, one is able to relinquish wealth;
when one leaves the home-life, one is able to relinquish the five desires and afflictions. Because of faith in the good, one maintains the precepts; by maintaining the precepts, one ceases evil.
Once evil has ceased, one should proceed to practice all manner of goodness. This practice of all manner of goodness necessarily depends upon..."

Through extensive learning, one hears the Dharma; because of hearing the Dharma, one is able to renounce. When one is able to renounce, wisdom arises. Therefore, these five matters are taught in this sequential order.

These five matters constitute the treasure, while shame and remorse serve as its guardians. Since the guardians are also considered wealth for the owner of the riches, these seven matters are collectively termed "wealth.
Although worldly people possess much wealth, it must emerge from the person and grow through cultivation. Thus it is with the Bodhisattva.
It is likewise so. By using one’s own treasures to instruct others, enabling every person to practice according to the teachings, one attributes the merit of this transformation to oneself;
there is no greater benefit than this.
15. Answer on Peaceful Sleep:
The four dhyānas serve as his bed and seat; born from pure livelihood, abundant learning increases wisdom, which serves as the sound of his self-awakening.
The bedding and seat are among the four requisites for practicing the Way, all of which are obtained through pure livelihood; the bedding and seat are one such requisite.
In the Western Regions, when those of noble and high status wish to rise from sleep, they play subtle music to awaken themselves.
The Bodhisattva is likewise. Among all dhyānas, the four dhyānas serve as the foundation, distinguishing them from the fundamental dhyānas of the non-Buddhists.
Arising from wrong livelihood, one brings all practices to rest.

At the time of entering dhyāna, one should awaken and rouse oneself with the wisdom increased by extensive learning, ensuring that one does not fall into the partiality and stagnation of being like a solitary wheel or a single wing;
only then can one ascend to the Great Way.
16. Answer regarding food and drink:
The food is the Dharma of ambrosia; the flavor of liberation is the beverage.
In the celestial palace of Śakra, there is the Pārijāta tree; from the tree grow flowers, and from the flowers is produced ambrosia, just as in the human world.
A hundred flowers produce honey. In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, [the gods] sport within the gardens, gathering ambrosia together to eat;
by this they are able to attain long life and immortality. Within the Buddha-dharma, one nourishes the life of wisdom with the ambrosia of nirvāṇa, causing it to endure forever without interruption.
Master Kumārajīva said: "There are four kinds of the flavor of liberation. First, the renunciation of the household life..."
There are five desires. Second, through the practice of dhyāna, one leaves behind the afflictions of worldly clamor. Third, through wisdom, one leaves behind deluded thoughts.
Fourth, through nirvāṇa, one leaves behind birth and death. There are also two kinds of liberation: first, liberation from afflictions; second, liberation from obstacles.
It is also said that the nature of craving, which knows no satiety, is called "thirst. When craving is severed, one attains liberation. This is liberation.
It quenches the thirst of craving; therefore, it is called "gruel" (*pāna*). The four flavors likewise remove the thirst of craving, and are thus considered "gruel.
○ Seventeen: On Bathing.
One bathes with a pure mind.
Master Kumārajīva said: "When the mind is pure, there is no defilement; this absence of defilement is itself bathing. It is also called 'wandering through the eight liberations.
[Section] Eighteen: Answering on Fragrant Ointments.
The category of precepts serves as fragrant unguent.
Among the noble and eminent of the Western Heavens, after bathing, they apply scented water to their bodies, which remains without dispersing for a long time.
I once saw in Panyu an offering of rose-water from Siam; it was contained in a vessel of five *he* and was valued at fifty pieces of gold. It is said that...
In the palace, one bathes by pouring drops of water over the body; the fragrance does not dissipate for a month.
This is its efficacy. For a Bodhisattva, the fivefold Dharma-body serves as the fragrance, and the fragrance of ethical discipline (*śīla-gandha*) is its beginning.
The above sections all answer [the question regarding] how that Bodhisattva is fully endowed with the great essence from beginning to end,
demonstrating that he has fulfilled both internal and external conditions to become a magnificent man and an extraordinary hero of the Buddha-Dharma royal family. The following text, however,
answers [the question regarding] the manifestation of his great function.
II. Manifesting Great Function (14 sections). First, the ability to crush and destroy afflictions.
To crush and destroy the thieves of affliction, one is courageous and robust, beyond compare.

There are three kinds of afflictions: first, the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which are severed when seeking self-benefit; second, the afflictions of dust and sand (*rajas-aṃśu*), which are severed when benefiting others.
Third is ignorance (*avidyā*). It is severed when awakening and practice are perfected. For those of sharp faculties and superior wisdom, severing these afflictions is like splitting bamboo:
once severed, all are severed. Therefore it is said that nothing surpasses courage and vigor.
Second, it is able to subdue demonic adversaries.
It subdues the four kinds of māras and erects the banner of victory at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The four māras are explained as before. Master Kumārajīva said: "In foreign lands, when one defeats an enemy and achieves victory, one erects a banner of victory."
The subduing of Māra at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) likewise symbolizes his supreme manifestation.
Third, he is able to manifest birth while remaining in the state of non-arising;
though he knows there is neither origination nor cessation, he manifests birth for the sake of others.
Master Zhao said: "To know that there is neither arising nor ceasing is to attain the Dharma-body; thus, there is no further portion of birth.
Because it appears as though there is birth for the sake of others, there is nowhere it does not reach."
Fourth, it can manifest all lands, manifesting them all completely, just as there is nothing the sun does not illuminate. As for these lands:
vertically, they consist of the Shared, Expedient, and True-Response [realms], which differ according to their ascent or descent; horizontally, they comprise the ten [directions].
Only then will there be the distinction between the pure and the defiled.
Fifth, they are able to make offerings to all Buddhas;
they offer to the immeasurable billions of Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions. Regarding these Buddhas and their own bodies, they harbor no thought of discrimination.
The Bodhisattva realizes non-arising and shares the same threefold merit as all Buddhas of the ten directions;
they possess one body and one wisdom, and their powers and fearlessnesses are likewise identical. Therefore, there is no thought of discrimination.
Sixth, they are able to constantly cultivate the Pure Land.
Although they know that all Buddha-lands and sentient beings are empty, they constantly cultivate the Pure Land to teach and transform all living beings.
The lands of all Buddhas and the multitudes of sentient beings are like flowers in the sky; fundamentally they do not exist, and thus all are empty.
Yet these lands and these beings are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi.
Therefore, one constantly cultivates the Pure Land and transforms sentient beings, realizing it and perfecting it.
7. Ability to manifest forms according to each type:
Among all classes of sentient beings, their forms, voices, and modes of conduct—the Bodhisattva of Fearless Power can manifest them all simultaneously.
The forms, sounds, and deportments of sentient beings of the ten realms appear all at once; this is because he has attained the Samādhi of Universally Manifesting the Physical Body.
○ Eighth, he is able to perceive demons and manifest as demons.
They discern the deeds of Māra, yet manifest compliance with them. Through the wisdom of skillful means, they are able to perceive them all according to their will.
Having already awakened to the nature of Māra, they subsequently manifest compliance; thus, they are not turned by Māra, but rather are those who can turn Māra.
9. They are able to manifest old age, sickness, and death;
they may manifest old age, sickness, and death to bring all sentient beings to maturity. Knowing them to be like illusions and transformations, they attain unimpeded penetration.
X. Being able to manifest the three calamities, part two. First, manifesting the great three calamities, part one. First, briefly manifesting the calamity of fire:

"Sometimes he manifests the burning at the end of the kalpa, where heaven and earth are all set ablaze. Sentient beings harbor the notion of permanence; [the Buddha] illuminates them so they may know impermanence."
Sentient beings often hold the notion of permanence, primarily based on the view that heaven and earth are indestructible.

They then claim that this body receives its mandate from heaven and receives its substance from earth; since heaven and earth are permanent, human life is likewise permanent. Thus, they constantly give rise to the view of permanence.
The Bodhisattva wishes to shatter their perceptions. Sometimes, when it is not the time of the kalpa-conflagration, he manifests as the kalpa-conflagration, causing the great earth to blaze forth;
even Mount Sumeru, though most solid, becomes mere dust—how much more so the sentient beings born therein, who are not eternal?
This briefly demonstrates the calamity of fire; the calamities of water and wind may be understood accordingly.
The two assemblies sought the Bodhisattva.
Countless billions of sentient beings came together to invite him, arriving at his residence all at once; he transformed them, causing them to turn toward the Buddha-way.
First, he manifests a fire disaster to make them realize impermanence; subsequently, their faculties are stirred, and they come to request deliverance.
(3) Regarding the four types of diverse guidance and instruction: first, he instructs through the arts and crafts.
Whether through the scriptures, incantations, and arts, or through various crafts and skills, he manifests the practice of all these to benefit all living beings.
(2) He transforms them by means of manifold paths.
"Among all the various paths and dharmas in the world, he has gone forth as a renunciant within them all; thus, he resolves the delusions of others without falling into false views.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Because they share common practices, they are moved by mutual affinity; first they are in harmony, and only later do they diverge. A renunciant possesses virtue."
Because he was revered as the preeminent teacher among all beings, he manifested his entry into the homeless life to cultivate virtue and lead others. Master Zhao said:

"Of the ninety-six types of heterodox practitioners, all leave home to seek the Way; following their example of leaving home, [the Buddha] sought to resolve their delusions, yet did not adopt their views."
Third, he transformed himself into various devas;
sometimes he became the sun or moon deities, or Brahmā, the Lord of the World.
Master Kumārajīva said: "At the beginning of the kalpa, there were neither sun nor moon, nor were there yet sentient beings; it was a time of primordial darkness."
Because they do not see the sun and moon, he manifests as the sun and moon so that they may obtain illumination.
Fourth, by means of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*),
he sometimes becomes earth and water, and at other times becomes wind and fire.

Master Kumārajīva said: "At the beginning of the kalpa, when the earth had not yet been formed, he used his supernatural powers to cause winds from the six directions to blow upon the waters, solidifying them to form the earth.
Or, when he saw people on a ship about to sink at sea, he manifested it as land so that they might find safety.
Wherever there was a need for water, fire, or wind, he provided exactly what was requested. He did this either by manifesting these elements or by means of his own body."
He does so. It is the same regarding food and medicine.
○ Second, showing the three minor calamities. Part one: rescuing from the calamity of disease.
During the kalpa when there is pestilence, he manifests as various medicinal herbs. If anyone should consume them, their illness is cured and all toxins are eliminated.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Some are made to eliminate their illnesses, while others attain the state of an immortal (ṛṣi). Through these means, they are transformed and led into the Right Path.
In foreign lands there are marvelous medicinal substances; some resemble human forms, while others resemble the shapes of elephants or horses.

Those resembling elephants or horses may have people mount them, and they travel directly through the void. Or, merely by seeing or hearing of these medicines, all various ailments are immediately [cured]."
This is the elimination [of suffering].
○ Second, saving from the calamity of famine:
During an eon when there is famine, he manifests his body as food and drink to first relieve their hunger and thirst, and subsequently teaches the Dharma to people.
III. Saving from the Calamity of Weapons (2). First, quelling strife through compassion:
During an eon of weapons, one arouses compassion for their sake and transforms those sentient beings, causing them to abide in the ground of non-contention.

Master Kumārajīva said: "In a future kalpa at the end of the age, when weapons arise and the human lifespan is ten years, Vāsulimitra will descend from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and be born into a royal family as a son of heaven. He will transform the people, saying:
'Our ancestors lived for an extremely long time; it is because of our current anger and lack of compassion that we have come to such a short life. Therefore, you all—'"
