They should practice a mind of loving-kindness. When the people obey this command, their evil intentions will gradually diminish. Thereafter, those born shall have a lifespan of twenty years.
Thus it continues in succession until the time of Maitreya, when the lifespan reaches eighty-four thousand years.
2. Harmonizing through Equal Power:
If there is a great battle array, he establishes it with equal power; the Bodhisattva manifests his majestic might to subdue them and bring about peace and harmony.
Master Kumārajīva said: "When two armies face each other, one assists the weaker side so that their strength becomes equal. Once the two forces are balanced, there is no longer victory or defeat;

thus, both sides attain mutual peace and security. If even a skilled acrobat like Yiliáo could bring about a cessation of hostilities by juggling balls, how much more so when the compassionate power of a Bodhisattva is extended—it naturally resolves all strife."
Eleventh, they are able to rescue those in the three miserable realms.
Throughout all lands, wherever there are places of hell, they immediately go there to diligently relieve their suffering and affliction.
In all lands where animals prey upon one another, he manifests birth among them to bring about their benefit.

Master Shi said: "In times past, when humans lacked propriety and righteousness and were cruel toward their elders, the Bodhisattva manifested as monkeys, elephants, and birds to encourage respect for seniors.
Thus, both humans and beasts cultivated goodness and lived in mutual harmony. As it is said in the Mahā... [text continues].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The text is abbreviated and omits the hungry ghosts (preta), but in a complete treatise they should be included.
12. To cause confusion:
He manifests the enjoyment of the five desires and also displays the practice of dhyāna, thereby causing the mind of Māra to become confused and agitated so that he cannot find an opportunity.
"A lotus flower blooming amidst fire—this may be called rare. To practice dhyāna while remaining within desire is likewise rare.
Master Zhao said: "If one says they are practicing dhyāna, yet they still experience the five desires; if one says they are experiencing desire, yet they manifest the attainment of dhyāna."
Its transformations are unfathomable; this is why Māra causes such confusion. Were it not for one who stills the turmoil and aligns with the ultimate purpose, who could reconcile these two?
Tanyue said: "When a Bodhisattva manifests the acceptance of desire, it is to use the hook of desire to draw others in and lead them into the Buddha-way.
It is solely because he wishes to cause them to enter the Buddha-way that he accepts desire, and yet he further practices dhyāna."
As for "Chan" (meditation), it is the Chan of the Great Samādhi of the Nāga. Those in the world who speak of "verbal Chan" should not use this as an excuse.
○ Thirteen: The Hook of Manifesting Desire.
Or he may manifest as a courtesan to attract those who lust after beauty; first using the hook of desire to draw them in, he subsequently causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom.
As for the "hook of desire," the Bodhisattva uses desire as a fragrant bait to hook the perverse thoughts of sentient beings and lead them into Buddha-wisdom.
This is because that which sentient beings crave is solely desire; if one were to attempt to lead them by means of renouncing desire from the outset...
To dramatize [the teachings] in this way is to violate their nature and reject the teaching.
Therefore, one first accords with their desires to hook them, gradually inducing them so that they finally enter the Buddha-wisdom before ceasing [the effort].
○ Fourteen: Miscellaneous Clarifications on Various Transformations, Part Six. First, benefiting the multitude through shared purpose (*samānārthatā*):
he may act as a village headman, or serve as a guide for merchants, or become a state preceptor or a high minister, thereby bringing benefit and profit to sentient beings.
2. Saving the Poor through the Two Treasuries:
For all those who are impoverished, he manifests as an inexhaustible treasury and thereby exhorts them, causing them to resolve upon the bodhicitta.
Third, to subdue pride and arrogance:
for those with a mind of pride and arrogance, he manifests as a great strongman to subdue all who are conceited, causing them to abide in the unsurpassed path.
Master Zhao said: "A mind of arrogance elevates itself like a mountain peak that cannot retain water.
The Bodhisattva manifests as a strongman to subdue that haughty mind, and only thereafter moistens it with the water of the Dharma."
Fourth, he bestows fearlessness.
To those multitudes who are terrified, he stands before them to offer comfort and reassurance; first he grants them fearlessness, and afterwards causes them to resolve upon the Way.
5. The Rishi Free from Desire:
Sometimes he manifests as a rishi free from carnal desire who possesses the five supernatural powers, guiding all living beings and causing them to abide in precepts, patience, and compassion.

Master Shi said: "In this world there are no sages or saints; sentient beings are inferior and base, and thus do not enter into the profound Dharma. Therefore, they are transformed through the precepts and patience.
(6) Servants and attendants provide service.
Seeing those who require service, he manifests as their servant. Having gladdened their hearts, he inspires them with the mind of the Way (*bodhicitta*).
According to whatever they require, he enables them to enter the Buddha-way; through the power of his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he is able to provide for all their needs in full measure.
The Dharma taught by the two fingers is immeasurable;
likewise, the Path is immeasurable. His practice has no limit, and his wisdom is boundless. He delivers and liberates countless multitudes.
Third, it is praised by all Buddhas.
Even if all Buddhas were to praise its merits for countless billions of kalpas, they would still be unable to exhaust them.
4. Conclusion and Exhortation to Practice:
Who, upon hearing such a Dharma as this, would not resolve to attain bodhicitta? Save for those unworthy persons who are foolish, deluded, and devoid of wisdom.
As explained above, the great essence and the great function are both complete within a single mind; they are established in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
This is what initiates the *saṃnāha* (armor) at the very first thought; this is what culminates in great compassion when responding to the perils of sentient beings.

Each and every thing is manifested as it is, without the slightest fabrication. All who possess a mind shall inevitably attain this; therefore, it is said: "Who, upon hearing such a Dharma, would not resolve to awaken?"

Regarding the bodhicitta: except for those whose sprouts have withered and seeds have rotted such that they do not become vessels for the Dharma—namely, those unworthy persons who lack the potential for bodhi, as well as those in the world who are ignorant, deluded, and dark, possessing no awareness or discernment—they are unable to give rise to this mind.
This chapter begins with the Buddha-way, proceeds through the lineage of the Tathāgata, and concludes by encompassing the Dharma-gates.
They belong together. The three characteristics of arising possess a distinct sequence.
This means that if a Bodhisattva wishes to practice the non-path in order to penetrate the Buddha-path, they must fully possess the sixty-two views as the seed of the Tathāgata.

Once that seed is obtained and one practices the Buddha-path, then the Dharma-gate will encompass them, and the great essence and great function will certainly be accomplished. If one were to judge this according to the classification of teachings...
The Perfect and Sudden [Teaching] may be understood; however, as for the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), this constitutes the primary thesis of this chapter.

Its general meaning must also be clarified. Why is this? For although the various methods of contemplation have many different approaches in their principles and purports, they are essentially and exhaustively subsumed within the three types of contemplative methods established by Tiantai. As for these three types, Master Jingxi...

In the *Zhiguan yili* (Examples of the Meaning of Stopping and Contemplation), it says: "Now, as for the three contemplations, their meanings are of three kinds. The first is 'contemplation according to practice' (*cong xing*). This involves contemplating the one mind within the myriad objects;
though the myriad objects differ, the principle of wondrous contemplation is equal. The contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth is precisely its intended meaning.
(Text) This corresponds to what is stated in the present sutra: "The Great Path of Bodhi should be sought within the mental activities of sentient beings."

Practicing on non-paths while penetrating the Buddha-path, and so forth—this is precisely the meaning of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* and other scriptures regarding the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Second, regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*): as in the passages concerning the Four Truths and the Five Practices, these enter into the single thought-moment of the mind.
This is considered "contemplation through circular observation" (yuan guan). (Text) This is found throughout this sutra; I cannot cite it in full here. Third is "reliance on phenomena and signs":
for example, Rājagṛha and Gṛdhrakūṭa are named based on their activities; by borrowing these phenomena as objects of contemplation, one guides those with attached minds.
This can be understood through examples such as the Vaipulya [sūtras] and Samantabhadra. (Text) This precisely corresponds to what is stated in the present chapter:
"True Wisdom is the mother of Bodhisattvas; Expedient Means is their father. Among all teachers of the multitude, there are none who are not born from these.
Ultimate emptiness and quiescence are the house; the garden of dhāraṇīs, and so forth," are all its meanings. By knowing this, one understands that [it is] like Heaven.
The contemplative methods established by the Tiantai school accord perfectly with the Buddha’s intent. If one now wishes to further cultivate contemplation and understanding, it is as follows:
when contemplating a single moment of mind, one finds that it fully encompasses the ten dharma realms. The nine realms are provisional, while the Buddha realm is real.

That which is contemplated is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; that which contemplates is real wisdom. Bodhisattvas take this as their mother, while skillful means (*upāya*) serves as their father.
Furthermore, such a mind is none other than the Buddha-mind; indeed, all the Teachers of the Multitude arise from it.
By observing these various instances through their common characteristics, one can understand this by means of the intellect, just as one recognizes the moon by leaving aside the pointing finger.
Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Scroll Nine Commentary on the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra:
On Non-Self, Scroll Ten Authored by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi, Mount Tiantai [Scroll Nine] [Scroll Ten] [The text continues with the commentary.]
○ Ninth, the commentary on the "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality," part two. First, the explanation of the chapter title:
*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Nine, "Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality.

"Non-duality" refers to the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). For this reason, at the beginning of the chapter, the Bodhisattva Dharmavikurvaṇa (Dharma-Sovereignty) offers these words:
It is stated that attaining this *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena) constitutes entry into the gate of the non-dual dharma (*advaya-dharmamukha*).
The final chapter describes the benefits, stating that five thousand bodhisattvas all entered the gate of the non-dual dharma and attained *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*.
This is the definitive doctrine; it is not subject to alteration. Second, there are the two: the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the world-realm (*dhātu*), both mundane and supramundane.

The "seeds" and "realities" are merely provisional designations among phenomena. As for the wondrous Dharma of non-arising, although it encompasses the three thousand realms, its single nature is pervasive and interfused;

fundamentally, it is not a matter of numerical categories. It is because sentient beings have themselves become turbid within the ocean of perfect enlightenment that the illumination of their true nature was initially lost.
To discard the ocean and recognize the bubble is to establish the duality of subject and object. Based upon ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), one falsely gives rise to designations;
based upon these designations, one vainly constructs numerical categories. "One" is the beginning of numbers, and "ten" is their end.

Having thus been established from this point, ten gives rise to a hundred, and a hundred gives rise to a thousand. Furthermore, based on these, one performs multiplication and division. From this point onward, [the process continues] without end.
This is indeed beyond reckoning. Now, having exhausted the source and observed the beginning, we see that one has already become deluded regarding the True and pursued the False.
Yet, by following the current back to its source, one must surely turn away from the False to return to the True. This turning from the False to return to the True must begin with the derivative.

Therefore, those guests who seek to return to the Origin first employ the method of contemplation (*guanfa*) to achieve this "non-attainment" (*bu*). For "non" (*bu*) signifies emptiness, non-existence, and relinquishment.

This is "Dissipation. These two are the numerical categories among substantial dharmas. When the numerical categories of substantial dharmas are destroyed, then conventional designations and names are forgotten.

When conventional designations and names are forgotten, then the affective delusions regarding substantial dharmas are destroyed. When the affective delusions regarding substantial dharmas are destroyed...
Then the afflictions of birth and death are empty, and one realizes the principle of the non-arising of bodhi and nirvāṇa.

Yet there are the teachings, the practices, and the principles. One must first receive the teaching of the non-dual dharma, then cultivate the practice of the non-dual dharma, and only thereafter realize the principle of the non-dual dharma.
As for the teaching of non-duality, it is empty and devoid of anything to be discarded or swept away.
The four meanings all explain the practice of non-duality; therein, the function lies solely in the elimination of conceptualization.

The principle of non-duality is realized solely through the testimony of emptiness and non-existence. Since a "gate" (mukha) takes the sense of that which enables passage, and gates are established according to the phenomena [they lead to], there are thus the gate of teaching, the gate of practice, and the gate of principle.
Some say: the two dharmas of teaching and practice are able to lead one to the principle; this is termed...

It may be said that "gate" (*mukha*) is appropriate. Since principle (*li*) is that which is penetrated, why is it also called a "gate"? The answer is: although principle is that which is penetrated, its nature is unobstructed;
it universally penetrates all phenomena (*dharmas*). Thus, it may also be called a "gate," and for this reason, principle is taken as the gate. Or, one might raise an objection:
[Objection: "Though 'two' is negated, what shall be done with 'one'? [Response: The explanation says: Since it is called "non-dual" (*advaya*), both "one" and [its opposite] are forgotten.
You say that "one" is preserved; your delusion is indeed extreme. [Objection: "Though 'two' is negated, what shall be done with 'three'?
What shall be done with ten, a hundred, a thousand, or ten thousand? [Response: The explanation says: "One" is the beginning of numbers. Since the root is absent, the branches [cannot exist].

To what could they be attached? This is especially so for that which is non-dual. Thus, the provisional enumeration of names is employed as a means to dispatch one toward the true dharma (*dharmatā*), serving as a preliminary introduction to wondrous contemplation.
The primary intent lies in the true dharma, not in the provisional names. Therefore, the various bodhisattvas...
There are those who take two dharmas as the starting point for their discourse, such as when the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara said:

"O virtuous ones, arising and ceasing constitute duality. Since dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, they are now without cessation. To attain this patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma.
There are those who take the three karmas as the starting point, and there are those who take the Three Jewels as [the starting point].
Regarding the term "extremes" (*dva*), such enumerations are not limited to these alone; why then should it be fixed at two? Someone may ask:
"How does this compare to the 'Ten Gates of Non-duality between the Original and the Traced' in Jingxi’s *Fahua wenju*? I reply:

Although this [text] encompasses the three aspects of teaching, practice, and principle, its primary intent lies in practice. That [work], by contrast, clarifies only principle. This is the first point of difference.
This "non-duality" refers to the method of dispelling and clearing away, wherein even the slightest sentiment is not retained.

That "non-duality" refers to the principle of integration and penetration, wherein all things are merged as one within the Dharma-realm. As it is said, "form and mind are non-dual": form is precisely mind, and mind is precisely form;
thus, all phenomena of form and mind are none other than the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). These two types of non-duality are not the same. How much less so... [the former]!
That sūtra belongs to the category of clarified butter (*ghṛta*), while this sūtra belongs to the category of fresh butter (*navanīta*). Their purity and mixture are naturally distinct;
they cannot be treated as following the same track.
[Section Two: Explaining the Text, Part Four. First, the various bodhisattvas speak on entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Second, first, Wei...]
At that time, when the householder Māṭhara questioned him, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: "O noble ones, how does a bodhisattva enter the dharma-gate of non-duality?
Each of you should speak according to what you find most appropriate."

Master Kumārajīva said: "The alternating use of existence and non-existence is the constant principle of the Buddha-dharma. Since the preceding chapter spoke of existence, this subsequent section speaks of the gate of emptiness.
Furthermore, from the beginning of this assembly until now, only two individuals have engaged in dialogue while the rest remained silent.
Now, wishing for each to manifest their own virtues, he asks them to speak exhaustively. It is also said that dispositions may differ, and thus there must be causes for awakening."

I urge each of you to speak of your realization to extensively dispel the delusions of the assembly. Now, when a supreme assembly clarifies its fundamental tenet, it must be considered beautiful only if it reaches a definitive conclusion.
As this Dharma seat is about to disperse, if we wish to investigate its profound significance and extensively expound upon non-duality, only then will we exhaust its wondrous essence.
Master Sengzhao said: "From the very beginning of this undertaking, although the teachings elucidated have differed, they are all the path of the Great Vehicle’s signlessness (*animitta*).
The path of signlessness is precisely the Dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*).
The Dharma-gate of inconceivable liberation is precisely the Dharma-gate of the primary truth of non-duality (*advaya*). This is what was established by Vimalakīrti when he manifested illness."
This is the foundation established by Mañjuśrī’s inquiry into the illness. Whether ordinary person or sage, none achieve the Way without passing through it.

Thus, it serves as the opening chapter of this work and the primary discourse of these words. When one investigates its ultimate destination, it is but one. Nevertheless, among students, there are various dispositions for opening the mind, and their methods of reception and practice differ.
Some contemplate arising and ceasing to return to the source; others infer existence and non-existence to realize the essence.
True. Some seek the One by investigating transgressions and blessings; others attain profound stillness by examining body and speech.
Although their paths differ, their ultimate convergence is no different. Because they are not different, one adopts what all people share in common to verify the great purport of this sutra.
○ Thirty-one bodhisattvas respond to the thirty-first [question]. The first [section] explains the entry into the gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of arising and ceasing.
Within the assembly, there is a bodhisattva named Dharmeśvara who says: "O virtuous ones, arising and ceasing constitute duality. The Dharma is fundamentally..."
It does not arise; now, it does not cease. To attain this *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena) is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma.
Briefly stated, there are three kinds of arising and ceasing: first, that which pertains to the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), namely the alternation of spring and autumn;

second, that which pertains to the primary retribution (*mukhya-vipāka*), namely death and birth after death; and third, that of the deluded mind, which does not abide for even a single *kṣaṇa*. Of these, the former two do not exceed the category of the secondary.
Section. Only the single kind of deluded mind is its root. If its root is destroyed, then the branches and twigs will wither of their own accord.

Now, that which arises and perishes is a phenomenon established through mutual dependence. Since phenomena are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning, where could there be arising upon which to depend for there to be cessation?
This is non-arising and non-ceasing; it is the Dharma-patience of non-arising, and one has thereby entered the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Not...

Contemplate these flowers in the sky: the void is fundamentally without flowers; their appearance is due to the cataracts of visual impairment. Since the cataracts themselves are originally non-existent, how could the flowers exist?
Even the place where the flowers arise cannot be found; how much less can there be their cessation? Thus, both birth-and-death and nirvana are all flowers in the void.
If one can know that the flowers of cataracts are all empty, then the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) is spontaneously realized and manifest.
This is the gate of teaching (*śāsana-mukha*). To observe in accordance with this is the gate of practice (*pratipatti-mukha*).
To enter into principle through such observation is the gate of principle (*tattva-mukha*). Hearing the teaching and observing the mind, one leaves behind the finger to see the moon;

one must not hold views of them being sequential or identical. This is entry into the gate of non-dual dharma (*advaya-dharmamukha*). As for the remaining thirty gates, one example serves as an illustration for all.
There is no need for further elaboration.

Regarding the classification by teaching (*yàojiào*): the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) belongs to the first stage (*bhūmi*) in the Separate Teaching (*biéjiào*), and to the first dwelling (*vihāra*) in the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).

By destroying fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*), one is able to realize and enter [this state] in both cases. Nevertheless, it is also called "common" (*tōng*); that is, the Bodhisattvas of the Common Teaching (*tōngjiào*), having entered the stage where what was to be done is accomplished (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), are also so named.
They realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

What differs is that the universal [teaching] destroys the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi- and bhāvanā-āsrava*), whereas both the distinct and the perfect [teachings] destroy the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*); thus they differ. This sutra is taught within the Vaipulya [period].
It is not problematic to judge the practitioners of the three teachings according to what each has realized.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": one contemplates that the single thought-moment is ever-new and does not abide, ceasing without pause for even a *kṣaṇa*.

This is the second [aspect]. Within a single thought-moment are the three thousand [realms]; within a single *kṣaṇa* are the nine periods of time. At the very moment of arising, there is cessation; at the very moment of cessation, there is arising.

These two dharmas of arising and cessation oppose and negate one another in their essential nature. Thus, while there is arising and cessation, fundamentally there is no arising or cessation; thus, the dharmas are fundamentally non-existent.
"Arising, there is now likewise no ceasing.
2. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality as explained in terms of "self" and "what belongs to self":
Bodhisattva Guptasena said, "'Self' and 'what belongs to self' constitute duality. Because of the existence of a self, there is that which belongs to the self. If there were no [self]..."
When there is a self, there is no "mine"; this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality.

"Self" takes the sense of being a sovereign master. Regarding all people in the world, that deluded mind which clings to itself as being able to act as a sovereign master over the world is entirely an object.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds: first, the innate; second, the discriminative.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* explains this as follows: "That which belongs to the self" (*ātmiya*) is, in brief, like that which was investigated in the seven locations of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

"Fundamentally there is no self" (*anātman*) is, in brief, like the refutation of the false mind in the three locations of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where the mind is sought throughout the three periods of time in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and found to be unobtainable, and where the mind is analyzed through the four propositions in the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and found to be non-existent. This is therefore...
Fundamentally, there is no "mine. Since it is established on account of the "self," and even the mind of "self" does not exist, where could that which is "led by" [the self] possibly reside?
When both "self" and "mine" are absent, then the principle of arising ceases to exist. Standing forth in solitary independence—this is what is meant by entering the gate of non-duality.
Regarding the classification according to the provisional teachings: the two kinds of self—innate and discriminated—belong to the delusions of thought within the realm of desire and form.
Merely destroying this self to realize non-arising places one in the stages of the Shared Teaching, specifically the stage of "Already Accomplished.

If, however, one destroys the attachment to self beyond the realm of desire and form to realize the Middle Way’s non-arising, then one’s position lies in the first bhūmi or the first vihāra of the Distinct and Complete Teachings. This sutra...

It is taught in the Vaipulya (fangděng) [sūtras], which encompass both the Shared (tōng) and Distinct (bié) [teachings] while correctly expounding the Perfect (yuán) Teaching. By means of these three teachings, there is no fault in the determination of the stages (bit).

Furthermore, there is no other way to understand through contemplation (guānjiě) than to investigate each of the three periods, the four propositions (sìjù), and the seven locations and three places (qīchù sānchù).
When sought, both "I" and "mine" are equally unobtainable.
○ Third, entering the gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of acceptance and non-acceptance:
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said, "Acceptance and non-acceptance constitute duality. If a dharma is not accepted, it cannot be apprehended. Because it is not..."
It can be attained; therefore, there is neither grasping nor abandoning, neither action nor movement. This is called entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Not blinking has three meanings: first, being like the gods; second, loving and revering the Buddha’s body, observing it with steady, unblinking gaze;
third, the mind being free from the dust of defilements, so that the eye of wisdom is always open. Master Dīpaṃkara said: "There are three meanings of 'receiving': from the six sense organs..."

In relation to the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), there are three types of feeling (*vedanā*): first, painful feeling, which arises conditioned by disagreeable objects; second, pleasant feeling, which arises conditioned by agreeable objects;

and third, neutral feeling, which arises conditioned by objects that are neither disagreeable nor agreeable. The faculties (*indriya*) and objects belong to the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Because of form, there is feeling; because of feeling, there is perception (*saṃjñā*);

because of perception, there are mental formations (*saṃskāra*); and because of mental formations, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Thus, among the afflictions and the cycle of birth and death for human beings, nothing is greater than this.
Regarding sensation (*vedanā*), to be able to be without sensation is to attain right reception (*samyag-vedanā*). It is for this reason that *samādhi* is called "right reception.

Nevertheless, right reception is attained only by depending upon false reception; as it is said: "If a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself is established through dependence.
Therefore, it is said that "sensation and non-sensation are two. Now, however, there is no dependence and no phenomenon that is established.

Therefore it is said: if a phenomenon is not grasped, it cannot be apprehended. Where there is apprehension, there is grasping and receiving. Since it cannot be apprehended, there is neither grasping nor receiving.

Where there is grasping, there is relinquishing; where there is no grasping, there is no relinquishing. Since there is neither grasping nor receiving, then even "not grasping" and "not receiving" do not exist.
Where there is receiving, there is conceptualization; where there is conceptualization, [there is further proliferation].

If both volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*), as well as what has been received and what has not been received, are both non-existent, then perception (*saṃjñā*), formations, and consciousness are all non-existent.
Therefore it is said: "no action, no formation. This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Regarding the provisional teaching (yàojiào) classification: there are the five aggregates of the stage of fragmentation (fēnduàn) and the five aggregates of transformation (biànyì).

When the five aggregates of fragmentation are forgotten, one takes true emptiness (zhēnkōng) as the Dharma of non-duality (bù'èr fǎ), which is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (wúshēng fǎrěn). This corresponds to the stage of "having already accomplished" (yǐbiàndì) in the general classification, and to the seventh stage (qī zhù wèi) in the specific classification.

Those at the stage of the seven degrees of faith can all enter it. However, if one says that one must first forget the five aggregates of the transformational realm before entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality and realizing the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
then it is only those dwelling in the first bhūmi of the Separate or Perfect [Teachings] who can attain this.

Regarding contemplative understanding: when the mental faculty (*manas*) encounters mental objects (*dharmas*), if it takes as its object the five past sense-objects that are contrary or adverse, it gives rise to painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*);

if it takes as its object favorable objects, it gives rise to pleasant sensation (*sukhā vedanā*); and if it takes as its object objects that are neither contrary nor favorable, it gives rise to neutral sensation (*aduḥkhāsukhā vedanā*).

Because of these, the subsequent three aggregates (*skandhas*) arise; thus, afflictions (*kleśa*) become vast and turbulent, and birth and death (*saṃsāra*) are endless—all of which proceed from this.

Śāriputra, if one can use the contemplation of emptiness to clearly perceive that the objects of the mind (dharmas) are fundamentally empty in their essence, then the three types of sensation will not arise, and one attains right reception (*samyak-samādhi*).
Furthermore, realizing that even sensation itself cannot be apprehended, how much more so non-reception?
Since both reception and non-reception are empty, there is no grasping, no fabrication, and no activity; this is the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Fourth, entering the gate of non-duality by way of the two dharmas of defilement and purity.
The Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa said: "Defilement and purity constitute duality. When one perceives the true nature of defilement, there is no appearance of purity;
this accords with the mark of cessation. This is called entering the gate of non-duality."
Afflictions and birth-and-death are both termed "defilements. Only by departing from these causes and effects and realizing entry into bodhi and nirvāṇa can one be called "pure.
This is the teaching of the provisional vehicles of the partial and small [vehicles]. For those of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, they perceive the true nature of defilement;
since the true nature of defilement is fundamentally free from pollution, why must they depart from the defilements of afflictions and birth-and-death in order to attain bodhi?

How pure is the nirvana of awakening! To be able to contemplate in this way is to accord with the characteristics of quiescent *tathatā*. Thus, defilement and purity are fundamentally non-dual in their nature; this is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. This is the person of perfect and complete realization who contemplates the afflictions and birth-and-death of the nine realms: that which is cultivated as defiled is itself the defilement of the nature (*dharmatā*). When the defilement of the nature is fused [with wisdom], it is no longer defilement. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-defilement. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-arising," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally unarisen, there is nothing further to be produced. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-arising. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-extinction," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally unextinguished, there is nothing further to be extinguished. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-extinction. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-coming," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally unarisen, they have nowhere from which to come. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-coming. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-going," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally unextinguished, they have nowhere to which they go. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-going. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-abiding," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally neither coming nor going, they have no place to abide. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-abiding. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-entering," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally non-abiding, they have no gate through which to enter. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-entering. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-exiting," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally non-entering, they have no gate through which to exit. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-exiting. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-dwelling," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally non-exiting, they have no place to dwell. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-dwelling. It is also called the "Dharma-gate of Non-attainment," for when one realizes that all phenomena are originally non-dwelling, they have nothing to be attained. This is called the "Dharma-gate of Non-attainment. Pervasive. There is no dharma that does not tend toward it; it spontaneously encompasses and attains the nature of purity. It is the very essence itself; there is no need for transformation or transference.
This is because True Suchness (tathatā) can follow defiled conditions to produce the nine realms; thus, one who is able to contemplate this accords with the characteristic of cessation.
It should be understood that this teaching belongs to the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun).

Regarding "contemplative understanding": when one contemplates the mutual encounter of the sense faculties and their objects, at the moment a thought arises, it necessarily belongs to one of the nine realms.
This is precisely the mind of affliction and the matter of birth-and-death; it is termed "defilement.

To realize that this cultivated defilement is itself the inherent nature of defilement is to perceive the true nature of defilement. The true nature of defilement is fundamentally pure from the beginning; this is what is meant by "being identical with defilement."
This is purity. How could there be a characteristic of purity obtainable apart from the nature free from defilement? To contemplate in this way accords with True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Being able to follow along with conditions of defilement and purity while maintaining the characteristic of quiescent extinction—this is contemplating the mind as it enters the gate of non-duality.
5. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of movement and thought.
The Bodhisattva Sunakṣatra said: "Movement and thought constitute duality. Where there is no movement, there is no thought;
where there is no thought, there is no discrimination. One who thoroughly penetrates this enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Where there is movement, there is thought; where there is thought, there is movement. Thus, movement and thought are fundamentally one dharma.

That they are now spoken of as two is merely a distinction between the beginning and the end, or between the coarse and the subtle. If one realizes that when the mind first arises, the mind has no initial characteristic, because it is already far removed from even subtle thoughts, how could there be any movement or thought?
It is only when the perfectly luminous awareness gives rise to objects of perception that [distinctions appear].
When the nature of illumination is forgotten, thought first arises. Illumination is movement; once the nature of illumination is forgotten, that thought becomes attached.
Therefore, when there is movement, there is thought, and thus duality first comes into being. When one does not think, there is no thought;
no-thought is non-discrimination, which is non-duality. Hence it is said: "This is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Regarding the classification according to the provisional teachings (*kyōkō-han*): both "movement" and "thought" can be spoken of in all three teachings.

If one takes the views and afflictions (*jenshi*) within the realm of conditioned existence as movement and thought, then using the contemplation of emptiness alone to clarify that movement and thought—this may be understood from the Shared Teaching (*tsūkyō*).
If one takes the ignorance outside the realms as movement or thought, and distinguishes between the partial and the perfect by discussing the number of their categories;

or if, regarding the stillness and movement, one distinguishes between the partial and the perfect based on whether the three contemplations follow a sequential or non-sequential order—this too can be understood.

Regarding "contemplative understanding": one contemplates the single thought-moment (*citta*). If quiescence remains for too long, drowsiness arises; if alertness is excessive, discursive thoughts arise.

Thus, movement and thought constitute a duality. If, during times of quiescence, one is constantly self-awake, and during times of alertness, one is constantly self-quiescent—this is what is meant by "non-movement" which is then "no-thought. No-thought is precisely non-discrimination. This is...
This is for the purpose of contemplating the mind to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
○ Sixth, entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality by way of the two dharmas of "characteristic" and "non-characteristic.

The Bodhisattva Universal Eye said: "The single characteristic and the absence of characteristics constitute duality. If one knows that the single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics, then it is also..."
Not grasping at signlessness, one enters into equality; this is the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality.

Initially, one gathers the manifold characteristics of all phenomena and returns them to the single characteristic of the mind; yet, although these characteristics return to the One, [they remain as they are].
There still remains the mark of "one"; the conditions have not yet been forgotten. One must eliminate even this "one" before the marks and conditions are finally severed.
Although it is said that this "one" is eliminated, this non-existence does not exist separately outside of the "one.
It is the very mark of the one mind; its essence is fundamentally without marks. Therefore it is said: "If one knows the single mark, it is itself the absence of marks. Since it is one...
That which has characteristics is itself without characteristics; thus, one does not abandon the single characteristic, nor does one grasp at the absence of characteristics.
By neither abandoning nor grasping, one enters into equality. This is what is meant by entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.

Regarding the classification according to the provisional teachings (*kyō-han*): if one employs the contemplation of the equality of emptiness (*kū-byōdō-kan*) to empty out both grasping and rejecting, then the Distinct, Shared, and Complete [teachings] can all be so described.

However, if one employs the wondrous contemplation of the Middle Way (*chūdō-myōkan*), neither abandoning the existence of the single characteristic nor grasping at the non-existence of formlessness, then by distinguishing between the "limited" and "unlimited" [aspects], they are established as the Distinct and the Complete; the meaning of this can be understood.

Regarding the practitioner who resolves through contemplation (*guanjie*): they contemplate that the nature of the single thought-moment (*ekacitta*) possesses the three thousand [dharmas], all of which ultimately converge into the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of that single thought-moment.
That thought is fundamentally empty; originally, it possesses no characteristics. Thus, the single thought is itself non-thought, and non-thought is itself the single thought.
Is this not like knowing that the single characteristic is itself the absence of characteristics? In this way, within the single thought-moment—
There is nothing to be relinquished; within non-thought, there is likewise nothing to be grasped. By means of equanimous contemplation, one contemplates the principle of equality.
This is called contemplating the mind as having a single characteristic that is without characteristics, thereby entering the dharma-gate of non-duality.
7. Regarding the two dharmas of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas as entering the gate of non-duality, the Bodhisattva Subāhu said:

"The mind of a bodhisattva and the mind of a śrāvaka constitute duality. When one contemplates that the characteristics of the mind are empty and like an illusion or a transformation, there is no mind of a bodhisattva and no mind of a śrāvaka. This is called entering the gate of non-duality."
The Bodhisattva’s mind of the six perfections is directed toward benefiting others; the Śrāvaka’s mind of the four noble truths is directed toward self-benefit.
The nature of these two minds is that their essence is entirely empty—like an illusion, like a transformation—and both are ungraspable. If they were graspable, they would be dual.
Because it is ultimately unobtainable, it is called the Dharma-gate of Non-duality. Regarding the classification of teachings:

if one enters by means of "true emptiness," whereby emptiness removes the two minds, this is the entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality according to the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching), which takes the nature of phenomena as its substance.
If one enters by means of the "Middle Way," whereby emptiness removes both emptiness and existence, this is the Middle Way of the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching) and *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching).
Contemplation. Distinguishing between the limited and the unlimited is entry into the gate of non-duality.

Regarding contemplative understanding: to contemplate that a single thought-moment encompasses the practice of the six perfections is the bodhisattva mind; to encompass the practice of the four truths is the śrāvaka mind.
To contemplate the characteristics of these two minds as empty and like illusions, seeking neither the śrāvaka mind nor the bodhisattva mind, is [the way].
They cannot be apprehended. This is the contemplation that the mind lacks these two characteristics, thereby entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
[8] Explaining the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of wholesome and unwholesome.

The Bodhisattva Puṣya said: "Good and not-good constitute duality. If one does not give rise to good or not-good, but enters the limit of signlessness and attains thorough penetration, this is called entering the gate of non-dual dharmas."
Master Shi said: "All contaminated wholesome states of mind, as well as wholesome actions of body and speech, and the uncontaminated [states] up to and including nirvana, are called 'wholesome.
All actions of body and speech produced by the afflictions are called 'unwholesome. Daoping said:
If unwholesome thoughts arise, they become the cause for the cycle of birth and death within the three realms and six paths.
If wholesome thoughts arise, they become the fruit of the two vehicles’ bodhi and nirvana that transcend the three realms.

One who seeks the Buddha-way must not only refrain from giving rise to unwholesome thoughts, but must not give rise to wholesome thoughts either; only then will one be in accord with the Great Way. —The Sixth Patriarch.
He said: "Do not think of good; do not think of evil. Which one is the original face of Elder Ming? This is indeed a statement worthy of consideration.
To judge it according to the teachings: if one takes true emptiness as the limit of formlessness, wherein both good and evil thoughts are transcended, then—
This belongs to the gate of non-duality for Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna).

If, however, one regards the "Middle" of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna) and the "Perfect Middle" as the limit of signlessness—neither good nor evil, and transcending the two extremes of emptiness and existence—then this belongs to the entry into the gate of non-duality for the Distinct and Perfect Teachings.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that although a single thought-moment possesses the nature of evil of the nine dharma-realms and the nature of goodness of the Buddha-dharma realm, the nature of evil and the nature of goodness are fundamentally interfused in essence, such that neither good nor evil can be predicated.
This is the entry into the non-dual dharma-gate of the signless limit through contemplating the mind.
9. Regarding the three dharmas of karmic offenses and defilements, the Bodhisattva Siṃha said:
"Offenses and merit are two. If one realizes the nature of offenses, they are no different from merit.
To decisively comprehend this characteristic with adamantine wisdom, such that there is neither bondage nor liberation—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Regarding the ten realms of existence (*daśa-dhātu*), one may discuss the accumulation of demerit and merit through their mutual transmission.

Only the realm of the Bodhisattva represents the gradual progression toward demerit, while the realm of the Buddha-Dharma represents the ultimate consummation of merit. This constitutes the second [point]. As the Sūtra says: "My own mind is inherently empty; demerit and merit have no master."
It is further said: "Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, one shines universally throughout the ten directions.

This precisely means that the nine realms are taken as the nature of evil, while the Buddha-realm is taken as the nature of goodness. Because the nature of evil is interfused and permeates all, there is no dharma that does not enter it;

it spontaneously encompasses the nature of goodness of the Buddha-realm. Therefore, it is said: "If one penetrates the fact that the nature of sin is no different from merit, one who can thus illuminate and realize this is..."
By means of adamantine wisdom, one decisively realizes that these characteristics possess no distinction between the bondage of the nine realms and the liberation of the Buddha-realm;
this is the entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

Regarding those who judge the teachings: they realize that the nature of sin is no different from merit. No teaching other than the Perfect and Sudden (the *yuanton jiao*) can dissolve this statement.

Regarding those who practice through contemplative understanding: they contemplate that within a single thought-moment, the ten realms are inherently complete; their substance is interfused, such that sin and merit are no different.
This may be understood by referring to the standard explanations.
10. Regarding the two dharmas of the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*, *anāsava*), the Bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
"The outflowing and the non-outflowing constitute duality. If one realizes the equality of all dharmas, then the notions of 'outflowing' and 'non-outflowing' do not arise;
one does not cling to signs, nor does one dwell in signlessness. This is the entrance into the gate of non-duality."
That which is with outflows (*sāsrava*) refers to worldly phenomena characterized by signs (*nimitta*). That which is without outflows (*anāsrava*) refers to supramundane phenomena devoid of signs.
If one were to give rise to discrimination between outflows and the absence of outflows, one would not perceive the equal nature (*samatā-dharmatā*) of all phenomena.
Now, this Bodhisattva realizes the equality of phenomena and does not discriminate between outflows and the absence of outflows; thus, they do not abide [in such distinctions].
One does not dwell even in signlessness; this is entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The criteria for judging the teaching may be understood by reference to the eighth [section].

As for the contemplative interpretation: one contemplates the Middle Way within the mind, which is the simultaneous negation of both extremes—namely, outflows and the absence of outflows, as well as signs and signlessness.
This is the contemplation of the mind for entering the gate of non-duality.
11. Explaining the entry into the gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned:
The Bodhisattva Pure Understanding said, "The conditioned and the unconditioned constitute duality. If one leaves behind all numerical reckonings, then the mind is like space."
Emptiness. To be unimpeded by means of pure wisdom is to enter the gateway of non-duality. The mind of an ordinary person is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
the mind of a noble one (*ārya*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). It is in contrast to the conditioned that the unconditioned is spoken of.
These are the two methods of reckoning: the conditioned mind and the unconditioned mind.

When one completely distances oneself from both these methods of reckoning, at that time the mind is like empty space and attains pure wisdom, being unimpeded regarding both the conditioned and the unconditioned.
This is what is meant by entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): if one uses the mind of true emptiness to distinguish between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this belongs to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

If one uses the mind of the Middle Way to simultaneously negate both the conditioned and the unconditioned, thereby distinguishing between the partial and the complete [truths], it is judged as entering the Distinct and Perfect Teachings (*biejiao* and *yuanjiao*).
Regarding contemplative understanding: one contemplates that when a single thought-moment belongs to the dharma-realm of the six classes of ordinary beings, it is the conditioned mind;

when it belongs to the dharma-realm of the Two Vehicles, it is the unconditioned mind. When one contemplates the realm of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through the pure wisdom of the Middle Way, remaining unimpeded by departing from these two extremes—this is called entering the gate of non-duality by contemplating the mind.
Twelfth, entering the gate of non-duality by way of the two dharmas of the mundane and the supramundane.
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said: "The mundane and the supramundane constitute duality. The very nature of the mundane is empty; this is itself the supramundane.
Within it, there is no entering and no exiting, no overflowing and no dispersing. This is called entering the gate of non-duality."
Regarding the emptiness of the nature of the world: the afflictions and birth-and-death of the world are themselves bodhi and nirvāṇa;
therefore, their nature is fundamentally empty. Precisely because they are fundamentally empty, they are themselves the supramundane bodhi and nirvāṇa.
Consequently, within this interval, there is no bodhi or nirvāṇa to enter, nor is there any birth-and-death or affliction from which to emerge.
It does not overflow into the mundane world, nor is it dispersed within the supramundane. This is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality. Regarding the classification of the teachings:
the nature of the mundane world is itself the supramundane; form is itself emptiness; it is not that form ceases for there to be emptiness. Three.

In all teachings, one may speak thus. It is not by restricting the discussion to the evil of cultivation (*xiu-è*) that one speaks of the evil of nature (*xing-è*); this refers to both the general and the specific.
To thoroughly comprehend this is the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
Regarding "contemplative understanding" (*guan-jie*): a single mind is fully endowed with the ten realms. Six realms belong to the mundane world; four realms belong to the supramundane world.
Furthermore, the ten realms fundamentally reside within a single thought-moment; this is the emptiness of the nature of the mundane world, which is itself the supramundane.

There is no sixfold realm of ordinary beings from which to emerge, nor is there any realm of the four types of noble ones into which to enter. It neither overflows nor disperses—this is called contemplating the mind as the entry into the non-dual dharma-gate of the mundane and supramundane.
13. Explaining the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of birth-and-death and nirvana, the Bodhisattva Good Intention said:
"Birth-and-death and nirvana constitute a duality. If one perceives the nature of birth-and-death, then there is no birth-and-death."
There is neither bondage nor liberation; there is neither burning nor extinction. To understand in this way is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
The "Chapter on Maitreya’s Inquiry into Illness" states: "All dharmas are the very mark of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirvāṇa*); they cannot be extinguished further.
This mark of quiescent extinction is itself the nature of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Since it is said that they cannot be extinguished further, there is no birth-and-death. Since there is none..."
Regarding birth and death: since there is no birth and death [to be found], what birth and death could there be to bind, and what nirvana could there be to liberate?

As for those who judge the teachings: if one perceives that the nature of birth and death is itself without birth and death, and understands "form is emptiness," this belongs to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
If one takes the "Middle" alone as emptiness, it belongs to the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao). If one takes the "Perfect Middle" as emptiness, it belongs to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Regarding the teaching on "contemplative understanding": one contemplates that the form of a single moment of birth-and-death is itself the mark of quiescent extinction; it cannot be further extinguished, and thus there is no birth-and-death.
Since there is no birth-and-death, there is no bondage. This very mind of birth-and-death is itself liberation; this is what is meant by "contemplation."
The mind enters the gate of non-duality.
14. Explaining the entry into the gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of exhaustion and non-exhaustion:
The Bodhisattva Pratyakṣadarśin said, "Exhaustion and non-exhaustion are two dharmas. Whether it be ultimate exhaustion or non-exhaustion, both are [non-dual]."
The mark of inexhaustibility is itself emptiness. In emptiness, there is neither the mark of exhaustion nor the mark of non-exhaustion.
To enter in this manner is to enter the gate of the non-dual dharma.
To destroy afflictions and exhaust birth-and-death is called ultimate exhaustion; if they are not yet exhausted, it is called non-exhaustion.
To have both exhaustion and non-exhaustion constitutes two dharmas, and is not entry into the gate of non-duality.

Only when one thoroughly understands that birth-and-death and afflictions—regardless of whether they are exhausted or not—are all the inexhaustible mark of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and since they are thus emptiness itself, [one enters non-duality].
How could there be any obtainable distinction between the two dharmas of exhaustion and non-exhaustion? This is what constitutes entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas.
Regarding those who judge the teachings: the characteristics of exhaustion and non-exhaustion both ultimately return to emptiness;
thus, while all three teachings may speak of them, one must rely on the perspective of emptiness to determine their partiality or perfection.
As for the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that a single thought-moment is emptiness, which is the aspect of exhaustion; it is the provisional, which is the aspect of non-exhaustion;

and it is the middle, wherein the aspects of both exhaustion and non-exhaustion are all aspects of inexhaustibility. This is called entering the dharma-gate of non-duality through contemplating the aspects of the mind’s exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
Fifteenth, entering the gate of non-duality by way of the two dharmas of self and non-self.
The Bodhisattva Samantarakṣa said: "Self and non-self constitute a duality. Since even 'self' cannot be apprehended, how could 'non-self' be apprehended?"
One who perceives the true nature of the self no longer gives rise to duality; this is the entry into the gate of non-dual dharmas.
The true nature of my self—that is, the sixty-two views mentioned in the preceding sutra—is the lineage of the Tathāgata. It is the "self" within the view of self.
Since this self is already of the lineage of the Tathāgata, it is the eightfold sovereign self and should be called the true nature.
Yet, this self is not a self, and thus cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be anything to be apprehended when one speaks of "non-self" in relation to this self?
Thus, self and non-self are non-dual in essence; therefore, this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Regarding the classification of teachings (panjiao): if both self and non-self are ultimately subsumed within emptiness, this is termed "non-duality" (advaya);

this can be spoken of according to both the Shared and Distinct Teachings. However, if the eightfold sovereign self is taken as the true nature, then it belongs exclusively to the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
Regarding contemplative understanding: one contemplates that within a single moment of mind there is the sense of a sovereign master, which is termed "self.
This self is fundamentally not a self; one realizes that no nature of self can be found. This is precisely the Tathāgata-lineage of the eightfold mastery over the self.
Thus, since even a "self" cannot be found, how much less could there be the attainment of "non-self" through the destruction of the self? Contemplating in this manner, [one sees] the self and...
There is no self; its essence is non-dual. This is the dharma-gate of contemplating the mind as neither self nor non-self.
16. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of explaining the two dharmas of clarity and ignorance.
The Bodhisattva Vidyuddeva said: "To speak of clarity and ignorance as two is dualistic. The true nature of ignorance is itself clarity; yet clarity, too, cannot be grasped.
It is free from all numerical categories. To be equanimous within this, without duality—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the dharma of the dark afflictions of sentient beings; clarity (*vidyā*) is the dharma of the awakening illumination of the *bodhi* of all Buddhas.
These are spoken of in terms of cultivating defilement versus purity, or cultivating evil versus good.

It is not that there is no distinction between light and darkness, nor any difference between the ignorant and the wise; therefore, clarity and ignorance are said to be two. Now, from the perspective of the reality of this ignorance...

Regarding nature: one contemplates the nature of defilement and the nature of evil. Although there are distinctions between cultivated defilement and cultivated evil, the essence of the nature of defilement and the nature of evil is non-dual.

Is it not like water and waves? Although the characteristics of water and the characteristics of waves differ in their movement and stillness, the moisture of the wave-nature and the water-nature are one and the same.
Water, waves, and the ocean are nothing other than the nature of moisture; they pervade all realms together.
This is true illumination. Illumination itself cannot be grasped; to grasp it would result in duality. With its nature being neither defiled nor pure, it is of a single flavor and equality.
This is what is meant by entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): if one discusses the mutual identity (*xiangji*) between the views and afflictions within the realm of desire and the three types of *bodhi*, this principle is present in the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
If one discusses the mutual identity between ignorance outside the realm of desire and the three types of *bodhi*, this exists only in the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuantun jiao*);
the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*) does not share in this portion.

Regarding contemplative understanding: when the sense faculties and their objects encounter one another, a single thought-moment arises—whether it be greed, anger, or delusion; this is precisely ignorance (*avidyā*).
By means of the wisdom of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), one abandons these three poisons; this is true illumination (*vidyā*). These constitute the two [aspects].

To realize that this ignorance is the cultivation of defilement, which is itself the defilement of the nature (*prakṛti-saṃkleśa*), and for that defilement of the nature to be interfused such that there is no phenomenon that does not accord with it, is to spontaneously encompass all things.
One attains the true illumination of intrinsic purity. One contemplates that the actual nature of ignorance is itself true illumination; yet one does not even grasp at this illumination.
Within this state, there is equality and non-duality. This is what is meant by contemplating the mind as the non-duality of illumination and ignorance.
17. Explaining the entrance into the dharma-gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the Bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"Form and the emptiness of form constitute a duality. Form itself is emptiness; it is not that form ceases to exist for there to be emptiness. The very nature of form is itself empty.

It is the same with feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Consciousness and the emptiness of consciousness constitute a duality. Consciousness itself is emptiness; it is not that consciousness ceases to exist for there to be emptiness."
The nature of consciousness is inherently empty. To attain thorough penetration into this is to enter the gateway of non-dual dharmas.

Although the five aggregates are equally the phenomena of birth and death acquired as the retribution of sentient beings, when they are distinguished, the aggregate of form belongs to birth and death, while the other four aggregates belong to afflictions.
Within these five aggregates of grasping, there exists the luminosity of Prajñā-wisdom; therefore—
Those who wish to attain the Way of the Buddha can illuminate that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty, thereby crossing over all suffering and calamity;
this constitutes the second [point]. Furthermore, one must thoroughly understand that form (*rūpa*) is itself emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and that emptiness does not arise from the extinction of form.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. Thus, the phenomena of form pertaining to a person’s birth and death, as well as the phenomena of the mind consisting of afflictions (*kleśa*), are utterly ungraspable.
It is attained; it is precisely bodhi and nirvāṇa, the luminosity of prajñā-wisdom. One need not seek prajñā outside the five aggregates;
this is what constitutes entering the gate of non-duality.

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): if one takes the illusory forms of the six realms of ordinary beings and the true emptiness of the two vehicles as mutually identical—such that emptiness does not arise from the extinction of form—this is the initial gateway of the Mahāyāna teaching for entering the gate of non-duality.

If one takes the illusory forms of the nine realms as identical to the true emptiness of the Buddha-realm, this is the final teaching of the Mahāyāna gateway for entering the gate of non-duality. If one takes [the forms of] the ten realms...

Illusory form is precisely the nature of the ten realms, whether defiled or wholesome, which is true emptiness; it is not an emptiness resulting from the extinction of form. This is the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden:
that form is itself emptiness, entering the gate of non-duality.

Regarding contemplative understanding (*guan-jie*): one contemplates the single-moment mind of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Because it possesses thought, it defiles the true principle; this is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).
Its reception within the mind is the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). The mind taking this concentration as its object is the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

The mental activity applying itself to this principle is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The clear, distinct discrimination associated with conscious awareness is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, if one employs contemplation to dismantle these five aggregates, this is precisely the empty truth of *prajñā*. Thus, form and the emptiness of form constitute two;

yet, if one can thoroughly realize that this very form is itself emptiness—rather than emptiness being the result of the extinction of form—and that the nature of form is inherently empty, and so on up to consciousness, which is likewise—then one who attains penetration therein is said to contemplate that "form is itself [emptiness]."
Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality through Emptiness. ○ Eighteenth:
Explaining the entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by means of the two dharmas of "different kinds" and "the kind of emptiness.

The Bodhisattva Mingxiang said: "The four kinds [of phenomena] are different; the kind of emptiness is different. These constitute duality. The nature of the four kinds is itself the kind of emptiness."
Nature is empty because the prior limit and the posterior limit are empty; thus, the middle limit is also empty.
If one can know all such natures in this way, this is called entering the gateway of non-dual dharmas.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* clarifies the seven great elements (*mahābhūta*). Of these, the first five—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—are the "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*);
the latter two—the visual faculty and consciousness—are the "retributive body" (*upapatti-vipāka*). Since this [text] does not discuss the retributive body, it speaks only of the five great elements.

Among these five great elements, the preceding four—earth, water, fire, and wind—are things that possess form; therefore, they are said to be "fourfold differences. The subsequent great element of space lacks...
Because they are characterized as things, they are both empty and not different; thus, difference and non-difference constitute duality.
Now, within the *tathāgatagarbha*, one contemplates that the nature of form is itself true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is itself true form;
even so, the nature of wind is itself true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is itself true wind. Therefore, these four natures are themselves the nature of emptiness. This...
Having already established through horizontal pervasion throughout the ten directions that there is non-duality, this very horizontal pervasion is no different from vertical exhaustion.
Thus, as the past limit and the future limit are empty, so too is the middle limit empty.
To be able to know that these various natures are neither arising nor ceasing, and have neither coming nor going—this is what constitutes entry into the gate of the non-dual dharma.

Regarding the classification of teachings: if one can merely understand that the four kinds of natures in the mundane world are themselves the nature of emptiness, this refers to the general and specific intentions [of the teachings].
If one can understand the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, such as "form is truly empty," and so forth, this is the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
Regarding "contemplative understanding": one contemplates that within a single moment of the conscious mind, the ten realms, the five aggregates, and the lands are inherently complete.
Each of these possesses four distinct elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—as well as the distinct element of space, making two categories. Such natures are all the Tathāgatagarbha:
nature-form is true emptiness, and nature-emptiness is true form. Throughout the past, future, and present limits, every thought-moment is empty.
Thus, by contemplating the mind and all natures, one enters the gate of non-duality.
(19) Regarding the two dharmas of the eye and form, the Bodhisattva Subhāṣita said:
"The eye and form constitute duality. If one knows the nature of the eye such that it is neither greedy for nor angry toward form,"
Delusion—this is called tranquility. Likewise, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and flavors, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena constitute duality.
If one knows the nature of the mind such that it is without greed, hatred, or delusion toward mental phenomena, this is called tranquility.
To abide therein is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.
Now, the sense organs and their objects form a pair, just as yin and yang are matched or as husband and wife unite to procreate a child;

this has been so for a long time. If, at the beginning of a kalpa, when the human race had not yet paired, beings were suddenly born through transformation, how could there be such a thing as "birth from birth"?
The same applies to the six sense faculties: if one can know the nature of the eye, then it does not depend upon [external objects].
Regarding form (*rūpa*): if one does not take form as an object, then the three poisons will have no cause, and the seed of consciousness (*vijñāna*) will have no objective support.

Therefore, those who study the Path value the knowledge of the faculties (*indriya*). This is like the invocation of Aṅgulimāla through *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, wherein it is said that the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) perceives all Tathāgatas with constant clarity and distinction;
this is the cultivation of the five faculties, complete and without deficiency.
In the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, it is stated in all such passages: "Furthermore, as in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*: 'When seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing;

seeing is already apart from seeing, for seeing cannot reach it. This clarifies that if one knows the nature of the eye is free from greed, anger, and delusion regarding forms, this is called 'quiescence' (*śānti*).
This is the meaning of entering the gate of non-dual dharmas."

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): this is indeed a teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*). If one judges it according to its meaning, it can also be practiced by those who follow both the Common (*tong*) and Distinct (*bie*) teachings.

Regarding the practitioner of contemplative understanding (*guanjie*): "contemplation" (*guan*) refers precisely to the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*); to speak further of "contemplating the mind" would be redundant.
Twenty: Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of giving and dedication.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said: "Giving and dedicating it toward omniscience constitute two. The nature of giving is itself the nature of dedicating it toward omniscience.
It is the same for upholding the precepts, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom in their dedication."
All-knowledge constitutes duality. The very nature of wisdom is the nature of dedication toward all-knowledge.
To enter into the single characteristic within this is to enter the gate of non-dual dharmas.
This refers to the two aspects of dedicating the six perfections of the phenomenal (sāṃvṛtika) teachings toward the six perfections of principle (tattvika) and omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
The former consists of the six perfections of phenomena; since the sixth perfection therein also belongs to the phenomenal, its wisdom likewise must be dedicated toward omniscience.
As for the six perfections of the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*), once one has practiced giving, one does not dwell upon forms, sounds, odors, tastes, or tangibles.
How much more so for wisdom! Now, by dedicating the six perfections toward the nature of wisdom, one enters into the single mark;
thus, one should accord with the Prajñāpāramitā, giving rise to the mind while having nothing upon which to dwell.

Regarding the classification of teachings: one need only observe the "one mark" into which [the practitioner] enters—whether it be emptiness, the Middle Way, or the merely conventional versus the non-merely conventional—to understand the three teachings of the Vaipulya gate.
Regarding the contemplative understanding (*kuan-jie*): it has already been explained above that one contemplates how a single thought-moment is replete with the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*).

One then dedicates these six perfections toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). Furthermore, one can thoroughly comprehend that the nature of the six perfections is itself the nature of the omniscience toward which they are directed.
Within this, one does not perceive any distinction between the mind of the six perfections and the mind of omniscience; this is the contemplation of the mind.
Entering the Dharma-gate of the Single Characteristic and Non-duality.
○ Twenty-one: Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by means of the two dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
The Bodhisattva Gambhīraprajñā said: "To regard 'emptiness,' 'signlessness,' and 'wishlessness' as two is dualistic. Emptiness is itself signlessness. It is wishlessness.
Marks are themselves non-action. If emptiness, signlessness, and non-action are present, then mind, thought, and consciousness are absent.
That which is a single gate of liberation is itself the three gates of liberation; this is entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
The single mind of a person is fundamentally empty from the beginning; it is also fundamentally without marks and without activity.
These three gates of liberation are likewise fundamentally one essence; they are given different names according to their respective meanings.

That people fail to realize this is because their conscious intellect conditions sensory objects and discriminates them, thereby rendering it not empty, attributing marks to it, and [attributing activity to it].
Thus one acts with the ear. By this, one is able to attain that which is without mind, thought, or consciousness, and immediately realizes the three gates of liberation.
Since these gates of liberation are of a single essence, one attains the three by means of the one, and manifests the one by means of the three.
This is what is meant by entering the gate of non-dual dharmas.
Regarding those who judge the teachings, all three liberations and four teachings may be spoken of; however, the primary intent here lies in the Mahāyāna.
It is simply that one observes whether it is through emptiness or the Middle Way, and whether it is categorized as Shared, Distinct, or Perfect.
Regarding contemplative understanding: one contemplates a single moment of mind across the three periods of time and its four characteristics, examining each one until nothing can be found.
It is primordially empty by nature and devoid of any marks. Who is the creator? When contemplating in this way, the functioning of mind, intellect, and consciousness ceases.
Emptiness is itself signlessness; signlessness is itself non-action. Within this single liberation, there are thus the three liberations.
This is the gate of non-duality regarding the three liberations through the contemplation of the mind.
Twenty-second: Entering the Gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of the Three Jewels.
