The Bodhisattva Śāntendriya said: "Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha constitute duality. The Buddha is itself the Dharma; the Dharma is itself the Saṅgha. These three..."
All jewels possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and are equal to empty space; all phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise so.
One who can practice in accordance with this enters the gateway of non-dual dharmas (*advayadharmamukha*).
The Dharma is original enlightenment (*benjue*); the Buddha is initial enlightenment (*shijue*); and the Sangha is the harmonious union of the initial and the original.
These are the true Three Jewels. When that original enlightenment is in a state of delusion and initial enlightenment has not yet arisen, then the Three Jewels are all hidden and do not manifest.
This is what is meant by the saying: "Throughout hundreds of thousands of myriads of kalpas, one does not hear even the name of the Three Jewels."
Once one has realized the originally inherent awakened nature, one employs the wisdom of initial awakening (*ādikṣaya-jñāna*) to illuminate original awakening (*mūla-awakening*).
When initial and original awakening merge as one, both initial and original awakening are forgotten. At that moment, the Three Jewels appear simultaneously.
Is it not the case that the Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Saṅgha? These Three Jewels are all without marks (*animitta*), equal to empty space, within the single mind.
Since this is so for all phenomena, it is because there is nothing that is not original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).

Regarding the classification of the teachings, while this principle may be articulated within all Mahāyāna schools, its primary intent lies specifically in the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*) teaching.
Regarding contemplative understanding: one contemplates that a single thought-moment is the inherent nature, essence, and magnitude of the Buddha-nature.

That which is contemplated is the Dharma Jewel of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*); that which contemplates is the Buddha Jewel of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*). When initial and original enlightenment accord with one another, this is the Sangha Jewel of their unified integration.
23. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of the body and the extinction of the body.
The Bodhisattva Unobstructed Mind said: "The body and the extinction of the body constitute duality. The body itself is the extinction of the body. Why is this so?"

One who perceives the true mark of the body does not give rise to the view of a body nor the view of the extinction of the body. Body and the extinction of the body are non-dual and without distinction.
To be neither startled nor afraid within this is to enter the gate of the non-dual Dharma.

"The body and the extinction of the body" refers to the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) extinguishing the physical body to enter the nirvāṇa of cessation without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*).

Because one is suffering and one is bliss, one is existence and one is non-existence, they constitute "two. "The body is itself the extinction of the body" means what is called seeing the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the body.
This is because, within the path of suffering, one is able to see the *dharmakāya*; therefore, one does not give rise to the view of a body or the view of the extinction of a body.

Cessation. Is it not the case that when the body and the cessation of the body are both absent, there is neither suffering nor pleasure, nor does one give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the body or its cessation?
When people of inferior faculties perceive this true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), few fail to be struck with alarm and fear.
Only those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence awaken to the fact that this *dharmakāya* is primordially present; therefore, they are neither alarmed nor afraid.
Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): the duality of the body and its extinction is the view and understanding of the Two Vehicles.

If one realizes that the body and its extinction are non-dual, then one can enter both the initial and final teachings of the Mahāyāna—namely, that "form is itself emptiness," and not that "emptiness results from the extinction of form.

To perceive the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the body and realize that the path of suffering is itself the *dharmakāya* is the capacity of those with the faculties for the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
This is the gateway to awakening into one's nature.

As for "contemplative understanding," it means contemplating that a single thought-moment is fully endowed with the five aggregates (*skandhas*). By illuminating and clearly realizing the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), one perceives that suffering is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
The body and the extinction of the body are non-dual and without distinction; this is called contemplating the mind and the body’s entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality.
(24) This is the twenty-fourth [section], which explains the entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality by means of the two dharmas of body, speech, and mind.
The Bodhisattva Supreme Goodness said: "The actions of body, speech, and mind constitute duality. These three types of action are all characterized by non-action.
The non-characteristic of the body is the same as the non-characteristic of speech; the non-characteristic of speech is the same as the non-characteristic of the mind.

That these three types of action are characterized by non-action is the same as all phenomena being characterized by non-action. One who can thus accord with the wisdom of non-action has entered [the Way]."
Regarding the Dharma-gate of Non-duality:
when the body performs acts of walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, or engages in grasping and moving about; when the mouth sings, chants, or speaks;

and when the mind reflects or deliberates—all these involve conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*). Yet, the three karmas are fundamentally empty; this is precisely the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*), which is entirely without conditioned activity. Although the three karmas...
Third: Since non-characteristic is one, the body is without the characteristic of activity, and likewise the mouth is without the characteristic of activity;

these are the three karmas as the primary retribution (*sambhogika-niṣyanda*). All phenomena are the secondary retribution (*āśraya-vipāka*). Although the secondary and primary differ, the principle of non-activity is the same.
Therefore, the non-activity of the three karmas is the non-activity of all phenomena. To be able to thus know wisdom in accordance with non-activity—this is [the third].
In order to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality,
those who classify the teachings (panjiao) maintain that this meaning also applies to the Mahāyāna; it is simply by means of the mark of non-action— whether as emptiness or the Middle Way—
that one distinguishes between the partial and the perfect.
The understanding through contemplation can be known.
○ Twenty-fifth, entering the gate of non-duality is explained by way of the two dharmas of merit and transgression.
The Bodhisattva Merit Field said: "Meritorious action, transgressive action, and immovable action constitute duality. The true nature of these three types of action is precisely [non-duality]."
Emptiness. In emptiness, there is no meritorious action, no sinful action, and no immovable action.
To not give rise to these three types of action is to enter the gate of non-duality.
There are three kinds of practice. There are those that are shallow and proximate; as Master Kumārajīva said: "Wholesome deeds of the desire realm bring about the retribution of pleasure;
unwholesome deeds, the ten paths of non-virtue, bring about the retribution of suffering; and immovable deeds are the practices of meditative concentration in the realms of form and formlessness.
There are also those that are perfect and sudden, which realize the nature of the three virtues and depart from the defilement of the three delusions.
Physical and verbal karmas that accord with principle and are without deliberate effort are called meritorious actions (*puṇya-karma*).

When one is deluded regarding the nature of the three virtues and defiled by the three afflictions, physical and verbal karmas that oppose principle and involve deliberate effort are called evil actions (*apuṇya-karma*).

To be able to thoroughly comprehend this, remaining constantly in meditative concentration without a moment of non-concentration, is called immovable action (*āneñjya-karma*). When the self-mind is inherently empty and neither sin nor merit has a master, movement [is transcended].
Since both the immovable and the non-immovable are not apart from the three natures, how could there be any distinction between meritorious action,
sinful action, and immovable action? Therefore, in daily life, when none of these three dharmas arise at all, this is called entering the gate of non-duality.

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): this principle also applies to the three vehicles of the Mahāyāna; however, it is only when interpreted according to the final explanation that it becomes perfect and complete (*yuan*).

Regarding the contemplative understanding (*guanjie*): contemplating the thoughts of the nine realms is termed "meritorious action" (*puxing`); contemplating the thoughts of the Buddha-realm is termed "virtuous action" (*fuxing`).
In a single thought-moment, all is empty and quiescent; all [phenomena] are simultaneously negated. This is called "immovable practice.
Such is the true nature of these three practices: it is emptiness. Being empty, the three practices do not exist. Within these three practices, nothing whatsoever arises.
This is the contemplation of the mind that enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
26. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of self and other.
The Bodhisattva of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra said: "To give rise to duality from the self constitutes duality. One who perceives the true reality of the self does not give rise to dualistic dharmas."
If one does not abide in these two dharmas, then there is no consciousness. That which has nothing to be cognized is the entry into the gate of non-duality.
As for the arising of duality from the self: because there is a self, there is "the other"; thus, duality is established. To perceive the true reality of the self—
Thus one awakens to the true self. The true self is no-self; when the mutual dependence of form is extinguished, dualistic dharmas do not arise.

When "self" and "other" are established, the discriminative consciousness of phenomena arises; when these two dharmas are forgotten, there is no such consciousness. Therefore, this is the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Regarding those who judge the teachings: if one merely forgets the phenomenal consciousness and perceives the partial, true self, this belongs to the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
If one perceives the Middle Way’s true self while forgetting both forms of consciousness, this belongs to the Distinct and Complete Teachings (Bie and Yuan).

Regarding the contemplative understanding: at the time of contemplating the mind, there is the apprehension of subject and object; because of "self," that [object] arises, and these constitute duality.
By illuminating the Middle Way within the self, one enters the contemplation that transcends dependence and forgets conditions—this is the Dharma-gate of the non-duality of contemplating the mind.
27. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of "having something to obtain":
The Bodhisattva Guṇakūṭa said, "The characteristic of having something to obtain constitutes duality. If there is nothing to be obtained, then there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
That which is without grasping or abandoning is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
All phenomena are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*). In delusion there is nothing to be abandoned; in awakening there is nothing to be grasped.
In the state of an ordinary person there is nothing lost; in the state of a noble one (*ārya*) there is nothing attained. Therefore, those who can awaken to this, regarding all phenomena—
Without grasping and without abandoning, one enters the gate of non-dual dharmas. The Heart Sūtra also says:
"Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva attains unsurpassed bodhi."

Regarding the "determiner of the teachings" (panjiao): it is the meaning of non-attainment (*anupalabdhi*), as explained in the *Heart Sūtra*. It universally encompasses the Mahāyāna teachings; this [text] is identical to that.

Regarding the "contemplative understanding" (guanjie): one contemplates that every single thought-moment is none other than the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, each and every one perfectly accomplished and entirely without attainment.
This is called entering the gate of non-duality by contemplating the mind.
28. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of light and darkness:
The Bodhisattva Candrottara said, "Darkness and light constitute duality. Where there is neither darkness nor light, there is no duality. Why is this?
Just as when one enters the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling, there is neither darkness nor light; so too it is with the characteristics of all dharmas."
To enter into equality within this is to enter the gateway of non-dual dharmas.
When obscured by delusion, there is the darkness of afflictions; after awakening to clarity, there is the true illumination of wisdom. Thus, there is delusion and awakening, and darkness and light.
Therefore, they are treated as two. Originally there was no delusion, and now there is likewise no enlightenment. There is neither darkness nor light; how could there be duality?

Thus, it is illustrated by the metaphor of the two vehicles entering the meditative absorption of the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*). Therein, the six sense faculties are entirely suspended and mental activity is completely extinguished.
Although days and nights pass, one does not perceive the difference between darkness and light. Is this true only of the mind? It is so for all phenomena as well.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between delusion and awakening, or darkness and light.
For those who classify the teachings (*panjiao*), the categories of delusion/awakening and darkness/light do not apply; all three teachings may be spoken of in this regard.
One need only observe their non-duality—whether they are characterized as emptiness or the Middle Way—to determine whether they are partial or perfect.

As for "contemplating the mind": one contemplates that the single thought-moment of ignorance is itself true illumination. Fundamentally, there is no distinction between light and darkness, nor any difference between awakening and delusion;
it is of a single flavor and equal. This is what is meant by contemplating the mind as entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
29. Entering the Dharma-door of Nonduality by way of the two dharmas of delighting in nirvāṇa and not delighting in the world.
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said: "Delighting in nirvāṇa and not delighting in the world constitute duality. If one does not delight in nirvāṇa..."
To have no weariness with the world is to be without duality. Why is this? If there were bondage, there would be liberation.
If there were originally no bondage, who would seek liberation? Without bondage and without liberation, there is neither delight nor aversion; this is entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

The reason why those of the Hīnayāna delight in nirvāṇa and loathe the mundane world is that they perceive the existence of the fetters of birth and death within the mundane world and the liberation of nirvāṇa within the supramundane; thus, they give rise to longing for the latter and aversion toward the former.
Therefore, these constitute duality. Now, the Mahāyāna bodhisattva understands that the world of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is itself the supramundane *nirvāṇa*.

Since it is fundamentally unbound from the beginning, what need is there to seek liberation? Thus, there is no distinction between longing for one and loathing the other; this is why they enter the gate of non-dual dharmas.

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): although the principle that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual is one, there is still a distinction between what is within and outside the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Now, as for the teaching that brings the two dharmas within the world into non-duality, this is the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).

As for bringing those outside the world into non-duality, it is divided into the Distinct and the Perfect Teachings (*biejiao* and *yuanjiao*) based on whether they are "partial" or "complete" non-duality.

As for the practitioner who enters through contemplative understanding: they contemplate that the single thought-moment of the mind of birth-and-death is itself the mind of nirvana. Birth-and-death and nirvana possess no dual characteristics;
there is neither bondage nor liberation. This is called entering the gate of non-duality by contemplating the mind.
Thirty: Explaining the entry into the gate of non-dual dharma by way of the two dharmas of the correct and the deviant.
The Bodhisattva Maṇicūḍarāja said: "The correct path and the deviant path constitute duality.
One who abides in the correct path does not discriminate between what is deviant and what is correct. To be free from these two is to enter the gate of non-dual dharma."
As for "false paths," the ninety-five kinds of mental activities that follow deviant tracks are all termed false paths.
As for the "right path," it refers to the teachings spoken by the Buddha; whether they pertain to the teachings for humans, devas, or the three vehicles, they are all termed the right path.

Furthermore, regarding what is false or right, there is no distinction between internal and external; one considers only the mind. This is what is meant by the statement: "To perceive the Buddhas through deluded conceptualization... the Buddha...
This too becomes erroneous. When one observes sentient beings with right wisdom, sentient beings are likewise wondrous.
Although one who makes this statement possesses the merit of discerning the correct, they have not yet grasped the principle of total integration.
Therefore, those who enter the direct path must forget both the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox; only then can they enter.

As for those who judge the teachings (*panjiao*), they transcend the duality of the heterodox and the orthodox. It can be said that the "Shared Teaching" (*tongjiao*) realizes that form is identical to emptiness through a contemplation that forgets conditions;
even those who enter the Path of Truth in the "Tripitaka Teaching" (*zangjiao*) are able to forget [dualistic attachments].

However, one must examine whether what is forgotten is heterodox or orthodox, and whether the "Dharma-gate of Non-duality" entered therein is emptiness or the Middle Way. When judging their respective teachings, there is no [fixed standard].
It does not conform to the compass.

Regarding the contemplation of liberation: one observes that when the faculties and their objects arise in opposition, thoughts belonging to the nine realms constitute cultivated evil and are all deviant paths;
thoughts belonging to the Buddha-realm constitute cultivated good and are the true path. These constitute two. To penetrate this, cultivated evil is itself inherent evil.
Cultivating goodness is itself the nature of goodness. As for the good and evil of nature, their essence is fundamentally interfused; thus, evil is precisely good, and good is precisely evil.
When one contemplates in this manner, one does not discriminate between the heterodox and the orthodox, thereby entering the contemplation that forgets conditions.
This is called contemplating the mind to enter the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
31. Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality by way of the two dharmas of reality and unreality.
The Bodhisattva Delighting in Reality said: "Reality and unreality constitute duality. One who perceives reality does not even perceive reality;
how much less so that which is unreal? Why is this? It is not seen by the fleshly eye; it is only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) that can see it. And yet, this wisdom-eye..."
To see nothing that is not seen—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
"Reality" refers to true emptiness (*śūnyatā*); "unreality" refers to illusory existence. One who has "true vision" is a person who has already realized true emptiness.
Since true emptiness is itself empty, what could possibly be seen? Therefore, one does not even see reality; for illusory existence is fundamentally non-existent.
Now it is further confirmed as real; how much more so could that which is not real be obtained? Therefore, the inquiry and explanation state: "It is not seen by the fleshly eye;
only the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*) can see it. Yet this wisdom-eye neither sees nor does not see.
Now, how could there be duality in neither seeing nor not seeing?"

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): from the perspective of what is seen by the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*), the provisional teaching aligns with the stage of "having already accomplished" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*); the distinct teaching aligns with the seventh stage (*bhūmi*);
and the perfect teaching aligns with the seventh level of faith (*śraddhā*). All of these possess this meaning.

However, as for the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who has attained the true wisdom-eye, he does not perceive reality or unreality through dualistic marks; he neither sees nor does not see, abiding solely in the Perfect and Sudden.
Regarding the contemplation of the mind: one contemplates that a single thought-moment is fully endowed with the ten realms. The nine realms are unreal; the Buddha-realm is real.
One who attains the true mark of all phenomena and sees according to reality does not even perceive the reality of the Buddha-realm, let alone the unreality of the nine realms.
Because the Buddha-realm is real, the nine realms are unreal; because the nine realms are unreal, they are the Buddha-realm.
The realm is real; not observing the single thought-moment through dualistic characteristics is the true eye of wisdom.
To neither see nor not to see is the gate of non-dual observation of the mind.
II. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva’s Exposition on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
First, the various bodhisattvas inquire about entering the dharma-gate of non-duality.
After all these bodhisattvas have each spoken, they ask Mañjuśrī: "What is the bodhisattva's entry [into the dharma-gate of non-duality]?"
The Gate of Non-dual Dharma.
Second, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī answers by using words to dispel words.
Mañjuśrī said: "According to my understanding, regarding all dharmas, there is no speech and no discourse; there is no demonstration and no..."
Consciousness is free from all questioning and answering; this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

The teachings on entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality provided by the thirty-one bodhisattvas have already involved verbal expression and were demonstrated to others through the exchange of questions and answers—all of which are accessible to the mental consciousnesses of sentient beings. Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, wishing to—

To obliterate emotional consciousness, one employs words to dispel it; yet, regarding all phenomena, one must be without words, without speech, without demonstration, and without consciousness, transcending all questioning and answering.
Only then can one enter the gate of the non-dual dharma (*advaya-dharma-mukha*). Within this, the single character "consciousness" (*shí*) is the central theme.
Its role in the classification of teachings and the contemplation of the mind is fully elucidated in the following chapter.
III. Vimalakīrti’s Discourse on Entering the Dharma-gate of Non-duality (3). First, Mañjuśrī asks about entering the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī asked Vimalakīrti: "We have each spoken for ourselves; you, O worthy one, should now speak."
"What is this entry into the dharma-gate of non-duality?
Vimalakīrti, the layman, answered by dispelling words with wordlessness;
at that time, Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word.
Then the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī praised his excellence, exclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent! That which is utterly devoid of letters and speech—this is the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality."
Four or five thousand bodhisattvas heard the Dharma and obtained benefit.

When this "Chapter on Entering the Dharma-Gate of Non-Duality" was being preached, within this assembly, five thousand bodhisattvas all entered the dharma-gate of non-duality and attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Master Sheng said: "Although Mañjuśrī clearly understood that there is nothing that can be said, he had not yet clarified that speaking itself is non-speaking.
This is why Vimalakīrti remained silent and spoke no word, thereby demonstrating that speech is not real.
If speech were indeed real, how could one remain silent? Master Zhao said: "To speak about the unspeakable is not as good as being unspeakable within the unspeakable. Therefore..."
There was silence. The aforementioned bodhisattvas placed their words within the realm of dharmalakṣaṇa; Mañjuśrī spoke regarding the wordless;
Vimalakīrti remained wordless within the wordless. These three were identical in their realization of the fundamental principle, yet their manifestations differed in depth.
Thus it is truly said that speech follows the wordless, and knowledge follows the unknowable.
Deng said: "To exhaust the source, one discards the oar; at the end of the road, one leaves behind the whip.

This is the inevitability of principle and that which all people equally recognize. To investigate the ultimate reality of non-arising, it is supremely vast and expansive; one encounters nothing before oneself."
Following this, there is no subsequent [reality]. It is that which the mind cannot reach and which speech cannot express; its arrival is ancient.
Therefore, the myriad phenomena of birth and death take consciousness as their root and speech as their expression.
Once speech has taken form, written characters compete to arise. Those who stray from the Way are numerous; they are confused by words and deluded regarding their nature. Following [this path]...
The Way is like the lost sheep at a forked path; with ten thousand streams and a thousand branches, all paths diverge and return to the source.
Were it not for Great Awakening (*Mahābodhi*), who could point the way back?

These Dharma-gates expounded by the thirty-three great Bodhisattvas are all the constant principles of Great Awakening and the swift path to non-arising (*anutpāda*). Some express the Way through words, while others...
Yet he employs speech to dispel it, or sometimes uses silence to dispel speech. Now, when one reaches the point where silence dispels speech, the Way has reached its ultimate.
Did not Mañjuśrī say: "In my view, regarding all phenomena, there is no speech and no discourse, no demonstration and no cognition;
they are free from all questions and answers. When the Way reaches this state, it may be said that the source has been exhausted. Truly.
This allowed Yimou and Vimalakīrti to each possess their own singular excellence.
Yet, since it was said that he had transcended all questions and answers, Vimalakīrti’s verbal threads had already revealed their sharp edge;
he could not avoid the single stroke of Mañjuśrī. Nevertheless, although the methods shown therein were different paths, the principle they employed was one and the same.
The merit is not different; it simply arises from inversion and origination. Taking the path as a temporary means to return home, the Way is transmitted through words.
Without words, there would be no way to point toward its essentials. Words are like dregs; yet without discarding words, one cannot obtain the pure essence.
Discarding words is still a form of speaking; without silence, one cannot realize the ultimate aim. Therefore, having realized this, one returns to the source, though the paths taken may differ.
They follow the same track. Is it not because, among the thirty-three gates, each gate requires these three stages?
First, one practices according to each individual gate; in the middle, one dispels them through wordlessness;
and finally, one realizes them through silence. Only then can one enter the gate of non-arising. Thus, as for Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...
That he alone sighed in admiration of Vimalakīrti was surely because he first attained the ultimate through silence;

it was not that silence could be exclusively favored while speech could be entirely discarded. However, as these matters involve the doctrines and principles of the teachings, their reasoning is subtle and profound.
Although the phrasing and flavor follow what has preceded them, let us attempt a detailed examination of their underlying understanding hereafter.
I hope that those who aspire to the Way may grasp its essential meaning and proceed with their cultivation. To further explain this significance, the text is divided into four parts:
first, clarifying the meaning of non-arising; second, clarifying the meaning of the gateway; third, clarifying the meaning of the non-dual dharma; and fourth, clarifying the meaning of entry.
The principle of non-arising is like a celestial king bestowing a magnificent mansion; therefore, it is elucidated first. Although it has been attained...
A great residence must be entered through its gates; therefore, they are explained next. Although one may find the gate, one must possess the method for entering it;
therefore, the third [topic] explains this. A gate is so called because it enables passage; it facilitates both exiting and entering; therefore, the fourth [topic] explains this.
The wise attain understanding through analogies; thus, they know that what I have further explained is not redundant.

First, to clarify the meaning of non-arising (*anutpāda*): the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* elucidates the five patiences (*kṣānti*). First is the patience of subduing (*avaivartika-kṣānti*); second is the patience of conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*); third is the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*).

These are set aside and not discussed here, as they precede the stages of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]. Fourth is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Their positions are at the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Distinct Teaching and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching. Although the previous explanation stated that the meaning applies to all three teachings, here we specifically refer to the Perfect Teaching;

from the first dwelling up to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), these are all stages of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Fifth, the patience of extinction (*kṣaya-kṣānti*):

both the Distinct and Perfect Teachings place this at the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*prabhāsvara-bodhi*). However, the Distinct Teaching only discusses the destruction of twelve grades of ignorance (*avidyā*). Regarding the... [text ends]
To say that the true cause of our own house serves as the ultimate fruit of your house is, for now, set aside without further discussion.

Rather, we shall speak only of the stage of Perfect Wondrous Enlightenment as the "Patience of Quiescent Extinction" (*śānta-nirodha-kṣānti*). Now, these two types of patience refer to the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) of birth, abiding, change, and extinction;
they are named precisely after the delusions that are to be destroyed. Therefore, they begin from the first dwelling (*prathama-bhūmi*).

Because it destroys the ignorance of the characteristic of arising, it is called "non-arising. Because wondrous awakening destroys the ignorance of the characteristic of cessation, it is named "quiescent extinction" (*śānti*).

Since this sutra clarifies the dharma realized by Bodhisattvas, it takes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) as the principle entered through the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
Therefore, in the opening chapter, the Bodhisattva Dharmeśvara explains the entry into the Dharma-gate of Non-duality.
At the conclusion of the chapter, it says that five thousand bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Thus, we know that the "Gate of Non-duality" is the innermost sanctum; furthermore, the patience of the non-arising of dharmas realized by the bodhisattvas is taken as its definitive essence.
Second, regarding the meaning of the "gates" (dvāra): "gate" is a metaphor. It is like a residence; if one wishes to reach the innermost sanctuary, one must enter through the gate.
The Dharma-gates of the Buddha are likewise so: since the Path enters by way of the gates, they are metaphorically called "gates.
However, there are three distinct types—the Gate of Teaching, the Gate of Practice, and the Gate of Principle—as previously explained. Now, specifically...
This clarifies the gate of practice. Therefore, it is called "entering the gate of non-dual dharmas. However, gates are established based on principle, and there are four such principles;
thus, the gates through which one enters are also established as four. Although there are four meanings, the principles are but three—namely, the Three Truths:
first, the principle of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), which establishes all phenomena; if there is a gate, it is entered through this. Second, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The principle [of the Middle Way] subsumes all phenomena; one enters it by means of the gate of emptiness.

Regarding the principle of the threefold truth, one simultaneously illuminates the two extremes of emptiness and existence, entering it by means of the gate of both existence and emptiness. This simultaneously negates the two extremes of emptiness and existence.

One may enter by way of a gate that is neither empty nor existent; however, the gate entered upon in this present chapter is precisely the gate of emptiness, because it is said to be "entering the gate of the dharma of non-arising.
Although it is the gate of emptiness, its meaning also encompasses the four [truths].
For example, the two dharmas pointed out constitute the gate of existence, while the non-dual dharma entered therein constitutes the gate of emptiness. Within these, there is also...
When both emptiness and existence are forgotten, as with birth-and-death and nirvana, neither is established; this is the gate of "neither.
Since there is "neither," how could there not be "both"? For the time being, the gate of emptiness is taken as the primary focus.
Master Tiantai, however, frequently established the "wordless phrase" beyond the four propositions to encompass the intent of transcending words.

One must understand that the principle of wordlessness also possesses degrees of excellence; it is not found solely in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), but is likewise present in the three preceding teachings.
Furthermore, it is not unique to Buddhism; even among the non-Buddhist paths of India and the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism in this land, it exists as well.
As the *Analects* states: "What does Heaven say? The four seasons proceed, and the hundred things are born."
"This is the 'silence' of the Master Kong (Confucius). The *Daodejing* says: 'The Way that can be spoken of is not the eternal Way.
Excessive words lead to exhaustion; it is better to maintain the center. This is the 'silence' of the Master Li (Laozi). Zhufu Zi said:

'In conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is a self (*ātman*) within the fifth [category], the Ineffable Treasury (*anabhilāpya-kośa*). This is the 'silence' of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) of the Western Heavens. [End of] Body.
The Master said: "I have heard that within liberation there is no verbal expression. This is the 'wordlessness' of the Tripitaka Teaching of the Hīnayāna.
That the three vehicles equally employ the path of wordless speech to realize the nature of phenomena and enter the truth—this is the 'wordlessness' of the Shared Teaching.
The 'Wordless Youth' in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*—this is the 'wordlessness' of the Distinct Teaching. Thus did the Tathāgata conceal [the ultimate meaning].
Vimalakīrti remained silent at Vaiśālī, and Śāriputra was silenced at Magadha; this is the wordlessness of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
People today like to take such wordlessness as the realization of the Way, regarding it as the Supreme Vehicle; one must not fail to understand this. Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Arising within arising cannot be spoken of; non-arising within arising cannot be spoken of; arising within non-arising [cannot be spoken of]..."
It can be spoken of. That which is neither arising nor non-arising cannot be spoken of. Beyond the four teachings and four gates, it is indeed true that each possesses a wordless phrase.
Regarding the third point, the meaning of the non-dual dharma: the non-dual dharma is precisely the non-arising into which one enters. As it is said:
This Dharma is precisely the entrance into non-duality. Since this is now the gate of non-arising, it is called "non-dual.

As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "arising and arising cannot be described," and so forth, regarding arising and non-arising—given that this current scripture contains thirty-three individuals each explaining the Dharma-gate of non-duality they have entered—one may infer from other locations and other scriptures that this is likewise the case.

There is also that which is taught: the entry into the realm of arising-arising is a dharma-gate that is neither one nor many; the entry into the realm of non-arising-arising is a dharma-gate that is both two and not one;
the entry into the realm of non-arising-non-arising is a dharma-gate that is neither two nor not-two.

This is briefly as in the preceding sutra: liberation comes from wisdom combined with skillful means; bondage comes from skillful means lacking wisdom; liberation comes from skillful means combined with wisdom; [bondage comes from wisdom lacking skillful means].
Skillful means are bound by wisdom; wisdom is non-duality, while skillful means are multiplicity. Entering into one's own practice is entering non-duality;
benefiting others is entering multiplicity. This meaning is distributed throughout the various sutras and can be fully encompassed within four statements, leaving nothing out:
namely, the dharma-gate of non-duality, the dharma-gate of multiplicity, and the dharma-gate that is neither non-dual nor multiple.
Gate. It is neither a gate of non-duality nor a gate of non-unity. Students should not cling to one corner or damage the other; this is the proper way.
Regarding those who enter the meaning [of the teachings], "entering" refers to the contemplation of phenomena (*dharmānupaśyanā*).

According to the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, and other scriptures, as well as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other treatises, which clearly elucidate the definitive meaning, there are three types of contemplation of phenomena: first, the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); second, [the contemplation of formlessness]; third, [the contemplation of wishlessness].

The contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*). Among the three [contemplations], this is the contemplation of the middle. This sutra also possesses these three according to its meaning, as already explained previously.

Entering into the meaning of the present text is precisely the contemplation of emptiness (*kong-guan*), because it employs the principle that "non-exhaustion does not obstruct. This accords with the aforementioned non-duality (*buer*).
Having already categorized this through the fourfold analysis (*catuṣkoṭi*), there are likewise four aspects to the present meaning of "entry" (*praveśa*).

First is entry into contemplation, which corresponds to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*’s contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional. Second is emergence from contemplation, which corresponds to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*’s contemplation of emerging from emptiness into the conventional.
Third is the contemplation that is both entry and emergence. Fourth is the contemplation that is neither entry nor emergence; this corresponds to the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
From the provisional [aspect] of emptiness, one enters the contemplation of the Middle Way. Because it simultaneously illuminates the two truths, this is the entry and exit of "both.

Because it simultaneously negates the two truths, this is the entry and exit of "neither. Contemplating by means of this, one knows that the meaning of "entry" likewise possesses four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Since the character "entry" (*ru*) is the contemplating subject—the contemplation—it must necessarily have an object of contemplation; this refers to the section below.

This refers to the term "character" (or "syllable"). However, there are two types of objects: the object of principle (*li*) and the object of phenomena (*shi*). The object of principle is the meaning of non-duality.

The object of phenomena refers to the two dharmas explained by the thirty-one individuals. These thirty-one dharmas do not go beyond the ten objects of contemplation (*shijing*) observed in the *Mohe Zhiguan*:
first, the object of the aggregates, bases, and elements; second, the object of afflictions; third, the object of illness; fourth, the object of karmic characteristics... [and so forth].
The objects of the five maras; the objects of the six dhyānas; the objects of the various views; the objects of overweening pride; the objects of the two vehicles;
and the objects of the bodhisattvas. As in the first case, that of arising and ceasing; the second, that of self and what belongs to self; the third, that of acceptance and non-acceptance;
the fourth, that of defilement and purity; the fifth, that of mental movement; and the sixth, that of the single characteristic and the absence of characteristics—these are all the *skandhas*.

The sixth is the realm of the *dhātus* (elements). The seventh is the mind of the Bodhisattva; it is the realm of the Bodhisattva. The mind of the Śrāvaka is the realm of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
The eighth, the wholesome and unwholesome, and the ninth, sin and merit, are the realms of the characteristics of karma.

The tenth, the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), half belongs to the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) and half belongs to the realm of the Two Vehicles. The eleventh, the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), is likewise...
Half belong to the *āyatanas* (sense bases), and half belong to the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). The twelfth [pair] is the mundane and the supramundane;

the thirteenth is birth-and-death and nirvāṇa—both of these belong to the same two categories as before. The fourteenth is the exhausted and the inexhaustible; the fifteenth is the self and the non-self.
The sixteenth clarifies ignorance (*avidyā*). The seventeenth is the emptiness of form (*rūpa-śūnyatā*). The eighteenth concerns the fourfold difference between space and the elements.
These five objects are halfly objects of phenomena (*vastu-viṣaya*) and halfly objects of principle (*tattva-viṣaya*). The nineteenth is the sphere of the eye and forms as an aggregate (*skandha*).
The twentieth is the object of the act of giving (*dāna-vastu*), dedicated toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*); this is an object of principle. The twenty-first...

Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are the objects of the two vehicles (the second). The twenty-second is the Three Jewels; the objects of the aggregates and sense bases, as well as the realm of principle.
The twenty-third is the body and the extinction of the body; the objects of the aggregates, sense bases, and principle.

The twenty-fourth is the three karmas; the objects of the characteristics of karma. The twenty-fifth is the practice of merit and demerit, as above, as well as immovable practice; these are the objects of meditative concentration.
The twenty-sixth is the entry into the aggregates and sense bases arising from the self. The twenty-seventh is the entry into the aggregates and sense bases of that which is apprehended.

The twenty-eighth is the entry into the aggregates and sense bases of darkness and light. The twenty-ninth is the entry into the aggregates and sense bases of delighting in nirvāṇa and not delighting in the world.
The thirtieth is the entry into the aggregates and sense bases of the right path and the wrong path. The thirty-first is... [end of fragment].
The one reality and the lack of reality both pertain to the objects of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) within the realms of phenomena and principle.

Although these ten [categories] do not cover everything entirely, to speak briefly, that which is observed is nothing other than the two objects of phenomena and principle. Why limit this to this alone? It is the same in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) and the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* (*Léngyán jīng*).
The three gates of contemplation (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) are none other than the objects of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

However, upon examining this text, although one or two [contemplations] encompass other objects, in reality, those concerning the aggregates, bases, and elements predominate. This is because the latter nine objects are contemplated only when they arise;
if they do not arise, they are not contemplated. Only the first object is present before the practitioner at every turn from the very beginning; therefore, it is clarified here.

These matters pertain mostly to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Once one has been able to understand this, then the classification of the teachings (*śāstra-vibhāga*) and the contemplation of the mind (*citta-avalokana*) can both be known.

*The Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra*, Chapter Ten: "The Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation."
The causal conditions of the Incense Accumulation [Buddha] reveal a principle of ultimate greatness, whereas Śāriputra’s mental desire for food is a matter of extreme triviality.
To employ a great crossbow by means of a minute trigger, or to produce a massive tree from a tiny seed—such is the nature of this event.
The causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma are truly inconceivable. [Section Two:
Explanation of the Sutra Text, Part Fifteen. First, Begging for Food at Fragrant Accumulation, Part Six. First, Śāriputra’s Thought on Food.]
Thereupon, Śāriputra thought to himself, "The time for the midday meal is approaching; where shall these bodhisattvas eat?

Master Kumārajīva said, "That Śāriputra alone should have raised this thought has three underlying meanings: first, that the substance of one's conditioned karma cannot exist without material support;
