The same applies to the assembly. Since you occupy the position of a senior disciple, it is fitting that you provide offerings for the multitude.
2. Knowing their thoughts, he rebukes and permits them. First, the rebuke:
At that time, Vimalakīrti, knowing their intentions, said to them: "The Buddha has taught the eight liberations; you, O worthy ones, have accepted and practiced them. How is it that—"
"Are you listening to the Dharma while eating mixed foods?
Master Zhao said: "The Buddha taught the eight liberations; these are the exquisite delicacies of desirelessness and the supreme nourishment for the Dharma-body.
You, O Benevolent One, have personally received them and yet claim to have no great cravings. Yet now, amidst the perception of mixed foods, you wish to hear the Dharma."
How could this be because there is no desire on your part to seek it out?
(2) Granting [the request]:
"If you wish to eat, wait but a moment; I shall cause you to obtain food such as you have never experienced before."
III. Displaying His Spiritual Powers to the Assembly (in eight parts). First, Manifesting His Realm:
At that time, Vimalakīrti entered into samādhi and, by means of his supernormal powers, manifested to the great assembly the world-system above.
Beyond forty-two Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands, there is a land named Saṃghagandha (Many Fragrances). The Buddha there is named Gandhavyūha (Accumulated Fragrance), who currently resides in that land.
Samādhi is the essence; supernatural powers are the function. The land of Many Fragrances is the form manifested within this essence and function.
It is like an elephant. When the water is clear, the moon appears; when the mirror is polished, the image arises. These three depend upon one another, and thus the great function is manifested.
Second, to manifest its fragrance.
This fragrance is the most supreme among the scents of humans and devas in the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions.
Both fragrant and foul odors are objects perceived by the faculty of the nose; the reason they differ is due to the distinctions in the karmic retribution and environments of sentient beings.
In the desire realm of this Sahā world, there are only defiled objects, resulting from defiled minds and evil conduct.
It is felt that those who dwell in the Pure Land possess only wondrous realms, brought about by their pure minds and virtuous deeds.

The Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) is the most pure among all pure lands; therefore, its fragrance is supreme. This, too, is merely a characteristic of the Pure Land of Common Residence (sāmbhogika-kṣetra).
Third, it is revealed that there are only bodhisattvas:
in that land, even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist; there are only assemblies of pure great bodhisattvas, for whom the Buddha preaches the Dharma.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, even the names of the three evil realms do not exist, let alone their actual presence; yet therein still exist those of the two vehicles.
In the Land of Fragrant Accumulation, even the names of the two vehicles do not exist; it is a land of supreme purity within the realm of shared purity.
The four lands are composed solely of fragrance.
Throughout their realms, everything consists of fragrant pavilions, fragrant grounds for walking meditation, and fragrant gardens and groves.
By contrast, the substance of the Sahā world is made entirely of earth, mud, tiles, and stones; compared to the Pure Lands, its impurity is evident.
He knows.
○ Fifth, the pervasiveness of the fragrance of food:
the fragrance of that food circulates throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions.
6. While they were sitting together to eat, that Buddha was just then sitting with the bodhisattvas to eat. At this time, Śāriputra here thought of food;
it happened to be the hour of noon for eating, and they were sitting there in that realm to eat, just as in this world.
The same applies here; thus, we know that this land is the Land of Common Residence (*sahā*).
Seventh, as for the offerings made by the various devas:
there are sons of gods, all of whom are named Gandhavatī, and they have all resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
They make offerings to that Buddha and the various bodhisattvas.
In this land, the monastics do not cook their own food, but beg for it from donors; in that country, the pure assembly likewise does not cook their own food, but provides for the various devas.
This is the reason for the distinction between the purity and impurity of these lands, arising from the nature of their respective karmic retributions.
Nevertheless, it is precisely because of this exertion that they are distinguished.
○ All eight assemblies witnessed this with their own eyes;
there was not one among these great multitudes who did not see it with their own eyes.
Since the retributions for purity and defilement are distinct, and the distance between the upper and lower realms is vast, this great assembly has witnessed it all with their own eyes.
This clearly demonstrates the sovereign supernatural powers of Vimalakīrti, which are inconceivable even by the standards of perception of the masses.
IV. Four Questions Regarding Who Shall Bring the Food. First, Vimalakīrti poses the question:
At that time, Vimalakīrti addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying, "O virtuous ones, who among you is able to bring the meal from that Buddha?"
2. Mañjuśrī’s Majestic Power:
By the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, the entire assembly became silent.
Although many bodhisattvas in the gathering possessed supernatural powers, if they had merely said, "I am capable," then the merit of Vimalakīrti [would have been eclipsed].
It was not revealed. Because the merit of this sutra has no [specific] destination, Mañjuśrī used his supernatural powers to cause the assembly to remain silent.
3. Vimalakīrti’s Shame.
Vimalakīrti said, "O virtuous one, this great assembly might find this shameful.
4. Mañjuśrī’s Exhortation:
Mañjuśrī said, "As the Buddha has taught, do not despise those who have not yet studied."
That Vimalakīrti initially did not deliver the food was also to demonstrate his modesty and brilliance.
That Mañjuśrī and the assembly remained silent was also to demonstrate their deference and yielding. Both feigned disagreement, desiring only to collaborate in fashioning the vessel of the Dharma.
5. Manifesting Transformation (Vikurvaṇā), Part Four. First, manifesting as a bodhisattva:
At that time, Vimalakīrti, without rising from his seat, manifested a bodhisattva before the assembly.
His physical marks and signs were radiant, and his majestic virtue was so preeminent that it eclipsed the entire gathering.
Second, he issued a command that they should go, saying to them:
"Go to the realm of the upper direction; you shall pass through as many Buddha-fields as there are sands in forty-two Ganges Rivers."
There is a land named Saṃghagandha; its Buddha is named Gandhottama. He is currently seated together with various bodhisattvas, partaking of a meal.
○ Third, he instructs him on how to address them:
"When you arrive there, speak these words on my behalf: 'Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One and pays his respects.'"
[He] measured [his distance], inquired after his well-being, and asked whether he was free from illness and affliction, and whether his physical strength was at ease.
"In the Pure Land of Fragrant Accumulation, the great assembly is free from disease; how much more so the Buddha’s own body?
That I now pose these questions is merely because I am employing the method of inquiring after the Buddha used in the Sahā world as a formal expression of reverence."
4. Fourth, one should state their vow:

"I pray that I may obtain the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal and perform Buddha-work within the Sahā world, so that those who delight in inferior teachings may attain the Great Way, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata may be heard everywhere."

He requested the fragrant food to perform the Buddha-work; therein lie two intentions: first, to transform those of small capacity toward the Great Vehicle; second, to manifest the fame and renown of the Buddha.
○ Sixth, the Bodhisattvas receive the command, in three parts: first, the deportment of the Bodhisattvas' departure.

At that time, the manifested bodhisattva ascended to the upper regions before the assembly; the entire multitude saw him depart, and he reached the World of Many Fragrances, where he prostrated at the feet of that Buddha.
II. Statement of the Message.
Furthermore, he spoke these words: "Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the World-Honored One.
He pays infinite respects and inquires after your well-being, asking whether you have little illness and little affliction, and whether your physical strength remains secure."
Third, he stated his aspiration:

"I pray that I may receive the remains of the World-Honored One’s meal. I wish to perform Buddha-work within the Sahā world, so that those who delight in inferior teachings may attain the Great Way, and so that the fame of the Tathāgata may be heard everywhere."
2. Those in the assembly questioned the Buddha:
"Those great beings, upon seeing the manifested bodhisattva, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence. From where has this superior person come?"
"Where is this Sahā world? Why is it called 'those who delight in inferior teachings'?

He asked the Buddha these questions because he perceived that the words spoken were unlike anything ordinary, and the traces manifested were unfathomable; thus, he marveled at what had never occurred before.
His inquiry consisted of three parts: first, asking from where the person had come; second, asking where the land was located; and third, asking why...
These are called minor dharmas; they are all things that have not yet occurred in Gandhavyūha.
III. That Buddha’s Response to the Assembly (in three parts). First, the response to the second question.
The Buddha addressed them, saying: "Below this world, past as many buddha-fields as the sands of forty-two Ganges Rivers, there is a world named..."
Sahā. ○ Second, the answer to the third question:
The Buddha’s name is Śākyamuni. He currently dwells in the world of the five turbidities and evil ages for the sake of sentient beings who delight in inferior teachings.
He expounded the Way of the Buddha.
○ Third, answering the first question in three parts: First, the Buddha’s direct answer:
"There is a bodhisattva there named Vimalakīrti, who dwells in the inconceivable liberation and preaches it for the sake of all bodhisattvas."
Because of this Dharma, he has dispatched an emanation to extol my name and praise this land, so as to cause those bodhisattvas to increase their merit and virtue.
II. Those in that assembly further asked:
That bodhisattva asked, "What kind of person is he, that he can manifest such transformations, possessing such power of virtue and fearlessness, and such supernormal powers?
The Buddha then answered him.
The Buddha said, "It is most great. To all the ten directions, he dispatches emanations to perform buddha-work and benefit sentient beings.
(4) That Buddha gave him food.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa took a bowl of various fragrances, filled it with fragrant food, and gave it to the manifested bodhisattva.
[The four bodhisattvas who came together: First, the bodhisattva desired to depart.

Then those nine million bodhisattvas spoke with one voice, saying: "We wish to go to the Sahā world to make offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha, and we also wish to see Vimalakīrti and the assembly of other bodhisattvas."
II. Permission and Admonition Regarding Fragrance (3). First, the admonition to restrain bodily fragrance:
The Buddha said, "You may go, but restrain the fragrance of your body so that those sentient beings do not give rise to thoughts of delusion or attachment."
2. Admonition to Abandon Your Original Form:
Furthermore, you must abandon your original forms so that those in that land who seek to become bodhisattvas shall not feel self-contempt or shame.
The Buddha’s body in the Pure Land is tall and majestic, and the bodhisattvas are likewise so, as described in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the Buddha Puṣpadantavimalaśrīcandra.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Wonderful Sound: "Your body is forty-two thousand yojanas in height, while my body is six million eight hundred thousand yojanas;
this is how it should be understood."
Third, the injunction not to hold them in contempt or create obstacles:
Furthermore, regarding them, you must not harbor thoughts of contempt or conceive of them as obstacles. Why is this?
Because all lands in the ten directions are like empty space. Moreover, because the Buddhas wish to transform those who delight in inferior teachings, they do not manifest their full purity.
It is the Land of Purity;
it is the land of retribution for sentient beings. Although it is manifested through their own karmic response, it is also due to the manifestation of the Buddha.
That the Tathāgata conceals the pure and manifests the defiled is appropriate for the way of transformation. One should not despise the defiled because of its impurity.
The three of them arrived together at the master’s chamber.
At that time, the transformed bodhisattva, having received the alms-bowl of rice, together with those nine million bodhisattvas, all relied upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power.
By the power of Vimalakīrti, they suddenly vanished from that world and, in an instant, arrived at the house of Vimalakīrti. There,
he transformed four seats and sat upon them.
At that time, Vimalakīrti immediately manifested nine million lion thrones, as magnificent and exquisite as those before.
All the bodhisattvas sat upon them;
together with the previous ones, there were nine hundred and three thousand two hundred in total. They were elevated eighty-four thousand yojanas high.
He sat upon his seat in the middle of the hall.
At that time, six transformed bodhisattvas offered food;
they presented bowls filled with fragrant rice to Vimalakīrti.
7. The fragrance of the food was heard from afar.
The scent of the food universally perfumed the city of Vaiśālī as well as the trichiliocosm.
8. Hearing the fragrance, they all came together. Part one: The assembly of Vaiśālī gathers. Part two: Candracchattra arrives with his followers.
At that time, the brahmins, householders, and others of Vaiśālī, having smelled this fragrance, felt their bodies and minds become joyful and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Thereupon, the elder Candracchattra, accompanied by eighty-four thousand people, came to enter the house of Vimalakīrti.
Second, the supreme salutation of joy:
seeing that there were many bodhisattvas within the chamber, and that the various lion thrones were high, broad, and magnificently adorned, they all rejoiced greatly.
They paid homage to the assembly of bodhisattvas and great disciples, then withdrew to stand to one side.
The two devas both arrived;
all the earth spirits, space spirits, and the various devas of the desire and form realms, having smelled this fragrance, also came and entered.
The House of Vimalakīrti. 9.
Vimalakīrti Invites Them for a Meal. Part Two. First, the Invitation to Eat:
At that time, Vimalakīrti spoke to Śāriputra and the other great śrāvakas, saying, "Venerable sirs, you may eat of the Tathāgata’s sweet..."
Regarding the rice flavored with dew:
why was it that only the śrāvakas were invited and the bodhisattvas were not? It is because a bodhisattva may eat, yet may also refrain from eating.
Because they may refrain from eating, they do not think of food; therefore, they were not invited. Because they may eat, for this reason they are also considered equal [to the śrāvakas].
It is food. Śrāvakas may eat it, yet they cannot do so without food; because they can eat it, they are mindful of food, and for this reason it is specifically mentioned.
Furthermore, it serves as a warning not to limit one’s intentions. Since Bodhisattvas are not of the class that requires such warnings, it is not included in their enumeration.
As for the Tathāgata’s meal of ambrosial flavor, first, its taste is sweet and delicious, which serves as a metaphor for—
Amṛta. First, as for those who obtain this food: they will certainly realize the fruit of amṛta.

Now, the five desires of the world can all cause people to give rise to greed and attachment, to create evil karma, and to summon birth and death; yet among these desires, the craving for flavors is the most [binding].
Furthermore, this is because it can give rise to the human mind's desires for sensory objects.
Now, however, the food of Fragrant Accumulation is perfumed by Great Compassion and produced from the Fivefold Dharma-body; it does not produce desire, yet it enables people to leave desire behind.
Those who are about to eat this food must reverse their habitual tasting and return to taste the source within.
It is unified with nirvana; therefore, it is called "the meal of ambrosial flavor.

Although practitioners today consume the food of fragmented existence, if they can turn back to taste its true flavor and return to tasting the primordial source, it may rightly be called "the meal of ambrosial flavor.
I address those who eat: do not taste it in vain.
II. Admonition Regarding Adornment: It is permeated by great compassion; do not consume it with a limited mind, lest it fail to digest.

Master Kumārajīva said: "The meaning of 'permeation' (vāsita) is threefold: first, the fruition of great compassion; second, that which is contemplated by the compassionate mind; and third, [the transformation] by means of..."
He gazes upon them with eyes of compassion. Upon eating this rice, they should give rise to the Great Mind and establish great undertakings; this is called repaying kindness.
Repaying kindness is what is meant by "digesting.
○ Tenth, the śrāvakas have few thoughts.
There was a certain śrāvaka who thought, "This food is little, yet this great assembly must each eat their fill.
(11) He cautioned against limited wisdom in two parts; first, the formal admonition.
The manifested Bodhisattva said: "Do not, with the meager virtue and limited wisdom of a śrāvaka, attempt to measure the immeasurable merit and wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The four oceans may run dry, but this food is inexhaustible. Were all people to eat it, taking morsels as large as Mount Sumeru, they could not finish it even in an entire kalpa."
II. The interrogation and explanation:

Why is this so? Because for one who is fully endowed with the merits of inexhaustible precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, the leftovers of what they have eaten can never be exhausted.
The food consumed even by the various devas of worldly merit is already inconceivable;
how much more so for those who have perfected the merits of the ultimate fivefold Dharma-body—how could they be conceivable?
12. The twelve groups of monks ate until they were no longer hungry;
yet, from the rice in their bowls, they all remained fully satiated, and it was still not exhausted.
13. Receiving food and attaining benefit, in two parts: first, having eaten, they were peaceful and happy.
All those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, devas, and humans who eat this food experience physical tranquility and happiness,
just like the bodhisattvas in the land of Sarvavyūharati.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, when it is time for a meal, exquisite bowls made of the seven treasures will each appear before them, filled with fragrant rice from which they may eat as they please.
This brings four benefits: first, it accords perfectly with their wishes and eliminates hunger and thirst.
Second, the four great elements are harmonized and free from conflict. Third, food is digested immediately upon consumption, leaving no residue.
Fourth, one does not give rise to attachment to flavors, but increases the aspiration for the human path.
○ Second, fragrance issues from the pores.
Furthermore, wondrous fragrances issue from all the pores, just like the fragrance of the trees in the Land of Universal Fragrance.
○ Fourteen: Mutual Inquiry into the Dharma, Part Six. First, this Bodhisattva’s inquiry into the Dharma, in two parts. First, Vimalakīrti’s inquiry.
At that time, Vimalakīrti asked the bodhisattvas from the Land of Fragrant Accumulation: "How does the Tathāgata Fragrant Accumulation preach the Dharma?
The two bodhisattvas replied:
"The Tathāgata of our land does not preach by means of words and letters; he causes all devas and humans to [realize the truth] solely through various fragrances."

They attain entry into the practice of the Vinaya. Each of the bodhisattvas sits beneath a fragrant tree; upon smelling this wondrous fragrance, they immediately obtain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues.
For those who obtain this samādhi, all the merits possessed by the bodhisattvas are fully perfected.

In all Buddha-lands, the Buddha-deeds performed arise from inversion and originate from it; the six sense objects serve as the primary factor, while the six faculties and six consciousnesses serve as their attendants.
Furthermore, these are unified and harmonized by means of the seven elements (*mahābhūta*).

It is for this reason that the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* provides twenty-five skillful means as the gateways to the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*) for those who enter. However, regarding these various [realms] for sentient beings...

Regarding the Dharma, there are those with sharp and dull faculties; one must select those with sharp faculties so that they may cultivate and study for a long time. One may preach the Dharma at both shallow and deep levels so as to reach those who are ready.
This is like the Buddha’s instruction to Mañjuśrī to select exclusively the ear-gate, and likewise the manner in which the Buddha-activities are performed in the Land of Fragrant Accumulation.
It is not that there are no other gates through which one may enter the Path; however, those sentient beings [there] possess the nose...

Their faculties are most sharp; therefore, they perform the Buddha-work solely through various fragrances. To say that "one immediately enters the practice of the Vinaya" refers to the initial gateway of the Threefold Training.
This is because those who have first entered the Path are able to cease evil and prevent wrongdoing as soon as they smell the fragrance.
Next, it says that "one immediately attains the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues. This further describes the effect of smelling the fragrance.
This is precisely the attainment of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). This samādhi is the Great Samādhi of the Perfect Center.
It is called "perfect" not merely because it is centered; within this center, all phenomena are inherently present.
Since it is termed the "treasury of all merits," what single dharma among all the merits of a Bodhisattva would not be fully contained therein? It is as follows:
The *Avataṃsaka* breaks through the delusions of ignorance and ascends to the first stage, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*). Therein, all objective realms are manifested;

this is the manifestation of the mind of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*), the principle. All wisdom is manifested; this is the manifestation of the mind of the revealing cause (*parijñā-hetu*), the gnosis. All merits are manifested;
this is the manifestation of the mind of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*), the practice. Because these three minds manifest simultaneously, it is called "all virtues."
The Treasury of Samādhis.
II. The Bodhisattvas’ Inquiry into the Dharma. A. The Bodhisattvas’ Question:
Those bodhisattvas asked Vimalakīrti, "In what way does the World-Honored One Śākyamuni now teach the Dharma?"
II. Vimalakīrti’s Response (in three parts). First, a general indication that the present Buddha is preaching the Dharma.
Vimalakīrti said: “The sentient beings of this land are stubborn and difficult to transform; therefore, the Buddha preaches for them words of firm severity.”
He subdues them by these means.
○ Second, specifically showing the present Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma:
He says, "This is hell; this is the animal realm; this is the realm of hungry ghosts; these are the various places of difficulty; these are the birthplaces of fools."
This is misconduct of the body; this is the retribution for misconduct of the body. This is misconduct of speech; this is the retribution for misconduct of speech.
This is misconduct of the mind; this is the retribution for misconduct of the mind. This is killing; this is the retribution for killing. This is taking what is not given;

this is the retribution for taking what is not given. This is sexual misconduct; this is the retribution for sexual misconduct. This is false speech; this is the retribution for false speech. This is divisive speech... [and so forth].
This is the retribution for divisive speech; this is harsh speech, and this is the retribution for harsh speech; this is idle chatter, and this is the retribution for idle chatter;

this is covetousness and envy, and this is the retribution for covetousness and envy; this is malice and resentment, and this is the retribution for malice and resentment; this is wrong view, and this is the retribution for wrong view.
This is stinginess; this is the retribution for stinginess. This is the violation of precepts; this is the retribution for violating precepts.
This is anger; this is the retribution for anger. This is laziness; this is the retribution for laziness. This is mental distraction; this is the retribution for mental distraction.

This is delusion; this is the retribution for delusion. This is the formulation of precepts; this is the upholding of precepts; this is the transgression of precepts. This is what should be done; this is what should not be done. This is an obstruction.
Obstruction; non-obstruction; incurrence of fault; freedom from fault; purity; defilement; with outflows; without outflows;
the false path; the true path; the conditioned; the unconditioned; the mundane; nirvana.
The Dharma taught by the Buddha always relies upon four kinds of *siddhānta*: first, the *loka-siddhānta*, which causes people to obtain the benefit of joy;
second, the *pudgala-siddhānta*, which causes people to obtain the benefit of generating wholesome states; third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*.

The first is the *siddhānta* of destroying evil, which enables people to obtain the benefit of breaking through [afflictions]. The fourth is the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, which enables people to obtain the benefit of entering into the principle.
Within these, furthermore, according to the differences between pure and impure lands, there are increases and decreases in the amount used.
If the world is considered as two types of *siddhānta*, then both the pure and the impure are employed.
For example, in the Land of Universal Fragrance (*Gandhavatī*), using fragrance as a means for Buddha-work is the *loka-siddhānta* (the worldly standpoint), which carries the meaning of "joy.

Causing devas and humans to enter into the practice of discipline (*vinaya*) carries the meaning of "producing goodness" for people. Upon hearing this wondrous fragrance, one immediately attains the treasury of all virtues.

"Merit" (guṇa) refers precisely to the meaning of entering into principle. This is because those with the roots of capacity in the Pure Land do not require harsh or forceful language to explain the methods of remediation;
therefore, such language is not employed in its entirety there. However, as for the Dharma taught by the Buddha in our Sahā world:
While all four *siddhāntas* (purposes) are employed together, it is primarily the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (the purpose of remediation) that is used most extensively.
This is why the layman Vimalakīrti spoke of it point by point, emphasizing how the sentient beings of this land are stubborn, fierce, turbid, and evil;
such is the nature of the teaching of remediation.
III. Third, the summary in three parts. First, the Dharma:
Because the minds of those difficult to transform are like monkeys, one must employ various methods to control their minds;
only then can they be tamed.
Second, the analogy:
It is like an elephant or a horse that is obstinate and untamable; one must apply various forms of torment, even to the very marrow of the bone, before it can finally be subdued.
Master Kumārajīva said: "Horses are of five types. The first is tamed immediately upon seeing the shadow of the whip.

The second is tamed only when it receives the whip. The third is tamed when pricked by a sharp awl through the skin. The fourth is tamed when the flesh is pierced. The fifth is tamed only when it reaches the bone.
Sentient beings, whether of keen or dull faculties, also have five grades. The first merely sees that others are without [faults]..."
First, he constantly contemplated the impermanence of his mind, and his heart was awakened. Second, seeing that his acquaintances were impermanent, his heart was awakened.
Third, seeing that his brothers and relatives were impermanent, his heart was awakened. Fourth, seeing that his parents were impermanent, his heart was awakened.
Fifth, seeing that his own body was impermanent, he experienced extreme suffering and distress; only after this was further compounded by harsh words did he finally [attain realization].
Then he attained awakening.
(The third section:
Thus, because sentient beings are stubborn and difficult to transform, it is only through all manner of harsh and urgent words that they can be brought into the discipline.
III. That Bodhisattva’s Praise of the Two. First, the praise of the Tathāgata:
When those bodhisattvas heard this teaching, they all exclaimed, “How unprecedented!
Just as the World-Honored One Śākyamuni Buddha, concealing his immeasurable power of mastery, delivers sentient beings by means of the Dharma that accords with their meager inclinations.”

Master Shi said: "When one conceals their traces and remains hidden while their brilliance persists, they naturally become like a poor beggar. By being like a poor beggar, they can interact with others;
once they interact, it becomes easy to be a neighbor. Therefore, they are trusted and delighted in by the poor."
II. Praising the Bodhisattvas:
These bodhisattvas are likewise capable of diligent humility; out of immeasurable great compassion, they have been born into this buddha-field.
IV. Vimalakīrti Manifests His Excellence: Part Two. First, a general statement that the merits of the bodhisattvas in this land are numerous.
Vimalakīrti said, "The bodhisattvas in this land possess a firm and steadfast great compassion for all sentient beings, just as you have said.
Nevertheless, the benefit they bring to sentient beings in a single lifetime exceeds that which would be achieved by practicing in those lands for hundreds of thousands of kalpas."

Master Kumārajīva said: "It is like a skilled physician who, encountering an epidemic during a kalpa of pestilence, applies his medical arts extensively and distributes medicines widely, thereby healing many and receiving immeasurable offerings.
It is the same for a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwelling in an impure land:

as evils increase all the more, his universal salvation becomes even more vast. By means of the ten dharmic medicines, he extensively relieves the multitude of ailments; thus his transformation is far-reaching."
The benefit is profound: in a single lifetime, one transcends ten thousand kalpas.
Second, the specific explanation of the ten matters in which the bodhisattvas of this land are superior. First, the heading:
Why is this so? Because in this Sahā world there are ten matters of wholesome dharma that are not found in other pure lands.
There is none.
○ Second, the explanation.

What are the ten? They are: gathering in the poor through generosity; gathering in those who violate the precepts through pure ethical discipline; gathering in [those who lack patience] through patience...

[He] subdues ill-will; through diligence, he gathers those who are indolent; through meditative concentration, he gathers those with distracted minds; through wisdom, he gathers those who are deluded.
He teaches the Dharma for removing difficulties to deliver those in the eight adversities; he delivers those who delight in the Lesser Vehicle by means of the Mahāyāna;

II. Specifically indicating the eight dharmas.
What are the eight? To benefit sentient beings without expecting a reward; to undergo all sufferings on behalf of all sentient beings.
They eliminate afflictions. They dedicate all the merit they have cultivated to others. With an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, they are humble and free from obstruction.
They regard all bodhisattvas as Buddhas. When hearing sutras they have not heard before, they do not harbor doubt. They do not conflict with the śrāvakas.
They do not envy the offerings given to others, nor do they exalt their own gains; rather, within these matters, they discipline their minds and constantly examine themselves.
To pass over [others' faults], not to speak of their shortcomings, and to always seek all merits with a single mind—these are the eight dharmas.
As for "sores," they are the flaws of jade and the blemishes of the body.
If a Bodhisattva possesses these, their conduct will not be pure enough, and they shall not be born in the Pure Land. That which Vimalakīrti taught was to demonstrate these eight practices.
To eliminate the eight faults and to bring benefit to sentient beings is truly the beautiful practice of a Bodhisattva. If one expects a reward for it, it becomes a flaw.
Furthermore, to constantly examine one’s own faults and not speak of the shortcomings of others is truly the beautiful practice of a Bodhisattva.
If one does not constantly seek all merits with a single-minded focus, it becomes a flaw. One should cultivate these eight practices.
Departing from these eight maladies, one truly practices the bodhisattva path as a flawless, exquisite jade. This is the swift divine power of the feet by which one attains birth in the Pure Land.

Master Zhao said: "The followers of the Two Vehicles regard the impermanent as impermanent; therefore, they weary of conditioned wholesome dharmas. They regard suffering as suffering;
therefore, they loathe the suffering of birth and death. They regard the non-self as non-self; therefore, they are indolent in instructing others.
They regard quiescence as quiescence; therefore, they desire perpetual stillness. The Bodhisattva does not regard the impermanent as impermanent; therefore, he is able to..."
He detests the roots of goodness; because he does not regard suffering as suffering, he does not loathe birth and death.
Because he does not regard non-self as non-self, he never tires of instructing others. Because he does not regard quiescence as quiescence, he does not enter into eternal stillness.
3. Non-abiding in seclusion:
while contemplating seclusion, one cultivates goodness with body and mind.

Master Kumārajīva said: "There are three kinds of seclusion: first, distancing oneself from the five desires of the human world; second, distancing oneself from afflictions; third, [distancing oneself from] all..."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is empty and detached. Now, while observing that its nature is empty and detached, one does not depart from the wholesome.
○ Fourth, non-abiding and having no place of return:
while observing that there is no place of return, one takes refuge in and proceeds toward wholesome dharmas.

Master Zhao said: "All dharmas have nowhere from which they come in the beginning and nowhere to which they go in the end. Although one knows there is no destination, one always returns to wholesome dharmas.
(5) Non-abiding in non-arising.
One contemplates non-arising, yet bears all beings by means of the dharma of arising.
Master Zhao said: "Though one perceives non-arising, one dwells in arising to sustain others."
6. Non-abiding in the outflow-free (anāsrava).
While contemplating the outflow-free, one does not sever the various outflows.

Master Zhao said: "Generally, all that is outflow-free shares the same nature as the conditioned (saṃskṛta); its essence is inherently markless (animitta), and it is entirely an unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) practice."
Furthermore, although they perceive the outflow-free (anāsrava), they remain possessed of outflows (sāsrava) in common with others. There are two ways in which they share these outflows:

first, there are those who have entered into saṃsāra through conditioned phenomena and have not yet actually severed their outflows; second, there are those whose outflows are already exhausted, yet who manifest as if they have not severed them.
7. Not abiding in anything, yet observing that there is nothing to be practiced, one teaches and transforms sentient beings through the practice of the Dharma.
Master Zhao said: "The nature of dharmas is without karma; what, then, is there to be cultivated? Although one knows there is no practice, the teaching must nevertheless be carried out."
This is the practice of the practitioner.
(8) Not dwelling in emptiness or non-existence:
while contemplating emptiness and non-existence, one does not abandon great compassion.
Master Zhao said: "The characteristics of all dharmas are solely emptiness and solely non-existence; yet, one does not abandon great compassion because of this emptiness and non-existence.
(9) Ninth, not abiding in the stage of the true dharma.
One contemplates the stage of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) without following the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
Master Zhaolun said: "The stage of the True Dharma refers to the ground for contemplating the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and attaining realization. Master Kumārajīva said:
"It refers to the dharma of attaining realization through non-arising and non-ceasing (*anutpādānirodha*)."
○ Tenth, the non-abiding contemplation that all phenomena are illusory, without solidity, and so forth.

One contemplates that all phenomena are illusory, lacking solidity, lacking a person, lacking a master, and lacking marks; yet, until one’s original vows are fulfilled, one does not let go of merit, dhyāna-concentration, and wisdom.
○ Three fetters.
To cultivate such a dharma is called the bodhisattva’s non-abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What is taught in this passage is the dharma-gate of liberation through both exhaustion and non-exhaustion; that is, not exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not abiding in the unconditioned.
The meaning of this is no different from what was taught by Vimalakīrti in the "Inquiry into the Illness of Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva" chapter.
Within the section on "Consoling and Encouraging Novice Bodhisattvas," it states that there is wisdom-conjoined-with-expedient-means and expedient-means-conjoined-with-wisdom;

that is, not exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while not dwelling in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). This extends to such passages as: "Though one practices in emptiness, one plants the seeds of the roots of virtue."

It merely differs in its phrasing and varies in its literary style; thus, by understanding that, one knows this, and by knowing this, one understands that—there is no need for further elaborate explanation.
II. A combined explanation of the four [aspects] based on two dharmas, in four parts. First, an explanation based on the pair of merit and wisdom:
Furthermore, because he possesses merit, he does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because he possesses wisdom, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Master Zhao said: "The preceding passage clarifies that the Bodhisattva does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
however, it has not yet explained the reason why he does not exhaust the one nor abide in the other. Now, the conduct of a Mahāsattva has its specific basis and its sublime aim;
therefore, I shall further clarify this in response. The accumulation of virtue must necessarily involve the ford of existence; if one were to abide in the unconditioned..."
If one were to act [in this way], then one's merit would not be complete. Master Kumārajīva said: "The preceding section manifested a single meaning;

now it clarifies that within a single gate both meanings are simultaneously present. If one does not abide in non-existence, then one does not exhaustively dwell in existence; if one does not exhaustively dwell in existence, then one does not abide in non-existence."
Second, an explanation based on the pair of the Great Compassion and the Original Vow:
Because of great compassion, he does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because he fulfills his original vow, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Third, an explanation in pairs regarding the collection of medicines and the administration of medicines:

because he collects the medicine of the Dharma, he does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); because he administers the medicine according to need, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Master Zhaolun said: "To gather fine medicine, one must go to perilous mountains; it does not emerge from a grand hall.
To collect the medicine of the Dharma, one must go to the realm of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*); it does not emerge from the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). He further said:
'If one abandons the conditioned, one becomes isolated from all living beings; how then could one follow them to bestow the medicine?'"
Fourth, an explanation by way of a pair concerning the knowledge of illness and the cessation of illness:
because he knows the illnesses of sentient beings, he does not abide in the unconditioned; because he extinguishes the illnesses of sentient beings, he does not exhaust the conditioned.

Master Zhao said: "To thoroughly understand all illnesses, one must necessarily know the location of the disease; how could this be something achievable through abiding in non-action (*wuwei*)? He further said:
'To extinguish the illnesses of sentient beings, one must necessarily apply treatment; how could this be something achievable by exhausting all conditioned phenomena (*yǒuwéi*)?"*
III. Conclusion:
"O noble sons, when Bodhisattvas practice this Dharma, they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor do they dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This is called the Dharma-gate of the liberation of exhaustion and non-exhaustion. You should all study it."
III. The Threefold Offering and Praise, Part Two. First, the Offering and Praise:
At that time, those bodhisattvas, having heard this Dharma being taught, were all greatly rejoiced.
They scattered various wonderful flowers of diverse colors and diverse fragrances throughout the trichiliocosm as an offering to the Buddha and to this [Dharma].
Having [heard] this sutra-dharma and all the bodhisattvas, they bowed their heads at the Buddha’s feet and, marvelling at such an unprecedented occurrence, exclaimed:
"Śākyamuni Buddha is truly able to exercise such skillful means in this regard."
"02. Returning to His Country.
Having spoken thus, he suddenly vanished and returned to that land.
The manner of the Bodhisattva Xiangji’s coming and going—whether manifesting or concealing himself—was not uniform; all were the inconceivable spiritual powers of a bodhisattva.
By the power of his supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*), the origins of his transformative traces each have their own underlying cause.

When he arrived, he manifested his coming so that the assembly might all behold it, for he intended to achieve the merit of self-benefit while simultaneously assisting in the flourishing of the Dharma.
Once he returned to his own land, he withdrew his traces to revert to his original state; thus he suddenly vanished, causing the assembly to fall into silent stillness.

Regarding those who judge the teachings: they do not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor do they dwell in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The Mahāyāna is identical to the three vehicles, such that all may speak of it.

For example, when a person of comprehensive capacity reaches the stage of "having already accomplished" (*kṛtāvibhūmi*), having realized the essence of the unconditioned, they immediately emerge from [that state] to assume provisional forms and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
By retaining residual habits to moisten their rebirths, they extensively deliver sentient beings. Is this not precisely "not exhausting the conditioned and not dwelling in the unconditioned"?

Indeed, when an ordinary person reaches the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) and has already destroyed the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*), they immediately cultivate the contemplation of emerging into the conventional (*niḥsaraṇa-prajñapti-vipaśyanā*).
Ascending through the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) and the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), these are all matters concerning the Bodhisattva’s benefiting of sentient beings.

Is this not precisely "exhausting the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) while not abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)"? Nevertheless, because their practice is divided into internal and external realms and lacks integration, they cannot equal those who follow the Perfect and Sudden Teaching (*yuan-dun-jiao*).
Within the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), there already exist both the six perfections of preaching the Dharma and those of concurrent correct practice;

how much more so when emerging from the eight stages of faith into provisional liberation, ascending to the [first] dwelling (*vihāra*) for perfect realization, and simultaneously illuminating both emptiness and existence, such that neither of the two extremes—the conditioned nor the unconditioned—is exhausted.
To simultaneously negate both emptiness and existence is to eliminate both the conditioned and the unconditioned; this alone constitutes the ultimate practice of a bodhisattva.

Regarding the contemplative understanding: one contemplates that the nature of the single thought-moment is simultaneously empty, provisional, and middle, and because it is simultaneously conventional, one contemplates existence.
To practice the bodhisattva path is because it is emptiness; to contemplate the unconditioned and cultivate the way to nirvana is because it is the middle way.
Thus, by simultaneously negating and illuminating the two extremes, one does not exhaust the conditioned nor abide in the unconditioned.

Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Scroll Eleven Commentary on the Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra: On Non-Self, Scroll Twelve Composed by the Śramaṇa Chuandeng of Youxi, Mount Tiantai [The following is the beginning of the text: Regarding the phrase "the body is not-self" (*anātman*): The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states: "The body is not-self. What is meant by "not-self"? It refers to the fact that the body is devoid of a permanent, unitary, and independent self-substance. Furthermore, it is because the body arises from the conjunction of various causes and conditions—such as the four great elements and the five aggregates—that it is designated as "body"; there is no self-existent entity therein. As the sūtra says: "The body is like a bubble, arising from the combination of various conditions; it has no master and is subject to decay. This is why it is called "not-self. Regarding the phrase "the mind is not-self": The sūtra further states: "The mind is not-self. What is meant by "not-self"? It refers to the fact that the mind is a succession of thoughts, arising and ceasing in every moment.

It is driven by the winds of afflictions and karma, and is subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death. Because it lacks stability and permanence, it is devoid of a true self. As the sūtra says: "The mind is like a monkey, leaping about in the forest of objects; it is like a flowing stream, never remaining still for a moment. This is why it is called "not-self. [End of excerpt]
○ Commentary on Chapter Twelve: "Beholding the Buddha Akṣobhya," Part Two. First, the commentary on the chapter title.
According to what is taught in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter Twelve, "Beholding the Buddha Akṣobhya," there are four points of meaning.
First, the method for contemplating the Buddha is clarified; second, the absence of extinction is clarified.
There is no birth. The third *vidyā* clarifies passing away from that place and being born here; the fourth *vidyā* clearly reveals the vision of Akṣobhya Buddha.
It is likely that the translator intended for the reader to first grasp this meaning and then behold Akṣobhya.

Thus, when beholding Akṣobhya, one must not lack the thirty-eight categories of the Dharma-body contemplation gates (*dharmakāya-dhyāna-mukha*), nor must one fail to realize that the Tathāgata dwells in neither passing away nor birth.
Birth does not preclude manifesting birth and non-birth within the Sahā world-system;

it is also intended to lead the reader, through the meaning of these subsequent words, to perceive our Śākyamuni Buddha as he reveals birth and death through the Dharma-body, which is itself devoid of birth and death.
Since the three texts have been summarized and only the vision of Akṣobhya Buddha is specifically designated, there must be a specific intention that is hidden therein.
○ Second, the explanation of the sūtra text has five parts. First, clarifying the method for visualizing the Buddha has two parts. First, the Tathāgata asks: "By what..."
Observing them with equanimity,
the World-Honored One then asked Vimalakīrti: "If you wish to see the Tathāgata, by what means do you contemplate the Tathāgata?"

Master Zhao said: "Previously, Mañjuśrī was commanded to come together with [the Buddha] to see the Buddha. Although he turned his gaze to conform to worldly custom, his underlying observation was not the same.
The Tathāgata perceived his intention in advance and intended to reveal the purpose of his coming observation, thereby clarifying that the Buddha's work is inconceivable;
thus, He knew and yet questioned him."
II. Vimalakīrti’s Response by Means of the Method for Contemplating the Buddha (in two parts). First, the general establishment of the great meaning.
Vimalakīrti said: “Just as one contemplates the true mark of one’s own body, so too does one contemplate the Buddha.”
Master Sengzhao said: "What is a Buddha? He is the designation for Great Awakening, which exhausts principle and perfects nature.
His Way is void and profound; it is already wondrously transcendent beyond the ordinary realm. The mind cannot be known through wisdom, and his form cannot be fathomed through images.
He acts in concert with the myriad things, yet dwells in the domain of non-action; he remains within the sphere of speech and calculation, yet he abides [in stillness]."
The Land of No Words is not existent such that it could be called non-existent, nor is it non-existent such that it could be called existent.
It is silent, desolate, empty, and vast; no thing can fathom it. Not knowing how to name it, we have arbitrarily designated it as "Awakening.
Its attainment is also the ultimate limit. Why is this? For those who are identical in their attainment, even their attainment is itself attained. Identical in...
As for "losing," one loses even that which is lost. Therefore, that which is true shares in the same truth; that which is false shares in the same falsity.

The Tathāgata’s numinous illumination harmonizes with the profound darkness, unifying them within that single *dharmatā*. The characteristic of the *dharmatā* is itself the characteristic of the Tathāgata.
Thus, a sutra says: "To see the dharma of the *dharmatā* is to see the Buddha. Vimalakīrti himself contemplates the *dharmatā* of his own body as the act of contemplation.
"Regarding the marks of the Tathāgata, the ultimate meaning resides herein.
Dīpaṃkara said: "As for 'observing the true mark of one's own body,' one first observes one's own pure *dharmakāya*.
Since this is the case for observing oneself, how could it not be so when observing the body of the Buddha? Therefore, it is said, 'it is likewise. This is the foremost and ultimate point."
All Buddhas and even Bodhisattvas of partial realization are without exception endowed with three bodies: first, the Dharma-body; second, the Reward-body;
and third, the Response-body. Master Tiantai said: "As for the Dharma-body, it takes the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as its teacher and model, and thus takes the Dharma-body itself as its body.
This body is not material substance, nor is it mind or intellect; it is not comprised within the aggregates, bases, or elements."

This is merely a forced designation of the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) as "body. As for the "life-span" of this *dharmatā*, it is not a life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) obtained through karmic retribution, nor does it possess any continuity or maintenance.
It is merely a forced designation of that which is non-transmigrating and immutable as "life-span.

This life-span has no measure of length, nor any measure of brevity; it neither extends nor contracts. It is merely a forced designation of the *dharmadhātu* as having a measure equal to empty space. This, then, is not a body.

It is the body that has no life-span, the life-span of no-life-span; it is the measure of the immeasurable. As for the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body), it is what is elicited through spiritual cultivation. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"That which is obtained through long-term cultivation of practice. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "Because the Great Parinirvāṇa is attained through the path of cultivation.

Thus, the wisdom of suchness (*tathatājñāna*) illumines the realm of suchness; the wisdom of bodhi and the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) are in mutual correspondence and in profound union. They are in correspondence.
It is like a box and its lid fitting together. As for their mutual merging, it is like water and milk merging into one.

The Dharma-body is neither body nor non-body; since wisdom likewise corresponds through this merging, it is also neither body nor non-body. We provisionally name this wisdom the "Reward Body" (Sambhogakāya).

The Dharma-life is neither life nor non-life; since wisdom corresponds to the profound mystery, it is likewise neither life nor non-life—it is only by force of designation that what is not life is called "life.

The Dharma-measure is neither measure nor immeasurability; since wisdom corresponds to the profound mystery, it is likewise neither measure nor immeasurability—it is only by force of designation that the immeasurable is called "measure.
As for the Responsive Body (Nirmāṇakāya), it means responding by taking on a body identical with the myriad things.
It should be understood that they are conjoined as a single life-force; it should be understood that they share the same measure of length and brevity.
When wisdom merges with the essence, it is able to give rise to great function, just as mercury mixed with pure gold can coat all manner of forms. So too, when merit is united with the Dharma-body.
He manifests and appears everywhere; he can manifest as a body or as no-body. He can manifest as eternal life or as impermanent life.

He can manifest as immeasurable or as measurable. Although this sutra speaks of contemplating only the Dharma-body, it is in fact the Responsive Body (nirmāṇakāya), not the Responsive Body being the Dharma-body.
Why is this? It is because the Tathāgata currently resides in the Āmra Garden.
Although it is said that he sits upon a lion throne of various jewels like the king of mountains, Sumeru, this is actually manifesting the superior within the inferior;
yet the traces of the eight phases of enlightenment remain distinct. As it is said, though he is not the three periods or the five aggregates, he is in truth the Nirmāṇakāya (Response Body);
thus he has a prior limit, entering the womb and coming forth, a subsequent limit, entering parinirvāṇa and departing, and an intermediate period of eighty years.

The marks and signs of his physical form are brilliantly radiant, and his wisdom and mental faculty are vividly clear. Therefore, the Great Being contemplates this very [form], yet finds each individual aspect to be non-existent;

this is precisely the Dharma-body. If one were to depart from the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) to contemplate it separately, how would this differ from the teachings that take principles as their object, severing the nine partial views to contemplate the true, eternal, and pure consciousness?

II. Specifically explaining the method of contemplation has three parts. First, the actual explanation of the method of contemplation has forty sections. First, contemplating through the non-existence of the three time periods:
I contemplate the Tathāgata as not coming from the past, not going to the future, and not abiding in the present.
The Tathāgata Śākyamuni is identical to sentient beings in that he possesses the past, future, and present.
Therefore, in the past, he descended from Tuṣita Heaven to enter the womb of his mother; in the future, he will depart from the Śāla grove into parinirvāṇa;

and at present, he is eighty-one years old, dwelling precisely within the Jeta Grove and the Anāthapiṇḍika Park. However, these manifested traces respond to the capacities of beings, and thus what is perceived differs according to their faculties.
What is seen by those of great capacity is the inconceivable eightfold manifestation. If one were to respond to the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), all eight aspects would be inferior;

yet when the Great [Vehicle] displays appearance and disappearance, it is like the waves of water—the entire body of the Dharmadhātu, wherein all eight are supreme and wondrous. In the Small Vehicle, birth and cessation constitute impermanence in essence;
it is like fire burning wood, ultimately resulting in ash and annihilation. Now, as for what is seen and observed by the layman Vimalakīrti:
This is the capacity of the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching. It is precisely because the manifested body comes from the past limit (*pūrvānta*) yet its coming is not seen;
it goes to the future limit (*aparānta*) yet its going is not seen; and it dwells in the present yet its dwelling is not seen.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "It comes from nowhere, nor does it go anywhere; for this reason, it is called the Tathāgata."
Second, by means of the contemplation of non-pañcaskandha:

one does not contemplate form, nor the suchness of form, nor the nature of form; one does not contemplate feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor the suchness of consciousness, nor the nature of consciousness.
This refers to the observation of the Dharma-body through the form and mind of the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

Specifically, the Response-body possesses the physical characteristics of the thirty-two marks and eighty minor signs, as well as the mind that transforms the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms.
When expanded, these constitute the five aggregates (pañca-skandha). Thus, for those with the ordinary fleshly eye or the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-eye, they observe form as form and mind as mind.
To take the mind as the object is called "contemplating form. The wisdom-eye of the Two Vehicles contemplates that form is like the mind.

The partially-realized Buddha-eye of Bodhisattvas contemplates the nature of form and the nature of consciousness. Now, you, Layman, employ the ultimate Buddha-eye to contemplate the form and mind of the Tathāgata’s response-body;
seeing that it is neither form, nor the likeness of form, nor the nature of form, you directly perceive the Dharma-body.
Third, by means of the contemplation that it is not the four great elements:
since it does not arise from the four great elements, it is identical to empty space.

As for the color of the response-body (nirmāṇakāya), since it must correspond to that of ordinary beings, it likewise necessarily coagulates the four great elements of paternal semen and maternal blood.
There is a body. Now, as observed by the householder with the Buddha-eye, it is that the four great elements are not the four great elements;
their form-characteristics are signless, identical to empty space.
Fourth, one contemplates through the non-existence of the six sense bases.
The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) have no accumulation. Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind have already transcended them.
Although the body possesses the six sense bases, because it is identical to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), one does not accumulate thoughts regarding the six faculties. "Already transcended" means:
This refers to transcending them.
○ Fifth, by means of the contemplation that [the self] is not within the three realms, one does not abide in the three realms; the three impurities have already been abandoned.
Although the response body (nirmāṇakāya) exists within the triple world, it is already unlike sentient beings in that it lacks the defilements of views and afflictions;
how much more so for the dharma body (dharmakāya)—how could it be stained by the three defilements, and why would it necessarily remain within the triple world?
6. By means of the three liberations, one accords with the three gates of liberation and fulfills the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*).

Although this may appear similar to that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) in terms of acceding to the three gates of liberation and possessing the three knowledges, one is nonetheless able to realize and enter into the reality of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Nature is itself Buddha-nature, because ignorance is itself the Dharma-body.
○ Seventh, the contemplation of identity and difference:
there is neither the characteristic of identity nor the characteristic of difference.

One should be identical with all sentient beings, mysteriously penetrating all things. The myriad dharmas within a single mind are called "one"; the single mind within the myriad dharmas is called "different.
When one realizes the myriad as one, they are not "one"; when one realizes the one as the myriad, they are not "different. This applies equally to form.
Since even form is thus, how could there be any characteristics of oneness or difference between phenomena?
8. By means of the contemplation of self and other:
there is neither the characteristic of self nor the characteristic of other;
one should be identical with all sentient beings. Yet, while self and other appear distinctly, they should be realized as the Dharmakāya, wherein self and other are perfectly extinguished.
9. To observe by means of taking signs within signlessness is neither signlessness nor taking signs;
it would be identical to the Two Vehicles, wherein there are no signs, yet it would be identical to ordinary beings, wherein there is the taking of signs. Thus, observation should be...
The Dharma. Therefore, it transcends both extremes.
10. By means of this "this shore" and "that shore" contemplation, he transforms sentient beings by being neither on this shore, nor on that shore, nor in the middle stream.
If he were identical to sentient beings, he would be on this shore. If he had already perfected the Buddha-way, he would be on the other shore.

To say he is here while having already ascended to the other shore, or to say he is there while still being identical to sentient beings—this means he is neither here nor there, but dwells in the middle stream.
These three are all manifestations of his traces. Now, observing this very [reality]...
It should be in accordance with the Dharma; therefore, it is neither this, nor that, nor is it a middle current.
○ Eleven: By means of quiescence and non-contemplation, one contemplates quiescent extinction, yet it is not eternal cessation.

To contemplate quiescence is for the whole to be identical with the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Furthermore, it is not that there is a permanent extinction; rather, the whole arises as the response-body (nirmāṇakāya). This is what is meant by:
"It is simply the Dharma-body, not [a separate] Dharma-body"; that is, the Dharma-body is necessarily identical to the response-body.
Twelfth, by means of this contemplation of "this" and "that":
it is neither this nor that; it does not rely on this, nor does it rely on that.
Because one should be identical with all sentient beings, one is personally not "this. Because one is entirely identical with the Dharma, one is personally not "that. However...
Thus, in this direction or that direction, in reality, one does not take this to be this, nor take that to be that.
○ Thirteen: Contemplating through wisdom and consciousness—it cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness.
If it could be known by wisdom (*jñāna*), it would follow *nirvāṇa*; if it could be cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*), it would follow birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
In reality, it should be identical to *nirvāṇa* yet does not follow *nirvāṇa; it should be identical to birth-and-death yet does not follow birth-and-death.
Now, observing that response (*ying*) is identical to phenomena (*fa*), and phenomena are identical to response—how could this be known by wisdom or cognized by consciousness?
To recognize this!
(14) To observe through darkness and light:
there is neither darkness nor light.
To be identical with the long night of birth and death is called obscurity; to be identical with the sun of wisdom of nirvana is called illumination.
Now, observing that what corresponds [to these] is precisely the Dharma-body, how could there be any such thing as obscurity or illumination?
15. Contemplating by means of names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*):
there is neither name nor mark;

this should be understood as being identical to [the nature of] Sahā. His characters are "Śākya," which is his name. A name is able to summon its essence (*tattva*), while the physical marks and radiant light are the marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Thus, responding while being the Dharma is called "responding without a name"; being the Dharma while responding is "appearance without appearance.
(16) Contemplation by way of strength and weakness.
There is neither strength nor weakness.
One should be equal to a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*); to possess heroic valor that covers the world is called strength. One should be equal to a Sugata;
to be compassionate, gentle, and loving toward all things is called weakness. Thus, when one accords with the Dharma, where then can strength or weakness reside?
Seventeenth, by means of the contemplation of purity and impurity:

if it were neither pure nor impure, it would have to be identical to the Land of Ultimate Bliss; yet it is pure because it is in a state of purity. It would have to be identical to the Sahā world; yet it is impure because it is in a state of impurity. However...
Thus, responding to the situation, it accords with the Dharma; thus, both purity and impurity are neither.
(18) Contemplating by way of being within directions and departing from directions:
it is neither within directions nor departing from directions.
If it were identical to the Sahā world, it would be situated within a spatial direction; if it were necessarily different from that person, it would be detached from spatial directions.
Thus, in accordance with its responsiveness, the Dharma-body neither has a location nor does it not have a location. Because it has no location, it is not situated within a spatial direction;
because it has no non-location, it is not detached from spatial directions.
19. Contemplating the conditioned as unconditioned:
it is neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
If it were conditioned, it would be identical to birth-and-death; if it were unconditioned, it would be identical to nirvana. Yet, it is precisely through such responding that—
Dharma. Who can name existence or non-existence?

He should have been identical to those of the world: born in the Lumbinī grove, pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, walking seven paces east and west to demonstrate, and uttering a lion’s roar, saying, "In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored.
Yet, in truth, responding to conditions as he did, the Dharma is fundamentally without demonstration or explanation; other matters may be understood by analogy.
21. Contemplating by means of the pāramitās:
there is neither giving nor stinginess; neither precept-keeping nor transgression; neither patience nor anger; neither diligence nor indolence; neither concentration nor distraction.
Neither wise nor foolish, neither sincere nor deceitful, he should appear identical to ordinary beings, yet possesses the seven obscurations;
these he destroys by means of the gates of the seven perfections. [He regards] his kingdom, city, wife, and children...
Like mucus and spittle, he left the city to become a renunciant, casting off his dark robes like skin. He gave rise to the patience of birth and the patience of the Dharma;
enduring hunger and cold, he practiced with diligence for six years until his body was withered and stood like a skeleton. With single-minded concentration, he sported within the various dhyānas.
By the power of wisdom, he tore asunder the net of ignorance. Not betraying his own spiritual nature, nor deceiving sentient beings, he thus responded accordingly.
The Dharma is fundamentally without stinginess; why then must one practice giving? It is fundamentally without deception; why then must one employ sincerity?
○ From the twenty-second [section] onward, it concerns the contemplation of coming and going, entering and exiting.
Neither coming nor going, neither emerging nor entering, yet one should manifest as dwelling together with others;
though there is coming and going, one should not be the same as ordinary people.

Emerging from meditation and entering meditation—thus, while responding to circumstances according to the Dharma, fundamentally there is no coming or going, even though the traces of emerging and entering can be sought.
23. Contemplation by way of the severance of the path of language:
all paths of language are severed;

At the outset, it should be identical to that of ordinary beings; therefore, it is a non-field of merit. Through cultivation, one accomplishes the Buddha-way; therefore, it becomes a field of merit. Thus, then—
It accords with the Dharma; as it is free from both [extremes], it is neither a field of merit nor not a field of merit.
○ Twenty-fifth: Contemplating those who are worthy of offerings and those who are not worthy of offerings.
It is neither worthy of worship nor unworthy of worship.
At the beginning, before it has become a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), it is not worthy of worship; later, having become a field of merit, it is worthy of worship.
Thus, while it is indeed worshipful as a phenomenon (*dharma*), the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) itself is neither worthy of worship nor unworthy of worship.
26. Contemplating through grasping and relinquishing:

that which is neither grasped nor relinquished should be identical to sentient beings; therefore, one relinquishes the afflictions of birth and death and grasps at bodhi and nirvana—this is precisely what accords with the Dharma.
Thus, it is neither grasping nor abandoning.
(27) Contemplating through both the characterized and the uncharacterized,
it is neither characterized nor uncharacterized.
It should be like a Wheel-Turning King; therefore, it possesses marks. Its essence is like empty space; therefore, it is without marks.
It is thus in accordance with phenomena, yet it is neither with marks nor without marks.

This passage directly regards the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) as being identical to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the dharma body; it views it as being beyond measure and exceeding all numerical categories.

Being free from all fetters, one should be the same as sentient beings; yet being possessed of all fetters, one should contemplate that phenomena are fundamentally free from fetters.
(33) Contemplate all sentient beings with various forms of wisdom.
The various wisdoms such as these are identical to those of sentient beings;

they are the Dharma that accords with reality. Although this wisdom is not something that can be attained by all sentient beings through the wisdoms of the three vehicles, it is equal despite being unequal, and identical despite being different—is this not precisely the Dharmakāya?
34. One contemplates all phenomena through their differentiation;
yet regarding all phenomena, there is no differentiation.
Because one should accord with sentient beings and preach the Dharma according to their capacities, there is differentiation. Now, one contemplates that which is responsive and the Dharma itself.
Therefore, regarding all phenomena, there is no discrimination.
(35) By observing through gain and loss,
one finds that in all things there is neither gain nor loss.
One should be the same as sentient beings: what they gain, one gains; what they lose, one loses. One should then contemplate phenomena:
that which is gained is not gained, and that which is lost is not lost.
36. Contemplating through turbidity and affliction, one who is without turbidity and without affliction should come to this Sahā world;

Now, observing that which is immediate and responsive, how could there be any turbidity or affliction?
(37) By means of the contemplation of activity and arising,
there is neither activity nor arising.

One should be identical with all sentient beings. Only upon attaining perfect enlightenment does one act and initiate [practice]. Contemplating that action is itself the Dharma, one acts and initiates while fundamentally being without action or initiation.
(38) This is contemplation by means of arising and ceasing.
If [the Buddha] were without birth and without extinction, he would be identical to sentient beings. Yet, he was born in the royal palace and entered parinirvāṇa at the twin śāla trees.

Furthermore, his accomplishment of the Way through the eight phases is likewise subject to the transformation of the four marks—great and small—which makes it appear as though there is birth and extinction. Now, if one contemplates that the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is itself the Dharma-body, it is like water...
Waves. Although the characteristics of waves differ, the nature of water itself is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Without fear and without sorrow; without joy and without weariness.

Now, observing that the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), there is neither fear nor...
Sorrow. There is neither joy nor weariness.

"Remaining unchanging while following conditions" means that the entirety of the responsive manifestation is itself the Dharma.

As these encounters occur repeatedly throughout the course of daily activity, if one can observe each instance in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*), then everything will be seen as nothing other than "remaining unchanging while following conditions" and "following conditions while remaining unchanging. A magician knows that he creates illusions through illusion; he certainly does not claim that his illusions are real. When a sage realizes that all is illusory and acts within that illusion, how could he still harbor views of existence, non-existence, birth, or death?

II. Showing the matters of death and birth.
Although the Bodhisattva dies, he does not exhaust his roots of goodness; although he is born, he does not increase various evils.
Master Kumārajīva said: "When ordinary people die, they give rise to evil and extinguish goodness; once born, their manifold evils increase."
The Bodhisattva is not so. Furthermore, ordinary beings exhaust their roots of goodness and thus end their lives;
with their perverted and evil minds flourishing, they subsequently undergo rebirth. The Bodhisattva is not so. Their Dharma-transformation is pure, and they proceed according to their will;
therefore, they do not suffer this affliction. Because they lack this affliction, although their traces appear to come and go, this is not what is meant by "passing away" and "being born."

Furthermore, previously, the absence of death and birth was clarified through the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); now, it is clarified through mastery over the transformation of dharmas (*dharmapariṇāma-vaśitā*).
If one seeks [the truth] within these two gates, then death and birth have no locus. To inquire about death and birth [in this context] is to miss the point by a great distance. Daoping said:

To wish to believe, accept, see, and understand it through a mind possessed of intentionality or through the clarity of the intellect—is this not indeed difficult? From here...
The following explains the purport of the sublime and profound sūtras. The profound sūtras spoken by all Buddhas are none other than the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Now, material sustenance nourishes the four physical elements, whereas the sustenance of the Dharma nourishes the Dharma-body.

This clarifies that the Dharma-jewel is profound, firm, and difficult to peer into. Master Daosheng said: "The *dhāraṇī*..."

the dharmas that accord with dependent origination are without self, without person, without sentient beings, and without life-span; they are empty, signless, and unarisen.

That which neither arises nor perishes contradicts the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). What is taught in the profound sūtras is that they are neither existent nor non-existent;
because they are neither existent nor non-existent, they accord with the dharma of dependent origination. Master Zhao said: "Dharmas arise from causes and conditions; they are born of conditions."
Thus, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Where there is no intrinsic nature, there is no master. Where there is no master, there is no self, person, or life-span.

It is solely emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-arising; this is what accords with the profound sūtras. Master Sengzheng said: "This is precisely the teaching of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*)."
